26 October
3903
New Zealand Society of Accountants Amendment Bill
WEDNESDAY, 26 OCTOBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 3.2 p.m.
Prayers.
NEW ZEALAND SOCIETY OF ACCOUNTANTS AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the New Zealand
Society of Accountants Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill contains miscellaneous
amendments requested by the New Zealand Society of Accountants. Clause 2 relates to the
determination of fees payable by members of the society. Fees are at present prescribed by
the rules of the society, but in future will be prescribed by the society in general without
requiring the approval of the Governor-General in Council. A limit is placed on the penalty
that can be imposed on the reinstatement of a member to a register when he has resigned or
been removed for being in arrears with payment of fees.
Clause 3 empowers the council of the society after due inquiry to remove from a register
the name of a person who has obtained membership by supplying false information. There is
a right of appeal to the committee of appeal. Clause 4 authorises accountants to practise in
partnerships of not more than 120 members. The present limit of 75 members will be too low
if some of the larger firms continue to expand. Clauses 5, 6, and 7 are designed to enable the
council to strengthen the society's fidelity fund. Clause 5 increases from $20 to $50 the
maximum annual fee that the council may prescribe as payable to the fidelity fund by
chartered accountants in public practice. Clause 6 increases from $20 to $100 the amount of
the levy that the council may impose on chartered accountants in public practice in any one
year to meet any insufficiency in the fidelity fund. The conditions under which the levy may
be imposed are widened to cover a likely insufficiency as well as an actual insufficiency.
Clause 7 removes the present limitation whereby annual fees for the fidelity fund may not be
prescribed while the fund exceeds $200,000.
Clause 8 validates previous actions by the society in general meeting, and the council, in
determining fees, levies, and penalties, and making rules, to the extent that such acts could
have been done if the present amendment had been in force. The action of the council in
increasing the annual fee payable to the fidelity fund from $10 to $20 with effect from 1 July
1976 without obtaining the prior approval of the Governor-General in Council is also
validated.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Does clause 8 indicate,
through its retrospective applications, that the society acted and then found it did not have
the authority to so act? I presume that is the reason, but I ask, too, whether the Bill has the
support of most members of the council alone, or is unanimously supported by members of
the society. In my time as Minister a few people objected even to membership of the society,
and I do not imagine they would go along with restrictive measures being placed on them by
the society. But if we exclude the one or two who, for conscientious reasons, object to being
members, can the Minister assure the House that the other members of the society in good
standing accept the Bill in its entirety?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): What the Deputy Leader of the
Opposition says is correct. The move was made, but the need for an Order in Council was
overlooked, and this validates it. As far as I am aware, there has been no complaint from
members of the council about the action taken by members of the society, and clearly the
council made the necessary moves for the change. I do not for one moment think that
accountants would object to the substantive clauses of the Bill. A fidelity fund is necessary
for professional bodies of this kind, and it is simply a matter of increasing the amounts that
may be ordered to be paid, and, as members will see, of facilitating these changes in the
future. It seems to be a bit archaic to require an Order in Council to deal with some of the
matters in the Bill.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Referring to clause 7, does the
society contemplate any limit to the fidelity fund? There have been, I think, two fairly
substantial defalcations that had to be covered. I understand the fund shows no strength at
present, but with the maximum annual fee increased to $50 it could be built up fairly quickly.
Is any policy to be followed, or has any indication been given by the society that the fund
contemplated in clause 7 will be unlimited?

## p. 3904 (#10) ############################################

3904
26 October
New Zealand Society of Accountants Amendment Bill
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Yes, the legislation proposes that it
be unlimited, but I am sure the society will not continue simply to bring in additional funds if
they do not appear to be needed. The great difficulty at present with this and at least one
other profession is that they are getting into very substantial sums indeed. The fund is a
protection not so much for the clients as for those associated with the clients. It is hardly a
protection for the accountants; they have to make the subscriptions. It is not proposed that
there should be a limit, but I think we can rely on the council not to take in funds in excess of
what is reasonably required in the circumstances from time to time. In my view it would be a
lot more than $200,000.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): Could the Minister throw some light on the
background of clause 4, increasing the acceptable number of partners from the present 75 to
120? I know it is a very long time since accountancy was confined to small partnerships of
three or four practising in one centre and not elsewhere, although I believe they still make up
the bulk of the profession. For many years one has become accustomed to accountancy firms
having branches at least in the four main centres and often elsewhere, and this necessarily
increases the number of partners needed for the business to be carried on. The same
tendency has manifested itself to a much lesser degree in the law, where it is not uncommon
now for a city firm to have a branch in the suburbs, or indeed in a provincial centre some
distance away-Auckland and Whangarei are examples. In one or two cases there has been a
bridging of the gap between Auckland and Wellington. But when one gets to an association
of 75 and upwards the whole concept of partnership seems to disappear-the relationship of
confidence that one partner must necessarily repose in the other, and the burden of
responsibility that he has to bear for the misfeasances of his partners.
The Minister will know that certain developments in the law have greatly widened the
area for which a person advising on financial matters can be responsible. Quite apart from
any protection of clients, I know the profession has been troubled to protect itself against
actions for which it may have no responsibility or control whatever. Has this been requested
by the body of the profession, or has it been submitted to an annual meeting? What are the
reasons for going beyond that? One comes to the notion when there are 75 associates, or
even fewer, that a corporate structure would be more suitable. I know that idea has been
considered by both the accountancy and legal professions. So far it has not matured finally in
the legal profession, but I believe more thought has been given to it by accountants. Can the
Minister tell me whether there has been any move by the society to put forward proposals
that would contemplate and authorise the incorporation of firms, perhaps those with a
number of separate branches? Does the same ruling apply to the accountancy profession as
to the legal profession, that where separate partnerships are established there must be
separate trust accounts for each, that aspect being definitely for the protection of the clients?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Let me deal first with the trust
account aspect. In the legal profession it is covered by regulations and has no direct
relevance to the accountancy profession, for which no regulation applies. This is simply a
practical matter arising from the fact that at least one, and I think more than one,
partnership in New Zealand is approaching the limit of 75. One finds it difficult to
contemplate a corporate structure for a professional practice. As the member says, it is true
that the question of shared liability arises, and there have been cases in the past-and
doubtless in the legal profession as well-in which the act of one partner has caused very
great financial loss to the whole partnership. I know of one case that financially crippled the
individual partners, who were men of considerable substance in the accountancy profession;
one junior partner's defalcations financially crippled them. Nevertheless, the profession
believes that that must be the manner in which it continues to operate. One could not
contemplate any kind of limited liability for a professional partnership-I think that would
be quite wrong.
The method of overcoming this difficulty is through the fidelity fund, but the answer to
the specific question is that at least one, and I think more than one, partnership is getting
close to the 75 limit, because the national firm is becoming quite typical, certainly of city
practices. Although it would be fair to say that few of them have as many partners in one
branch as the biggest of the legal firms, some nevertheless have quite large numbers of
partners. Multiplied by several cities the figure of 75 is a bit much, but 120 should hold the
position for a long time. I do not think more than one or two firms would need to extend
beyond 75. The provision has been requested through the council of the society, and I would
be of a mind to accept the request, although it would not apply widely, and I doubt whether
many members of the society would have strong views on it, anyway.
Bill introduced and read a first time.


## p. 3905 (#11) ############################################

26 October
3905
Racing Amendment Bill
RACING AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That the Racing Amend-
ment Bill be introduced. The Bill amends the Racing Act 1971. There are a number of
significant amendments that are of some importance to all facets of the racing industry, but
perhaps rather more important to those involved with greyhound racing. Indeed, they could
be regarded as being momentous for the sport of greyhound racing, as totalisator
betting-albeit on a restricted basis-is being made available on greyhound racing meetings
for the first time in this country. As from the start of the next racing year—that is, 1 August
1978-restricted totalisator betting will be available to followers of that sport.
The introduction of the Bill, therefore, represents a long-awaited day for the enthusias-
tic band of people who administer greyhound racing. The sport was introduced into New
Zealand in about 1890, and since bookmaking was made illegal in 1920 it has been struggling
to pay its way—as its only means of raising revenue has been the rather limited opportunity
offered by equalisator betting. For many years the sport has been seeking the benefits of on-
course totalisator betting, and in this respect to be placed on the same footing as racing and
trotting.
The new concept of on-course totalisator betting introduced in the Bill is described as a
restricted totalisator licence. It is restricted in the sense that it is different from the normal
totalisator licence, which includes the opportunity to use the totalisator not only for on-
course betting, but for off-course betting as well. The extension of off-course betting to
greyhound racing is a matter for the future, and this fact is accepted by those involved in the
sport. In the meantime, greyhound racing will have the opportunity to demonstrate its ability
to conduct on-course betting at the club level, and to gain from this experience the public
knowledge and confidence in the administration of the sport on a national basis that would
be an essential prerequisite to any extension of betting facilities.
The restricted totalisator licence is expected largely, if not entirely, to replace the
equalisator licence, under which greyhound racing clubs and a few of the smaller horse
racing clubs-sometimes colloquially referred to as "picnic" clubs-have been operating.
The Bill also provides for the official body controlling greyhound racing-the Greyhound
Racing Association-to be represented on the New Zealand Racing Authority. The associa-
tion will have one nominee on the authority.
The New Zealand Racing Authority itself is being given some additional powers by the
Bill. It will in future have direct power to act in certain areas where at present it has only
advisory powers; for example, in the determination of the distribution between racing,
trotting, and greyhound racing of the total number of totalisator licences to be issued in any
racing year. The Bill next goes on to provide that the authority will have power to adjudicate
in disputes between the racing and trotting conferences and the Greyhound Racing Associa-
tion, and in such disputes between clubs as may be referred to the authority by the respective
regional body. The Bill also amends section 36 of the principal Act by making it permissible
for the totalisator to be opened for betting 10 times at any one racing meeting. The present
legal maximum is nine. The opportunity to run an extra totalisator race will make it more
attractive for clubs to provide opportunities for the qualifying of maiden performers, and will
be of benefit particularly in those areas where it is difficult for owners to get their horses
accepted for totalisator races.
Quite apart from the above amendments, which generally are related to the conduct of
racing, there is one further important amendment affecting the age at which people may bet.
The Bill proposes to take a more realistic view of the legal betting age. At present this is 20
years. It is proposed that, in line with many other areas where the legal age has been lowered
from 20 to 18 years, this be done for betting also.
Those are the major amendments that the Bill will make to present legislation affecting
racing. It is expected that it will command a good deal of attention from various interests
within racing in its three forms-galloping, trotting, and greyhound racing. The provisions in
the Bill have been discussed fairly widely with those involved in those three forms of racing.
Nevertheless, I think it is appropriate that it be referred to a select committee.
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): I appreciate the Minister's telling us that the Bill will be
referred to a select committee, because I think some matters might be of concern. I
appreciate also that there will be restricted totalisator betting on greyhound racing. I know
that the New Zealand Greyhound Racing Association has been wanting this for some years.

Racing Amendment Bill
Now that it has moved to Mt. Smart stadium, where it is attracting quite good crowds, I
wonder why the Minister is giving it only a restricted totalisator licence, and why the
association is not being given parity with trotting and racing, which would help it enorm-
ously, because of the growing popularity of the sport and the large following in
Auckland—and I should imagine there would be a following in the rest of the country.
Formerly, the deputy chairman of the New Zealand Racing Authority was elected by
the members of the authority. Why has the Minister decided to change this-in clause 3-so
that he elects the deputy chairman? There seems to be no rhyme or reason for the change.
Surely the members of the authority, with their experience, and their knowledge of their
fellow members, can decide for themselves who should be the deputy chairman, as they have
done in the past. Why has the Minister suddenly taken it into his head to change this rule,
depriving the members of the authority of the opportunity to elect the deputy chairman, and
enabling the Minister, in some sort of authoritarian manner, to elect the deputy chairman?
The Minister said that he has had discussions with the various parties involved. I should
like to know the nature of the discussions, and whether the question of the restricted
totalisator licence for greyhound racing figured in the discussions with the trotting and racing
people, and if they were responsible, because of some sort of rivalry, for the restrictions
being placed on totalisator betting on greyhound racing. The Minister did not say what the
outcome of the discussions had been. I wonder if the trotting and racing people were happy
about greyhound racing having a special totalisator, or was this brought in by the Minister as
a result of the many requests that I know he has had from the greyhound racing people to
give them a full totalisator licence? As the Minister knows, they have experienced enormous
problems in trying to establish the sport. They were at Kumeu for some years, racing their
dogs under extremely difficult conditions. The move to Mt. Smart has been part of a
development of the sport, and one would have expected that they would be given a full
totalisator licence to enable the sport to grow-as should be done, and has been done in
other countries. Can the Minister assure me that the greyhound racing people are happy
about the special totalisator rights?
I approve of the Bill's being sent to a select committee, because I am sure that
submissions will be made about it. I want the Minister to tell the House and the country why
he has taken away the democratic right of the New Zealand Racing Authority to appoint its
own deputy chairman, and given it to himself.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I shall reply to the member for Grey
Lynn immediately, because the questions he asked are of interest to the House. The
greyhound racing industry itself requested a restricted totalisator at present. It agreed with
the Racing Authority and myself that it had to prove it could run the totalisator, and that, at
an appropriate time, the Racing Authority and the Minister who happens to be in charge of
racing at the time will look at the whole matter and see whether it is possible to give the
greyhound racing industry TAB facilities. Again, the Racing Authority recommended that
the deputy chairman should be appointed by me.
Hon. M. Rata: Why?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: Because it believed that the deputy chairman, who at times acts as
chairman, should be devoid of sectional interests. That is a very responsible reaction from
the Racing Authority. There could be an occasion when, say, the galloping interests could
dominate while the chairman was away. The chairman, in particular, is very keen that the
deputy chairman should be free of those sectional interests, and I believe that it is the right
thing to do.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): I have a couple of questions to
ask about clause 8, which deals with the general powers of the authority. It seems that a very
important and possibly far-reaching power has been slipped into the legislation. I refer to the
authority's power to distribute and determine licences issued in the various areas. I am a
little concerned that this might well mean the death knell of some of the smaller country
clubs, such as Kumara-about which the Prime Minister had something to say on a previous
occasion-Kurow, and Dargaville, when the heat comes on.
What factors would concern the authority when distributing licences? If a club-for
example, Kurow-found itself under pressure, what right would it have to resist any change
in the reallocation of licences proposed by the authority? I have had only a cursory glance at
the Bill, and that matter might be mentioned, but I cannot find anything at the moment that
suggests there is adequate protection for clubs of this kind. For some years now they have
had to fight to survive, although many of them, remarkably, have been able to stand on their
own feet. It would be a retrograde step if clubs that cater for areas that otherwise would not

Racing Amendment Bill
have much opportunity to participate in this sport found themselves forced to the wall simply
because an authority is vested in a group such as this, without adequate means of protection
available to the clubs.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): The power given in the proposed new section 13 (3)
in clause 8 is not only new, but also devoid of any criteria that can be taken into account by
the authority when redistributing licences. That is a major addition. Members will recall
that, when he was Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister reminded a club that if it
took certain action it could confidently look forward to obtaining a licence. The Government
has now proposed to transfer that power to the authority without indicating in the Bill what
criteria will be used when redistributing licences. It is simply stated that it will be done after
an Order in Council has been issued.
Can the Minister give an absolute assurance that all present licences will remain?
Members will recall that clubs can face the onerous task of putting another club out of
business. We should not casually permit the introduction of a Bill that appears to slip in a
major power. The Government should amend the Racing Act to give effect to a simple guide
that the authority shall have due regard to the Government's policy conveyed to it in writing.
That would be more flexible and simple, and would take into account the social and other
consequences. The increased authority will serve the present interests as well as greyhound
racing.
How is it proposed to license greyhound racing under the powers vested in the proposed
new section 13 (3) in clause 8? In some areas the annual race meeting is the only big event in
the district. There is nothing in the Bill to satisfy us that the authority will take account of
that sort of circumstance. Unless that is spelt out clearly, the House cannot be expected to
support the provisions contained in clause 8. The greyhound people have worked hard for
many years, and, with the introduction of this Bill, many people will say that the Govern-
ment has gone to the dogs. Be that as it may, I am sure that the efforts of the greyhound
people have at long last brought to the Government a realisation of its responsibilities. I
earnestly suggest to the Minister that a simple section empowering such a major authority
requires further elucidation before the Bill should be allowed to be introduced.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I know that members opposite have
had very little time to study the Bill, so I shall refer the member for Northern Maori to clause
16. If he reads clause 8 he will see that the proposed new section 13 (2) states: “. . . the
Authority may, at the request of the Minister or on its own initiative, from time to time
advise the Minister . . ." The authority has no power to approve extra days. On each
occasion it must recommend to the Minister. The Government will always have control of
the limit, which I will mention in a moment.
Let me say also that the authority only recommends the total number of licences for the
various conferences. For instance, it will be seen in clause 16 that the authority can
recommend to me not less than the following numbers of licences for totalisator clubs:
galloping clubs, 290; trotting clubs, 182; hunt clubs, 17. For restricted totalisator clubs the
numbers are: galloping clubs, 10; trotting clubs, 10; greyhound racing clubs, 60. It is the
authority's responsibility to recommend the number of days for each type of racing, not to
decide on the method of allocating those days. That will be the responsibility of the
individual conferences and the association, but, under the proposed new section 37 (2) in
clause 16 the authority can increase the number of days by 11. Even so, it has power only to
recommend to the Minister; the final decision rests with the Minister and the Government. If
the Government considered that too many racing days were being recommended it could
decide not to grant an application. I want to make the point again that the authority only
recommends the total number of days or nights for trotting, galloping, or greyhound racing.
The decision on which clubs are allocated the licences rests with the Racing and Trotting
Conferences and the Greyhound Racing Association. It will be up to the three organisations
to decide on the allocation of those permits.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): The New Zealand Greyhound Racing Associ-

Greyhound Racing Association compared with that payable by the two conferences. At the
moment, as the member is well aware, there is a totalisator duty on racing and trotting of 8.5
percent on win and place betting. A commission of 8 percent is paid to the clubs on on-
course betting. On TAB betting they get 7.5 percent, which is taken by the Totalisator
Agency Board. A large proportion is later allocated to the clubs. The greyhound racing clubs
will pay totalisator duty of 5 percent on all bets placed. In addition, racing and trotting clubs
are levied 0.5 percent for an amenities levy and 0.5 percent goes to the stake subsidies
scheme a total of 17.5 percent. The Government has decided that the 5 percent totalisator
duty will be payable by the Greyhound Racing Association in the first year or so, probably
until the time the clubs are given a TAB licence, when it could be increased to 8.5 percent.
But they will be given a commission of 12.5 percent to bring them up to a total deductions
level of 17.5 percent in line with the trotting and racing clubs. I am sure that, as an
accountant, the member for Wigram will appreciate that it would make things a little difficult
if we did not have the same figure for greyhound racing and trotting and galloping. I believe I
have answered all the questions raised.

Forest Protection, Lakes Okataina and Tarawera
6. Mr LATTER (Marlborough), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East), asked the
Minister of Forests: In view of the public concern about the felling of native forests in the
Lakes Okataina and Tarawera area, can he indicate what methods have been adopted to
protect these forests?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The felling of native forest in the Lake
Okataina-Lake Tarawera area is on land leased from Maori owners by the Tasman Pulp and
Paper Company. Forest bordering the lakes themselves is largely Crown administered scenic
reserve and is thus protected. Forest on the adjacent leased land has been examined by a
forest ecologist and one area identified for reservation for scientific purposes. Other areas
will be reserved, where appropriate, for soil and water conservation.

Electronic Snooping
7. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Justice: What has the Government done
to honour its election promise that: “National believes that when any Government depart-
ment or other organisation collects confidential information regarding any individual, it has
an obligation to ensure that it remains confidential. Thus we will pass new laws to protect
access and guard against any form of electronic snooping"?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The first part of the statement quoted is
an affirmation of the duty of public and private persons to keep information received in
confidence confidential. I adhere to and repeat that principle. Happily, in New Zealand, the
abuse of information received on a confidential basis is not such as to render general
legislation of any urgency. In the specific case of the Law Enforcement Data Bank at
Wanganui, the Government has legislated to provide the most complete protection practic-
able against any disclosure of confidential information. Over and above that the Human


## p. 3912 (#18) ############################################

3912
26 October
Oral Answers to Questions
Rights Commission will be charged under clause 58 of the Bill now before Parliament with a
general oversight of the privacy field and will have the functions, among others: (a) to
inquire into any law, practice, or procedure, or any technical development, if it appears to
the commission that the privacy of the individual is being or may be unduly infringed
thereby; and (b) to report on the need for legislative, administrative, or other action to give
better protection to the privacy of the individual.
Mr Hunt: In view of the Minister's two quotations from a Bill yet to be passed by this
House and also the fact that other Bills yet to be passed say that the provisions of any other

Hon. DAVID THOMSON: By taking an intelligent interest in it.

discussions with the Minister of Maori Affairs on the proposals. Under the new Reserves
Bill, when it becomes law, such a proposal would, of course, require a change of reservation
to be advertised and indeed the uplifting of a reservation.

Wainuioru Water Scheme
14. Mr COUCH (Wairarapa) asked the Minister of Works and Development: When will
the Wainuioru water scheme in the Wairarapa be able to proceed, and what is the estimated
final cost?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Acting Minister of Works and Development): The estimated
final cost for the Wainuioru rural water supply scheme is $946,000 of which one-
half-$473,000-will be met by Government grant. The estimated costs include both the off-
farm works and the on-farm works necessary to complete the scheme. The proposed scheme
has recently been considered in detail by the Water Resources Council. The council has
recommended it to the Government for approval once the required water rights have been
considered and issued by the regional water board. Part of the Government grant is available
for scheme work to commence in the current financial year—that is, the year ending March
1978 once the required approvals have been given.

Socialist Unity Party and Federation of Labour
15. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour: In view of the speech which
the Minister of Fisheries gave to the Leeston branch of Federated Farmers as reported in the
Evening Post of 18 October, in which he said that “not many people realise that half of the
Federation of Labour Executive are members of the Socialist Unity Party”, will the Minister
give the basis on which his colleague made this statement and will he inform the House of the
names of these S.U.P. members and where his colleague obtained this information?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I am advised by my colleague that the
newspaper report was a very abbreviated comment on an answer he gave at Leeston, and
that his remarks of S.U.P. involvement in the trade union movement were intended to refer
to their leadership in some of the important Federation of Labour district councils. The
honourable member has indicated to me that he did not intend to convey the impression that
half the national executive of the Federation of Labour were members of the Socialist Unity
Party, and regrets that such inference may have been drawn. As far as my colleague is aware,
only one member of the S.U.P. is on the executive of the Federation of Labour.
Mr Isbey: In view of the Minister's answer, has his colleague denied the reported
statement?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I am not my brother's keeper. I understand there has been
correspondence with the Minister, but that is not within my province as Minister of Labour.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the regret expressed by his colleague, will the Minister take
any steps to ensure that other colleagues do not pursue the course that his colleague had
inadvertently publicly stated?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: If the information given to me by my colleague is correct, then
what he said is right. I would think that at least half the officers of trades councils in New
Zealand would be members of the S.U.P.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Erosion
16. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister in Charge of the Earthquake and War
Damage Commission: What action has been taken to date on the recommendations of the
commission relating to flood, landslip, and sea erosion and referred to in its report for the
year ended 31 March 1977?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the Earthquake and War Damage
Commission): Following the Wellington and Hutt Valley floods of 20 December 1976 the
commission submitted a scheme for consideration whereby relief could be made available to
home owners for flood, landslip, erosion, or other disaster-induced problems affecting
residential sections. The proposal is that local authorities be empowered to set up local relief
schemes funded and administered at local community level, and tailored to meet the special
needs of the community. The commission's recommendation was referred to the Territorial
Local Government Council for consideration. A committee representing the council, the
Department of Internal Affairs, and the commission has met on two occasions to consider
the proposal. At the request of this committee the proposal is to be referred to the local


## p. 3916 (#22) ############################################

3916
26 October
Oral Answers to Questions
government consultative committee at its next meeting with the Minister of Internal Affairs,
which will be held about the end of next month. I feel the scheme proposed by the
commission is the only practicable and equitable way home owners can be provided with a
measure of relief for uninsurable property losses, and I have strongly urged that the proposal
be fully investigated with a view to early implementation.
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister say when this proposal will be implemented?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: As I have said, the proposals have been referred to the local
government consultative committee, and will be considered at its next meeting. I should like
to see the scheme accepted and implemented as soon as possible.
Mr Brill: The scheme outlined by the Minister proposes that the indemnity would be
funded by rates. Can the Minister give any indication of the extent of rating that would be
required to fund such a proposal?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The proposal is that the fund would be established with an initial
charge of 5c for every $100 of land value, which would be the equivalent of $5 for every
$10,000 section. After the fund is established it is considered that a charge of 1c for every
$100 of land value would be sufficient. That would mean that the average family with a home
on a section valued at $10,000 would pay $1 a year into the fund.
Hon. Michael Connelly: In the time he has been in charge of the Earthquake and War
Damage Commission has the Minister received any other recommendations to assist home
owners, and, if so, what were those recommendations?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No, I have received no other recommendations. The present
recommendation is an expansion of a proposal put forward in 1974, and it is the only one I
have received.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Maui Technicians-Recognition of Training Course
17. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Education: Does the Trade
Certification Authority intend to give official recognition to the training course provided at
the Taranaki Polytechnic for technicians working on the Maui development by issuing some
certificate of proficiency, and, if not, can he explain why?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Two distinct issues appear to have been
run together in this question, and two separate statutory bodies are in fact involved: they are
the Trades Certification Board and the Technicians Certification Authority-there is no
Trade Certification Authority. Neither body has considered, or has been asked to consider,
the issue of any special form of certificate for the courses referred to at the Taranaki
Polytechnic. The courses were provided in 1976 to offer an introduction to industrial
instrumentation for people with suitable previous qualifications or experience in related
fields. At that time no approved pattern of training in industrial instrumentation existed.
The Government has now approved the introduction of extended trade training for the
industrial instrumentation trade from 1978.
Hon. F. M. Colman: To what extent does the Department of Education enter into the
provision of courses for development work such as that undertaken at Maui and other parts
of the country, and does the department try to provide technicians with the skills and
qualifications needed for such work?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: There is some confusion in the member's mind. The Trades
Certification Board issues certificates only after the full requirements for proficiency in a
trade are met. This may well include examination where the person has suitable qualifica-
tions or experience, and in some cases those provisions may be exempted. On the other
hand, the Technicians Certification Authority is a separate body, and it has no power under
the Act to award certificates. After the completion of a course the authority would issue the
certificates on the basis of its own Act. The member is asking what happens in a complex
case. In this case the Taranaki Polytechnic set up a course to provide instrumentation for the
people working the Maui gasfield. Following the last Budget, a course has been set up for
trade training in instrumentation.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Lambing and Calving Percentages
18. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Agriculture: What estimates of
lambing and calving percentages have been made by his department in the Wairarapa,


## p. 3917 (#23) ############################################

3917

Southern Hawke's Bay, and Central Hawke's Bay areas, and how do they compare with the
1976-77 figures?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Agricul-
ture. The Ministry conducts a national sample survey of lambing percentages at tailing time
each year, and the results are normally published in December. The results from the 1977
survey in the areas asked about are not yet available. Statistics required for the calculation of
calving percentages for beef cows are available only after the 31 March Department of
Statistics census of livestock numbers. Accordingly, no survey-based estimates of lambing
and calving percentages in the areas concerned are available at present. Officers of the
ministry have been in contact with farmers in the areas concerned, and with allied groups,
and it is thought that lambing percentages in some areas might be up to 10 percent lower
than last year.
Mr Falloon: Has the Minister heard that the highest lambing percentage drop is
estimated to be between 30 percent and 40 percent, and in some cases up to 50 percent, and
that in calving there have been much greater losses of cows than in any previous year?
Hon. V. Š. YOUNG: I have heard reports of such losses. I have given the average figures
for the districts. This year has been a good lambing year and some farmers have not been so
detrimentally affected. Some farmers have been severely affected, and I understand that
those figures will be included in the surveys of the districts.

Timber Requirements—Self Sufficiency
20. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) asked the Minister of Forests: What proposals
does the Forest Service have to ensure that regions such as Taranaki and Wellington become
self-sufficient in timber requirements?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Exotic production forests have been
established by the Forest Service at Te Wera, Taranaki; Lismore, Wanganui; Waiterere and
Santoft, Manawatu; and at Ngaumu, Wairarapa, essentially to satisfy the requirements of
local populations for sawn timber for building and general purposes. It is envisaged that the
continued development of these State forests will adequately cater for the sawn timber
requirements of the lower North Island in the foreseeable future, including most of the large
urban Wellington demand.

Questions and Replies
Fishing Foreign Investment
3. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Finance: Does he intend to raise the
limit for foreign investment from 24.9 percent for joint fishing ventures?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The Government is at present
studying the various alternatives for the best utilisation of New Zealand's fishing waters,
following the passing of the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Act 1977. The
question of joint fishing ventures is naturally of particular importance, and an announcement
will be made shortly. I should point out that 24.9 percent is not necessarily the maximum
percentage of foreign equity permitted in a fishing venture. Foreign investment policy has
been to treat each application on its merits, and where particular advantages can be shown
which justify a higher percentage than 24.9, approval can be given accordingly by the
Overseas Investment Commission. This policy will continue in the future.
(7/10/77)

Breast Prostheses
8. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) asked the Minister of Health: How many benefits have been
paid to women who have had a mastectomy operation since the introduction of the subsidy
for the first breast prosthesis?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: This benefit was introduced on 29 July 1976
and provided for the full cost of the initial breast prosthesis required after a mastectomy
being met up to a maximum of $30. Statistics on the number of prostheses subsidised are not
available, but $7,409 was expended on the subsidy from 29 July 1976 until 31 March 1977.

Breast Prostheses
9. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) asked the Minister of Health: Is it correct that there is a 60
percent mark-up on oil-filled breast prosthesis, and, if so, what steps is he prepared to take
to enable women to purchase first and subsequent prostheses at cost price?


## p. 3923 (#29) ############################################

26 October
3923
Questions and Replies
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: I am informed that there is about a 60
percent mark-up on this form of prosthesis, but the reasons for this include: that the fitting is
a time-consuming process, customers usually trying the prosthesis under a wide range of
different sorts of garments; the range of shapes and sizes of such prostheses may mean the
carrying in stock of 30 different varieties; the demand for and consequently the turnover of
these garments is small; fitting needs to be carried out by senior and well experienced staff.
Such prostheses currrently retail at about $31.60, which is only slightly above the Govern-
ment subsidy. In view of difficulties of fitting and distribution of these prostheses, the
present system appears to be satisfactory, and no change is envisaged. With the need to
restrain Government expenditure, there is no proposal to extend the subsidy to replacement
breast forms at the present time.
(11/10/77)
University Sessional Assistants-Wages and Conditions
10. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: What provisions are
there for holiday pay, sick pay, method of appointment, tenure position, negotiation of wage
rates, and conditions of employment for those who serve as sessional assistants at the
universities and at Lincoln College?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The term "sessional assistant"
does not define a formal grade of salaried staffing which is defined in the same way
throughout the universities. It covers a wide field of employment, varying in the nature of
the duties, the duration of appointment, and the qualifications and standing of the appoin-
tees. In some universities the term includes positions which in others are called correctors,
markers, demonstrators, tutors, oral tutors, laboratory supervisors, project markers,
specialist testers, and part-time lecturers. The appointees range from unskilled handymen or
clerks to undergraduates, graduates, and retired professors. The duration of appointment
ranges from an hour or two, to a week, a term, or a session, the last covering an academic
year. Appointments are usually for less than a year, and are not permanent. Rates of
payment vary according to the nature of the work and the experience and qualifications of
the appointees; payment is by the hour, the week, or the session, and in some cases explicitly
includes holiday pay. Each university has its own method of determining its rates of
payment, and, where appropriate, regard is paid to the salary scales of permanent staff. The
diverse nature of the whole group rules out formal salary negotiations except in those
universities where the term is closely defined.
(12/10/77)

14. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General: (a) How many people were
awaiting telephone connections as at 1 October 1977; (b) can he indicate the total numbers
awaiting connections in Auckland, Christchurch, Wellington, and Dunedin respectively as at

4754; and Dunedin district, 1104. The estimated loss of revenue for the 12-month period
ended 1 September 1977 is $2.8 million.

Health Tax on Cigarettes and Beer
15. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Health: Has he seen the report of a
speech given by the member for New Lynn and reported in the New Zealand Herald on 29
September saying that, "of the $27.5 million a year expected from the extra 1c health tax on

3930
26 October
Questions and Replies
cigarettes and beer the present Government was spending only $4.8 million on community
health-the rest is going into its superannuation fund", and, if so, does that statement reflect
the facts, has the Minister made the facts public, and does he know of any incorrect figures
having been released that could lead to a genuine misunderstanding of the facts in this

Abortion Admissions to Public Hospitals
18. Mr FENTON (Hastings), on behalf of Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), asked the
Minister of Health: Has he seen the statement on page 50 of the public health report that of
the 4500 abortion admissions to public hospitals annually about 3000 are the result of
"botched up back-street abortions", and can he confirm the accuracy of these figures?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The statement made on page 50 of the
public health report quotes an article in the New Zealand Law Journal, No. 15, of 22 August
1972, by Mr W. A. P. Facer. In it the author refers to the average number of cases requiring
public hospital treatment for abortion between 1950 and 1968 as being 4488. Mr Facer has
worked for the Abortion Law Reform Association as a research officer. On the basis of an
estimate made by a British gynaecologist (Diggory, 1966), that two-thirds of British cases
admitted to hospitals were in his view due to criminal attempts, Mr Facer said that if this
proportion is valid in New Zealand it would mean an annual average of about 3000 criminal
abortion cases. There is no way of confirming the accuracy of these figures, as the true
incidence of criminal abortions cannot be absolutely determined.

Tongans in New Zealand
21. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Has he seen the
statement by New Zealand's former immigration officer in Tonga, Mr D. Gordon, in the
Dominion of 30 September, that the money earned by Tongans in New Zealand is urgently
needed in the islands and that letting people work in New Zealand is a more positive form of
aid for ordinary citizens than aid projects, and, if so, is he considering making representa-
tions to the Minister of Immigration to achieve this?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: Few
would disagree that the money remitted home from Tongans working in New Zealand is a
valuable increment to incomes in Tonga. The Government has introduced special work
arrangements for people from the islands. I would, however, disagree that to allow people to
work in New Zealand is in itself a more positive form of assistance than our official aid
projects. Remittances may ease hardship, but they do little to remedy its cause. Through our
aid programme, the priorities of which are set out in consultation with the island govern-
ments, and through the Pacific Islands industrial development scheme, the Government is
working with the island states to help them boost productivity, to create new jobs, and to
expand the opportunities available for people in their home countries, thereby offering
people a real alternative to having to leave their homes in search of work.
(6/10/77)
Health Tax on Beer and Cigarettes
22. Mr FENTON (Hastings), on behalf of Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), asked the
Minister of Health: Has he seen the statement in the New Zealand Herald of 29 September
by the member for New Lynn that the present Government is spending only $4.8 million of
the beer and cigarettes tax on health, and can he reiterate the correct position?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: I have seen the member's assertions as
published. They are quite fallacious. For the current financial year it is estimated that $18
million will be received from the extra tax on tobacco and alcohol. Of this, $200,000 has been
transferred to the Education vote for the extension of nursing training in Waikato and
Southland, and $17.89 million to the health vote for allocation as follows: additional costs on
established community care programmes, $6,171,000; new policies in community care,
$11,043,000; allocation towards supplementary estimates for community care, $586,000. The
total is $17.8 million. In the light of this, I am mystified by the member's reference to an
allocation of only $4.8 million from this tax for health purposes.

future infringements are given to fishing vessels caught within the 200-mile economic zone?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: The Exclusive Economic Zone
(Interim Measures for Foreign Fishing Craft) Regulations 1977 came into force on 1 October
1977. Copies of these regulations; including maps showing the areas closed to trawling by
foreign fishing vessels, have been delivered to foreign boats, both at sea and in port. Foreign
vessels breaching these regulations would initially be given a warning, but if caught again
they would be liable for prosecution. Naturally, any foreign fishing vessels caught fishing
within our 12-mile territorial sea would be apprehended immediately.

Employment for School Leavers
35. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he seen the front page
story in the Christchurch Star of 28 September headlined Job hunters face a bleak outlook.
which deals with the difficulties facing this year's school leavers; does he agree with the
analysis of the youth unemployment situation contained in that article; and what steps is he
taking to ensure that the estimated 65 000-plus school leavers and graduates who are due to
enter the job market in the next 3 months will be meaningfully employed?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: I have seen the article in the
Christchurch Star of 28 September referring to school leavers. The member for Grey Lynn
will recall that I have already indicated that unemployment levels, including those on special
work, are not expected to drop below 12 000 to 13 000 during the coming summer. As the
honourable member will know, several factors determine the number of school leavers
entering the work force in any year. These include examination results, the numbers
proceeding to tertiary education, the availability of the desired job, and parental concern
that their sons and daughters should not leave school unless they have a definite job
arranged. Because of these factors the actual number of school leavers entering the work
force this year will not be known until early next year. A survey of senior secondary school
students intentions is now being undertaken, and this will give some indication of the
numbers likely to be seeking to enter the work force. When the results of this survey become
available the school leaver situation can be closely monitored and action taken if necessary.

Kauri Planting
39. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Forests: In view of the recent
increase in the price of kauri timber and the limited amount available, has he any plans for
planting kauris as part of the afforestation programme?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: The Government's objective is the
perpetuation of native forests both as natural forests and as managed stands. This policy
requires that the regeneration of species and stands will have high priority, and in certain
circumstances artificial enrichment of natural regeneration is beneficial. The present cut of
kauri is quite small, and it is the aim to sustain this by managing those stands that have
regenerated over the last 100 years, supplementing natural regeneration with enrichment
planting.

Technical Institute Staffing
41. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: What are the broad
details of the new arrangements for staffing at technical institutes as notified to institute
principals on 29 June this year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: The arrangements for tutor
staffing in technical institutes, as notified in the circular of 29 June, are an outcome of
discussions which have been held with principals for some time. Each institute has been
given an overall tutor staffing allocation for the current 1977 teaching year. This allocation to
each institute has taken into account the growth in student numbers in courses for which
there is a permanent commitment, and other new developments, as well as the institute's
proposals for other courses. In calculating the increase over the 1976 staffing figures the
Department of Education first took into account for each institute its growth in courses
taught towards examinations for the Trades Certification Board, the Technicians Certifica-
tion Authority, the Society of Accountants, and the New Zealand Institute of Management,
as well as all full-time courses. Institutes have been asked to manage their provision of all
other courses so that their total tutor staffing allocation is not exceeded. Until this year, the
department has controlled total tutor staffing levels for all institutes by approving the staffing
for each individual course. The new arrangements enable the department to approve all
acceptable course approvals for each institute provided that it does not exceed its overall
tutor staffing allocation. These arrangements give institutes greater freedom in deciding
upon which courses to offer.

Market?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry)
replied on behalf of the Acting Minister of Overseas Trade: My department has examined
the potential of the North American market on behalf of many individual apparel manufac-
turers. While present prospects for developing sales of New Zealand apparel on the
Canadian market are not good because of the import quota system imposed by the Canadian
Government in late 1976, access to the United States market is unrestricted. Several New
Zealand manufacturers have proved that they can sell there competitively and that the
United States market can offer substantial prospects for increased exports of apparel.

Textile and Garment Manufacturers Federation to undertake an in-depth study of the
United States market. Details of the composition of the study team, the areas to be visited,
and the timing of the study are presently being discussed by officers of my department and
representatives of the federation.

Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: The amount of family benefit

introduced tax relief of up to $13 a week for families with young children. In Australia the
level of family allowance payable in respect of three children totals A$14.50 a week, but the
average male wage in Australia is A$198.70 compared with $141.27 in New Zealand.

families on low incomes in Australia.

Down Under the Plum Trees
54. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast),
asked the Minister of Education: Could he inform the House whether his department will
follow the Indecent Publications Tribunal decision that the book Down Under the Plum Trees
can be used for children of any age "while receiving instruction from parents or pro-
fessional advisers", and, if so, would he advise just who can be classed as a "professional
adviser"?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: My department has noted the
decision of the Indecent Publications Tribunal, and recognises that this book could, under
the conditions set down by the tribunal, be used in schools if a teacher were to be recognised
as a "professional adviser". The Supreme Court did, however, say this: "We consider that
the question of who is a 'professional adviser' is a question of fact to be determined by a
court faced with this question, particularly under prosecutions under section 21. It will be for
the person accused of committing an offence to justify himself under this section. It may be
that the term can be called 'imprecise', but it is deliberately designed, we think, to cover a
great variety of people who might legally have the advice and instruction of young people as
their responsibility." Any school contemplating using the book should, in my view, await a
decision from the court on the definition of a "professional adviser”.

Immigrants from Pacific Islands
55. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Immigration: In view of the statement in
the Dominion of 30 September by New Zealand's former immigration officer in Tonga, Mr
D. Gordon, that New Zealand's immigration clamp down had hit the hopes and ambitions of
the ordinary man in the islands and restricted the development of housing because of the
decrease in money remitted from New Zealand, will he take these factors into account in
future when deciding immigration quotas from the islands?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: The Government does not have a
quota system for persons entering New Zealand from Tonga as visitors, workers, or
permanent residents. I take it that the "immigration clamp down" mentioned in the
statement in the context of Tonga is a reference to steps taken by the Government to stop
short-term visitors from coming to New Zealand on the off chance of finding employment,
and the channelling of prospective workers into the official work permit scheme. There has
been no clamp down in the last 2 years. The only changes that have been made have
extended the period of stay up to a maximum of 11 months, established a loan fund for the
payment of fares, extended the period of time for workers to repay fares to 20 weeks, and
allowed specific workers to be nominated by employers or sponsored by friends in New
Zealand. I have not seen any figures in recent months concerning a decrease in money
remitted to Tonga from New Zealand. If there has been a reduction I should like to examine
the reasons, because there has been a substantial increase in the number of persons on work
permit schemes, and 66 percent of the Tongan overstayers who registered under the stay of
proceedings have provisionally been granted permanent residence. In these circumstances
they are in a better position to send money home than was the case when they were here
illegally.

Immigrants from Pacific Islands
69. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Immigration: In view of the statement in
the Dominion of 30 September, in which New Zealand's former immigration officer in
Tonga, Mr D. Gordon, stated that his hardest task in Tonga was explaining to people why
they could not go to New Zealand even if they had job offers, could he specify the criteria
used for accepting permanent or temporary immigrants from the islands?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: Tongan citizens may come to new
Zealand for temporary employment, in accordance with the provisions of the official work
permit scheme agreed between the New Zealand and Tongan Governments. Under the
scheme, offers of employment from New Zealand employers are lodged with district offices
of the New Zealand Department of Labour for forwarding to the Tongan Department of
Labour, Industry and Commerce. There is no provision for employment offers to be made
directly to workers in Tonga, although employers may nominate particular workers.
Employers are required to make financial and other commitments, and the Department of
Labour checks that no suitably qualified workers are available locally to fill the vacancies.
The Tongan Government is responsible for the final selection of workers, who must be
between 20 and 45 years of age and of good health and character. The policy covering the
permanent entry of Tongan citizens to New Zealand places a high priority on family
reunification and other humanitarian factors. New Zealand has given an undertaking that
the migration of skilled workers from Tonga, as with other developing countries, will not be
encouraged. Applications solely on occupational grounds are therefore not accepted.

Mercury Level in Fish
100. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Health: Can he state the level of
mercury allowed in fish by Department of Health regulations, and also the maximum level
recommended by the World Health Organisation?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied on behalf of
the Minister of Health: The maximum level of mercury allowed in fish sold in New Zealand
is 0.5 parts per million—that is, 0.5 mg of mercury per kilogram of fish. The World Health
Organisation has not set a specific recommended maximum level for mercury in fish. Rather,
it has set a provisional tolerable weekly intake for mankind from all sources, including fish,
of 0.3 mg per person or 0.005 mg per kilogram of body weight.

Motorcar Spare Parts
102. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has he
seen a statement in the Auckland Star of 5 October by an importer of thermostats to the
effect that "Motorists are being swindled by the system of snowballing percentages on car
parts", and, if so, what action is being taken by his department to protect motorist
consumers?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied: I have seen
the article referred to. The maximum mark-ups that may be applied to car parts are fixed by
the Stabilisation of Prices Regulations 1974. In terms of those regulations, importers,
wholesalers, and retailers are permitted to apply a lawful percentage mark-up to the into-
store cost, which includes duty and sales tax. This year the Government established the
Commission of Inquiry into the Distribution of Motor Vehicle Parts, and included in its
terms of reference is one dealing with the reasonableness or otherwise of the profits realised
by distributors of motor vehicle parts. The commission is required to report its findings by 30
November.

Disarmament
110. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Since the General
Assembly of the United Nations will in mid-1978 devote a special session to disarmament,
what will New Zealand's role be at this special disarmament session, and will any initiatives
be taken by the New Zealand Government to halt the tragic build-up in military expendi-
ture, especially on nuclear weaponry, that has been evident in the last 30 years?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: New
Zealand is one of the countries which co-sponsored the resolution at the General Assembly
last year calling for a special session. The Government therefore welcomes the special
session and will do everything possible to ensure its success. Our role will be similar to that
adopted by New Zealand in other disarmament discussions—namely, the expression of a
sensible and reasoned voice seeking to assist in establishing a consensus that will set the
international community on the road to more assured progress on disarmament issues in
future years. We are not on the 54-member preparatory committee for the special session
and the scope for any initiatives is limited in the preparatory stages. We do, however, follow
the committee's work in New York closely and have made our views known to the
committee. We also submitted a paper commenting on the agenda and objectives of the
special session. The Government also plans to publish a green paper on disarmament before
the special session with a view to acquainting the public of the various disarmament issues
that will be considered at that session.

percent of total Government expenditure. It is estimated that in the year ending 31 March
1978 net expenditure on national superannuation will represent 52.81 percent of total social
welfare expenditure and 11.32 percent of total Government expenditure.

Aranui Manning
113. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Railways: Has he seen the report in the
Dominion of Friday, 7 October 1977, on the likely cancellation of the 10 a.m. sailing of the
Cook Strait ferry Aranui due to a crew shortage, and, if so, could he advise: (a) was the
sailing cancelled; (b) how many crew were involved; (c) what were the reasons for the crew
shortage; (d) of which union were they members; (e) what is the total manning scale of
members of that union on the vessel; and (f) how many passengers were inconvenienced?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: Yes, I have seen the report
in the Dominion of Friday, 7 October 1977, concerning the likely cancellation of the 10 a.m.
sailing of the Cook Strait ferry Aranui due to a crew shortage. To answer the specific
questions asked by the honourable member: Yes, the sailing was cancelled. Twenty-three
members of the provedore section of the crew exercised their right under the Shipping and
Seamen Act 1952 to give 24 hours notice to relinquish their positions. After leaving the
vessel no other members of the Federated Cooks and Stewards Union of New Zealand were
available to fill the jobs. The normal complement of cooks and stewards on the vessel is 27.
About 267 persons were booked for the sailing, and they had their travel arrangements
altered. However, nearly all the people were conveyed on the Aratika or Arahanga the
same day.

Nuclear Disarmament
126. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: In view of
the special session of the General Assembly of the United Nations, which will be devoted in
mid 1978 to the question of nuclear disarmament, will he advise: (a) whether New Zealand
will be participating; (b) what specific proposals the Government intends to initiate; and (c)
whether he proposes to publicise within New Zealand any views to highlight the significance
of this special United Nations session?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: New
Zealand will certainly be participating in the special session next year, as I indicated
yesterday in answer to the question referred to by the member for New Lynn. New Zealand
is not on the 54 member preparatory committee for the special session, and, accordingly, the
scope for initiating proposals before the special session itself is limited. However, the
Government is doing everything possible within its resources to make a positive contribution
to the session. At home, the Government is preparing a green paper on disarmament for the
special session, with a view to acquainting the public of the various disarmament issues that
will be considered at that session. The Minister of Foreign Affairs has also proposed that a
link be established between the Government and the public to facilitate the exchange of
ideas and opinions on disarmament issues in advance of the special session. At the special
session itself New Zealand will, of course, be prepared to initiate any proposal it deems is
required to make the special session a success. However, the session will not constitute a
disarmament negotiating forum but rather a general conference devoted to the principles,
programmes, and machinery of disarmament. It will be a success if it provides a better
framework for the progress in disarmament in future years. New Zealand's contribution will
be tailored to meet this objective.

Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands) replied on behalf of the Minister of Police: In
most establishments where meals are served over a long period to large numbers of people
the quality and quantity of meals fluctuates from time to time. This is certainly the case in
respect of meals served to recruits at the police college at Trentham, despite the fact that
meals and facilities are constantly inspected and reported on by college supervisors. The

just north of Porirua. In the meantime the Police are endeavouring to find a satisfactory
solution to messing problems at the Trentham college. One positive step that has been taken
is the recent establishment of a position as police catering officer. Applicants for the new
position have already been interviewed, and, when the person to be appointed takes up his
duties, the situation at Trentham will be high on the list of matters requiring his expert
attention.

Free Enterprise
142. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Prime Minister: How does he relate the
statement of the chairman of Tappenden Industries Ltd as reported in the New Zealand
Herald of 7 October that "free enterprise is being whittled away" with the National Party's
traditional claim of unqualified support for free enterprise?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister) replied: It is not possible to relate the
statement in question to National Party philosophy in any way; nor do I accept the
statement. The same statement further suggests the extent of rules and regulations which
now enwrap profit-seeking organisations are getting close to choking them to death``,
referring to the retail car trade. The facts simply do not bear this out. The figures released
just last week by the Minister of Trade and Industry show that new car sales are running at
an acceptable level and that used car sales have actually increased for the 9 months ended
September 1977. I am obliged to point out that, while the National Government whole-
heartedly believes in free enterprise, it makes no apologies for the existence of controls in
this sector, as these controls are designed to achieve the most favourable balance between
the needs of the commercial sector, the New Zealand consumer, and the economy as a
whole. This was promised in the 1975 National Party manifesto, which stated that the
National Government would provide "a balanced legislative and administrative approach to
the needs of both consumers and the commercial community".

Customs Revenue from Opium-smoking Equipment
146. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Customs: Is it correct that the Customs
Department is collecting revenue from imported equipment which was primarily designed to
be used for the smoking of opium?


## p. 3961 (#67) ############################################

26 October
3961
Questions and Replies
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied: It is an offence under the Misuse
of Drugs Act 1975 to be in possession of any needle, syringe, pipe, or other utensil, for the
purpose of committing an offence against that Act. The range of equipment which could be
used for the smoking of controlled drugs, including opium, is extremely wide and extends
from simple household items such as tinfoil and household spoons to various kinds of pipes,
many of which can also be used for smoking tobacco. To the extent that any of these goods
are dutiable my department collects revenue on them. Because of the obvious difficulty in
making an effective Customs Import Prohibition Order to cover all goods that might be used
in taking opium, the law enforcement agencies involved in the fight against drugs have in the
past relied on the offence provision in the Misuse of Drugs Act. However, in view of recent
publicity on this matter I have asked my department to re-examine the matter to determine
whether it would be possible to impose a prohibition aimed specifically at such equipment.
(18/10/77)
Fire Safety Regulations
147. Dr WALL (Porirua) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: Does he intend to follow
the recommendation of the New Zealand Fire Service Commission and the "Sprott House"
Commission of Inquiry supported by the New Zealand branch of the Institution of Fire
Engineers (mentioned on page 18 of the commission's report), that local authority bylaws on
fire safety be replaced by statutory regulations?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: The recommendation referred
to has not been acceptable to successive Governments, which have preferred that fire safety
standards should be applied through bylaws adopted by territorial authorities rather than
regulations promulgated by the central government. Successive Governments have also
preferred that the standards to be applied should be determined and revised from time to
time through the consultative process of the Standards Association of New Zealand. This
process provides much more flexibility for amendments made necessary by technological
developments and the special requirements of individual districts. Fire safety bylaws must be
adopted by all territorial authorities, and all must have the prior approval of the Minister of
Local Government. I do not consider that there is any indication that the situation is in need
of any change at this stage on the lines suggested.
(18/10/77)

Unemployment Statistics
154. Mr ISBEY. (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour: Has he seen the report by
Robin Turkel in the New Zealand Herald of 13 October on unemployment in New Zealand,
which is summed up in the paragraph, "Since the first step towards solution of any problem
is recognition of its existence, it would seem time for New Zealand to compute its jobless the
way most other developed countries do-as a percentage of the work force rather than
merely registered unemployed", and has he any intention of following this
advice?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The Government has already taken
initial steps to study the feasibility of an alternative measure of unemployment. A technical
working party comprising members of the Department of Labour and the Department of
Statistics is investigating the feasibility of conducting a household labour force survey similar
to those carried out in some other countries. Many technical questions need to be answered
if such a survey is to be reliable. The working party has addressed itself to these questions, as
well as making detailed studies of overseas surveys, and its report is now in the final stages of
preparation. If a decision is made to adopt a household labour force survey to measure
unemployment, the registered unemployment series would continue to be published as a
measure of those unemployed persons seeking the assistance of the Department of Labour.
The system adopted in New Zealand is the same as that in Australia.

Telephone Service-Emergency Dialling
156. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General: Has he seen the comment
on page 13 of the New Zealand Fire Service Commission report that "The introduction of
the emergency (111 dialling) telephone service has not proceeded as speedily as the New
Zealand Post Office equipment allows", and what is he doing to speed up installation?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: Yes, I have seen the comment
about the introduction of the 111 emergency telephone service. The Post Office makes
provision for the introduction of the 111 emergency telephone service each time a manual
telephone exchange is converted to automatic working, but the introduction of the
emergency service is contingent on all three services-ambulance, fire, and police-being
able to accept calls on a 24 hour basis. All three services have not been able to provide a 24-
hour answering service in some cases, and the 111 emergency service has not proceeded in
these areas because of that. It is not possible to introduce the 111 emergency service until
exchanges are converted to automatic operation.

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I find it interesting
that the Opposition should attack a success story. The fact of the matter is that when the
member for Mt. Albert was Minister of Trade and Industry there were factory closures, and
the cost of living rose as never before. He inherited a position with the cost of living
measured by the consumer price index at 5 percent; when he went out of office it was 15.7
percent, and rising. We have been coping with the rising tendency and with the inbuilt
factors ever since, but we have got it down to about 14 percent from the 17.7 percent it had
risen to as a result of the actions of the Labour Government; and, as the Prime Minister said,
it will continue to come down on an annual basis.
We hear a great deal from Labour members about factory closures. In 1974, under the
Labour Government, there were 260 factory closures, and in 1975 there were 423. More than
700 factories closed during the last 2 years of the last Labour Government. More people are
employed in factories in New Zealand today than when Labour was kicked out of office,
despite the problems we face-and I do not deny those problems. As Minister of Trade and
Industry I am concerned about them, but there are more people employed in manufacturing
units today than when the Labour Government went out of office.
The member for Mt. Albert commented on NAFTA. I believe that the deal the Minister
of Overseas Trade and I were able to negotiate in consultation with Australian Ministers is a
good one for New Zealand manufacturers, and especially the apparel industry. We
negotiated in April for 4 000 000 garments to be exported to Australia during a period of 12
months. In the 2 or 3 months preceding the negotiations 1 000 000 garments above the
previous year's quota had been produced in New Zealand, and when the manufacturers
came to me I made arrangements with the Australians for them to take the 1 000 000
garments, thus giving a total of 5 000 000. In addition, we have another 1 500 000 for the
period of 18 months, including the first 12 months of the agreement and the next 6 months.
We have been able to negotiate on behalf of New Zealand manufacturers for the right to
export 6 500 000 garments to Australia. The Australians have not been selling successfully in
New Zealand. This is a negotiation, and in a negotiation the other party expects to be able to
get something out of it. We have agreed with the Australians to a reduction in duty for 6
months only, plus monitoring by the Department of Trade and Industry of any imports that
come in.
Now, the reduction in duty from 32.5 percent to 15 percent still means that during that
time New Zealand will continue, both within the agreement and outside it, to have access to
Australia on the basis of 6 percent, 7 percent, and 9 percent. Those are our duty rates. That
is what we pay to get into Australia on this narrow 6-months agreement. During that time
Australia will still have to get over a barrier of 15 percent. The other Australian manufac-
tures that come in under the normal import licensing system-and for the last 3 years under
successive Governments New Zealand importers have brought in about $700,000 worth of
apparel from Australia-will still be liable for 32.5 percent. And when the 6-month period is
over the substantive duty rate will revert to the rate for normal imports-32.5 percent. This
is a special agreement to enable the New Zealand manufacturers to sell an additional
