is desperately needed. The reaction from the Associate Minister of Finance was, "The
Government is looking at the situation." That is typical of Tory philosophy: don't do
something, just stand there—and that is exactly what the Government has done. Why has it
not acted over the past months to relieve the pressure placed on people by direct taxation?
Why has it not increased the limit on loans available from the Housing Corporation, to
stimulate the building industry and to assist young people? Why has it not directed more
money to the Development Finance Corporation, to enable that body to assist front-line
industry and so provide employment opportunities? Why does the Government not offer
some relief to hard-pressed families, and why does it not increase the family benefit, as was
recommended by the Kennedy-Good report in 1976? We have seen no action from the
Government.
Mr FENTON (Hastings): We have just heard an amazing speech, delivered with the
usual effrontery by the man who led New Zealand into disaster in 1973, and who has no right
to talk about the economy in any sense of the word. When he was the Prime Minister, the
public told his Government that it should not just stand there, but do something; however,
the Labour Government took no decisive action at all. The figures on which his whole
speech was based were begging at every turn.
The fact is that the Leader of the Opposition is so far out of date that he does not realise
that today the external deficit, which was boosted by the former Labour Government to a
record $1,000 million, has been reduced to $480 million, and the giant internal deficit before
borrowing of $1,400 million, which resulted from the Labour Government's recklessness, is
now down to less than $400 million-all within 2 years. Those guilty members on the
Opposition benches-and I cannot repeat this too often, because they deserve to hear
it-condoned a policy that they now protest about loudly: an unconstitutional and unlawful
overexpenditure, without sanction, of $239 million. That indicates the record of Opposition
members, who now have the absolute gall to stand in the House and criticise the Govern-
ment for acting honestly and in the best possible way in its endeavours to rescue the country
from the utter shambles in which it was placed between 1972 and 1975 by an inept,
ineffective, and incompetent Government.
Opposition members talk a great deal about housing and employment, and attribute the
lack of these to the Government's policies. Under the former Labour Government the
housing industry was badly run down, because that Administration boosted house building
to a tremendous extent without in any way controlling it. As a result, the industry ran wild,
with no control of any kind. When the National Government assumed office, housing was far
from healthy and the Government was faced with a total overexpenditure of about $170
million. In other words, the former Labour Government had spent all the kitty; the building
industry and services were hopelessly overextended, to the point where more and more
people found they had to wait longer and longer to acquire their own home.
During their period in office, members opposite managed to double the prices of houses
and treble the prices of sections. They thereby committed every person who was waiting for
a house to the terrible possibility—which then became a probability and finally a fact that
they would have to find twice the deposit, borrow twice the amount, and, of course, pay
twice the interest when purchasing a home. I remind members opposite that interest rates
first rose to about 20 percent under their administration and not during the term of the
National Government. Although during the time of the former Labour Government there
was an all-time record in the number of second and third mortgages registered, Opposition
members are now criticising the present figures.
Members opposite dare to stand in the House and criticise the National Government for
trying to disentangle the country from the shambles in which they placed it. Of course, that
typifies, exemplifies, and characterises Opposition members, who claim to be democratic
socialists and pretend to know something about the economy and financial affairs. They also
claim, heavens above, to know something about humanity, but they caused the people to
suffer economically and in every other way. The people are now suffering to a lessening
extent as a result of the National Government's policies; with inflation and the economy
under control, the country will finally be a much happier place in which to live.
The hour set down for the suspension of the sitting having arrived, the motion lapsed.

CARTER OBSERVATORY AMENDMENT BILL
Bill reported without amendment.
In Committee
LAND AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The Bill, which now contains 7 clauses, deals with administrative matters. Clause 1
relates to the short title. Clause 2 will enable the Minister to delegate a number of his powers
to officers of the Department of Lands and Survey-for example, under the Counties Act
1956 the Minister's consent is required to the stopping and closing of roads by county
councils. In most cases these decisions are of a relatively minor nature only and should be
delegated; the amendment will relieve the Minister of the need to consider every case. In
most instances roads have already been closed.
Clause 3 simplifies certain procedures regarding the Land Settlement Board. While the
board has the power to purchase land, it does not have the authority to lease it; in the past,
leasing has been at the direction of the Governor-General. It is reasonable that the board
should have its own leasing powers. Clause 4 relates to the good husbandry of land under
pastoral leases; it is an additional clause provided since the Bill was first introduced, and is
purely a tidying-up clause. Where section 122(10) of the Land Act refers to the administra-
tive division of the Supreme Court, the amendment simply changes that to refer to the Land
Valuation Tribunal.
Clause 5 brings the provisions of the Land Act relating to reviews of interest rates into
line with those of other Government lending institutions. At present the principal Act
provides for 5-yearly reviews, and this is amended to 3-yearly reviews. Clause 6 amends the
general offence provisions of the Land Act to provide that information for all offences under
the Act is to be laid within 1 year.
In the Committee stage of the Bill I intend to introduce a Supplementary Order Paper
to include in the Bill a new provision that will involve the redesignation of the post of
Assistant Director-General of the Department of Lands and Survey as Deputy Director-
General.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Opposition supports the Bill and welcomes the
extension of the Minister's powers of delegation; it welcomes also the provisions for the
leasing of private land and the cropping of pastoral land. Although it is a short Bill, it is
important.
The Minister will remember that, during the debate on the estimates, the Opposition
questioned the extension of the powers of the Land Settlement Board. The new section
108(2), inserted by clause 4(1), deals with afforestation and gives the board powers it did not
have before. Page 10 of the department's report states: "There are numerous cases where a
small area of a farm could best be planted in trees but the farmer cannot raise finance on
which to apply for a Forestry Encouragement Grant. In the interest of good land use and in
cases where pastoral farming would continue to be the predominant activity on the property,
marginal lands finance should be available for use as the local share for such small
afforestation projects."


## p. 3982 (#88) ############################################

3982
26 October
Forest and Rural Fires Bill
The report also mentions the acquisition of "stepping stone" units, and I wonder if the
Bill takes these two important matters into account. It might be possible to align these to the
provisions of the Bill. The issue is important, particularly to farmers on uneconomic land,
and I suggest that between now and the Committee stage the Minister should carefully
consider the questions that were asked during the debate on the estimates. I support the Bill.
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I thank the member for Western Maori for his

suggests.
Bill read a second time.
FOREST AND RURAL FIRES BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. This is the third time the House has had before it a comprehensive fire control measure
designed to protect the trees and grasslands on which we as New Zealanders place such
store. The first measure was the Forest and Rural Fires Act 1947, which provided new and
comprehensive local organisations with full powers to prevent and fight fires in country
areas. Experience showed some need for improvements in organisation, and these were
incorporated in subsequent legislation.
I think I should comment briefly on the general problems of the overlapping jurisdic-
tions of fire authorities. There are five independent aspects of fire control: (a) the prevention
of the spread of fire from or on to a property, achieved by the forest and rural fires
enactments; (b) the prevention of damage to the soil of a property, achieved by the Soil
Conservation and Rivers Control Act 1941; (c) the protection of trees, pastures, and so on,
on Crown land, achieved by the Land Act 1948; (d) the protection of State forests, achieved
by the Forests Act 1949-although relevant portions were transferred to the Forest and
Rural Fires Act 1955; and (e) the protection of private land carrying vegetation, achieved by
common law rights of owners-for example, the refusal to allow anyone to light fires.
Although a given property may be affected by any or all of these controls, they all
represent independent jurisdictions. Clause 14(2) of the Bill enables them to co-operate, but
any attempt to compel one interest to administer the jurisdiction of another would mean
unskilled intervention in another's specialist field. One of the problems arising out of these
overlapping jurisdictions is that a farmer may have to apply to more than one body for
permits to light a fire. Representations were made to the select committee by national water
and soil conservation organisations; the New Zealand Catchment Authorities Association;
the Marlborough Catchment and Regional Water Board; and the New Zealand Counties
Association-all calling for some integration of fire control arrangements, this to be done by
fire plans drawn up by the fire authorities.
That is a most welcome attitude, and the Bill goes far to accommodate it; but I must add
a word of caution. The fire authorities are available as co-ordinators, using fire plans as a
joint record of arrangements, but no one may operate a takeover by, as I have said,
intervening in another body's specialist field. Regarding jurisdictions, the co-ordination, co-
operation, and good understanding of the roles of the various bodies concerned are vital to
effective fire control. As was said often during the preliminary discussions on the Bill, fire
does not respect jurisdictions.
I conclude with a comment on financial practicability. Some proposals, such as that
universal firebreaking be required, are ideal, but cannot be applied except where landow-
ners can meet the cost. Otherwise, the owners will be forced off, leaving the land derelict
and a still bigger menace. This is why clause 27 of the Bill is directed only at exotic forest
owners and at land subdividers, as these folk are using their land commercially and expect
large returns. If poor hill country carrying scrub is planted in exotic trees, it becomes good
commercial land able to pay for such firebreaks, when soil conservation does not preclude
this.
Financial practicability is likewise the basis of the levies made under clauses 45 and 46.
The levies are calculated on a land value tariff—that is, they fall so heavily upon forests that
little is left for neighbouring farmers to pay, if the farmland is considered liable at all in a
particular case.
Financial practicability is also a main feature of the new concept of forest areas. As well
as improving the intensive protection of forests against risk, to the advantage of a fast
enlarging primary industry, the forest areas will considerably ease the cost of fire control that


## p. 3983 (#89) ############################################

26 October
3983
Forest and Rural Fires Bill
at present falls upon county councils.
The Bill will be followed by revised regulations, which will be prepared as thoroughly
and as openly as was the Bill. I acknowledge the work that was done by certain members of
the Forest Service in developing this legislation, and I mention the work of Mr Buist, who
worked on the Bill for some time when he was the office solicitor. He moved about amongst
the various local authorities, Federated Farmers, and other groups, gaining unanimous
support for the measure.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): As the Minister pointed out, this is a major Bill
providing for the protection of our forest areas. Opposition members said on its introduction
that they wanted to be sure that all those concerned in the protection of our forests had been
consulted. I thank all those who made submissions to the committee. This very important
Bill is a culmination of bipartisan activity; it has been around the House for some time, and
the Labour Government shared in its preparation. It is about time that everybody in the
country got together; I am thinking particularly of local authorities, Federated Farmers, and
those who have been most responsible, as well as those who are interested in afforestation.
The establishment of a fire authority, particularly in rural fire districts, will do much to
enhance the protection I referred to earlier.
The Bill is a move in the right direction, and will help protect the forested areas that are
so important to our economy and to the people as a whole. I have great pleasure in
supporting the Bill, and I think the Minister will agree that all Opposition members did much
to help the committee. The department was helpful too, and I thank the legal advisers who
took part in the committee hearings.

Prayers.
NOTICES OF MOTION
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Before I call the next order of business, which is notices of
motion, perhaps I could again draw the attention of honourable members to what I believe is
a rather dubious procedure. The House has required the Speaker to vet notices of motion,
but in doing so it has given the Speaker virtually no authority to do anything worth while
with them. Twelve were presented to me today—a round dozen-and I notice that there are
already 24 on the Order Paper. We have a 50 percent rate of inflation. Not one of them will
be debated, as far as I know, and I wonder what we achieve by having this spate of notices of
motion. There will be another page and a half on the Order Paper-the Government Printer
may be pleased about that. Members will be able to let off some steam, and I think that is a
good idea.
However, it appears to me that some of the notices of motion are repetitious, if not
tedious; some border on the frivolous; some appear to be more interested in the person of a
member than the policy of a party; and some contain accusations that make it difficult for me
to decide whether or not to accept the motions on the ground of whether they can be
authenticated, but I suppose I must accept them as posing material for debate. I invite
members to reconsider their attitudes to notices of motion. I am quite happy to vet them as
far as I can-which is to a very limited extent—and to accept them, but I doubt very much
whether they really achieve anything to the benefit of Parliament as a whole.
LAND PURCHASE BILL
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That the Land Purchase Bill be
introduced. The Bill is a consolidation of the Land Settlement Promotion and Land
Acquisition Act 1952, and the amendments to that Act. Members will be aware that the
Government withdrew the Land Settlement Promotion and Land Acquisition Act 1975,
which was introduced by the previous Labour Government and referred to the Lands and
Agriculture Committee. The present Government considered that it would be in the
interests of all concerned to replace that Bill with a consolidation of the present Act.
Part I of the present Act, which relates to the compulsory taking of farm land for the
settlement of discharged ex-servicemen, has not been brought forward into this Bill. This
provision has not been used since the passing of the original Act, and with the operation of
the civilian land settlement scheme it is no longer necessary.
Part I of the Bill I am now introducing relates to the control of sales and leases of farm
land to prevent undue aggregation, and it is under this provision that major changes are
proposed. The transactions to which the Bill applies are basically the same as in the present
Act, except that the existing area limitation of 2 hectares or more has been increased to 4
hectares, and the term of leases of farm land has been extended from 3 years to 5 years. The
present provision that allows a 10-man company to acquire farm land without having to
obtain the consent of the Land Valuation Tribunal is being replaced. The Bill provides that
in future an interest of 25 percent or more in a farm-land owning company will be treated as
a substantial interest in land, and that any person who holds such an interest or holds land in
his own right must obtain the consent of the tribunal to purchase further land as an individual
or to purchase shares in a farm-land owning company. A farm-land owning company will
also require the tribunal's consent to purchase further farm land or shares.
The general criteria in deciding whether undue aggregation will result are, in some
cases, the same as in the present Act. The notable exceptions are the provision relating
aggregation to the requirements of the purchaser and his family, which has been omitted,
and the provision concerning the holding of shares in a farming company, which has been
included. The tribunal is required to have regard to whether the acquisition would be in or
against the public interest. For the purposes of the Bill, the criteria for determining the
public interest are: first, to ensure and preserve the diversification of the ownership of farm


## p. 3985 (#91) ############################################

27 October
3985
Land Purchase Bill
land by individuals, or, in the case of farming companies, the diversification of the ownership
of shares in such companies; and, secondly, that farm land of good productive capacity is
retained as farm land in so far as this is compatible with other matters of public interest.
In addition, a further criterion has been included: whether, in the opinion of the
tribunal, any proposed change of use of the land for commercial exotic forestry or other
purposes will be beneficial or detrimental to the interests of the community in which the land
is situated. A major change is that, if land in the transaction is, in the opinion of the tribunal,
substantially undeveloped, the only criterion to be considered is the ability of the purchaser
or lessee to bring the land up to its productive capacity. The intention of this provision is to
seek to attract investment into the development of lands that might otherwise remain
unproductive. The period for lodging an application to the tribunal has been extended from
1 month to 3 months.
Part II of the Bill deals with the control of acquisition of land by overseas interests, and
is basically unchanged from the provisions in the present Act. The only major change is the
inclusion in clause 16 of the provision that the Governor-General may by Order in Council,
on the recommendation of the Minister, declare any land or any class or classes of land to be
not subject to the provisions of that part of the Bill. The Bill will be referred automatically to
the Lands and Agriculture Committee.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): The marked difference between this proposal and
that which the Government decided not to proceed with is a clear indication of the
philosophy of each political party towards the ownership of land. Whereas the Labour Party
has always advocated that all land should be owned, managed, and controlled by New
Zealand citizens, the Government has opted out of its responsibility to ensure that land is
not transferred to overseas companies and is not unduly aggregated by anyone.
Clause 16 of the Bill includes a provision that the Governor-General may by Order in
Council declare any land to be not subject to this clause. What is the purpose behind that
provision? Why does the Minister not set down the criteria, rather than have the declaration
made by Order in Council? After all is said and done, there is sufficient control now, with
the Overseas Investments Commission, monopolies Acts, and so on, to govern the need for
maintaining investments from overseas without forgoing the ownership of our land by
overseas companies or persons. We should adhere firmly to the principle that all land should
be owned, managed, and controlled by New Zealand citizens for all time, much as we should
like to mortgage land to overseas vested interests on the pretext that they may invest funds
here.
The major change in clause 16, to exempt certain classes by Order in Council, is a move
that should not be encouraged, and I trust that the committee, when considering the Bill, will
give some thought to whether this power should be vested in the Executive. Why has this
course of action been adopted? Why has the Government decided that it might do this by
Order in Council? It is seeking a power that should be properly set out in the statute, so that
everyone understands the New Zealand laws about the ownership of land. Be it farm land,
or any class of land, it is worth protecting by law.
The Government has the Opposition's support in updating the provisions to ensure that
there is no undue aggregation of land. Could the Minister indicate whether Maori land

of persons involved, I am sure there is no breach of the proposed or existing law.
I repeat that an opportunity has been missed of stating that neither Parliament nor the
people will tolerate the ownership of land or properties by other than New Zealand citizens
or those permanently resident in this country. Other countries have adopted that principle,
and understandably so. I do not think the Executive should seek the power to exempt certain
classes of land, or to enable certain transactions to be made by Order in Council. That is a

The Minister will know that not only farm land, but also other valuable property, has

no difficulty about that so far. However, small but important areas of land, not necessarily
farm land, have been sold to overseas interests. Such transactions should be controlled, and

always considered that that practice has a good deal of merit, because, unfortunately, there
is a bleeding of capital from the farming industry into the cities. Farmers constantly invest in
the cities surplus capital and assets and the proceeds from the sale of farms. That happens
frequently, and I have always thought that there was considerable value in the reverse
process.
Certainly, most of the Queen Street farmers I have met do not make excessive profits;
they are very much hobby farmers, and they increase production but do not make excessive
profits in my experience. They invest in the rural industries capital produced in the city, and
that is something to be desired from an economic point of view-not something to be
criticised. I rose to make that point, because it is very easy to make accusations, claims,
criticisms, and condemnations if one does not think the procees through. The movement of
capital from the city to the country is desirable, in my view.

Teaching Staff-Primary and Intermediate
1. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Education: What has been
teacher reaction to the introduction of continuous staffing at primary and intermediate
school level?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): Comments I have received from

Zealand Educational Institute, indicate that generally speaking the new primary staffing

average waiting time for those making application before they receive funds if they qualify?

Marketing Corporation, it is expected that approved withdrawals should be paid out within 1
month of application. Prior to this revision the average waiting time would have been longer.

Canterbury Forests-Sale of Windthrown Logs
6. Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora) asked the Minister of Forests: What are the total receipts
from the sale of windthrown and burnt logs from the Canterbury forests, and what return on
investment does this represent?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): To 30 September 1977 receipts for sales of
windthrown and burnt logs from State forests in Canterbury totalled $17.26 million. The
total direct cost of the recovery operation over the same period is $13.74 million giving an
excess of revenue over expenditure of $3.47 million. In addition, $5.58 million of overseas
exchange was earned from the export of logs from private forests. Their costs are not known;

Zealand Electricity Department sought State Services Commission approval for the pur-

Roading Expenditure-Avalon Bridge
10. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Works and Development: With
the extra $11,800,000 available to the National Roads Board for State highway and local
authority works, could consideration be given to providing a four-lane bridge across the Hutt
River at Avalon, instead of a two-lane bridge?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Acting Minister of Works and Development): The original
decision of the National Roads Board to approve a two-lane bridge across the Hutt River at
Avalon was based on the estimated traffic volume that would use the crossing. The overall
scheme has been so designed that when traffic growth approaches the capacity of the two-
lane structure the additional lanes can be built. Until such time as this demand is substan-
tiated by the use of the new structure it is premature to give approval for a four-lane
structure.
Mr Lambert: Can the Minister give an assurance that when the traffic volume indicates
that there should be four lanes the finance will be available?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I do not know that I can assure the member that finance will
be available, but I can assure him that the bridge is being constructed so that when the need
for four lanes arises it can be met in the most reasonable way. However, that is at least 10
years away. It might interest the member to know that the volume of traffic expected to use
the bridge is about 6000 vehicles a day, whereas the bridge that is being constructed will have
a capacity of between 12 000 and 15 000 vehicles a day.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Would it not be preferable to give consideration to other urgent
works in the Hutt Valley, such as a bypass in Upper Hutt, before the development of the
four-lane bridge?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! It may be preferable, but not on this occasion. The
question related to a four-lane bridge across the Hutt River at Avalon. It did not relate to
other urgent works, and if the member wants to ask about other works he can put down
another question.

Shipping Corporation
16. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Transport: In the light of his answer
in the House that the New Zealand Shipping Corporation was subsidised to an amount of $4
million, can he indicate (1) where this is shown in the annual report of the corporation; and
(2) whether this sum should be offset by the profit in the accounts?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Transport.
"The total cost to the Government for providing the Shipping Corporation service to the
Cook Islands and Niue and a coastal shipping service was, as I indicated on 19 October, $4.2
million for the year ended 31 March 1977. Page 11 of the Shipping Corporation's annual
report shows that $2.99 million was received from the Government by way of charter and
management fee. The remaining $1.2 million was paid directly to the Shipping Corporation
by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as reimbursement for expenses incurred in operating the
Cook Islands and Niue service. It was for this reason that this figure was excluded from the
corporation's annual report. In reply to the second part of the question, offsetting the profit
in the corporation's accounts against the subsidy paid would have the effect of cross-
subsidising loss-making services by profit-making services. This is not desirable. In directing
the Shipping Corporation to provide shipping services to the Cook Islands, Niue, and the
New Zealand coast, which operate at a loss, successive Governments have undertaken to
ensure that the corporation would not be financially disadvantaged."
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Wheat Acreage
17. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Agriculture: What acreage of
wheat is necessary for New Zealand to reach self-sufficiency, and what acreage has been
sown during the winter and spring of 1977?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I reply on behalf of the
Minister. The area necessary for a self-sufficiency of wheat is estimated at about 100 000
hectares. The area sown in 1977 will not be known until the end of November. However, on
present information a slight decrease from the 93 700 hectares sown in 1976-77 is expected.
Mr Elworthy: Is it expected that last year's planting of 93 000 hectares will produce self-
sufficiency this season?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: As I understand it, last year 93 000 hectares gave us self-
sufficiency. We expect a slight drop in the area planted this year, but it is too early to be final
on that.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Old People's Homes-Licensing
18. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Mr HUNT (New Lynn), asked
the Minister of Health: What is the current practice for the licensing of old people's homes,
and is there any intention to introduce more stringent regulations?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): Licensing of old people's homes is governed by
the Old People's Homes Regulations 1965. These provide for the licensing of premises that
are mainly for the aged or infirm and where there are six or more persons over the age of 65
who pay for their lodgings and one or more meals a day. Application for a licence is made to
the medical officer of health in the district concerned. Provided the premises comply with the
requirements of the regulations, a licence is issued by the head office of the department. An
inspection of all licensed premises is made annually through the office of the medical officer
of health. It is known that the standard of care and facilities provided in some rest homes
leaves a lot to be desired. The regulations have been revised, and I can assure the
honourable member that they will lay down more stringent requirements in order to
safeguard the interests and well-being of residents. A draft revision of the regulations has

Post Office Publicity
20. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui),
asked the Postmaster-General: What efforts were made to inform business houses of the
recent postal changes, and when were such people told of the changes in envelope size
requirements?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): The intention to introduce a standard
letter postage rate was announced on 4 November 1976. However, general publicity about
standard letter envelope sizes began as far back as 1970. Close liaison has been maintained
since then with key organisations such as envelope manufacturers, the printing and station-
ery trade, and chambers of commerce. These organisations, together with large customers,
were specially notified in late 1976 about the changes. Further publicity was released in June
1977, and this included the distribution of a pamphlet to all business firms. Details of the
principal rates and charges to apply from 1 October 1977 were announced on 22 July 1977.

URGENT QUESTION
Tourism-Coach-Drivers' Dispute
Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Labour, as an urgent question: Is he aware
that as of midnight tonight, 27 October, overseas tourists will be stranded throughout New
Zealand, and will he inform the House: (1) the present average coach-driver's wage, the
amount of increase sought and the amount of increase agreed to; (2) the approaches he has
made to the employment group concerned to avoid this stoppage; and (3) what last-minute
moves he intends to make this afternoon to avert this situation which will cause irreparable
damage to our tourist industry?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I am now aware that as a result of proposed
strike action by some drivers tomorrow overseas tourists and others who rely on these
services may be stranded temporarily-some for 24 hours. I am unable to give the
honourable member the present average coach-driver's wage as the remuneration of these
drivers varies considerably depending on the utilisation of vehicles, hours worked, tips, and
so on. When negotiations broke down the employers had offered a 7 percent increase in
wage rates, and were discussing an industry allowance of $6 a week and a rearrangement of
drivers' holiday entitlements. I am advised that the union sought a 30 percent wage increase
plus substantial improvements in other allowances and conditions in the award that would
have increased drivers' take-home pay considerably. I am also advised that the union has
now made a fresh application for conciliation proceedings, and that all parties have agreed
upon a conciliation council being set up on this application on 1 November. In view of this, I
am completely at a loss to understand why some drivers should take futile strike action
tomorrow when constitutional means for settling the dispute and the issue are under way.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

He had told the Minister of a person who was worse off. When on the age benefit, that

received $266, plus the $149 superannuation from his previous job. However, tax amounted
to $67, leaving a total of $348-$5 more a week, but he had lost the television and telephone
concessions, and was worse off. That example had been presented to the Minister, and
during his absence overseas the Acting Minister, the Minister of Trade and Industry, had
admitted that that person was worse off by virtue of his special circumstances. With national
superannuation the difference between promise and performance was glaring.
The Minister had attended a meeting of pensioners in Wellington, and on 25 August an

country, resented being told they were better off, and had accused the Minister of breach of
promise. They were not $18 a week better off as they had been promised by the National
Party before the general election.

those who were entitled to the benefit would receive sympathy and understanding from the

and would report to the Minister as soon as it had completed its work; and the report would

New Zealanders who were in receipt of national superannuation had gone through two
world wars and the great depression of the 1930s. They had been taxed hard to compensate
for costs and for reconstruction after the second world war, and from 1972 to 1975 their
savings had been eroded by inflation during the term of the Labour Government. Those who
were receiving national superannuation deserved it. If the Labour Party's superannuation
scheme had continued, taxpayers would have paid an extra $168 million this year by way of
compulsory payroll tax and compulsory employer subsidies. National superannuation had
been brought in without increasing tax rates. It now stood at 70 percent of the average
ordinary-time weekly wage, and would increase to 80 percent on 31 August 1978.
The National Government considered that people were entitled to financial security in
their retirement, and to retain their dignity. National superannuation was payable as of right
at 60 years of age provided a person had the necessary qualification of 10 years' residence in
New Zealand. There was no means test. National superannuation was adjusted every 6
months in line with increases in the consumer price index as worked out by the Department
of Labour.
National superannuation did not discriminate against women who stayed home to look
after their families. All had an entitlement on reaching the age of 60. The introduction of
national superannuation had given financial independence and dignity to older people. In
addition, it was a portable benefit, and could be paid into any trading bank, trustee savings
bank, or Post Office Savings Bank account. It was the most generous social welfare benefit
ever paid in New Zealand. Money was available to meet the cost, and also to meet the added
cost of the benefit when it was increased to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly
wage on 1 August 1978. About 1000 people in every electorate who were drawing national
superannuation for the first time were very grateful that it had been introduced.

metropolitan areas could not be met; if they were, there would be no funds for the remainder
of the country.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) said, in confirmation
of the statement made by the member for Northern Maori, that in December 1976 the
Director of Roading had advised the Hokianga county clerk that the National Roads Board
had resolved that special assistance was conditional upon the proposed local authority
reorganisation taking place.
New roads were needed in subdivisions in Wairoa Borough. The building of the eight
houses allocated by the Government had been slowed down because there were no roads
into the subdivisions. It was difficult to develop urgently needed residential areas when roads
were not provided. Wairoa was a relatively large borough of 5500 people; it had 24 miles of
roads and needed more to better service the borough's 1500 acres. A 3:1 subsidy of $6,000
had been made available for the present year, barely enough to build one asphalted and
curbed driveway. The money had been allocated for McLean Street, but, with the price of
concrete curbing and asphalt, it was enough for only a fraction of the street.
Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora) said that the Opposition claim that there was insufficient
work for private contractors did not apply to the Rangiora electorate. The Waiau bridge was
to be rebuilt. The Waiau irrigation scheme would revolutionise that part of North Canter-
bury by eventually irrigating 17 000 hectares. Many more employment opportunities would
be offered as a result of the change in the nature of farming in the area. It was estimated that
permanent work on constructing the scheme would be available for 50 or 60 people; and
temporary workers would be required also. Because of changes that would take place in the
district when the scheme was fully developed, population of the local townships should
increase by 200 or 300. That would provide more employment opportunities, and a more
diverse base to what was now basically an agricultural area.
The Loburn irrigation scheme in the Rangiora electorate had been approved during
1977. Expenditure on that scheme would amount to about $300,000, and work would be
commenced this year. It was one of the schemes that had apparently been shelved by the
Labour Government when it came into office. Another proposed scheme in the Rangiora
electorate was the Glenmark irrigation scheme, which he hoped would be built in the
Waipara area. It was a new concept, and would serve about 20 farms varying in size between
50 hectares and 200 hectares, in a dry area. Many of those small farms would be regarded as
sub-economic if farmed by conventional methods. It was proposed to divert winter flood
waters into 28 storage ponds.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) said that the Waiau irrigation scheme had
been approved in principle by the Labour Government, and, but for the change of
Government, would have been 18 months under way. The Loburn irrigation scheme had
been scheduled, and would have been approved by the Labour Government long before it
had been approved by the National Government. Since the change of Government, there
nad been a definite slowing down in development. The roading vote had been effectively cut
by $30 million. Delayed irrigation and development schemes in the South Island had caused
a major setback.

Appropriation Bill-Estimates
The works programme was a major instrument of Government economic policy, a
major spender, provided considerable employment, and undertook development and
services important to industry and to farming. That role of the Ministry of Works and
Development was more important still when private spending fell because of international
economic conditions, yet during the past 2 years the Government had effectively cut total
works spending by about $300 million. That had compounded the decline in the economy,
had helped to create large-scale unemployment, had rendered idle many contractors and
builders, with their plant and equipment, and had forced experienced builders and contrac-
tors to the wall. The Government was now contemplating an emergency Budget to try to
remedy the situation.
In the Christchurch area major roading projects, including the southern outlet, had
been at a standstill. Coinciding with the abandonment of the Rolleston new town project, in
Christchurch there had been increasing bankruptcy and liquidation of building and construc-
tion firms, large-scale and increasing unemployment, and reduced turnover and profitability
in factories and retailers' establishments that otherwise would have provided building
services and supplies, and domestic equipment and needs. That had happened at a time of
unsatisfied demand for housing in Christchurch. The abandonment of the Rolleston scheme
had meant a loss of housing and development expenditure to the Christchurch area of $400
million. In addition, at least $100 million had been lost in industrial plant, and domestic
supplies and equipment.
The abandonment of Rolleston had cost Christchurch at least $500 million. If the
planned expenditure in the Christchurch region had gone ahead, there would have been a
demand for building and construction, and allied manufacturing and related services. There
would, have been no bankruptcies or unemployment. The city would have been more
prosperous. The reduction in the works programme had meant that not only Christchurch,
but all New Zealand had been affected. The Government's mismanagement of the works
programme had helped to create the present economic situation. The Government had been
forced to reconsider its policy, and would shortly be bringing down a programme to set it
right.
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central) asked Opposition members whether a Labour
Government-if there ever was another Labour Government-would recommence the
Rolleston project.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Yes, it would be rebuilt.
Mr COMBER said he wondered what people in regional towns such as Ashburton and
Timaru would think of that. Under the former Labour Administration they had feared for
their future because of the Rolleston project.
He paid tribute to the commissioner and the Ministry of Works and Development. The
architectural, civil engineering, mechanical, electrical, and power divisions of the ministry
were involved in work in every electorate, as were the town and country planning and water
and soil divisions. In the Wellington Central electorate the ministry was involved in the first
stage of the new National Library, the tender let for the Chief Post Office, the new Court of
Appeal building, the Correspondence School in Molesworth Street, and the Beehive-the
Executive Wing of Parliament Buildings opened by Her Majesty earlier this year. One
project of special concern to him was the Wellington motorway and the second Mt. Victoria
tunnel. In times of restraint some things had to go by the board. How could Opposition
members reconcile their advocacy of first, more planning, and, secondly, reduced taxation?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Acting Minister of Works and Development) said that the
recent allocation of additional funds meant that $90,000 had been approved for the sealing of
a section of State Highway 12 in the Hokianga district. An additional $6,000 had been
granted for Wairoa-the exact amount asked for in the half-yearly review. The development
that would have taken place at Rolleston was instead taking place within the confines of
Christchurch City. In 1975-76, $2,464,000 had been allocated to irrigation construction; the
amount for 1977-78 was $2,575,000. The amount allocated to rural water supplies in 1975-76
had been $1,225,000, and for 1977-78 $3,065,000. That was not a reduction in money or in
real terms. In 1975-76, $924,000 had been allocated to irrigation maintenance, and this year
the amount to be allocated was $1,300,000-again not a reduction in either money or real
terms. A complete review of the Glenmark scheme had proved necessary, and the estimated
cost was now about $1.2 million. Further assessment of the dam site qualities, the
economics, and management were well in hand. An early submission for consideration and
approval was expected shortly. The first funding had been tentatively programmed for the
1978-79 financial year, and was expected to be about $500,000.

Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
FRIDAY, 28 OCTOBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 9 a.m.
Prayers.
BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Next week we will have estimates on
Tuesday and Thursday.
MINISTERIAL STATEMENT-ECONOMIC MEASURES
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): With the leave of the House, I wish
to make a ministerial statement.
Mr SPEAKER,
The Government's economic strategy has been, and continues to be
to adjust the level of economic activity to the maximum that is sustain-
able considering the realities of our external trading situation. Over the
longer term this is being accomplished through measures which are
aimed to shift resources into export activities, dampen the demand
for imports and increase the efficiency in the use of all resources.
Much has been accomplished. The deficit in our overseas exchange
transactions has declined from $1,067 million or 11 percent of GNP
in the year ended June 1975, to $531 million or close to 4 percent of
GNP in the year ended June 1977. This has been achieved by main-
taining a rapid growth in exports while at the same time moderating
the growth of imports. Moreover, increased livestock numbers resulting
from the Livestock Incentive Scheme will contribute greatly to
expanding the export capacity of the economy.
Switching resources between sectors to achieve further progress is a
slow process and requires careful management. The Government is
determined to ensure that the levels of unemployment of people and
resources do not rise above the minimum that is consistent with the
need to shift resources into those areas that have high priority in the
attainment of our national economic goals. To rechannel resources and
control the flow of imports it is necessary to keep a fairly tight rein.
on the economy. It is equally important for the Government to react
promptly to changes in the short-term prospects for the economy to
ensure that a generally tight policy stance does not bring forth- a con-
traction greater than is necessary to adjust the economy to the external
conditions.
A delicate balance must be struck between the needs for short-term
stability in the economy and the longer run balance of payments


## p. 4014 (#120) ###########################################

4014
28 October
Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
strategy. Wherever possible the policies to maintain production and
employment should also be geared to helping us pay our way in the
world over the longer haul.
The present state of the world economy does not offer us much hope
for a rapid growth in the sales of our exports. It was clear from the tone
of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the
Commonwealth Finance Ministers that growth in our major markets
will not be as great as was expected earlier in the year. Also, we will
continue to face difficult problems of access to markets in many
countries. In the domestic economy, sales throughout 1977 have been
running below production with the result that stocks are accumulating.
Production is now being cut as firms reduce stocks. This de-stocking
occurs periodically and in normal circumstances would last about 3
to 6 months, after which production would recover. However, because
of the less optimistic external situation and a decline in business con-
fidence, there is a risk in the present circumstances that the usual
recovery after a de-stocking phase might be delayed. This would occur
if there were significant lay-offs by firms leading to reduced incomes
and spending. Production would not recover and unemployment would
increase.
The Government is introducing measures to ensure that spending
does not decline and that business confidence is maintained. This is
aimed at forestalling increases in unemployment that might otherwise
occur and keeping up the momentum of resource switching. It is
emphasised that these measures are not designed to bring about a
substantial reflation of the economy but a stabilisation of demand within
the framework of longer term adjustment policy. Together with fiscal
and monetary measures to accomplish a moderate stimulus, measures
are being announced to encourage further the growth of exports and
the better use of resources. Along with new policies in the agricultural
and manufacturing sectors, there are measures to promote the training
of people in skills that are important for their own personal develop-
ment and for the future of the economy. Measures are being announced
to create jobs directly for those who become unemployed. Our present
economic difficulties have highlighted the particular problems of youth-
ful unemployment which have intensified in many countries. New
proposals to cope with these problems are also being announced.
In formulating the new policies, the Government treads a narrow
path between too much and too little stimulus. Excessive stimulus would
fuel an inflation that is too high and expand a foreign deficit that, in
spite of the decline, is too large to be sustainable in the longer term.
Such a stimulus would slow the shifting of resources into the export
sectors and force us to mortgage further our future with overseas


## p. 4015 (#121) ###########################################

28 October
4015
Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
borrowing. Until the goals of the balance of payments strategy are
attained or there is a fortuitous improvement in our terms of trade, a
moderate level of overseas borrowing will have to continue to sustain
employment. New Zealand's credit rating in the world is now restored
to the highest level and finance is available on favourable terms. It will
be difficult for New Zealand to eliminate the imbalance in its overseas
accounts completely so long as the surplus run by the oil exporting
nations and a few major industrial countries amounts to more than $40
billion. However, it cannot be stressed too strongly that the Govern-
ment is determined to hold to its promises to bring the economy steadily
back into balance.
The major risk inherent in the new moves is that they may encourage
excessive wage increases and cause them to be transmitted more readily
into price increases. These new policies therefore place a responsibility
on employers and employees to show restraint in wage negotiations.
Otherwise they will result in inflation rather than greater employment
and production and the Government will have no option but to return
to a tight monetary and fiscal stance.
Some of the major points of the policies being announced are
summarised below:
Fiscal Policy
• A special supplementary family benefit of $25 per child is to be
paid on 29 November 1977.
An across-the-board cut in personal income tax of 5 percent is to
be applied from 1 February 1978.
An additional $16 million is being approved for works that do not
have high import content, can be put in place quickly, and are
in areas where the need for stimulus to the building industry
is high.
These measures, together with the fiscal effects of the other
measures being announced and other supplementary appropria-
tions to be tabled shortly, are expected to increase the deficit
before borrowing for the year ending 31 March 1978 by approxi-
mately $180 million.
Monetary Policy
Trading banks are to be directed to give higher priority to lending
to finance stockholding.
• Reserve asset ratio policy is to be eased by increasing the margin
of trading bank "free reserves".

in addition to the normal family benefit payable on that date.

children, the cost of the special supplementary benefit will be $25

Hire Purchase Restrictions Eased
The Hire Purchase and Credit Sales Stabilisation Regulations 1957
will be amended to exempt from restriction the category of “other
consumer goods". The present restriction on this class of consumer
goods is that the deposit must be a minimum of 10 percent of the
purchase price and the remainder must be repaid within 30 months.
The amendment will not affect the present restrictions on colour
television sets, new and used motor cars and motor cycles, but will
exempt "other consumer goods" such as white ware, black and white
television sets, and other household appliances.
Boosting Exports
Manufactured exports have been and are continuing to grow rapidly,
and the Government is already providing substantial assistance to
exporters of these products. However, some impediments to continued
growth have been identified and there are areas where additional
Government assistance is justified. These include export incentives,
access to equity and working capital, market development costs, and
attitudes and information.
The cost of these additional measures is estimated at $1.5 million in
the current financial year and $3.5 million in a full year.

Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
PRE-EXPORT FINANCE
The Development Finance Corporation will be authorised to make
short term loans for working capital requirements for export projects
where soundly based manufacturing units cannot reasonably cover their
needs from normal commercial sources. The loan finance will be at
rates of interest comparable with those charged by trading banks for
export finance. The difficulty which has been encountered, particularly
by smaller businesses, is one of absorbing, some months in advance of
receipts from the planned export sales, the increased costs of additional
raw materials and components needed for the manufacture of the extra
exports, and the costs of overseas market development.
EQUITY FINANCE
The Development Finance Corporation will be further expanding
its range of services to provide equity finance for small and medium-
sized firms which are being inhibited in their attempts to export by their
inadequate equity capital resources.
The implementation of these policies will play an important role in
the necessary movement of resources to companies with export potential
as well as relieving some pressure on the banking system for export
finance.
EXPORT SUSPENSORY LOANS
The official limit on the size of projects eligible for assistance under
the export suspensory loans scheme administered by the Development
Finance Corporation and the Rural Banking and Finance Corporation
is to be extended to $400,000, with a maximum loan of $100,000. In
special cases, larger loans for larger projects may be considered.
MARKET DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE
The administration of the existing 40 percent New Market Develop-
ment Grants Scheme is to be liberalised so that there is more emphasis
on progress payments, an extension of the basic term to 2 years, and a
more flexible definition of a new market. More extensive use of progress
payments will provide some assistance to exporters with cash flow
problems. The term of the grants (basically 1 year with a possible
extension on merit) is being extended because of the time and cost
involved in developing a new market.
EXPORT OF SERVICES
The Government has approved the inclusion in the Export of Quali-
fying Services Taxation Incentive of royalty and "knowhow" receipts
from the granting or the sale of New Zealand technology (both indus-

Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
Employment Policies
TRAINING PROGRAMMES
It is probable that if jobs are not available there will be a marked
retention of pupils at school and there will be pressure on secondary
school staffing, on the careers guidance services, and the pre-leaving
preparation programmes in schools. To help take up the younger
unemployed the Government has decided to institute special training
programmes, using existing facilities at technical institutes and schools.
The courses will be either general pre-employment courses in a range
of skills, or training for specific skilled or semi-skilled occupations
mounted to match local needs so far as possible to meet the demand
for specific skills as well as the younger unemployed persons available.
The courses will vary from 4 weeks to 20 weeks in length and teach
such specific skills as farm fencing, steel bending, and office methods,
or general skills training. Unemployed persons undergoing such courses
will continue to be paid the unemployment benefit (for courses of 20
weeks or less) but will go on to the standard tertiary bursary for any
full-time courses offered.
FARM EMPLOYMENT SCHEME
This scheme will be available to all farmers throughout New Zea-
and will provide subsidised employment of either a skilled or unskilled
nature for unemployed persons. The subsidy will be one-third of the
ruling rate for farm workers in the region concerned, with a minimum
subsidy of $40 a week and a maximum of $50 a week. (After allowing
for the tax that would be paid by the employee in subsidised employ-
ment, these rates approximate the single rates of unemployment
benefit). The scheme will be open to single and married persons.
The subsidy will be available only in respect of additional jobs
created, i.e., an increase in the number of jobs over the corresponding
period of the previous year. The scheme will come into effect immedi-
ately and will continue until 31 October 1978 at which stage it will be
reviewed.
In making placements under the scheme, priority will be given to
farmers needing labour for development programmes, especially those
in the Livestock Incentive Scheme.
The fares of unemployed workers travelling to an agreed location.
for interview by farmers with a view to placement under the scheme
will be met by the Department of Labour.

STUDENT COMMUNITY SERVICE PROGRAMME
To provide jobs for tertiary students over the summer vacation and
to lessen the extent to which tertiary students compete with school
leavers for job opportunities, a Student Community Service Programme
is to be instituted. This programme will give students temporary work
involving a form of community service. They will be employed by
voluntary agencies, local authorities, a Government agency, or alterna-
tively will work together as a co-operative on a particular project. This
programme will last for a maximum of 3 months this summer.
ADDITIONAL DETACHED YOUTH WORKERS
The present programme, funded by the Department of Internal
Affairs is to be expanded to provide for a total of 20 detached youth
workers. Under this scheme, young persons whose backgrounds
prejudice their chances of coping, and yet who possess some talents of
value to the community, are organised positively in their employment
and recreation through such means as work co-operatives.
YOUTH INITIATIVES FUND
A fund will be established to finance, by grant, projects involving the
Student Community Service Programme and the expanded Detached
Youth Worker Scheme. The fund will also finance projects proposed by
young people of a social, cultural, recreational employment, or com-
munity nature and could vary from marae improvements to travelling
artistic shows.
MAORI TRADE TRAINING SCHEME
The Maori Trade Training Scheme is to be expanded to include
as many as possible of the applicants from rural designated areas in
order to prevent their remaining unemployed in their home locality.
This year only 314 of the 664 applications for traineeships under the
existing scheme could be accepted. It has been decided therefore to


## p. 4025 (#131) ###########################################

28 October
4025
Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
introduce the following new training courses in 1978, providing places
for an additional 132 trainees: ladies hairdressing, at Manukau; fitting
and welding, at New Plymouth; painting and decorating, at New Ply-
mouth; fitting and turning, at New Plymouth; joinery, at New Ply-
mouth; panelbeating, coach and bodybuilding at Manukau; meat
retailing, at Manukau; secretarial, at Manukau; general merchandis-
ing, at Manukau. Expansion of this scheme will cost up to $550,000 in
a full year.
AUCKLAND URBAN TRADE TRAINING SCHEME
The Government has decided to introduce a pilot scheme for full-
time pre-apprenticeship training for young people in Auckland who
would otherwise be unemployed. It will operate on the same lines as
the Maori trade training scheme but will be open to young people of
all races. The scheme will consist of two carpentry and joinery courses,
one motor mechanics course, and one fitting and turning course, all at
Manukau Technical Institute. Places will be provided for a total of 56
trainees. The scheme will cost $200,000 in a full year.
ACCELERATED MAINTENANCE SCHEME
A sum of $5 million will be made available for a programme of
accelerated maintenance in public sector buildings, but using private
sector contractors. The expenditure is limited to labour and basic
equipment costs and will provide employment for 250 persons for a
year.
EMPLOYMENT AND VOCATIONAL GUIDANCE SERVICE
The continuing increase in the number of people enrolling with the
Department of Labour's Employment Service has greatly increased
the workload of the existing 100 employment officers, with a consequent
increase in the average period of unemployment per person and a reduc-
tion in field work. An additional 73 employment officers will therefore
be appointed and spread among the 22 departmental districts. The
appointment of these additional officers should lead to an improvemen
in placement activity, particularly among the younger unemployed.
Purchase of additional motor vehicles will also enable field work to
be stepped up.
The Department of Education will also appoint an additional 19
vocational counsellors, who will be appointed immediately and who
will be spread among the existing seven centres.
The extra cost of these measures will be $160,000 in 1977-78 and
$455,000 in a full year.

Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
Monetary Policy
A number of measures are to be adopted with the objective of
achieving some easing in monetary conditions. These monetary measures
are consistent with the general aim of mild stimulation of the domestic
economy and some will also serve to complement the major reforms.
of the financial system initiated in March 1976.
In addition to the general measures, specific measures are being
taken to increase the amount of credit available for housing, local
authorities, and stockholding.
STOCKHOLDING
In order to avoid too severe a contraction of economic activity as
a result of efforts to reduce stock levels quickly it has been decided that
the Reserve Bank will direct the trading banks to give a high priority
to granting credit to those clients having difficulty in financing existing
stock levels.
RESERVE ASSETS RATIOS
To facilitate the directive on the financing of stocks, the reserve asset
ratio policy applied to trading banks will be eased by allowing the
banks some additional margin of "free reserves".
GOVERNMENT SECURITY INTEREST RATES
As a contribution to easing the pressure on interest rates, Govern-
ment stock interest rates for 1- and 2-year stock will be reduced imme-
diately. At the same time small upward adjustments to Treasury bill
rates will produce a more satisfactory rate structure for Government
securities and encourage more widespread use of Treasury bills as
a market instrument.

RESERVE BANK LENDING RATES
The Reserve Bank has agreed to give immediate consideration to
reducing its lending rate for borrowing by the trading banks for reserve
assets ratio purposes from its present level of 12 percent.

Ministerial Statement--Economic Measures
LIFE INSURANCE COMPANIES
Life insurance companies are currently subject to investment controls
and directives which require them to hold 30 percent of assets in public
sector securities, of which 20 percent must be in Government securities,
and to maintain a further 20 percent of assets in housing and farming
investments.
To enable the life offices to participate more actively in industrial
development projects, their public sector security ratio will be reduced
by one percentage point by lowering their Government stock obligation
to 19 percent. The Reserve Bank will request the life offices to invest
the $24 million released by this move in private sector industrial pro-
jects, particularly those with an export orientation, including agricul-
ture.
LOCAL AUTHORITY SECURITIES
Trading banks are now to be permitted to invest in local authority
stock. Their holdings will not comprise part of their reserve assets. Life
insurance companies will in future be permitted to meet their ratio
requirements by acquiring local authority securities on the secondary
market as well as from new issues.
These measures will assist local authority financing, enhance the
marketability of local authority securities, and help generate an active
secondary market for such stock.
LOCAL AUTHORITY INTEREST RATES
There will be no change at present in interest rates on local authority
securities, thus widening the margin between short-term Local and
Central Government securities and consequently assisting the local
authorities in their loan raising efforts.
COMPENSATORY DEPOSIT SCHEME
A compensatory deposit scheme will be introduced next March under
which the Reserve Bank will re-deposit with the trading banks the
large net flow of funds to the Government during the month of March.
Such deposits will be repaid by the banks gradually over the March-
April-May period, thus smoothing the substantial fluctuations which
occur each year at that time. The uncertainty surrounding monetary
conditions in the month of March will be reduced and the pressure on
short-term interest rates will be eased.
Agriculture
Farm incomes are expected to remain at sufficient levels to sustain
investment and growth in productive capacity over the next 12 months,
though at a lower rate than the previous year. While the Government


## p. 4028 (#134) ###########################################

4028
28 October
Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
sees no immediate need for additional measures of farm income support,
it will ensure that the momentum of development through the Live-
stock Incentive Scheme is maintained.
It is equally important that the farmer's efforts to increase produc-
tion should not be frustrated by problems of processing or marketing.
The measures announced today will assist efficient development in these
two areas, both for traditional pastoral products and for the non-
traditional products, which have shown considerable export potential.
KURAL BANK FUNDING
The Rural Banking and Finance Corporation is to be allocated from
the National Development Loans Account for 1977/78:
(a) an additional $10 million for development lending and livestock
incentive suspensory loans; and
(b) a further $10 million for refinance of borrowings from other
sources undertaken by farmers engaged in genuine develop-
ment. The interest rate will be 9 percent, the bank's
refinance rate.
HORTICULTURAL MARKETING
The Government will discuss with the Export-Import Corporation,
and other interested parties, the need for market research and
the possible establishment of a horticultural marketing unit for the
purpose of co-ordinating the export production, marketing, and pro-
motion of horticultural and other non-traditional agricultural products.
The major factors holding back the horticultural industry from a
rapid increase in export returns have been identified as uncoordinated
marketing, and lack of market information upon which to match
products with customer requirements. It is considered that these factors
could be tied together by a small, commercially-oriented unit.
Through such a unit the corporation would carry out marketing
operations on request, complementing the marketing services provided
by the private sector. Care would be necessary to ensure that the
corporation's activities did not conflict with those of established
exporters.
ASSISTANCE TO FURTHER PROCESSING OF MEAT PRODUCTS
As certain processed meat products have now been included in the
Increased Exports Taxation Incentive Scheme the manufacturers of
these products will become eligible for export suspensory loans, through
the Development Finance Corporation. The target level of exported
production at which the suspensory loan may be converted into a
grant will be 60 percent of output exported within a specified time.


## p. 4029 (#135) ###########################################

28 October
4029
Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
DAIRY INDUSTRY PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT FINANCE
The Rural Export Suspensory Loan Scheme is to be extended to
include capital expenditure by the industry to manufacture new export
products. Diminishing access to traditional markets now requires an
expansion of diversification into export products suited to particular
alternative markets. The coverage would include processes to utilise
more fully the solids-not-fat in milk (in particular, whey), the
development of varietal cheese types, instant products, plants incor-
porating stricter hygiene standards, the development of consumer
packaging, and, for the new products, the associated laboratory facilities.
Because the dairy industry comprises co-operatives which are in
general non-taxable, the suspensory loans will be of amounts up to
20 percent of qualifying expenditure, rather than the normal 40 percent.
The upper limit of qualifying expenditure will normally be $500,000
(giving a maximum suspensory loan of $100,000) but this sum may be
exceeded in exceptional circumstances. Applications for these loans will
be considered by the Dairy Industry Loans Council with final approvals
being given by the Rural Export Suspensory Loans Committee.
The export target will be 60 percent of the output of the project in
3 of the first 5 years. The loans may be turned into a grant if this target
is achieved.
Apart from the advances to the Rural Bank the annual cost of these
measures will be of the order of $10 million.
Regional Development Programme Extension
At present the manufacturing and processing sectors are eligible,
under the Government's regional development policy, for staff training
grants, investigations and establishment grants, and pioneer status
suspensory loans, subject to certain detailed criteria. The Government
has decided that these facilities should also be extended to the agricul-
ture, horticulture, fishing, forestry, mining, and tourism sectors. The
Government will also introduce an alternative basis for claiming under
the suspensory loan scheme within the regional development pro-
gramme, namely the number of permanent new full-time employment
opportunities created by the project.
High Priority Activities
The 1977 Budget announced the development of a scheme for a
limited number of manufacturing activities which are to be judged,
on the basis of a few, clear cut, largely objective, quantitative criteria,
to be making an outstanding contribution to growth and to the
country's balance of payments. Such activities were to be granted "high
priority" status and so be eligible for assistance designed to encourage
their growth.


## p. 4030 (#136) ###########################################

4030
28 October
Ministerial Statement-Economic Measures
Qualifying criteria have now been established. In any year, a manu-
facturing activity will be entitled to high priority status if it meets the
following criteria:
(i) the activity must be, in the Government's view, capable of
being isolated from other productive activities undertaken
by the firm;
(ii) the activity must have, in the preceding year:
(a) had a minimum domestic value added in New
Zealand of 75 percent (after allowing for both direct and
indirect imports, but excluding capital);
(b) exported a minimum of 20 percent of its production,
based on factory door value, the minimum rising in annual
steps of 2 percent to 30 percent over 5 years;
(c) sold the remainder of its production on the New
Zealand market for an ex-factory selling price not more
than 10 percent higher than the f.o.b. export price;
(d) had total energy inputs from outside the company
not exceeding 7 percent of the factory door value of
production;
(iii) the production from the activity must be of a sort that would
be eligible for the increased exports taxation incentive if it
were exported.
The assistance measures are designed to aid the growth of these high
priority activities not only by helping to improve the tax-paid profit-
ability but also by easing the problems and delays associated with
obtaining licensing approvals and assistance from Government and
quasi-government agencies, and banks.
Once an activity has been granted "high priority" status, it will be
entitled to:
(a) priority rating for finance from trading banks and the Develop-
ment Finance Corporation;
(b) priority treatment for import licensing;
(c) exemption of the production of the high priority activity from
price control and consequential increases in the profit ceiling
of the qualifying firm;
(d) special consideration for export suspensory loan assistance;
(e) an investment allowance (in substitution for all other investment
allowances) of 40 percent on new plant and machinery
purchased after the activity has been granted "high priority"
status;

4031

(f) exemption from the 10 percent sales tax on plant and machinery
purchased after the activity has been granted "high priority"
status.
The range of measures will be extended to include special considera-
tion for other appropriate discretionary policies administered by
Government departments.
Applications for approval for "high priority" status under the
scheme should be made to the Department of Trade and Industry.
Legislation will be introduced to implement the scheme which, initially,
will have a specific lifespan of 5 years.

Kauri Sawn Timber-Price
2. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of Forests: Has he seen the statement in an
article in the New Zealand Herald of 3 October 1977 which claimed that an increase in the
price of State-owned kauri would lead to greater pressure for the purchase of kauri still in
private ownership, and, if so, does this statement clearly reflect the situation?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): Yes, I have seen the statement, but I consider
that it does not clearly reflect the situation regarding the sale of kauri in private ownership.
Kauri sawn timber has been exempt from price control since 1952, and selling prices are
determined by negotiation between the sawmiller and an intending buyer. Because of the
scarcity of this timber, and its intrinsic value for special purposes, such as boatbuilding,
prices obtained are high. The price obtained for State-owned kauri is calculated by deducting
from the already determined selling price for sawn timber, reasonable costs of logging and
sawing the wood. It therefore follows that the real pressure on the resource originates from
the high prices users of kauri sawn timber are prepared to pay for a scarce resource, and not
from Forest Service log prices.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Trade Negotiations
3. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Will he list the
successes that he has had in his negotiations abroad since taking office?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): In May 1976 I
attended the fourth United Nations Conference on Trade and Development in Nairobi, and
was then able to introduce New Zealand's revised scheme of tariff preferences for develop-
ing countries, which was warmly received by the developing nations attending the confer-
ence. In September 1976, at the NAFTA ministerial meeting held in Canberra, the Minister
of Overseas Trade and I reached agreement with Australian Ministers to extend the NAFTA
for a further period of 10 years. In April of this year, when I attended the ministerial
meetings of the Asian Development Bank and the Economic and Social Commission for
Asia and the Pacific, I took advantage of these visits to call on trade Ministers of the ASEAN
countries and undertook the initial negotiations that led to the Government introducing the
ASEAN in-store promotion programme in New Zealand. I have engaged in continuing


## p. 4039 (#145) ###########################################

28 October
4039
Oral Answers to Questions
negotiations with Australia over the past 18 months, although it has not been necessary for
me to journey to Canberra to bring each of these to a conclusion. In this context I list as
successes the arrangements concluded for reciprocal trade on apparel, footwear, and
textiles.
Hon. W. W. Freer: How does the Minister classify as a success the immediate advantage
given to the Australian clothing industry when the New Zealand industry cannot possibly
enjoy a similar advantage before the middle of next year?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The apparel agreement must be seen in the light of
the two periods negotiated--one for 12 months, which ends in February 1978, and the other
for 6 months, which ends in August 1978. Those agreements allow New Zealand to send
6 500 000 garments into Australia. So far Australia has sent only 92 000 garments into New
Zealand. The Government felt that to get agreement on these last 1 500 000 garments it
would be necessary to give Australia a further opportunity, through the tariff and for this
6-month period only, to secure some sales in New Zealand.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the fact that the Minister has just agreed to halve the tariff
on Australian exports to New Zealand, how can he justify the statements made earlier this
year that the original agreement he had reached on clothing was a success, and a fair one for
both countries?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: It was, and it is, a success story. The earlier
agreement was for 1 year, and the second agreement was for 6 months. The agreements were
for apparel only, and for a 6-month period only, so as to negotiate that 1 500 000. We did not
have a chance of getting those 1 500 000 garments into Australia for that 6-month period
unless we allowed Australia to export in return.
