Social Welfare-Disability Allowance
4. Mr COOPER (Otago Central), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East), asked
the Minister of Social Welfare: How many applications for a disability allowance were
received, how many were processed, and how much in total was paid out in the years 1975
and 1976?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Statistics are compiled for financial
years only. In the year ended 31 March 1976, 532 applications for disability allowance were
received, of which 374 were processed. During the year ended 31 March 1977, 2134
applications were received, and 2061 were processed. Separate statistics on disability
allowance expenditure are not kept. However, at 31 March 1976, 250 disability allowances
were in force at an annual value of $60,036. At 31 March 1977 1619 allowances were in force
at an annual value of $544,708.
Mr Lambert: Were disability allowances paid before 1975, and, if so, are records of such
payments available?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The benefit was one of the recommendations of the 1972 royal
commission, most of which were introduced before the National Government went out of
office in 1972. Finance was made available for the recommendation. The legislation
introducing the disability allowance was passed at 3 a.m. on 10 October 1975, which was the
last day of the session before the general election.

for the elderly?

improved benefit. They are considerably greater than the amount a young member like the
one asking the question would receive, and at this stage, bearing in mind our priorities,
which at the moment are definitely children's health, these benefits are thought to be
adequate.

College had three positions; one appointment has been made and two are under offer. The
positions are in English, accounting, and commercial subjects.

NEW ZEALAND SECURITY INTELLIGENCE SERVICE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): I move, That the New Zealand Security
Intelligence Service Amendment Bill be referred to the Statutes Revision Committee. I do so for
the following reasons. First, by refusing to send the Bill to a committee, the Government has
precipitated a controversy that has resulted in the Government's backing off, taking the Bill
back to caucus for deliberation, and bringing it back to theHouse with further amendments.
There seems to be no reason for Parliament's not considering the Bill further, and the select
committee system gives the public an opportunity to participate.
Secondly, a measure of this kind cannot be debated effectively when the House has not
been given a firm assurance that the Bill represents the Government's final view of the
matter. After all, we have read about proposals to make amendments, and it is quite likely
that, after debate in the House and the consideration of any submissions that are forthcom-
ing, more amendments could be made. There seems to be no reason for not referring the Bill
to a committee so that it can be examined and considered in a formal and proper way from
the parliamentary point of view. It could be that the Government is still undecided about
some precise aspects of the legislation, and, if the Bill were referred to a committee that
would hear submissions, the Government could be assisted to make up its mind.
Another reason for suggesting that the Bill be referred to the committee is the
widespread editorial comment throughout the country. I could mention a number of papers,
but I have in mind the Christchurch Press, which commented that efforts should be directed
to providing security against the misuse of security methods. The Press pointed out that one
answer is to define the purpose of interception warrants in a way that would minimise the
political element and exclude self-serving political ends. I have in mind also the views
expressed by the editor of the Christchurch Star who, when referring to the widespread
public concern, said that by refusing to send the Bill to a committee the Government was
excluding not only fringe groups, but also responsible bodies-the New Zealand Law
Society, for instance, and of course the Ombudsman.
The editor also said, on the main issues of telephone tapping and interception of mail,
that the New Zealand Law Society had said it wanted a tighter definition of circumstances so
that the interception would be restricted to matters that clearly related to security. Some of
the Government's proposed amendments cover these matters, but a broader consideration
of these key issues could be of benefit. The Christchurch Star also pointed out that the New
Zealand Law Society had suggested giving an independent authority the power to investigate
on its own initiative the issue and execution of warrants, and complaints from the public.
Surely, until a firm provision of this nature is written into the Bill, there is good reason to
hear the views of people who might want to comment.
Another important reason for referring the Bill to a committee is that Sir Guy Powles,
whose report initiated the legislation, said that the Bill differs from his report, and that—and
this is significant-his proposals would work only if taken as a package deal. The Govern-
ment should remember that democracy is a delicate system that is vulnerable to abuse. There
is already unease in the community about the Government's actions in the constitutional
field, which some would say could have an impact on parliamentary democracy, and that
should not be overlooked.
By not referring the Bill to a committee the Government is failing to use the forms of
Parliament which, in the evolution of parliamentary democracy, have been found necessary
to deal with the sort of public controversy that such Bills create. A further reason—and an
important one that should commend itself to the Government-for referring the Bill to a
committee, is that by failing to do so, the Government provides a platform for the sort of


## p. 4047 (#153) ###########################################

28 October
4047
New Zealand SIS Amendment Bill
people whose activities, it alleges, make a Bill of this kind necessary. I recall the Prime
Minister's statement, reported in the Dominion of 26 August, that: "I have no urge to
provide a sounding board for these fringe elements that in my view get far too much publicity
anyway." If the Bill had been referred to a committee, and these people had had the
opportunity to express their point of view, there might have been far less controversy than
there has been.
Another good reason for the Bill to go to the committee is the inconsistency of this
Government compared with a previous National Government. On an earlier occasion, when
legislation of this kind was before the House, the then National Government welcomed the
opportunity to send the Bill to a committee, and it also welcomed the views and suggestions
of Her Majesty's Opposition. The final reason why the Bill should go to a committee is the
continuing public controversy. Members of Parliament are still receiving telegrams and other
correspondence, and there is still comment in the news media. Recently I referred to the
Prime Minister a telegram I had received from an important institution in my own electorate.
I believe that, because of the continuing controversy, it is in the public interest to refer the
Bill to a committee. It would also be the best way of devising better legislation and
minimising the prospect of further controversy.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I do not support the proposal.
Mr Rogers: Yes, we know that.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: My reason is that, first of all-
Mr Rogers: Yes, that's right.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I do not know whether the member will continue what he

number of submissions have been received, each of which has been carefully perused and
matched up with the Bill in terms of desirability and practicability. As a result, a consider-
able number of amendments have been made, and they are in the Supplementary Order
Paper in front of us.
Many of the submissions from quite responsible organisations showed a lack of
understanding, not just of what was in the Bill, but also of what was in the principal Act, and
of the manner in which the Security Intelligence Service works. The member for Wigram

together with the Supplementary Order Paper, represents the Government's final view.

No, it is not. It is agreed that there has been wide public debate. It is interesting that after

Bill. I do not intend—and indeed, Mr Speaker, you would not allow me to give a detailed

points as being material that could well have been, and still could be, studied by a committee
in order to determine whether the general approach to the Bill was appropriate, and whether
the details in it are adequate or too far reaching.
The Bill was aimed at ending an existing evil that remained undealt with, and
presumably still operates. The Bill now before us is likely to aggravate that evil-the
increasing use by private detectives and other people of electronic bugs. The thrust of the
Listening Devices Bill was to discourage resort to them. It forbade them entirely in private
hands, and placed strict limitations on their official use. It allowed no extension to the
provisions of the Post Office Act, which, as I said, have been in operation for 50 years. It had
nothing to say about tapping telephones, or tampering with mail. Indeed, it referred only to

loss of principle is worth the putative increase of security? These discussions may be of mild
embarrassment to friendly countries, but I am sure they would take the point. Whatever may
be said by those obsessed with security, New Zealand is not subject to the risks of subversion
and terrorism properly feared elsewhere. Ironically, the principal reason for that state of

qualities as the most precious objective of politics. They are certainly worth any passing
diplomatic difficulty with friendly countries. Nothing, of course, removes the duty to keep
and use the information coming into New Zealand's hands with utmost care."
I believe that the last sentence really puts the seal on the matter, in that there is a
recognition of the responsibility we must face and accept in relation to the handling of
sensitive and confidential material. We must give an undertaking, and be seen to give it, that

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The question before the House this
morning is not whether the Bill should pass, but whether it should be referred to a select
committee for still further investigation. It is now more than 2 years and 2 months since the
then Prime Minister, the present Leader of the Opposition, asked Sir Guy Powles to
undertake a study of the need for a Security Intelligence Service in New Zealand. Is more
inquiry needed? There is an air of rather desperate anxiety about the arguments of the
member for Wigram and the member for Henderson, now that they are being dragged,
however unwillingly, to the moment of decision making.
That was why, in 1975, the present Leader of the Opposition asked Sir Guy what he
should do. There was dissension in his party. The member for Henderson and the Deputy
Leader of the Opposition adopted different positions on the need for a Security Intelligence
Service, or for an Official Secrets Act. The present Leader of the Opposition could not make
up his mind then, and it is quite evident that 26 months later he and his party are still not able
to make up their minds.
The 10 reasons listed by the member for Wigram are almost farcical. He said that the
Government has given further consideration to the Bill without public participation. Of
course there has been public participation, not only during the weeks the Bill has been in the
House, but for more than 15 months since Sir Guy Powles's report was made public. Why
should the Government not give further consideration? It said it would. We wanted public
opinions to be expressed, and thank goodness they have been, and we have given more
consideration to the Bill. The member for Wigram said that the Government has not given a
final view. Does the Opposition want law like the laws of the Medes and the Persians? There
must be continued concern about such serious matters, but we must make a decision on what
needs to be done now.
The member said that public evidence could help the Government. It has helped the
Government. We have had responsible reaction from such organisations as the New Zealand
Law Society. The member for Wigram, as a further reason, referred to editorial comment
about widespread public concern. Well, why should there not be such editorial comment?
That is what the newspapers are for. They are the fourth estate, and we are glad to have their
comments. Those who write the editorials are changing their views as they see the
amendments being offered by the Government.
A further reason given by the member for Wigram was that Sir Guy Powles says that the
Bill differs from his report. Of course it does. Where Sir Guy Powles's recommendations
were found not to be practicable, the Bill has had to differ. Sir Guy does not suggest that he
is omniscient-he is much too modest and distinguished a New Zealander to make such a
claim. Democracy is a delicate creature, and we have this organisation to maintain
democracy; I am glad to say that few Opposition members would deny that. Certainly
Labour leaders in the past-the late Norman Kirk for instance, and even the present Leader
of the Opposition—have not denied the need for a Security Intelligence Service.
Another reason given by the member for Wigram was that, by refusing to refer the Bill
to a committee, the Government is failing to use the forms of Parliament. What are we doing
now but using the forms of Parliament in public debate to proceed to the clause-by-clause
consideration of the Bill and the proposed Government amendments to it? Let us be done
with this argument, and get to the Committee stage before the House goes off the air.
Another reason put forward by the Opposition was that by failing to send the Bill to a
committee the Government is providing a platform for the sort of people whose activities it
alleges make a Bill of this kind necessary. What a silly, inconsistent reason. The Opposition
has dragged in anything to postpone the moment of decision.
The member for Henderson took the matter even further. His reasons were not almost
farcical; they were farcical. He claimed that the Government was not as well informed as the
Opposition. What a silly statement. No doubt he was referring to the mock select committee
set up by the Opposition. He referred to the timing of the debate. Obviously, a lack of
opportunity for propaganda was his concern. He alleged a cavalier and offhand attitude on
the part of the Government, but the Government has shown a very serious attitude to
everything connected with this Bill.

Clause 2. Interpretation.
(1) Section 2 of the principal Act is hereby amended by inserting, in their appropriate
alphabetical order, the following definitions:
"Intercept', in relation to any communication not otherwise lawfully obtainable by the person
making the interception, includes hear, listen to, record, monitor, or acquire the
communication, or acquire the substance, meaning, or purport thereof; and "intercep-
tion" has a corresponding meaning:
"Interception warrant' means an interception warrant issued under subsection (1) of section
4A of this Act, as inserted by section 4 of the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service
Amendment Act 1977:
"New Zealand Intelligence Council' means the Council of that name established in accord-
ance with an approval given by the Prime Minister on the 3rd day of February 1975:
"Terrorism' means advocating, threatening, or using violence to coerce, deter, or
intimidate-
"(a) The lawful authority of the State in New Zealand; or
"(b) The community throughout New Zealand or in any area in New Zealand for the
purpose of furthering any political aim:"
(2) Section 2 of the principal Act is hereby further amended-
(a) By omitting from the definition of the term "Commissioner", the word "appointed", and
substituting the words "holding office":
(b) By inserting in the definition of the term "security", after the word "sabotage", the word
"terrorism":
(c) By omitting, from the definition of the term "State Services", the words "Armed Services",
and substituting the words "Armed Forces".

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Broadcasting Complaints Committee-"Dateline Monday" Programme
1. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), on behalf of Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau), asked the
Minister of Broadcasting: In view of the apology that the Broadcasting Complaints
Committee has offered to Mr Ian Fraser regarding his opening remarks in the "Dateline
Monday" programme which it investigated, and the importance placed on those remarks by
the committee in its report, saying. that it "put all the excerpts from the interview with Mr
Minogue into a false context", is it intended to ask the committee to review its findings?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): The procedures under which
complaints are dealt with by the Broadcasting Corporation are prescribed in section 25 of the
Broadcasting Act 1976. The Minister of Broadcasting plays no part in any of these
procedures. However, the statement to which the honourable member refers did cover his
final point in its concluding sentence: "The committee wishes to make it clear that its other
findings remain unaltered."
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Kauri-Regrowth
2. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister of Forests: To what extent is the
regrowth of kauri being encouraged, and what areas are to be set aside for regeneration and
restocking?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): As far as possible, kauri forest areas are being
managed according to the kauri management policy, the prime objective of which is to
perpetuate kauri as a species in the interests of science, and for public enjoyment, both as
natural stands and managed forests. The policy is implemented to manage and regenerate
kauri by tending areas of natural regeneration, by periodic releasing and thinning of pole and
immature stands, and by the artificial re-establishment of seedlings on selected sites. To
date, 400 hectares of kauri forest have been formed by direct planting or supplementing of
natural regeneration.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Inflation-proof Bonds-Applications
3. Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition), on behalf of Hon. R. J.
TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition), asked the Minister of Finance: What propor-
tion of initial applications for the new inflation-proof bonds has been for the maximum sum
of $1,000, and what proportion has been for smaller sums up to and including $200?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): To date, the Reserve Bank has been
receiving a steady flow of applications of up to 140 a day. One thousand nine hundred and
fourteen applications, totalling $1,592,600, had been received up to and including 28
October. Of these, 8.6 percent are for $200 or less, 16.4 percent are between $200 and
$1,000, and 75 percent are for the full amount of $1,000.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Does the Minister have any figures to show whether a significant
proportion of the high number of applications for $1,000 are multiple applications from one
family?

Unemployment, New Plymouth
5. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Labour: Will he confirm that
the rise in the number of registered unemployed in New Plymouth between 30 September
and 14 October is the highest in the country, almost 30 percent of the total New Zealand rise,
and, if so, can he give a reason for this increase and state what measures his department is
going to take to alleviate the problem?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I can confirm that the increase of 259 in the
number of persons registered as unemployed in the New Plymouth district between 30
September and 14 October was the highest in the country. The whole of this increase was
caused by the enrolment of 271 workers who had been suspended by the local freezing works
because of an industrial dispute. Normal work has since resumed, and the number of
registered unemployed workers in the New Plymouth region is now at approximately the
level recorded prior to the dispute.
Hon. David Thomson: Will the Minister confirm that the local freezing works from
which these people were registered is not in New Plymouth City, but in Waitara?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Yes, I can confirm that. The 300 freezing workers suspended
were from Waitara freezing works.
Mr Bell: Could the Minister confirm that during that same period the decrease for the
Gisborne employment area was 63 persons?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: If I allowed the Minister to answer that we could get a series of
questions asking for figures for places all round the country.
Mr Friedlander: Can the Minister give any figures more recent than those referred to in
the question?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The latest figure I have available for New Plymouth, which is as
yet unofficial, is the number registered as unemployed on 28 October-which would be just
before the works fully resumed. It is 410, which is a very marked reduction.

Pacific Islands Industrial Development Scheme
7. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert),
asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: When was the Pacific Islands industrial develop-
ment scheme first announced, when did the only firm to enter into the scheme so far
commence operations in Samoa, and has the scheme been extended because of this lack of
success under its previous terms?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The scheme was
announced on 31 November 1976. J. Wiseman and Sons Ltd, the first company to gain
approval to set up a venture under the scheme, commenced production in Western Samoa
on 14 September. The extension of the scheme which I announced last week was designed to
broaden it in a way which our experience had shown to be desirable. It did not stem from a
lack of success of the scheme. I do not accept pessimistic claims that the scheme has been
unsuccessful. The large amount of interest among New Zealand manufacturers and the
significant number of companies which are investigating the establishment of ventures under
the scheme belie such claims.
Mr Malcolm: In view of the fact that a seminar was held in Auckland recently for
business houses to discuss the effects and possibilities of the scheme, can the Minister
indicate whether a large body of support for the scheme is growing in the manufacturing
industry?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Yes, the seminar chaired by the member for Piako
was successful. As a matter of fact, today I have had the Tongan delegation with me
discussing the scheme and other trade between Tonga and New Zealand. More than 129
inquiries have been made to my department concerning possible entry into the scheme by
New Zealand manufacturing firms.
Mr Rogers: How many people are employed by Wiseman's in Samoa, and how many
new jobs did the venture create?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I do not have the exact figure. About 10 to 12
people were trained in New Zealand by the company with financial assistance that is
provided under the scheme. They have gone back to Western Samoa to operate the factory
and to train other people who will be interested in it. I could get the exact figure for the
honourable member.
Mr Malcolm: Is the Pacific Islands industrial development scheme a reflection of the
very genuine attempts on the part of the National Government to give practical support to
our Pacific neighbours?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Yes, and I have evidence that it is much appreciated
by Pacific Island Governments.

Pacific Islands Production-Access to New Zealand Market
9. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert),
asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: What steps are being taken to allow greater access
to the New Zealand market for Pacific Islands products so that it will be worth while for
companies to take part in the Pacific Islands industrial development scheme?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The Government
believes that provisions offered under the generalised systems of preference of the major
industrial countries and the Lome Convention agreement provide attractive opportunities
for New Zealand firms to establish operations in the Islands under the scheme in order to
export to third countries. However, it has also been made quite clear that under the Pacific
Islands industrial development scheme there is provision for special access for products of
ventures established under the scheme to be considered on an individual basis.
Mr MacDonell: Will the Minister have talks with his colleague, the Minister of Customs,
to ensure that prohibitive tariffs and duties are not applied to those goods when they come
into the country?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I have already had talks with the Minister of
Customs. We see eye to eye on this matter, and wherever possible assistance will be given in
respect of tariffs on goods from those Pacific Island countries.
Mr Malcolm: Is there any opposition to the freer access of Pacific Islands manufactured
products by either the Manufacturers Federation or the Federation of Labour; and, if so,
which of the two organisations is the more intractable on the matter?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: There is no opposition at present from either
organisation to the Wiseman's venture. Interim access was negotiated after consultations
with the Manufacturers Federation and the Federation of Labour, and I have assured those
two bodies that there will be consultation in every similar case. However, we can do a great
deal more under the normal import licensing provisions in conjunction with individual
manufacturing firms, and that was the line we took in the discussions held this morning.
Hon. M. Rata: To what extent is the entry of goods manufactured in the South Pacific as
a result of the Government's policy inhibited by tariffs such as those suggested in the scheme
concerned?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Only to a very limited extent, but that question
would be better directed to the Minister of Customs, who handles tariff matters.
Mr Malcolm: Was the announcement in Auckland of the commencement of the
Wiseman's project in Western Samoa greeted by loud opposition from some quarters; and, if
so, was it from manufacturing quarters or from trade union quarters?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: There was some criticism of the provision for goods
to come back into New Zealand, but after consultations with both the Manufacturers
Federation and the Federation of Labour that opposition dissolved, and agreement was
reached on this particular project.

Dance Bands and Decibels
10. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Labour: Under what
union are members of a dance band registered, and will the new regulations limiting the
noise level at work places to 85 decibels apply, and, if not, why not?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Persons employed in dance bands would be
eligible for membership of the New Zealand Musicians Industrial Union of Workers. The
only Acts at present administered by the Department of Labour that contain noise control
provisions are the Factories Act 1946, the Construction Act 1959, and the Agricultural
Workers Act passed this year. Consideration is currently being given to the need to
incorporate similar noise control provisions in other statutes administered by the department


## p. 4065 (#171) ###########################################

1 November
4065
Oral Answers to Questions
so as to afford protection to persons in a wider range of occupations in which excessive noise
may be encountered. The reference to regulations limiting noise levels to 85 decibels is not
correct, as no legislative change has occurred. The position is that a recent review of the
evidence relating to noise-induced hearing loss has indicated that a reduction of the level
originally adopted by medical officers of health as a basis for determining the degree of
hazard was necessary to protect a greater percentage of the work force.

CHILDREN AND YOUNG PERSONS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I move, That the Children and
Young Persons Amendment Bill be introduced. The Children and Young Persons Act 1974
introduced substantial changes to the procedures under which the Department of Social
Welfare carries out its responsibilities in relation to juvenile offending and other problems
concerning the welfare of children and young persons. Perhaps the most significant change is
the legal distinction now made between children and young persons. Children are defined as
persons under 14 while young persons are defined as those aged 14 or over but under 17
years of age. The main thrust of the Act is to provide for child offenders to be dealt with
through care, protection, or control proceedings rather than through criminal prosecutions,
and to provide for such proceedings to be handled by the newly created children's boards
rather than the courts. The new provisions were universally welcomed both before and after
the Act came into force from 1 April 1975 and I am happy to report that they have, in
practice, greatly improved the child care services provided by the Department of Social
Welfare. However, over the 2½ years the Act has been in force it has become evident that
certain sections of the Act need amendment to clarify the original intention and to facilitate
more effective operation of the legislation. Many of these changes are of a relatively minor


## p. 4070 (#176) ###########################################

4070
1 November
Children and Young Persons Amendment Bill
nature but I would draw members' attention to three important amendments.
As I have explained, under the Act as it is at present worded, all children under the age
of 14 years who offend against the law are dealt with through care, protection, or control
proceedings rather than criminal prosecutions. This is a basic principle of the Act, and one
which, in the Government's view, should be maintained. Nevertheless, it is considered that
an exception should be made to this principle if the actions of a child have resulted in loss of
life. I am referring to cases in which a child is alleged to have committed murder or
manslaughter. Section 15(10) of the Act provides for the exclusion of such cases from the
jurisdiction of children's boards. Section 25(4) provides that the preliminary hearing of a
charge of murder or manslaughter against a young person shall be heard in a children and
young person's court. Clause 5 of the Bill provides for a child of or over the age of 10 to be
charged with murder or manslaughter as if the charge were being brought against a young
person.
Clause 13 is also worthy of comment. This will give a children and young person's court
the power in appropriate cases to call for a psychiatric examination of a child or young
person before the court. The clause will also enable the court, if there is medical evidence to
support such a course, to order that a child or young person be detained in a psychiatric
hospital for a period not exceeding 1 week so that a psychiatric assessment can be carried
out. The need for this amendment was highlighted in the report earlier this year of Mr
Mitchell, Stipendiary Magistrate, on the circumstances surrounding the treatment given to a
13-year-old Niuean boy in Lake Alice Psychiatric Hospital.
Clause 15 makes it clear that the Director-General of Social Welfare can, in appropriate
cases, arrange psychiatric. treatment for, or seek admission to a psychiatric hospital of, a
State ward in accordance with the normal conditions set out in the Mental Health Act. The
need for this amendment arose because there is some confusion as to whether the director-
general has the necessary legal authority to arrange such an admission. Clause 15 will
overcome this difficulty. It will not be appropriate for a child, or in some cases a young
person, to serve a term of imprisonment in a penal institution. For this reason, clause 18
gives authority for a child or young person to be detained in a social welfare institution
approved for the purpose by the Minister of Social Welfare in consultation with the Minister
of Justice.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I have listened to the Minister's explanation, and
agree that the three points he mentioned are of some moment, and that the present law has
caused some concern. It is appropriate that these points be reconsidered, but whether the
manner of the consideration is appropriate is something we will look at when we have had
more time to study the Bill. I should like to take up clause 18, which deals with the matter of
a young person or a child who is serving a sentence of imprisonment, or who has been
sentenced to a term of imprisonment, but for whom prison is inappropriate-with which I
think all would agree. Concern has been expressed, particularly in Auckland, that a young
person, having been remanded before a finding of guilt or innocence is determined, has been
detained in Mt. Eden Prison. I know circumstances do occur in which almost every
expedient has been tried and found failing; in which people have been remanded and have
not been able to be kept in custody, yet have a history that shows that their liberty should be
constrained pending trial. However, apprehension has been expressed at the insufficient
provision for dealing with people under the age of 16 who are facing criminal charges of
some seriousness, and who are remanded and find themselves quartered in Mt. Eden, which
is a most unsuitable location for them. Has the department considered including some
provisions for this in the Bill? Is it a matter that is causing it concern in the way it has caused
the rest of community some concern?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The matter of care facilities is
causing concern to both the Department of Social Welfare and the Department of Justice,
and discussions are being held on the provision of more suitable facilities. The Department
of Social Welfare does have some secure accommodation, but it is not suitable for holding a
child for any length of time.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: In view of the concern that has been expressed is it proposed to
send this Bill to a committee?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: It is not intended to send the Bill to a committee, but I hope we
will have an answer fairly quickly on the accommodation problem.

Adjournment-Economic Measures
ADJOURNMENT-ECONOMIC MEASURES
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I have received the following letter from the Leader of the
Opposition: "I formally notify you of my intention to move today, pursuant to Standing
Order 89, that the House do now adjourn for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of
urgent public importance, which requires the immediate attention of the House and the
Government; namely the financial statement presented to the House by the Minister of
Finance on Friday last. The text of this was read by the Minister, and it was accompanied by
an appendix, which he referred to but did not read. The whole document became available
to members during that sitting, and this is the first opportunity of discussing it in the
Chamber, and indeed the only opportunity of debating it there as a whole."
Standing Order 90 sets out the criteria which the matter proposed to be discussed must
meet in order to fall within Standing Order 89. The matter relates to the ministerial
statement made to the House last Friday. As such, I have little difficulty in concluding that it
complied with three of the four criteria set out in the Standing Order in that it is not framed
in general terms, it deals with a particular case of recent occurrence, and it involves the
administrative and the ministerial responsibility of Government. The remaining requirement
is that the matter requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government. I have
considered carefully whether the matter fulfils this provision. As the Leader of the
Opposition mentions in his letter, the House will not have an opportunity of debating the
statement as a whole. Some of the measures contained in it will be the subject of legislation,
which will be debated when the legislation is introduced. However, other measures are
administrative in nature, and the House will have no obvious means of debating them.
I feel also that I must weigh the importance of the package of measures announced on
Friday. The statement contained a number of changes in policy, which, when considered as a
whole, do, it seems to me, warrant the other business of the House being set aside in this
instance. For these reasons, I am prepared to accede to the application of the Leader of the
Opposition. I therefore ask those members who support the proposed motion to rise in their
places.
At least five members having risen in their places,
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition) said: I move, That the House do
now adjourn. Last Friday, Parliament almost, but not quite, got back into the business of
government. The Prime Minister presented an economic package of some significance, but,
despite a claim that he felt otherwise, he determined that Parliament would not debate that
package at the time of its introduction. The reasons were apparent. As I have said, the mini-
Budget is a pathetic copy of the proposal the Labour Party presented to the country 8 days
before. The package is the first open admission by the National Government that its
policies-if one could call them that—have failed.
In 2 years the Tory Government has produced economic disaster. Confidence has
collapsed, and there has been a consequent sharp reversal in investment. The latest figures
given by the Minister of Labour show that unemployment is increasing by 200 workers each
working day. People are packing up and emigrating at an even faster rate than unemployed
people are being stood on the sidelines. Inflation, which is now almost entirely home-grown,
and promoted by the National administration, is still on the way up. The last three quarters
have shown an increase in the annual rate of inflation.
Most people would admit that the industrial scene is in disarray. The workers and their
wives and families wait with concern, to the point of fear, thinking about what the next turn
of the screw will bring. The retired have found that they must start putting aside money to
meet the tax bill that will be levied in 1978. The economy is grinding to a halt, and young
people leaving school and university face the bleak prospect of second-choice or third-choice
employment. Worse still, many thousands of school leavers will have no job at all.
For several months before the Budget was introduced, the Opposition urged the
Government to take positive action to reactivate the economy before it was too late, but the
plea was rejected each time it was made. Finally, on 20 October the Opposition produced an
economic package and invited the Government to implement it. The package provided, first,
for an immediate injection of capital into front-line industry; secondly, for immediate
assistance for the prospective home owner, with consequential benefits to the beleaguered
building industry-home units being built in 1977 are almost 10 000 fewer than the number
built several years ago; thirdly, for a December tax holiday on the first $200 to $250 earned,
depending on the marital or family status of the taxpayer; fourthly, for a family benefit
increase of 50 percent for children under 10 and 100 percent for children over the age of 10,
to inject purchasing power into the economy at a time when it was most needed to help the


## p. 4072 (#178) ###########################################

4072
1 November
Adjournment-Economic Measures
family and stimulate the retail trade, thereby giving confidence to manufacturers; fifthly, for
a Christmas bonus for the elderly, for the same reasons; and sixthly, the development of a
skills programme to provide employment for young school leavers.
The package provoked an immediate response from the Associate Minister of Finance,
who said that it was too costly, impractical, and inflationary, and that the Government was
watching the situation. The Government has been stirred into action, and on Friday it
produced another mini-Budget, or several pages of excuses. Last night the Associate
Minister of Finance gave more excuses and some proposals. It is clear from the comments
made by the Associate Minister of Finance last night that the Government has accepted
unemployment at levels comparable with those of the 1930s. The document produced by the
Minister of Finance has a certain amount of gobbledygook. An example is a sentence on
page 3, which reads: "The Government is determined to ensure that the levels of unemploy-
ment of people and resources do not rise above the minimum that is consistent with the need
to shift resources into those areas that have high priority in the attainment of our national
economic goals." I suppose in simple language it means that the country will have
unemployment, but the Government hopes that the levels will not be too horrendous. The
ideal of full employment has been thrown out of the window.
On the other side of the ledger, it is not clear what the Government considers its
priorities are. When the Prime Minister was the Leader of the Opposition in 1975 the two
factors that concerned him most were inflation and imports. The mini-Budget has made no
attempt to attack either problem. What do the 73 000 young people leaving secondary school
and university think of a Government that accepts that the country should have unemploy-
ment at the levels of the 1930s?
The document has few other claims. It mentions the balance of payments, which
deserves closer examination, because it implies that the Government has achieved great
reductions in the deficit. This matter can be put into perspective only when one realises that
in its last 6 months the Labour Government reduced the balance of payments deficit by $266
million, whereas in its first 18 months-three times as much time-the third National
Government has reduced the deficit by $272 million, even though export earnings have
increased by $1,000 million. That could hardly be considered a success story by a self-styled
economic genius.
I turn now to the specific proposals in the document put forward by the Minister of

One proposal that will have an immediate effect is the lump sum payment in November

Associate Minister of Finance, is made by a Government that has already budgeted for a 26
percent tax increase. There is the height of generosity for you! The Government budgets for
a 26 percent tax increase for the 1977-78 financial year, and says, "For the last 2 months we
will give you a 5 percent cut on that increase, so all you will have to pay is a 25 percent
increase in your total tax bill." What is most important is that the proposed relief will
certainly not go to those in need, but to those with the highest incomes. This is very simply

proposal means that the weekly relief to the Prime Minister will be of the order of $17.53.

Inflation showed almost the worst performance by the Labour Government. It was
going to knock it for six, but knocked it for only three. When it took over in 1972, the rate of
inflation was 5½ percent; the following year it was 10 percent; the next year 12.6 percent;
and in the last year 15.7 percent. Up, up, up, up it went, and it was three times as bad when
the Labour Government went out as when it took over, with the increase accelerating and
continuing. Even the member for Northern Maori would concede that.
Hon. M. Rata: No, I wouldn't.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: He said he would not; he did not know. Many members of
that Cabinet did not know what the rate of inflation was, and the member for Northern
Maori has just admitted it. And there were massive subsidies, paid out of the taxpayers'
pockets, on top of the 15.7 percent a year rate of inflation. The subsidies have diminished,
and the basic rate has stabilised and is moving down. There is no doubt about that. When the
Labour Government went out of office in 1975, unemployment was higher than it had been
when it took over in 1972. It is going up now, and that is what this mini-Budget is all
about-to curb it, to hold it. Without the mini-Budget it could go up sharply next year. But
the Leader of the Opposition is quite wrong. Two or three times recently I have heard him
say that unemployment is at the 1930s level. What nonsense! It has been about 10 000,
12 000, 15 000, 17 000-including those on special work. Back in the 1930s, when the
population was a little over half the present population, the figure was between 50 000 and
100 000. It is now about one-fifth or one-sixth, relatively, what it was in the 1930s. If New
Zealand had the same proportion of unemployed as Australia has, the figure would be about
75 000-about four times greater. So much for the claptrap of the Leader of the Opposition
about unemployment.
One of the best tests of the Government's economic management came recently when
an independent American organisation sent someone to New Zealand to look at our
economy, and we were given a triple A rating in terms of international credit-absolutely the
top line, the highest credit rating possible. In Washington a few weeks ago, I talked to the
man who came here and did the study, and he said, “I am not looking at the trouble you are
in now. I am looking at what New Zealand is likely to be like 7 years from now. You are
borrowing on 7-year terms. In my view, your economic policies are sound. You have a sound
economy fundamentally. As far as I am concerned, you are triple A, a stable country, and,
with good economic management, you will be able to pay your debts."
Mr Falloon: Who said that?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: This was an independent New York organisation, whose
reputation depends on its ability to forecast correctly the way economies will go. That is the
best independent assessment that this country has had in recent times, and it is right up on
the top line. In the New York market we borrowed on better terms than the European
Investment Bank, which has behind it the credit of the Common Market. We are borrowing.
We have a proposal in front of us now to roll over a borrowing of $400 million that was made
by the Labour Government in 1974. That has to be borrowed soon with a little bit extra, but
at much better rates than the Labour Government borrowed at. We are repaying it more
than a year before we need to, because we are getting much better rates. We will save on the
deal, instead of paying the interest rates that the Labour Government arranged. Its credit
was not as good as all that, yet members opposite are now criticising the present Govern-
ment. We will borrow at lower rates and save on the deal, just as we did with the Swiss loan
arranged by the Labour Government, which we repaid early.
The National Government's credit is good. There is no doubt that careful balancing is
necessary. Following my discussions in Washington with world finance ministers, central
bankers, and private bankers, it became clear that the New Zealand economy would not get
much of a lift next year from international economic events. On my return to New Zealand
investigations were set in train resulting in the mini-Budget, which could have been
announced earlier, but without such a feel for the international situation.
The Labour Government did nothing. I remember one of New Zealand's most eminent
economists saying, at the beginning of 1975, that the Labour Government's policy was
borrow and hope. That is why it was thrown out-it borrowed, and hoped everything would
come right. Since 1973, New Zealand's terms of trade-the relationship between what its
exports will buy, and imports—have decreased by 40 percent. It now takes fewer bales of
wool to buy a tractor than it did in 1973.

Opposition members laboured mightily over their own package, and produced their

from him in meeting some of the country's economic problems. In fact, the House might well

In its package the Opposition pre-empted next year's income tax and pushed in too
much money, which would have been inflationary. The Labour Party's proposal failed to
inject funds at either the right level or the right quantity. It would have set inflation off
again, with the accent on the housing field. What a performance the former Labour
Government had in housing! While it was in power housing prices increased by 100 percent,
land prices by 160 percent, and building prices by 66 percent. In the last year under National
house prices increased by 3.78 percent, and section prices by 5.93 percent. But, Opposition
members came up with a proposal that would have set off an artificial demand for houses.
There is no point in building houses if there is no demand for them.
The package introduced by the Government is tailored to meet New Zealand's
economic needs-and even the Leader of the Opposition has admitted that it is not
inflationary. Now, that is an admission for you; I think even he is beginning to understand
the need for economic management and strategy. I remind the House that in its two Budgets
the Government has set out clearly the two pillars of its economic strategy: the need for
restraint and balance in the internal economy, and the need to increase our exports and our
overseas income.
In terms of that policy the package we are considering stands forward as a means of
keeping the economy in balance. I do not mind standing here on the conservative side of the
House and claiming to be a trimmer supporting the need for balance in economic manage-
ment, even if Opposition members constantly refuse to admit such a requirement. The
economy requires constant trimming. At the time the Budget was presented we said that we
would keep the situation under review. The changing economic circumstances, particularly
in the major overseas economies—our major trading partners—with a decline in their
growth and in the level of growth expected, have forced us to re-examine our economic
situation. So we have come forward with a mild stimulation to the economy.
It is a carefully packaged mini-Budget, which will bring the required impetus to the
economy without inflation. That was a point forgotten by the Leader of the Opposition when
he put forward his own mini-package, but he admits that the Government's is not infla-
tionary. We want to maintain demand and spending now, before Christmas. We want to
maintain business confidence and activity; and the leaders of the manufacturers indicated in
their discussions with the Prime Minister this morning that our mini-Budget will do that. We
also want to maintain the drive for exports—and we certainly have not had much help from
the Opposition on that score.
Let us look at the package. In terms of its fiscal measures, we have put in an immediate
injection of money that will help to boost Christmas spending and maintain business activity.
The business community and the public can have confidence that there will be another step,
another injection, required in a stagflation situation, with the income tax rebate in February.

As the Prime Minister said, income tax assistance has already been given to those in receipt
of a lower wage, and the House has passed measures to implement the Budget announce-

particularly the central institutions—the banks, the savings banks, the life offices, and the
Post Office.
In moving money through the banks into the economy we are providing for
employment-the type of activity that members opposite claim they want. I remind the
House that in our Budget we have put employment at the top of the list of the major
indicators. Any New Zealander with any experience or knowledge of people would wish that
to be the case. Employment is the major requirement for our people, but we cannot provide
it regardless; we have to balance it with the other indicators-our balance of payments,
inflation rate, and Budget deficit. The indicators have to be balanced together. If we are to
earn our way in the world we have to shift resources-not only material, but also human
resources-into the export industries. That is the basis of our mini-package, if members
opposite will only try to understand it.
Our employment record is the best of all the OECD countries, and, with the measures
the Government has taken, it will remain so despite the gross distortions of Opposition
members. Nobody on this side of the House wants unemployment. But where it is inevitable
we will provide measures to try to assist in finding jobs, in creating jobs, and in training
people for jobs. It is well known that untrained people will find it difficult to obtain work in
an increasingly technological society, with an economy demanding more trained people. It
starts right in the field of education, and in the drive and urge of society. This Government
will not baulk at the problem because of some criticism from the Opposition.
Now, with the New Zealand economy in trouble, the measures in this mini-Budget will
help us face up to our problems. I remind the House that we have the best employment
record of any of the OECD countries. We have put together a package in the building and

emphasis on the use of monetary policy and our financial institutions to support our export
industries. This package will help us, in the terms put in the 1977 Budget, to bring restraint
into the economy while we build up our capacity to export. I cannot overemphasise the
importance of this to New Zealand's future.
We are facing real challenges abroad because the world economy is not responding as
quickly as we had hoped. So we must use our own economic resources. We must be prepared
to borrow overseas at reasonable levels to maintain activity. We cannot overborrow to
maintain high wage claims-and I make an emphatic plea for wage restraint at this time in
terms of economic management and growth. We shall not win the battle for a strong New
Zealand economy in the face of excessive wage claims and union militancy. We must hold
together. This mini-package is designed to assist the mass of New Zealanders, as well as our
economy and society, to adjust to difficult economic circumstances. We shall keep the needs
of our economy under review month by month, and will ensure that economic activity is
maintained. I am sure the House will endorse the purpose behind this package.

The Leader of the Opposition was critical of the Government's attitude to the Export-
Import Corporation; he said we had criticised it before but now we were supporting it. The
fact is that when the legislation was introduced by the Labour Government it contained some
very bad provisions. The National Party, as a private-enterprise party, quite properly
criticised it. In the original Bill the Labour Government provided for the corporation to
compete in New Zealand with retailers and manufacturers. After hearing representations at
the select committee and the criticism of the then Opposition the Labour Government
removed the provisions, giving the Export-Import Corporation the power to compete with
retailers in New Zealand, but it did not take out the provisions allowing the corporation to
compete with manufacturers either in New Zealand or overseas. It certainly did not remove
the power of the corporation to compete with exporters-manufacturers or otherwise.
When the National Government came into office the caucus commerce committee,
under the chairmanship of my Parliamentary Under-Secretary, the member for Tauranga,
worked for some weeks on the legislation and on the work of the corporation. I arranged a
series of meetings with the staff of the corporation, board members, and also organisations
in manufacturing and commerce who were concerned at the workings of the corporation,
and it was found that the corporation had not been competing with New Zealand industry.
This Government will see that it does not, but we were not prepared to trust the socialist
Government on this. The Government has seen to it that the corporation has acted in the
interests of the people, including traders and exporters, and it is endeavouring to extend the
corporation's services.
Exporters and manufacturers are now moving into markets on the west coast of
America and in other parts of the United States. Many exporters were concerned at the
powers given to the corporation by the Labour Government. This Government has seen to it
that the corporation has acted in the interests of exporters, and that it has not competed with
them. On the other hand, it has provided services; and the people will continue to support
the National Government's working this way with the corporation.

Concern had been expressed about the flooding of productive land as a result of the

The difference in terms of orchard land in production that would be inundated was 47
hectares. Under scheme H, 60 hectares of productive orchard land would have been
inundated; under scheme F 107 hectares of productive orchard land would be inundated.
The difference between the two schemes was the loss of 11 orchards in the Cromwell Gorge.
The value of those orchards' production had to be set against the significant increase in the
energy value of scheme F. At about $100 million, scheme F was less costly, and could be
built more quickly. It had been carefully thought out and studied in great detail. It would
come into production 4 years before scheme H would have, because one less dam was
needed, and could produce more energy and more power.

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) said that the Labour Party had
won the 1972 election, not because of its regional development policy, but for other reasons.
The Labour Government had introduced a form of regional maintenance policy that in the
beginning had seemed to have much to commend it, but clearly, because it was not related to
the true resources of the area, had been destined always to be a policy without real
substance. The National Government had, over a period of nearly 2 years and in a number
of ways, slowly and steadfastly turned the main thrust of regional development towards
resource development; and it would continue to do so.
It was nonsense to suggest that, because the total amount spent on regional develop-
ment had decreased a little, the Government had made severe cuts. In each of the last 2
years the Government had provided more money for regional development assistance than it
had been able to spend. In 1973-74, the Labour Government had voted $3 million, and had
spent $898,000. In 1974-75, it had voted $5 million, and spent $4.9 million. In 1975-76, when
there had been both a Labour Government and a National Government, $5.7 million had
been voted, and $4 million spent. In 1976-77, the National Government had voted $5
million, and $3.5 million had been spent. There had been no question of budgetary restraints
stopping expenditure. The estimates showed that for 1977-78 the Government had budgeted
$4.3 million.
The facts clearly showed that in each of the years under both Governments the amount
voted had exceeded the amount asked for. The National Government's policy restraints in
1976 had been necessary to contain the inherited 28 percent per annum growth rate in
Government expenditure. The restraints had since been removed, and the recent mini-
Budget had provided for an expansion of schemes and proposals for further regional
development work. One of the principal items of regional development under the Labour
Government had been an organisation called Matai Industries, which had ended up an
unmitigated disaster. Under the National Government regional development was strong and
healthy, and was being serviced by good people in Wellington and in the regional develop-
ment councils. More importantly, the main thrust was towards resource development.

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-URGENCY
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That urgency be accorded formal
business, the introduction of three Government Bills, the introduction of the Social Security
Amendment Bill, the third reading of the Moneylenders Amendment Bill, the Human Rights

Corporation Amendment Bill (No. 2), and further consideration in Committee of the New

I take this rather unusual course because I want members to know what I think should
be in front of us today. Of the three Government Bills to be introduced, two at least are non-
controversial. There may be a little discussion on the other one. So that members can
perhaps time themselves and discuss what they wish to discuss, I take the unusual course at
the commencement of business of moving urgency for what I see as an appropriate amount
of business for today.

the notice on two grounds: first, it has very little substantiation; and secondly, it is not only
insulting but also frivolous.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I regret very much that the Standing Orders give me very little
room for manoeuvre. Against my better judgment and against my advice in 1974-and I was
a lone voice on the Standing Orders Committee-the House agreed with the recommenda-
tion made by the Standing Orders Committee at the time that the Speaker should be asked
to vet notices of motion. In asking him to do that the House asked him to weed the garden,
as it were, without giving him any weedkiller; he is required to do the job with his bare
hands. All I am allowed to do is to take notice of Standing Order 103, which reads: "Notices
of motion shall not—(a) Contain any unbecoming or offensive expression or any expression
or words which would not be permitted in debate; (b) Contain any statement of facts or
name of any person unless they are strictly necessary to render the notice intelligible and can
be authenticated; (c) Anticipate discussion of an order of the day." Those are the only
guidelines, the only criteria, I have to enable me to take action on notices of motion.
I have looked at that notice of motion, and I shall have another look at it. I saw the
reference to ducks, and thought that it was only a part of the culinary flavour of the whole
notice.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: The Peking flavour was there too, of course.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Do you prefer the Moscow flavour? Would a Muscovy duck be
better?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: It might be better if I had a look at it later on, out of the

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Parliament Grounds-Barricades
1. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt), asked
the Minister in Charge of the Legislative Department: Why was the barricade put in position
at the top of the library steps for the SIS demonstration on Tuesday, 18 October, still firmly
locked in position over Labour weekend?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister in Charge of the Legislative Department): I am
sorry that after all the fuss there has been over this question I cannot give the answer directly
to the member for Hutt. After the demonstration on Tuesday, 18 October, the police asked
Legislative Department staff to retain the barriers in position in case of further demonstra-
tion against the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill, and also for the
ceremony of the swearing-in of His Excellency the Governor-General on Wednesday, 26
October. It was agreed, provided that barriers across all accessways could be removed. The
Ministry of Works and Development was asked to arrange accordingly, and unlocked the
barriers on Wednesday morning, 19 October. Through inadvertence, the one at the top of
the library steps was not unlocked at that time. No complaint or request for the removal of
the barrier was received until 25 October. The barrier was then removed. Keys are held by
Police, Ministry of Works and Development, and Legislative Department staff, so that the
barriers can be removed quickly when required. I suggest that, if the member for Hutt has
any difficulty in the future, he should approach the Clerk of the House, who I am sure will
put everything right without any delay whatsoever.

5. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Transport: Has he any intention of
changing the present regulations covering the survey of fishing vessels to include craft of less
than 35 ft?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Transport. His reply is as follows: "I have no immediate intention of changing the present
regulations covering the survey of fishing vessels of less than 35ft in registered length. This
matter is regularly kept under review, but as there are over 1000 such vessels between 20ft
and 35 ft in length to survey all or even a proportion of these vessels would require a
substantial increase in marine division survey staff. Suitably qualified surveyors are
extremely difficult to recruit at present, due to an industry wide shortage. Discussions are
being held between the marine division of the Ministry of Transport and the Fishing Industry
Board to find alternative means of ensuring that fishing vessels under 35 ft in length are
brought up to and kept in an acceptable standard of seaworthiness."

me, as it is to the industry. It is a very difficult problem to control, but we have not lost sight
of it.

units, and the medical officer of health need only request this service. I can assure the
honourable member that the Department of Health is keeping the matter under constant
surveillance, and should additional mobile X-ray services be needed they will be supplied.

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Social
Security Amendment Bill. The Bill, which amends section 69c of the Social Security Act
1964, is a small Bill, but none the less one of considerable importance to all who care for a
disabled person in their own home. It is a Bill which, recognising that those who care for a
disabled relative do so at considerable financial cost to themselves, endeavours to provide
some small measure of relief for their humanitarian action.
The proposal that a disability allowance be payable for a disabled child has been
recommended on many occasions during recent years. The 1972 report of the Royal
Commission of Inquiry into Social Security in New Zealand stated: "Many severely handi-
capped children are cared for in their own homes. As in the case of disabled adults, their
disability may lead to much extra expense, and again a widely varying range of circumstances
may apply. We consider, therefore, that the disability allowance which we propose for
disabled beneficiaries should also be available for handicapped children. However, children
do not receive invalidity or sickness benefits so that the first basis of entitlement to an
allowance is not present. We consider therefore that the disability allowance should be paid
without income test to the person receiving the family benefit for the child."
The report continued: "We justify the waiving of the income test on the grounds that


## p. 4108 (#214) ###########################################

4108
2 November
Social Security Amendment Bill
parents, by caring for the child at home, are often saving the State the very considerable
costs which would be involved in caring for the child in a hospital or other institution."
Similar recommendations were made in 1973 in the third report of the Royal Commission of
Inquiry into Hospital and Related Services, and again in 1975 in Board of Health Report No.
24, Children with Handicaps. Conscious of the fact that the same need and justification for
financial aid could apply to families caring for an elderly disabled parent in the home, I have
widened the eligibility for the disability allowance so as to include all disabled persons
irrespective of age.
Clause 2 inserts into the interpretation section of the principal Act the definition of a
disabled person, in line with that found in the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act
1975. Clause 3 extends the right of appeal under section 121(2) of the principal Act to include
the disability allowance. Clause 4 is a rewriting of section 69C of the principal Act, under
which every disabled person will be entitled to a disability allowance provided that person
was born in New Zealand or has resided continuously in New Zealand for not less than 12
months, and is likely to remain permanently in New Zealand. Provision is made for the
Social Security Commission to exercise its discretion over the issue of and the rate of a
disability allowance in certain circumstances. Clause 4 inserts into the principal Act the
proposed new section 69D, under which the commission may require an applicant for a
disability allowance to submit to an examination by a medical practitioner. The proposed
new section 69E makes provision for a right of appeal on medical grounds where a claim for a
disability allowance is declined.
In March 1970 the then Intellectually Handicapped Children's Society, now the Society
for the Intellectually Handicapped, presented as part of its submission to the royal commis-
sion eight statements from parents of disabled children to illustrate their financial needs.
Today I can table at least 10 letters from parents in the Hamilton area who have documented
their needs. I cite the case of an 11-year-old multi-handicapped girl who costs her parents $17
a week for pre-school education while her older normal brother receives free education; the
case of a 5½-year-old intellectually handicapped girl living with her parents in Te Awamutu
whose education at the Christopher Park Pre-School Special Care Centre in Hamilton,
taking travel, accommodation, and other expenses into account, costs her parents $40.50 a
week exclusive of medical and home expenses; the case of an 8-year-old spina bifida boy,
where extra car mileage due solely to the boy's disability amounts to more than 1000
kilometres a year; and the case of a 13-year-old hyperactive mentally retarded girl whose
monthly clothing replacement cost is $60. Unfortunately the measure proposed may be too
late to help those whose cases were outlined in the 1970 submissions, but I pray that we may
still be able to help today's and tomorrow's parents and guardians of the disabled.

The Bill, however, goes further than that, and defines a disabled person as "any person
who suffers from physical or mental incapacity or impairment to such a degree that he is
seriously and permanently limited in the extent to which he can engage in the activities,
pursuits, and processes of everyday life". The Bill does not limit assistance to children or to
those who already qualify for the invalid benefit. It opens up the field so that people will
receive a benefit as of right—they will not have to go to the Social Welfare Department and
produce proof of income. That can make it extremely difficult for some people, particularly
those looking after disabled persons. I am reminded of a story told to me by the member for
Lyttelton about a couple living in her electorate. The wife is a multiple sclerosis sufferer, and
requires six changes of clothes each day. They live in a State house, and do not know
whether they qualify for any benefit. It may well be that they do, but because of the means
test they have not bothered to find out.
The principle behind this Bill is that people will qualify automatically if they ask for the
benefit. The Pukeora Home in my electorate is one of the finest institutions in New Zealand
for disabled persons. I should like it to be possible for those who make their home at
Pukeora to go home to their parents more often. Under this legislation they would qualify

they can at present. A maternity annexe at Woodville is being converted to a 5-day hostel for
disabled students, who travel up to 4 hours a day to a school in Woodville that is specially
designed for their purposes. Under this legislation the parents of those children would have
some help in looking after the children when they go home at weekends, and the children
would be able to mix in the community and with each other. I support the Bill for the reasons
I have outlined, and ask the House to commend it.

IMMIGRATION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): I move, That the Immigration Amendment
Bill be introduced. This six-clause Bill makes a number of amendments to the Immigration
Act 1964. The proposals contained in it give legislative effect to the Government's election
promise to review the work permit system and ensure that the number of permits is related
to economic requirements. The opportunity is taken to incorporate other amendments in
order to improve the law on the detection and deportation of overstayers.
Clause 2 relates to visitors entering the country, and makes it an offence for them to
seek to engage in employment unless they have been authorised to do so. Clause 3 is a
machinery provision extending the present provision about false representation in obtaining
a permit or an extension of a permit. Clause 4 relates to overstayers and persons illegally in
the country, and makes it an offence for an employer to employ a person who he has reason
to know does not have permission to work. Clause 5 makes provision to allow the Minister of
Finance to require a deportee to meet deportation costs. Clause 6 introduces an amendment
to give the Minister power to revoke the mandatory penalty of deportation for persons
convicted of being in New Zealand illegally if, in the Minister's view, there are exceptional
humanitarian circumstances that would make it unduly harsh or unjust to deport the
offender. I propose to move that the Bill be referred to the Labour Committee.

LOCAL LEGISLATION BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Local
Legislation Bill be introduced. This Bill is the usual measure brought down each year,
containing provisions affecting particular local authorities or other public bodies. Each
clause has been promoted by the local authority concerned, and deals with matters of a
relatively minor, non-contentious nature. This year there are 18 clauses. Some clauses
validate certain irregularities in actions already taken by local authorities, others authorise
specific proposals to be carried out if there is no provision in existing general legislation.
Government departments with an interest in particular clauses have been consulted,
and all members of Parliament whose constituents are, or may be, affected by individual
clauses have been advised by the local authority or public body concerned, as required by the
Standing Orders. I have not received any objections to any of the clauses in the Bill.
Standing Order 272 requires that the Bill be now referred to the Local Bills Committee,
where each clause may be examined in detail.

Apple and Pear Marketing Amendment Bill
APPLE AND PEAR MARKETING AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Associate Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Apple and
Pear Marketing Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill makes various amendments to the
Apple and Pear Marketing Act 1971, mostly at the request of the Apple and Pear Marketing
Board and the New Zealand Fruitgrowers Federation.
It is appropriate that I should draw the House's attention to the fact that in 1974 the
Apple and Pear Marketing Board and the New Zealand Fruitgrowers Federation commis-
sioned the Massey University market research centre to carry out a study on the New
Zealand pipfruit industry. The Massey report and its recommendations were considered at
the Fruitgrowers Federation conference in Hastings last November-and again this year, I
might add. Following consideration by the conference, a series of recommendations for
restructuring the pipfruit growing industry were submitted to the Government. Some of
these recommendations involved amendments to the Act. The Government has been giving
careful consideration to the industry's submissions, and has agreed to introduce an approp-
riate amending Bill.
Clause 2 empowers the board to handle, as well as apples and pears, such other
horticultural products as the Minister of Agriculture may from time to time approve. The
compulsory acquisition provisions will not, of course, apply to any other products the board
may handle. This extension is to allow the facilities of the Apple and Pear Marketing Board
to be used when this is considered to be useful. Associated with this provision, the board
will be empowered, with the consent of the Minister of Finance, to acquire shares in
companies dealing with fruit other than apples and pears-for example, shares in a co-
operatively owned cool store.
Clause 4 relates to the determination of the average price, and the provisions of the
apple and pear industry stabilisation scheme are being amended to bring them more into line
with those applying in other primary industries. In particular, the "cost of production"
criterion is being removed from the list of criteria the Apple and Pear Prices Authority is
required to take into account when fixing the annual average price. The effect of this is that
the authority will have more regard to market returns in fixing the price.
At the same time, however, the restriction on the seasonal movement in the annual
price is being widened to allow for changes of between plus 10 percent and minus 5 percent,
instead of the present plus or minus 5 percent. I am sure this will be welcomed by the
industry.
Associated with this change, any distribution of board profits is to be subject to the
approval of the Minister of Agriculture, as is the case now in the dairy industry.
Under clause 6 of this amending Bill, no more than half of the season's profit can be
distributed without the consent of the Minister of Finance.
Clause 5 makes provision for an industry levy on all sales of apples and pears. The rate
of the levy is to be fixed by the Apple and Pear Prices Authority after taking into account the
cost of producing apples and pears, the state of the industry reserve account, and the state of
the pipfruit growing industry generally. The purpose of the levy is to help finance the cost of
processing apples and pears, to help reduce any deficit in the reserve account, and to
promote the interests of the apple and pear growing industry. The Bill provides that the rate
for the first season in which a levy is set shall not be more than 0.25c a kilogram, which is
about 5c a case, and that, whenever it is changed, it cannot be increased by more than 10
percent over the previous rate.
Clause 7 contains the other principal amendment made by the Bill. This makes it clear
that the board has the sole right over exports of apples and pears. This was always thought to
be the case, but, in view of some doubts that have been expressed, it is intended to make this
requirement perfectly clear. Because the quality of apple and pear exports is of paramount
importance in international marketing, it is essential that New Zealand safeguards its status
as a producer of quality exports, and the Apple and Pear Marketing Board is the appropriate
organisation to ensure this objective is achieved. This sole right to export does not, of
course, apply to any products the board might become involved in handling, other than
apples and pears.
The provisions in the Bill are supported by most members of the apple and pear
industry. The industry is anxious that the Bill should be passed before the end of this month,
so that its provisions-particularly those relating to the fixing of the average price-are in
