specifically ask that the cost of production be withdrawn.
The Leader of the Opposition drew attention to the fact that in the tobacco industry the
cost of production is an important factor in establishing price. The obvious difference
between the two industries is that the tobacco industry is producing entirely for the local
market, while the apple and pear industry has its prices determined eventually by what the
world market will pay. That is why the cost of production criterion was removed. We had to
ensure, as we do in our major primary producing industries, that the price we pay the
producer over time reflects what the market will pay in any given situation.
The other question asked by the Leader of the Opposition related to the payout of any
surplus by the board now being determined after consultation with the Minister of Agricul-
ture. It is agreed that this was not a specific request by the industry, but it is a practice that
has become accepted within the producer boards, and the Labour Government in 1974
introduced exactly the same provision in the dairy products prices legislation. It is something
that has come into play with this type of legislation in the last few years. The apple and pear
industry was under the constraints of the combined Ministers-the Minister of Finance and
the Minister of Agriculture-when it was heavily in debt to the Reserve Bank. Fortunately,
market forces have ensured that this is not so at present, but the restriction incorporated in
the Bill is not strongly opposed by the industry.

POTATO GROWING INDUSTRY BILL
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Commit-
tee to present the report of the committee on the Potato Growing Industry Bill. The
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table. The Bill is a major achievement for the potato growing industry,
and is a culmination of about 8 years of discussions, submissions, and representations. For
the first time the growers are brought together, thus enabling the industry, which is
susceptible to numerous market fluctuations and seasonal conditions, to be more orderly.
Sitting suspended from 5.30 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.
Mr TALBOT: Before the adjournment I was reporting back on the Potato Growing
Industry Bill. At that stage members seemed to think that I had done my chips, but I had
not. The Bill will go a long way towards bringing together the main-crop potato growers.
Legislation has been discussed for 7 or 8 years. The committee received a total of 16 written
submissions, 15 of which were heard by the committee. Several amendments were made to
the Bill. The title has been amended to the Potato Industry Bill by the deletion of the word
"growing". Once the Bill is passed the New Zealand Potato Growers Board will be called
the New Zealand Potato Board. That is an important amendment.
Clause 5 deals with the election of certain nominees, and the committee made an
important amendment, which provides that all registered growers are eligible to vote for
nominees for both the Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation and the Potato Growers
Federation in elections for ward representatives. Previously, the Bill provided for only main-
crop growers to vote for nominees of the Potato Growers Federation and early-crop growers
for nominees of the Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation. The amendments are very
important and should help to overcome some of the objections expressed in submissions that
the industry should not be divided into early-crop and main-crop growers. Although the two
federations will still be putting forward separate nominations, all registered growers within
the ward will be eligible to vote.
Two amendments were made to clause 13. The second amendment is to subclause
(3)(m), which provides for the board to engage in publicity on quality standards. This has
been expanded to include publicity on variety characteristics of potatoes, and the subclause
has been moved up the list of board functions to become the new paragraph (i), which has
become known as the Shearer amendment.
Clause 17 deals with the annual registration of potato plantings. The minimum area of
potato plantings that must be registered has been increased from 0.2 hectares to 0.5 hectares,
and all persons planting more than that area must pay the registration fee. The amendment
has been made for practical reasons, as 0.2 hectares was considered too small an area for
registration.
In clause 18 the maximum registration fee prescribed in the Bill has been removed. The
fee will be set by the board, with the approval of the Minister, at the level considered
necessary to fund the board's operations. Clause 23, dealing with the potato surplus disposal
account, has been considerably amended, and a new clause, 23A, has been inserted.
Subclause (1) has been amended by replacing the present subclause, which specified that
$750,000 should be set aside for the disposals account, with a subclause that provides for the
board to set aside all the accumulated funds it considers will not be required to exercise its
other functions and powers. The reason for the change is that the surplus payments by the
board this season depleted the board's funds to below the $750,000 level. Subclause (2) now
provides for the interest on the disposals account to be used solely for the disposal of
potatoes, but the fund itself may also be used for disposals after a unanimous vote of the six
grower members only of the board, and the approval of the Minister. This is a major change,
and allows the fund as well as the interest to be used for the disposal of potatoes. At the same
time it is a safeguard against indiscriminate use of funds that have been built up from grower
money, by requiring the unanimous support of the six growers before its use.
The new clause 23A deals with the special levy to replenish the potato surplus disposals


## p. 4125 (#231) ###########################################

2 November
4125
Potato Growing Industry Bill
account. It has been inserted to provide for the replenishment, if necessary, of the disposals
accounts by means of a special levy on growers or classes of growers. The special levy is to be
recommended to the Minister only on the unanimous vote of the six grower members of the
board, and no more than one such recommendation can be made to the Minister in any year.
This new clause is also a major change. It allows the disposals account to be replenished, but
provides the same safeguard of unanimous grower member support as is provided in clause
23 (2), if the fund is to be used. Submissions received by the committee were divided over
whether replenishment of the fund should be allowed by any means or not at all. The
provision of a special levy with adequate safeguards should meet many of the objections.
The legislation as reported back will not please all growers. Some will be disappointed
that clause 4 has not been amended to provide for six grower representatives to be elected
from six wards. To have done that would have been to break an agreement made with the
industry by the Minister. Also, as was submitted to the committee by Federated Farmers, it
would have worked against, not towards, complete unification of growers. As reported back,
the Bill legislates on the undertakings given by the Associate Minister of Agriculture to the
Potato Growers Federation, the New Zealand Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation,
and the Potato Board. The Government and the Minister are to be congratulated on
introducing legislation which, as soon as it becomes law, will help to bring together into one
unified industry all those involved in potato growing.

Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): The Opposition wants to place

considerable evidence to show that the change in the Bill was in fact already producing
increases in interest rates. The Government tried to make out that such increases were
perhaps coincidental, and were certainly due to no part of the Bill. It is only a short measure,

widely than that point; but in the course of the discussion much mention was made of one
particular stock and station company, Dalgety's, which had announced in its annual report
that because of the situation it faced it would be increasing interest rates to farmers as a
direct consequence of the Bill's becoming law. It was pointed out to the Government that
whether or not it was intended that the Bill should have the effect of increasing interest rates,
the fact was that the Bill was being used by people who lend money to increase the rates at
which they lent that money. Further evidence came from an insurance company, which made

HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a third
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I take the opportunity of summarising briefly
some of the discussion that took place in the Committee of the Whole. Attention was first
directed to the interpretation clause, and I must say I find it unacceptable that we should
have a definition of "ethical belief" which says that it means "the absence of a religious
belief”. If the words were "included the absence of a religious belief” I could take it, but if
you were to tell the average churchgoer that he was there because he lacked ethical belief, I
am sure he would look at you in amazement. This phrase will be put on the statute book, and
in future will arouse the caustic comment it deserves.
There is some discussion, too, on "marital status", which, as defined originally,
included de facto marriages, but that has been dropped from the Bill. By doing so, the
Government has evaded, far from solving, problems posed by the increasing numbers of
couples who choose to live together without the benefit of a marriage ceremony. This is
evidence of the Government refusing to face up to division within its own ranks. As it now
stands, the Bill goes forward with less capacity to deal with this social phenomenon than it
did originally.
Clause 5, dealing with the functions and powers of the commission, was the subject of
an amendment moved by my colleague the member for Southern Maori, to make special
provision for the protection of children, and no doubt she will have something to say about
that.

## p. 4128 (#234) ###########################################

2 November
Human Rights Commission Bill
Clause 5A deals with reports to the Prime Minister, and we submitted an amendment
there to stress the paramouncy of Parliament rather than that of the Prime Minister, and to
1equire that some, at any rate, of the reports which are provided for here shall be directed to
Parliament as a legislative body, still preserving the cloak of confidentiality for those
recommendations that deal with proposed Government policies, because I believe the
commission should be free to have an intimacy of association between itself and the
Government as to matters that are still under discussion, and any Government should have
freedom of action until decision is crystallised.
Clause 14 is the initial clause of Part II, dealing with the topic of unlawful discrimination
as a whole, and is directed to the topic of employment. That, of course, is a fruitful field for
discrimination, and any realistic history of the development of the master-and-servant
relationship will necessarily be littered with examples of victimisation. Many of these are
directly political matters. Others have strong political overtones, and although it is undoub-
tedly necessary to outlaw discrimination as the Bill does, on the grounds of sex, marital
status, or religious or ethical belief, that in our judgment is not sufficient. To give adequate
immunity it is necessary to add to those categories the possibility of political belief. That is all
the more important in view of the attitude of the Government to those voters who have had
the temerity to proclaim their opposition to the Government.
Every elector is entitled to a secret vote, but if he cares to reveal his political affiliation
or just express openly a lack of confidence in the Government, or even open hostility to it,
then he should not be victimised thereby. Events over the last 2 years demonstrate the need
to protect those who have dared to differ. In reply to our move, the Government said it was
not necessary, that nothing had happened to show a need for this, and that the present law
was satisfactory. Be that as it may, we are, by this Bill, changing the law by saying that you
cannot discriminate on certain stated grounds. As a result there is the clear inference that
makes it impossible to sack a worker because of religious conviction, but, by clear inference,
this very action makes it lawful to sack a worker for political reasons.
The Minister of Justice said that he would not contemplate having a communist on his
payroll. If every employer adopted the same attitude, that would deny to communists the
right to earn a living. They would be rusticated and abandoned, not for anything done, or
even said, but because of thoughts, and that would apply to people of other political
persuasions. If the Government believes that any party should be banned, it has the
parliamentary numbers to say so, and do so, and it should not be resorting to back-door
subterfuge to achieve that end.
Part VI deals with industrial unions and professional and trade associations, and was the
subject of a great deal of discussion which will be adverted to briefly by some of my
colleagues. Finally, I want to close by contrasting the timidity with which this Bill defers to
other legislation with the manner in which another measure before us has a much bolder and
more drastic approach. Clause 82 (2) states, "Except as expressly provided in this Act,
nothing in this Act shall limit or affect the provisions of any other Act." In other words, it is
subservient to the whole of the statute book, and has to be read subject to anything else that
is there. Contrast that with this clause which appears in a Bill we will be debating later
tonight, and which is the main operative clause, "This section shall have effect notwithstand-
ing anything to the contrary in any other Act." That is a provision which enables that section
to override the whole of the statute book, and as I have said is in stark contrast to the
timidity with which this Bill approaches the very important question of human relationships
and human rights.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The Minister in reply.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Mr Speaker-
Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon): Mr Speaker-

to take into account the political beliefs of its own employees. The Minister of Justice asked
the association representatives whether they would be prepared to accept as a secretary of
the association or as a leading officer a person holding, as a political belief, that there was no
such thing as civil rights. The association said immediately that it would not be prepared to
accept such an employee.

Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): In the Committee stage of the Human Rights Commission Bill
Labour members pointed out very clearly some of its deficiencies. It could possibly be
accepted that some Government members had good intentions about the Bill, but, unfortu-
nately, one is reminded of the old axiom that the road to hell is paved with good intentions.
Clause 59 is an example of this, exactly and specifically. The main thrust and intent of clause
59 has nothing whatsoever to do with human rights. Clause 59, as was pointed out in the
Committee stage, stems from the manic attitude that the National Government has towards
industrial unions, and from the rather basic antipathy of Government members towards the
trade union movement. It is unfortunate, because in a way it will be part of the catalogue of
errors committed in the name of industrial legislation since this Government has been in
power. We have seen the result of those errors in the industrial legislation passed, and the
record number of industrial stoppages, the highest since the 1951 dispute.
The member for Lyttelton labours under a misconception about the Bill. She said she
was proud to read this morning that a woman jockey had won a race, and that this Bill had
made it possible. The Bill has not yet been passed, so how could the Bill have made it
possible for a woman jockey to win a race? This is one of the many misconceptions contained
in clause 59, which suggests that an individual within an organisation should have the right,
despite the democratic decisions of the majority of its members, to go outside an organisa-
tion and do something that is possibly detrimental to it. It was pointed out in the Committee
stage that clause 59 completely contravenes ILO convention 89, which deals with the
freedom of organisations. Under that convention organisations are free to determine their
own rules without interference by other authorities, including the Government.
We have in Part VI of the Bill something that is detrimental to the ordinary person who
is involved in the trade union movement. An example of what can occur was seen in a recent
dispute in the timber workers' union, where officials who were democratically elected by
members apparently lost the support of some members, and, whatever the rights and wrongs
of the group involved in the dispute, the members of that group took action against the
democratically elected officers of the union. Clause 59 will encourage that sort of behaviour
within organised, responsible trade unions and will destroy majority decisions, destroy
democratic organisation, and invite anarchy within the trade union movement. The clause
will also enable a few within a union to disrupt and intimidate, contrary to the union's rules.
There is no need to have clause 59 or Part VI of the Bill because, under the rules of the
Department of Labour, every union must have a disciplinary code attached to its rule book.
That code provides protection for individual members in disputes with officials or other
members of the union. I remember clause 14 of the watersiders' disciplinary code, which
stated that any union member could take action against an official if he thought that the
official was bringing the union into disrepute. If the union had a member like the member for
Awarua, who is trying to interject, any union member could take action against that member
for his manner of behaviour within the confines of a responsible Parliament, and he would be
disciplined by the union within the framework of those rules. A disciplinary code can go into
the rule book only after it has been approved, at a union meeting, then examined, analysed,
and finally accepted by the Department of Labour-and this is where it should belong. It
should belong within the rules of a union. The Minister of Justice was Minister of Labour for
a while, and he would appreciate that the rules accepted by the Department of Labour cover
union discipline, which is something that is needed. If we needed to protect individuals, this
clause would have been far better protecting the shareholders of some of the big finance
houses that have collapsed. The member for Awarua, who has this mad passion against trade
unions, should have come forward with a clause to protect the shareholders who lost their
life savings when some of the big finance houses collapsed.

The question of the third reading not being a proper occasion for referring to arguments
is reinforced in Speaker's ruling 39/5, which states: "In a third reading debate a member may
advance any reason why a Bill should not be passed but he does not give in detail arguments
in support of the point. He may comment on an amendment he put forward in the
Committee but must not argue its merits." In other words, it is an occasion for drawing
attention in passing to amendments that were defeated, but not for a long discussion on
matters that were defeated by way of amendment in the Committee.
The honourable member is quite entitled to refer to the amendment she moved, or any
other amendment for that matter, for the purpose of placing it in the records of the House,
but the Speakers' rulings make it quite clear that it is only for that purpose. Amendments can
therefore be recorded for reference, but the member cannot argue at length the merit of her
amendment. That was the point I was trying to make to the honourable member for Kapiti
when I interrupted his speech. He was expounding on an amendment that had been defeated
in the Committee of the Whole House. However, I think the honourable member for
Southern Maori was referring to clause 5(c). I gathered from what she was telling me that it
had been argued in the Committee of the Whole that the amendment that she proposed to
protect children was not necessary, because it was dealt with in clause 5(c). In that case, she
was quite entitled to discuss something that is in the Bill as it is written before us, but she is
not entitled to talk at length about the amendment that she proposed. I hope that I have
made it clear to the member.

From research and statistical data it is clear that the New Zealand environment is not

economic conditions can profoundly affect a child's personal health and development.
Presumably, therefore, people concerned about that aspect of human rights will be able to
make submissions to the commission under clause 5(c). I assume also that people who are

to make submissions to the commission under that provision. New Zealanders who are

5(c), particularly as cases of child abuse range in severity from relatively minor injuries to
severe injuries that result in the child's death. The latter comment applies particularly to pre-
school children. It is known that, for every case reported, there are many others that receive
no publicity, and we find that the evils of poverty are the main cause of child abuse.
Presumably New Zealanders who are concerned about the fact that a family's income
deprives that family of access to goods and services and therefore deprives the children from
adequate care will also be able to make submissions to the commission under clause 5(c). I
presume too that those who are concerned about the effects of financial hardship, unemploy-
ment, and illness of a parent, with the consequent inadequacy of income through the social
security benefit—and it is inadequate, particularly at times of crisis, such as when parents
separate-will be able to make submissions to the commission. Presumably New Zealanders
who are concerned about the children at risk in custody proceedings and decisions will also
be able to make submissions. I think, for instance, of those who are concerned that, ideally,
the present custody and access laws should be changed so that custody can continue to reside
in both parents, and who may very well want to urge under the provisions of clause 5(c) that
child advocates be provided to plead the case on behalf of children.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I am delighted that the honourable

towards children's rights or the rights of the aged, the sick, the pregnant woman, or any
group whose human rights are not clearly understood in our community. I do not think that
in my parliamentary career I will be associated with a Bill more important than this one. I am

ments some time next year, but I have to be very careful in finding and selecting the right

Human Rights Commission Bill
made by the weak against people in those organisations. As I have said, 3 years ago nine

powerful and unscrupulous men in that organisation.
Clause 59 enables a member of an organisation to complain to the commission if the
organisation of which he is a member, or any officer or agent of that organisation, in carrying
on or purporting to carry on the affairs of the organisation, threatens him with the use of
violence in order to induce him to agree to a course of action. That person makes a
complaint to the commission, and if it is possible to resolve his complaint within the relevant
industrial jurisdiction, the commission is then obliged to send it for industrial jurisdiction.
Surely members opposite are not saying that a New Zealander who happens to be a member
of a trade union or any other professional organisation should be denied the resolution of his
simple human rights or that he should be denied his dignity as an individual?

because of their concern with human rights. As I have told the House, I think of the
Ombudsman Act 1962, the Race Relations Act 1971, and Equal Pay Act 1972. It was at the

discrimination against women in employment. As the member for Lyttelton has pointed out,
this Bill now gives effect to this undertaking given in 1972, and although we lost that
election, we committed ourselves to that course. This third National Government is now
bringing forward the Human Rights Commission Bill, and I am quite certain it will be
welcomed by the vast majority of people as another step forward in a society which concerns
itself with the human rights of every individual.

Clause 4. Issue of interception warrant.
The principal Act is hereby amended by inserting, after section 4, the following section:
"4A. (1) On an application made in writing by the Director, or by a person authorised in writing
in that behalf by the Director, the Minister may issue an interception warrant authorising the
interception or seizure of any communication not otherwise lawfully obtainable by the person
making the interception or seizure, if he is satisfied by evidence on oath given by the Director, or
by the person so authorised, that-
"(a) The interception or seizure is necessary either-
"(i) For the detection of activities prejudicial to security; or
"(ii) For the purpose of gathering foreign intelligence information essential to secur-
ity; and
"(b) The value of the information sought to be obtained is such as to justify the particular
interception or seizure; and
"(c) The information is not likely to be obtained by any other means.
"(2) Any such interception warrant shall:
"(a) Specify the type of communication to be intercepted or seized; and
66
"(b) State the identity of the persons, if known, whose communications are sought to be
intercepted or seized, or (where the identity of the persons is not known) the place in
respect of which communications may be intercepted or seized; and
"(c) Specify the person who may make the interception or seizure; and
"(d) Contain such terms and conditions as the Minister considers advisable in the public interest;
and
"(e) Be valid for the period specified therein.
“(3) Any such interception warrant may include-
"(a) A direction to any person or persons or class of persons employed in the State Services,
otherwise than in the Police or the Armed Forces, to give such assistance as may be
specified in the warrant in making the interception or seizure; and, where any such
direction is given, the warrant shall also contain a direction that the services of the
persons who are directed to assist shall be made available to the Security Intelligence
Service by the Ministers of the Crown and the officers and employees of the State
Services who are in any way in control of the persons who are directed to assist:
"(b) A request to any other person or persons or class of persons to give such assistance as may
be specified in the warrant in making the interception or seizure; and, where any such
request is made to any persons who are in the employment of another person, the
warrant shall also contain a request that the services of the persons who are requested to
assist shall be made available to the Security Intelligence Service by the employers of
those persons and all other persons who are in any way in control of the persons who are
requested to assist.
"(4) The Minister shall, as soon as practicable after the close of each year ending with the 31st
day of March, review all warrants issued under subsection (1) of this section for the preceding 12
months, and prepare and lay before Parliament a report relating to the interception warrants issued
for the purposes of subparagraph (i) of paragraph (a) of subsection (1) of this section and the
interceptions and seizures made for those purposes in the immediately preceding year, which
report shall not disclose information that is prejudicial to security, and shall have regard to—
(a) The number of warrants issued for the purposes of that subparagraph; and
(b) The average length of time for which the last-mentioned warrants were in force; and
(c) The methods of interception and seizure used under the last-mentioned warrants,―
and shall provide a general assessment of the importance of the warrants issued for the purposes
of that subparagraph.
"(5) Every person who, by any interception warrant issued under subsection (1) of this section, is
authorised to intercept or seize any communication, or is directed or requested to give any
assistance in making the interception or seizure, is justified in making the interception or seizure,
and in taking any reasonable action necessarily involved in making or assisting to make the
interception or seizure, in accordance with the terms and conditions of the warrant; and
"(a) No civil or criminal proceedings shall lie against him by reason of his so doing; and
"(b) The issue of the warrant shall not be subject to judicial review under Part I of the Judicature
Amendment Act 1972 or otherwise.
"(6) Subsection (5) of this section is in addition to and not in derogation of any other enactment
relating to the execution of warrants.
"(7) This section shall have effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other Act."

The ACTING DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: I have to report that I have been asked to recall

Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I requested that you be recalled, Mr Speaker,
because I believed that there was a basic misunderstanding about what the member for
Onehunga said, and what the Chairman took from his statement. Under Standing Order
184, the Chairman took the statement as a personal reflection upon the private affairs or the
integrity of the Prime Minister. That would be so if the member for Onehunga said that he
believed that the Prime Minister was someone who was not trustworthy, or that he had
abused a situation; but, in fact, all that the member for Onehunga stated was his own
personal view about whether he thought a certain person should be trusted in a particular
position. I draw to your attention the fact that in this Bill the Prime Minister, by reason of his
being the head of the Security Intelligence Service, is given certain powers, and whether or
not he is the proper person to be in that position becomes relevant. The member for
Onehunga stated a view that is clearly strongly held, that he personally did not trust the
Prime Minister in that position. This is a debating chamber, and that is a strongly held view.
It is not one that has been ruled out before.
There is no requirement upon members of the House to trust each other. We are
required to address each other respectfully, but we do not have to say that we trust each
other. Indeed, I imagine a number of members opposite could probably say fairly strongly

Mr ACTING SPEAKER: It is unfortunate, on any occasion, that the Committee should
have to request the attendance of the Speaker to adjudicate on a ruling given by the
Chairman, or on procedures required to be taken by him. I am not required to rule on the
question of relevancy, even though the matter was referred to by the Minister of Justice.
Indeed, if I were asked to do so, I would have no hesitation in saying that I have no
jurisdiction. Speaker's ruling 47/2 states: "In Committee the Chairman of Committees is (1)
the sole judge on the question of relevancy; and . . . (4) any such ruling of the Chairman can
only be corrected or reversed by the House itself by resolution upon motion with notice."
Two matters have been brought to my attention. The first is whether the use of certain
words is unparliamentary, or whether they infringe Standing Orders, the procedures of the
House, or Speaker's rulings. The second is whether the member for Onehunga is defying a
ruling given by the Acting Chairman of Committees to withdraw certain words. As I
understand it from what honourable members have told me, the matter of the appropriate-
ness or otherwise of the words attributed to the honourable member for Onehunga was
raised after the Acting Deputy Chairman of Committees had required the words to be
withdrawn. The Minister of Energy Resources has told me that there were two or three
requests for the words to be withdrawn, and it was after that that the matter was raised.
One or two members have pointed out that this is a debating chamber and that we must
accept that at times debating will be robust. I certainly would not wish it to be otherwise, but
when words or expressions used go beyond being robust it is a different matter, but it is
difficult for me as Acting Speaker who was not present at the time to decide, because as I
know from experience, words used may be offensive in a certain context or used in a certain
manner. I believe that the best judge of whether the words are offensive or otherwise must
be the person presiding over the House or Committee at the time, who, in this instance, was
the Acting Deputy Chairman of Committees. So it seems to me that if he considered the
repeatedly used words "I cannot trust that man" offensive in terms of Standing Order 184,
which states that "All imputations of improper motives, or unbecoming reference to a
member's private affairs, and all personal reflections, shall be deemed highly disorderly,"
then he was in a position to judge. He considered the words in the manner in which they
were used to be an infringement of that part of the Standing Order which involves personal
reflections.
Another honourable member thought that the Acting Deputy Chairman was correct in
deeming them to be highly disorderly, and if they were highly disorderly then they must be
withdrawn, which leads me to the second point. Under Standing Order 37 any Acting
Chairman has all the powers, responsibilities and prerogatives of the Chairman of Commit-
tees as though he had been in the chair at the time. Therefore there is no question about the
Acting Deputy Chairman's ability in regard to the lawfulness of his requirement to the
member to withdraw the words. At that stage the honourable member for Onehunga put
himself in a position of defying a ruling given by the Chairman. In other words he is putting
himself offside of rulings made in the House.
The ruling given by the Chairman on this occasion must be upheld if, in his opinion, he
considered the words to be offensive in terms of the Standing Order, and he was quite proper
in requiring them to be withdrawn. Had there been any doubt about the offensiveness or
otherwise of the phrase or expression used, then the proper time to have raised that with the
Acting Deputy Chairman of Committees would have been then and there, and not after he
had apparently decided that the words should be withdrawn, and had required the member
to do so. It was at that stage, when he refused to withdraw them, that the Chairman's ruling
about the appropriateness of the words was apparently brought up. In my opinion, that was
too late. I therefore uphold the ruling of the Acting Deputy Chairman of Committees, and
require that the member for Onehunga should withdraw the expression attributed to him
that he cannot trust this man, in relation to the Prime Minister.
Before I finally require him to do so, I should point out again to honourable members
that although this is a robust debating chamber it is not one where robustness should extend
or degenerate into an attack on the person of a member. There is always a motion before us
that a certain clause stand part, that a certain Bill be read a second time, or whatever, and
that should be the motion exercising the attention of members, and not whether an
honourable member is young, old, male, female, silly, wise, or whatever. Those matters are
irrelevant. I invite honourable members to ponder them carefully, because one argumentum


## p. 4147 (#253) ###########################################

2 November
4147
New Zealand SIS Amendment Bill
ad hominem, if my Latin is correct, will lead to another, one attack on a person will lead to a
counter attack on another person and, at that stage, I am sure that honourable members are
well aware that we are leading ourselves towards disorder, and therefore to a termination of
the proper business of the House.
I therefore require the honourable member for Onehunga to withdraw the expression
that he cannot trust this man. Perhaps the honourable member did not hear me. I repeat that
I now require him to withdraw the expression that was taken exception to in the Committee
of the Whole, and that he was required by the Acting Deputy Chairman of Committees to
withdraw the expression, "I cannot trust this man."

4A. Destruction of irrelevant records obtained by interception-The principal Act is
hereby amended by inserting, after the said section 4A, the following section:

seizes any communication in accordance with any interception warrant shall, as soon as
practicable after the interception or seizure,—
"(a) Destroy any copy that he may make of the communication or any part thereof,
and any record, whether in writing or otherwise, of the information obtained
by that interception or seizure, except so far as the information recorded
therein relates directly or indirectly to the detection of activities prejudicial to
security or comprises foreign intelligence information essential to security:
"(b) Where the communication has been seized from mail in transit, return it to the
mail for delivery in the normal course:
"(c) In the case of any other letter or document or thing that has been intercepted or
seized, return it to the place from which it was intercepted or seized if the
Director considers that it is practicable to do so.
"(2) Where the Director considers that the return of any communication to the mail
might lead to consequences that would endanger life or property, and in any other case
where the Director considers that it is not practicable to return any letter or document
or thing to the place from which it was intercepted or seized, the Director shall, as soon
as practicable after the interception or seizure, consult the Solicitor-General as to the
disposition of the communication, and shall dispose of it as the Solicitor-General may
require.
"(3) Every person who knowingly fails to comply with the foregoing provisions of this
section commits an offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine not exceeding
$1,000."

Speaker's Ruling on Third Readings
THURSDAY, 3 NOVEMBER 1977
Mr Acting Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
SPEAKER'S RULING ON THIRD READINGS
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: This may be a convenient time for me to read a ruling which
the Leader of the Opposition asked me to consider yesterday in relation to what would be
appropriate material in a third reading debate, particularly in view of the changes made in
the Standing Orders procedures in 1972, following the elimination of the debate on the
report back from the Committee of the Whole.
Our volume of Speakers' Rulings is dated 1969, which predates the change in Standing
Orders that deleted the debate on the question that the report be agreed to. The essence of
rulings 2, 3, and 4 on page 36 and the rulings on pages 38 to 40 appears to me to be, in
relation to the scope of the debate on the third reading, as follows: (1) Members must
confine themselves to the general principles of the Bill as it emerged from the Committee.
The debate on the third reading is narrower than that on the second reading, so that matters
reasonably related to the Bill, which may be discussed during the second reading, must be
excluded from the third reading. (2) Amendments that have been agreed to in the
Committee of the Whole may be referred to and their principles discussed, because they are
now included in the Bill. (3) Amendments considered in Committee but not agreed to may
be referred to for the purpose of recording them, but their merits must not be argued and
they cannot be discussed at length. They are no longer part of the Bill as it emerged from the
Committee. (4) Amendments ruled out of order must not be discussed. I am supported in
this by a ruling given by Mr Speaker Whitehead on 12 September 1973, in Hansard, Volume
385, at page 3535: "As for the parts that have been taken out, I see nothing wrong with a
member making reference to the fact that something was deleted from the Bill, but I do not
expect him to debate the part that was taken out. There is plenty of scope for the member to
speak to the Bill, but there is no arrangement in the third reading for discussion of matters
that are not now in the Bill. We should not be discussing the Bill that was presented to the
House last year. We are discussing the Bill as it has emerged from the Committee stage."
Later he said: . . . if parts of the Bill were deleted in that way it would be wrong for
members to debate the parts deleted. When I say 'debate' I mean debate the merits of the
parts that have been deleted. I see nothing wrong with a passing reference, but I do not want
debate at this time on the merits of the parts of the Bill that were deleted.” Of course, that
ruling was made by Mr Speaker Whitehead after the change in procedures recommended by
the Standing Orders Committee and agreed to by the House in 1972. I hope that is of some
help to the Leader of the Opposition.
66
Rt. Hon. W. Rowling: I don't know that it helps me much.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Well, I hope it clarifies the matter anyhow.
ELECTORAL AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Electoral Amendment
Bill be introduced. At the time of the passage of the 1975 Electoral Amendment Act the
National Party, then in Opposition, made it quite clear that it opposed some of the measures
included in that Bill. I must say that those measures had been widely canvassed in a special
select committee, and evidence had been heard on the proposals. This short Bill aims to
restore a number of the provisions of the principal Act to the position prevailing prior to the
enactment of the 1975 amendment. I propose to go through them as they are listed in the
explanatory note to the Bill.
The 1975 amendment provided that any candidate who was a school teacher or staff
member of a university and was supervising students preparing for examinations could
receive remuneration during the period he would otherwise have been required by law to be
placed on unpaid leave of absence. Now, as a result of administrative difficulties at the
primary and secondary schools level, it has been decided to limit that provision to university
staff only.


## p. 4158 (#264) ###########################################

4158
3 November
Electoral Amendment Bill
The meaning of "ordinarily resident in New Zealand" is expanded to cover children of
public servants serving overseas. That amendment is necessary as a result of the lowering of
the voting age to 18.
The Bill restores the residential requirement for registration in any electorate from 1
month, as at present, to 3 months, as it was previously. That provision is to be found in
clause 4.
The prohibition on inmates of penal institutions voting in parliamentary elections is re-
enacted, and the requirement that a list of all candidates and polling places be delivered
before polling day to each residence in every electorate is repealed.
Clause 7 repeals the contentious provision that permits a person to vote if he is entitled
to be registered but is not registered, and believes on reasonable grounds that he is, or
should have been, registered as an elector. Honourable members will recall that this caused
a great deal of confusion and the Chief Electoral Officer found that it was difficult for
returning officers in the last general election to determine whether the applicant had
reasonable grounds for believing he was, or should have been, registered as a voter.
The maximum amount of a candidate's election expenses is being raised from $2,000 to
$4,000, and the previous provision that permitted the use of loudspeakers, despite any local
bylaw to the contrary, is being repealed in line with our belief that this matter is more
properly left to the control of local authorities.
Clause 10 places a restriction on election advertisements. Under this clause it will be an
offence to publish an advertisement on behalf of a candidate without the candidate's
approval. Advertisements published with a candidate's authority and relating to him solely
as a candidate for a particular electorate will form part of his election expenses. This will
mean that advertisements at the national level, such as those relating to party leaders, will
not be included within the leader's election expenses.
The Government is aware that a number of measures contained in this Bill may be of
interest to political parties who are not represented in this Chamber, and others. I therefore
intend, at the appropriate time, to move that the Bill be referred to the Statutes Revision
Committee for study, knowing that most of the clauses were widely canvassed and con-
sidered in 1975.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): With some sadness I rise to note the untimeliness
of this move by the Government. Only last weekend we put the clocks forward an hour.
Here the Government is setting out to put them back by a number of years. I had intended
challenging the Minister to refer the Bill to a select committee so that the public could
express views on those provisions that set out to repeal what was done during the Labour
Government's term of office a few years ago. If those had been the only provisions in the
Bill, I imagine that the Minister would have driven on regardless. Fortunately, one or two
new provisions deserve, and certainly ought to receive, the scrutiny of the public-apart
from the desirability of having evidence taken on the measures we put on the statute book.
I shall advert to some of these. At first glance, clauses 2 and 3 seem to deal with matters
that call for a review. Clause 10, though lengthy and somewhat complex, appears to set out
to deal with a problem that could lend itself to a great deal of abuse, and I believe has been
the subject of abuse in the past-either consciously or unconsciously, intended or
unintended-whereby some candidates have deliberately set out not to know that others
were incurring expenditure on their behalf-a kind of injured innocence on their part. Some
candidates in parties which had better remained unnamed have lent themselves to this kind
of practice, having made it known that so long as something was done without their
knowledge they would not object. As a result, a substantial amount was spent on their behalf
to their advantage, but without their provable knowledge and, I think, to the public
detriment. If this clause enables that type of activity to be controlled and curbed, I certainly
favour it.
Regarding the other provisions, I genuinely believe the changes they set out to revoke
were moves towards a better democracy. They widened the area of the democratic process
which, by definition, ought to be agreed to and supported unless there are disadvantages that
can be discerned and demonstrated.
The shortening of the residential qualification from 3 months to 1 month was a good
move, having regard to the transient nature of much of New Zealand life at present. One
does not have available at short notice statistics showing how many changes of residence
there have been, particularly in suburban electorates, but they are very great and tend to be
on the increase. People should be entitled to vote in the area in which they are living, so long
as they have been there for more than sufficient time to avoid the charge of being


## p. 4159 (#265) ###########################################

3 November
4159
Electoral Amendment Bill
carpetbaggers. We believe that a month is adequate and that those who live in an electorate
for a month are rather more involved with that electorate than the electorate from which
they departed within the preceding 3 months. Our change was a good one.
The provision that clause 5 repeals extended the right of voting to persons in penal
institutions, and again I think that is democracy in being. It is true that some people made
the point that those who were sentenced to a term of imprisonment should be called upon to
forfeit some of their rights, which of course they do by their very incarceration. I still think
that they should not be deprived of the right of political representation of some kind. For
many years back, before we changed the law, there were people in penal institutions who did
have the right to vote, although it is acknowledged that it was seldom exercised, because no
facilities were provided for taking that vote.
Clause 7 repeals an experimental and radical change in the electoral law, which gave a
person the right to vote if he claimed that on reasonable grounds he was entitled to be on the
roll. Admittedly, in practice, this gave rise to some problems, but they could have been
ironed out in a progressive manner rather than in the negative way the Government has
chosen to adopt, by taking away the whole proposal.
Clause 9 gives back to local bodies a power that few abused, I grant, but some were
prone to abuse. By virtue of the powers vested in them by local legislation, some local bodies
did deprive candidates—and that meant all candidates in those electorates-of the right to
bring their message to the people. The use of loudspeakers has not been abused nor is it
likely to be abused. If it were, the people to put a stop to it are the electors themselves. No
intervention by a local body is needed to ensure that the inhabitants of an area are not
unduly interfered with through noise. The Labour Government made a good move, and the
present move to do away with it is a bad one. I am glad the Bill is to be referred to the
Statutes Revision Committee, and I shall be very interested to hear evidence either for or
against the Bill.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I was a member of the select committee
that considered the previous amending Bill in response to which some of the proposals in this
Bill have come forward. I do not accept for one moment that any provision in this Bill is a
move away from the democratic process. The clause to which reference was made in that
connection does exactly the opposite. Considerable concern was expressed when the Labour
Government, with its large majority in the House, forced through the provision which took
away from the elected representatives of the people the right to say whether there should be
noise pollution in their municipalities. Local bodies had always had the right to say whether
people could go around the streets using loudspeakers for electoral purposes. The Labour
Government, over the protests of the National Opposition, took away that right, but I do not
know that it achieved anything by it. We propose, in a democratic fashion, to give that right
back to the local bodies.
Clause 7, to which the member for Henderson referred, is small but important, because
it clears up an untidy matter that was the brainchild of one of the Labour members in
Government. In plain non-legal language, it said that if a man thought he was entitled to
vote then he was so entitled, but even after that provision had been passed it turned out that
the Labour Government did not know what it had been legislating for, and thousands upon
thousands of such votes were disallowed at the last general election. It would not work, it
could not work, and it never should have been enacted. There should be clear law defining
the right of an individual to vote, and accordingly we are going back to the point where there
was clear law. The legislation that was enacted did not do what was claimed for it, and in fact
the Labour Government did not know what it was enacting.
There could be argument about some of the other matters, such as whether people in
prisons should get a vote for the first time. One of the difficulties that arose here was the
question of which electorate such people should vote in. There are at least three possibilities,
none of them very satisfactory, so we are going back to the position that existed for so many
years.
I do not propose to debate this introduction at length. It carries out an undertaking we
gave when the previous amendment Bill was passed-that on becoming the Government we
would reverse some of those measures.
I believe that the increase in the maximum amount of election expenses is reasonable,
because, looking at the returns for the last election, it is obvious that many candidates were
pressing right up to the limit, and I am sure that many of them would not have been too well
pleased at a close scrutiny of their expenses. The limit should should provide reasonable
elbow-room so that candidates do not spend the last allowable dollar, thereby implying that
9 Vol. 415

they managed to press the amount down and squeeze it, whereas close inspection would

attempts to make the matter clearer. That is all I want to say at this stage, except to confirm
that the Bill has been brought in in accordance with an undertaking we gave at the time the

INDECENT PUBLICATIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Indecent Publications
Amendment Bill be introduced. This three-clause Bill makes important changes to the
provisions of the principal Act that govern interim restriction orders. As the law now stands,
when the Indecent Publications Tribunal has made a decision allowing the sale of a
publication, any interim restriction order that it has imposed on the sale of that publication is
automatically lifted. The problem caused by this automatic revocation was illustrated in the
recent experience concerning the publication entitled Down Under the Plum Trees. It will be
recalled that the tribunal's decision generated a controversy that culminated in an appeal
being lodged to determine the validity of the tribunal's finding. However, during the time
the appeal was pending and being determined, considerable numbers of the publication in


## p. 4167 (#273) ###########################################

3 November
4167
Indecent Publications Amendment Bill
question were sold.
As the appeal was dismissed, that feature of the "Plum Trees" case, as it turned out,
was of no significance, but it nevertheless pointed up the practical difficulty that, in similar
circumstances when an appeal was allowed, the decision of the Supreme Court could well be
robbed of its significance if the publication in question had in the meantime been distributed
and sold. Accordingly, the Bill provides that an interim restriction order imposed by the
tribunal, if not revoked by the tribunal, does not lapse until either the 28 days in which an
appeal may be brought have elapsed, or, if an appeal has been brought, that appeal has
been determined.
The Bill also provides for a judge of the Supreme Court to impose an interim restriction
order on the application of a person appealing against the tribunal's decision, or to revoke
such an order on the application of the respondent in any appeal. The purpose of this is
simply to ensure that the court does not lack power to consider the question of an interim
restriction order in cases in which no such order is in force when an appeal is filed.
Although it must be accepted that the continuation of any interim restriction order for
28 days after the tribunal has cleared a publication for sale may cause inconvenience, it must
be noted that there will not be such an order in every case considered by the tribunal. I shall
go more fully into that when the Bill is read a second time.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The Minister describes the Bill as being
important, but it is essentially procedural, and, as far as I can see, little objection can be
taken to patching up a gap than manifested itself in the case referred to by the Minister. As
he said, it was not harmful in that case because of the outcome of the appeal upholding the
decision of the tribunal. However, I can see that there could be a problem in a reverse case. I
hope that it will be availed of as little as possible, and that appeals from the tribunal may be
heard and disposed of within the present maximum period of 3 months. That may be
possible, with the increased numbers now sitting in the Supreme Court, though one notes
with regret the increasing incidence of sickness among the ranks of Her Majesty's judges.
However that may be, I am sure the Minister would not wish to see the provision put
into operation any more than is absolutely necessary and that the existing procedure can be
gone through sufficiently expeditiously for the appeal to be dealt with, heard, and disposed
of within the existing time span of 3 months.
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): At present, the Indecent Publications Tribunal has the right to
make an interim restriction order of up to 1 month, with an extension of up to 3 months. The
Bill ostensibly alters that provision to allow the interim restriction order to continue until
such time as the final decision is made, either by the tribunal, the chairman, or the Supreme
Court.
Could the Minister confirm whether the incentive for the chairman, the tribunal, or the
Supreme Court to make a decision without allowing the matter to drag on ad infinitum will
be eliminated? For example, if a book is given an interim restriction order and may be read
only by people over the age of 18 or 20 until a decision is made under the terms of this
legislation, it could still be circulated and read before an order is made to ban it. I think the
present period of 1 month-or 3 months-is a reasonable time for the tribunal to decide
whether a book has literary qualities, or is pornographic.
The proposed new section 14A(9) in clause 2 states: "The chairman or the tribunal may
on the ex parte application of any person interested or on his or its own motion revoke an
interim restriction order. . . ." It therefore appears that the chairman of the tribunal can
terminate or alter an interim restriction order on his own volition without consulting his
colleagues who may have made the original order. Is that correct?
Hon. David Thomson: I am advised that the Bill does not change the present law as far
as the powers of the tribunal are concerned, but does give power to the Supreme Court to
impose an interim restriction order. These powers are set out in clause 3.
Mr ISBEY: The chairman of the tribunal may on the ex parte application of any person
interested, or on his own motion, revoke an interim restriction order. So an interim
restriction order can be imposed by a tribunal, but the chairman by himself can revoke that
interim restriction order, which does not appear to me to be an effective or judicial function
for a chairman by himself. Will the Bill go to a select committee?

1. Mr KIRK (Sydenham), on behalf of Mr BLANCHFIELD (West Coast), asked the

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I have read the article referred to, and
have also received a number of submissions both from manufacturers and from the
Sheepskin and Leather Products Manufacturers Association regarding the effect of the
imposition of sales tax on sheepskin car-seat covers. Details of sales of car-seat covers and of
other sheepskin products by a comprehensive range of manufacturers were recently
presented to Cabinet. It was agreed that no special provision should be made for sheepskin
car-seat covers, but that I should obtain information of sales over a longer period of time and

Mr Kirk: Is the Minister aware that the President of the New Zealand Sheepskin and

that quarter. I remind the member, however, that when sales tax is imposed on any item, it is

that they have been badly hit. I cannot accept any claims at face value without thorough
investigation of the worthiness of their arguments.
Mr Falloon: Have the manufacturers examined the potential for remission of customs

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I would have to confirm that point.

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I fail to see how that question bears on the subject at hand.
Hon. F. M. Colman: The Minister said that the worthiness of the case would be
considered. Would that not have been considered before the Government made its decision
to impose the levy?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: Naturally, very close attention is given to the effects of the
various measures provided in the Budget, but when we have reaction from people affected it
takes time to check on the validity of their cases, and the case of the sheepskin car-seat
covers is a particularly good example of that.

Foresty Encouragement Scheme-Planting of Special-purpose Species
10. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Forests: What encouragement is
given forestry encouragement grantees to diversify their planting into species that will
provide special-purpose timbers?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I reply on behalf of the Minister of Forests.
The forestry encouragement grants scheme is available to all landholders who wish to
undertake afforestation with any commercial species. Every project is considered on its
merits, and the only limitations imposed are the suitability of site and location for utilising
the material growth. Courses and field days are held for those interested in special-purpose
species, and the New Zealand Farm Forestry Association is actively supporting trials into
alternative shelter and production species. Landowners are becoming more aware of special-
use species, and recent applications approved show a growing preference for alternative
species where quality growing sites are available. A survey is being undertaken to ascertain
the most suitable special-purpose species for specific districts, and the results will be made
known to intending grantees to encourage diversification in the future.

Pacific Island Workers and Industrial Relations Act
11. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Immigration: Has his department
taken any steps to inform workers from the Pacific, either before or after arrival, of their
obligations as employees under the Industrial Relations Act and the awards and agreements
made under it?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): Under the memoranda of understanding
concerning the official work permit scheme, which was agreed between the New Zealand
Government and the Governments of Fiji, Tonga, and Western Samoa, it is the responsibil-
ity of the Island Governments to select workers and to provide them with pre-departure
instruction on working and living conditions in New Zealand, and on union membership,
and to improve where necessary their ability to communicate in English on arrival. Suitable
information on such matters is available to the Island Governments through the New
Zealand high commission in Suva, Nuku'alofa, and Apia. When employers seek authority to
bring workers to New Zealand under the official work permit scheme they are advised that
they have a responsibility to inform workers of their rights and obligations. After arrival in
New Zealand, workers from the Pacific have access to the same sources of information on
these matters as all New Zealand workers.

Drownings and Water Safety Campaign
17. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: Has he read the
article in the Sunday News of 30 October which reads: "Last weekend, the first of the

Mr COMBER (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Internal Affairs): The
Minister of Internal Affairs replies as follows: "I have seen the article, which went on to say,
'It is over to the public to take notice of the publicity and to be more careful.' The New
Zealand Water Safety Council is continually appraising the direction of its publicity. It has
expert knowledge and professional service to do this, and it also knows it has my full support
for its efforts."
Mr Isbey: Does the Minister have full confidence in the methods by which the New
Zealand Water Safety Council operates since it has only an executive director domiciled in

Mr COMBER: The Minister has total confidence in the personnel of the Water Safety
Council, which has available to it the expertise of the Tourist and Publicity Department and
an advertising agency. Members of the council also include the Ministry of Transport (the
small boats safety campaign) and the Department of Health (health education campaign).
It might be helpful to the member and the House to observe that only last week I drew to the
council's attention a photograph which had appeared in a Wellington daily newspaper
depicting six people-and from my observation three were adults-in a small dinghy. Two at
least were standing, and none was wearing a lifejacket.

people, and with it being the start of the summer season, will the Minister carry out an
investigation into the operations of the New Zealand Water Safety Council to ensure that the
number of drownings is reduced completely for this season?
Mr COMBER: Obviously no such guarantee can be given, but we are monitoring the
effects of the publicity campaign. The grant this year has been increased from $130,000 to
$166,000. The main publicity for the summer season will start on 14 November, with water
safety week, and will continue through to about April. The council also tries to sustain
unpaid media coverage, and I also observe that the small boats safety campaign started at
Labour weekend.

who had given a great deal of their time and ability to regional development had had to write
to the Minister-as regional councils had done-expressing frustration about the Govern-
ment's indifference and lack of industrial development aid.
The Minister had been asked to revert to the previous higher levels of incentives. Many
Southland factories had closed, and factories in other areas would close if the Government
did not adopt a more positive attitude. The Wairarapa Regional Development Council had
told the Minister that higher rail freight charges would encourage more industries to
Auckland and Wellington. Rail charges in Southland had risen by more than 80 percent, and
companies there could not compete unless they were given some incentive.
Today Comalco, the largest employer in Southland, had told its staff that their jobs
were in jeopardy because of the Prime Minister's actions-which ran counter to the principle
of regional development. The Labour Government had commenced re-negotiations with
Comalco that would have ensured continuity and expansion of the company's activities. The
high cost of development affected industry from one end of the country to the other. The
Government was determined to increase freight rates; so industry had to be close to the
largest markets-Auckland, the Waikato, and Wellington.

started with a great deal of hullabaloo and ballyhoo in 1973 had quickly shown that once

clear that they were pleased that the refinements and trimmings that the Government had
found it necessary to make last year had been reinstated this year. Regional development
had received special mention in the recent mini-Budget.
Statistics he had received from the Department of Labour had a direct bearing on the
position of factories in the 11 regional development areas. In Northland from January 1976
to the end of September 1977, 19 factories had closed and 16 factories had opened. Fifty
people had been employed in the factories that had closed and 77 people were employed in
the factories that opened—a net gain of 27 jobs. On the East Coast 4 factories employing 21
people had closed and 6 factories employing 13 people had opened—a net gain of 2 factories
and net loss of 8 jobs. The East Coast was the only regional development area where there
had been a net loss of jobs. In the King Country 5 factories employing 27 people had closed,
and 11 factories employing 28 people had opened—a gain of 6 factories and 1 job
In Taranaki 25 factories employing 104 people had closed and 45 factories employing
132 people had opened-a net gain of 20 factories and 28 jobs. In Wanganui 14 factories
employing 80 people had closed and 20 factories employing 91 people had opened—a net
gain of 6 factories and 11 jobs. In the Wairarapa 18 factories employing 103 people had
closed and 20 factories had opened creating 171 jobs-a net gain of 2 factories and 68 jobs.
In Marlborough, an area that had developed late, 3 factories employing 8 people had closed
and 9 factories employing 34 people had opened—a gain of 6 factories and 26 jobs.

FINANCE BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): I move, That the Finance Bill be
introduced. This is the annual washing-up Bill dealing with miscellaneous financial matters.
Clauses 2, 3, and 4 re-enact various provisions of earlier Finance Acts and consolidate and
simplify those provisions that still have effect. Clause 2 relates to free travel for disabled
servicemen from the two world wars. Clause 3 deals with the Nauru and Ocean Island
phosphate trade. Clause 4 consolidates legislation relating to war memorials. Clause 5
relates to the Statutes Amendment Act 1937, which is repealed by clause 21 of the Bill. The
clause preserves the effect of section 17 of that Act, which precludes the payment of damages


## p. 4193 (#299) ###########################################

4 November
4193
Finance Bill
for pain and suffering resulting from accidents causing death if the cause of action arose
before 1 April 1974.
Clause 6 saves the effect of any provision that may later be inserted into the Act in the
event of the repeal of the enactment inserting it. Clause 7 enables the making of Orders in
Council authorising contributors to the Government Superannuation Fund to contribute to
the fund on the basis of salary increases delayed by the wage freeze. Clauses 8, 9, and 10 are
to form part of the Gaming Duties Act 1971. These provisions are associated with changes
contained in the Racing Amendment Bill that is now before the House. The effect of the
proposed amendments to the Gaming Duties Act is that restricted totalisator clubs will pay
totalisator duty at the rate of 5 percent of gross investments as compared with 8.5 percent
and 9 percent payable by totalisator clubs.
Clause 11 repeals the Linen Flax Corporation Act 1945, abolishes the corporation, vests
the assets subject to the existing liabilities of the corporation-in the Crown, and author-
ises the sale of the corporation's assets. Clause 12 authorises the payment in accordance with
an agreement of $100,035.61 by the Natural Gas Corporation to Shell BP and Todd Oil
Services Ltd which, because of the Stabilisation of Prices Regulations 1974, could not
otherwise be paid. The amount is taxable.
Clause 13 validates the actions of the Ashley and Manawatu pest destruction boards in
purchasing houses for occupation by employees of the Agricultural Pests Destruction
Council. Clause 14 validates the transfer from the general funds of the Earthquake and War
Damage Commission to the disaster account of $5 million to meet claims resulting from the
floods in Wellington and the Hutt Valley on 20 December 1976. Clause 15 validates the
payment of standard tertiary bursaries before the making of the regulations authorising their
payment. Clause 16 validates the payment of secondary school bursaries at the rate of $400
per annum from the final term of 1976; the regulations authorising payment at that rate were
not made until August 1977.
Clause 17 validates the payment of certain motor vehicle allowances in connection with
brucellosis and tuberculosis tests before the making of the regulations authorising their
payment. Clause 18 validates excess unauthorised expenditure in the 1976 financial year by
the board of trustees of the Maori Education Foundation. The statutory limit is $200 and the
amount expended in that year was $555. Clause 19 authorises a temporary increase for the
year 1977 from $1,000 to $2,200 in the level of unauthorised expenditure by the University
Grants Committee. Clause 20 authorises, with effect from 15 June 1977, the transfer of up to
$4 million from the Consolidated Revenue Account to the motor vehicle third party
indemnity fund to meet any shortfall in the fund. The amount of $2 million was transferred
on 15 June 1977. Clause 21 repeals 17 Finance Acts and several other spent statutes.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
STATE SERVICES CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): I move, That the State Services
Conditions of Employment Bill be introduced. This is a Bill to consolidate and amend the
State Services Remuneration and Conditions of Employment Act 1969. The broad purpose
both of the current legislation and of this Bill is to provide a system for prescribing conditions
of employment in the State services-including arbitration when necessary-and for co-
ordinating the actions of the various State services employing authorities in their dealings
with the employee organisations.
The Bill results from three distinct considerations. First, the recommendations of the
1972 Royal Commission on Salary and Wage Fixing Procedures in the New Zealand State
Services; secondly, the experience of employers in operating under existing legislation; and
thirdly the Government's programme of industrial reform arising from its election policy. In
a climate of considerable public interest and allegations of State pay leadership the 1972
royal commission concluded "that the balance of probabilities suggests that many State
servants must be ahead of their private sector counterparts". There has been much
disagreement about the extent of that pay leadership, but it is generally accepted that it
existed to some degree.
Accordingly, this Bill, while remaining firmly based on the fair external relativity
principle of the 1969 Act, introduces a sophisticated procedure for making deductions from
the general adjustments made regularly to State services pay scales. These deductions are
designed to compensate for adjustments and increases already paid out, and so to eliminate
the element of double counting which the royal commission had found to occur. In the
10.


## p. 4194 (#300) ###########################################

4194
4 November
State Services Conditions of Employment Bill
interim this has been counteracted in negotiations. The deductions under the proposed
system are subject to 3-yearly review and appeal to the new Arbitration Court. Linked with
this new system of general adjustments are a number of associated changes, including
replacement of the half-yearly survey system by annual adjustments.
Moving away from the royal commission's findings, the one major deficiency encoun-
tered by employers operating under the 1969 Act is the lack of clear guidance in setting pay
scales when the category of workers concerned does not occur in employment outside the
State services. In these circumstances external relativity becomes impracticable, and it is
reasonable to look to recruitment and retention of staff as the yardstick in setting conditions.
In fact, the State Services Tribunal has ruled that for State employees with no outside
counterparts the recruitment and retention criteria of the 1969 Act cannot apply. That has
been rectified in this Bill, but only to the extent that those criteria can now lawfully be taken
into account.
Other improvements in procedures include a right for employee organisations to take a
dispute to arbitration without having to wait for the employing authority to issue a
determination. Also, a voluntary mediation service on the lines already available in the
private sector is established. Arising from the Government's own policy of industrial
reforms, including the other Bills involved in the package to come in shortly, this Bill
reconstitutes the present State Services Tribunal and the single service tribunals to mesh in
with an Arbitration Court in the private sector. These changes, which include a change of
name to Public Sector Tribunal, will make no difference to the arbitrating bodies already
familiar to State employees. In accordance with Government policy, however, the proposal
will provide for a degree of common membership of tribunals between the public and private
sectors, and this, by the pooling and monitoring of information about wage movements,
should greatly increase co-ordination in wage fixing throughout the economy.
Finally, the Bill introduces into the State services controls on unjustified industrial
action already implemented in the private sector. Penalties are provided for two types of
offence only: for strikes and lockouts in export slaughterhouses and essential services
without giving the required notice of intent; and, secondly, for strikes and lockouts over
matters broadly concerned with the interpretation of existing agreements in cases in which
procedures for settling the disputes are available. The scope of the penalty provisions has
been overstated by opponents of the Bill. The major purpose of this section is to ensure that
all employment is the same and that disputes are settled with the minimum of disruption. In
line with corresponding provisions in the Industrial Relations Act, the motivation for the
proposals in this Bill lies in the vulnerability of our export trade to industrial strife, and in the
commitments that were made at the last elections. On penal provisions the parties had
clear that responsible groups who abide by the procedures laid down have nothing what-
soever to fear from this section of the legislation.
soever to fear from this section of the legislation.

Bill will not be referred to a select committee.

can decide whether we want to examine it further or would rather not have it at all. The 1974
Standing Orders Committee reiterated the recommendations of the 1972 Standing Orders
Committee. The recommendations were accepted by the House and have not been changed.
The only change made in 1974 was to limit the time of the introductory debate to 2 hours, to
be divided equally between the Government and the Opposition.

explanatory note to them stated that the new regulation 64(a) authorised the State Services
Commission to suspend from duty without pay any employee who refused or failed to carry
out his normal duties. Regulation 64(b) enabled employees to be laid off work without pay
where, by reason of the failure of any group or class of employees to carry out their normal
duties, there was insufficient work for them to perform. Regulation 64(c) provided that
nothing in the regulations would prevent disciplinary action being taken against an
employee.
Part VIII of this legislation will not come into force unless there is an occasion when, in
the Minister's and the Government's opinions, it is necessary. The short title stated that Part
VIII shall come into force on a date to be appointed by the Governor-General by Order in
Council, and different dates may be appointed for the purposes of different provisions of
that part of the Bill or for the purposes of different groups or classes of employees of the
State services. So part of the regulations that have been in force will, with the passing of this
Bill, no longer be in force should there be problems, except by Order in Council.
