WANGANUI COMPUTER CENTRE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): I move, That the Wanganui Computer
Centre Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill makes four substantive amendments to the
Wanganui Computer Centre Act which was passed last year. These amendments have all
arisen out of suggestions made by the Privacy Commissioner and the policy committee, who
have now had the opportunity to observe the workings of the computer centre and the
legislation.
The first proposal will permit the authorised users of the computer system to place
fictitious information on the computer system for the limited purposes of training
employees, testing the system, and detecting any misuse of the computer system. This is in
keeping with the general spirit of the Act, which aims at ensuring that there is no
unwarranted intrusion upon the privacy of the individual. To use live information for these
purposes would be contrary to that principle. At the same time, however, considerable care
has been taken to ensure that the use of fictitious information is controlled.
The second change relates to the power of the Privacy Commissioner to obtain evidence
in the course of his inquiries. The Privacy Commissioner is now given powers to obtain
evidence that closely parallel those possessed by the ombudsman. The third change allows
the Privacy Commissioner, with the prior approval of the Governor-General in Council, to
delegate part of his powers under the Act to any one of his staff. The powers he may delegate
are receiving requests and acquiring information under section 14(1), and receiving and
investigating, but not reporting on, complaints under sections 15 and 16. The final change is
to the offences section of the Act, where a number of new offences have been created.
I am sure that this brief outline of the Bill will indicate to members that the Government
is taking steps to ensure that the balance achieved by the Wanganui Computer Centre
legislation between the needs of society and the rights of the individual is being maintained,
as recommended by the policy committee and the Privacy Commissioner.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
CUSTOMS ACTS AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That the Customs Acts
Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. This Bill amends the Customs Act 1966, the
Distillation Act 1971, and the Sales Tax Act 1974. It is basically in two parts. The first part
relates to the introduction of a new customs tariff, which it is proposed to bring into force on
1 July 1978. The second part relates to various amendments to the three Acts mentioned
earlier.
In view of its size and complexity it will be helpful to the House if I deal in some detail
with the proposal for the new tariff. Honourable members will be aware that the Govern-
ment confirmed a proposal by the previous Government that the current customs tariff
should be reviewed over a period of 2 years by an inter-departmental committee of officers
from the Customs Department and the Department of Trade and Industry. The committee
undertook a massive task, and I take this opportunity of thanking the chairman and
members for the work they put into their task. The review called for submissions from
interested parties, particularly manufacturers and importers, and also consulted, where
appropriate, with other Government departments and various trade groups. The end result
is the schedule to the Bill-all 555 pages of it: A substantially different form of tariff from the
present one is proposed. Two columns are provided for rates of duty-Normal Tariff and
Preferential Tariff. The "British Preferential" heading disappears. A third column is
provided to improve the collection of statistical data.
Anyone familiar with tariff documents will immediately appreciate the benefits of the
new layout. The actual number of tariff items has been reduced from about 4700 to about
2500, but at the same time about 6000 statistical items are provided. The Tariff Review
Committee's terms of reference requested the committee to review all tariff items; to
recommend a revised and restructured tariff compatible with modern trading conditions and
industrial requirements, and which would facilitate more adequate collection of statistical
information; to incorporate various nomenclature amendments recommended by the
Customs Co-operative Council in Brussels; to incorporate various amendments arising from


## p. 4209 (#315) ###########################################

4 November
4209
Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
a revision of the Standard International Trade Classification for Statistics; to take into
account trade policy considerations; and, finally-within the limitations of information
available to arrive at an assessment of the appropriate tariff rate necessary to accord
domestic industry a reasonable level of protection against competing imports, disregarding
the existence of other forms of protection; for example, import licensing. I wish to make it
clear that although the committee's terms of reference stated that it should disregard the
existence of import licensing in recommending a tariff rate, the Government does not intend
that the proposed tariff should replace the import licensing schedule.
In deciding what should be an appropriate tariff level many factors were considered by
the review committee. Examples not listed in any order of priority are: the capacity of the
industry to supply the local market; the New Zealand content of the goods concerned;
export performance; the extent to which domestic industry is dependent on or required to
use locally produced raw materials; the landed cost of competitive imported products; the
existence of substitute products; trade commitments under GATT, trade agreements,
NAFTA, and the generalised system of preference; whether or not an item has been
reviewed by the former Tariff and Development Board and the Government's decisions on
the board's recommendations; whether or not revenue is to be a consideration in recom-
mending a rate; the rates proposed for domestic raw materials in relation to the rates
proposed for end products using those materials; the effectiveness of current rates as a
measure of protection in relation to the volume of trade; whether or not the proposed rates
should be agreed to subject to a further study or investigation of the industry concerned.
With regard to the last consideration the committee has listed 10 industries-the
packaging, rubber, margarine and associated butter substitutes, starch, plastics, footwear,
consumer glassware, radio and television, wine, and motor vehicle industries. When the
reports from the former Tariff and Development Board on the rubber and packaging
industries were considered by the Government it was decided that these industries should be
the subject of further investigation. The margarine and associated butter substitutes and the
maize starch industries are in the early stages of development. The motor vehicle industry
has never been assessed in depth. The glassware, footwear, plastics, and radio and television
industries all requested high rates of duty, which the committee found difficult to sustain
without further investigation. The wine industry could, in the future, be seeking significant
increases in its current protective rates. In addition, there have been considerable changes in
the industry since the last investigation by the Tariff and Development Board. Within the
next few weeks the Government will be looking at what future action should be taken with
respect to these particular industries.
Reviewing the tariff has been first and foremost an administrative exercise, and the new
tariff does not incorporate any revolutionary change in our trade policy. Its aim was not to
remove tariff protection across the board, although some changes have been made. Some
trade interests asked for a level of protection that would have virtually excluded competition
from imports. The review committee's brief was to give industry an adequate-not
total-level of protection.
I turn now to the Government's proposals for appeals against the proposed tariff. The
former Labour Government and the National Government have agreed that once the new
tariff is implemented appeals would be considered against the new rates and its structure.
Because of the complexity and the interrelated nature of tariff items it is desirable that, in
general, appeals should not be considered until the tariff has been tested in practice.
Nevertheless, there may be some exceptional circumstances-more particularly related to
the structure of tariff items rather than the rates-where appeals could be considered before
the tariff is actually tested. To provide the public with a single point of reference it is
intended that all appeals should be initially directed to me, as Minister of Customs. Appeals
will then be considered by officials from the Customs Department and the Department of
Trade and Industry, but in some cases Treasury and also other departments could be
involved, as the need arises.
On matters considered to be of importance, officials will be required to prepare a report
for consideration by the Cabinet economic committee. If, however, the appeal does not
appear to be of great importance, the Customs Department, after consultation with other
departments involved, will prepare a report and submit it for a decision to the appropriate
Ministers. Normally I would expect the Cabinet economic committee to refer some of the
more important appeals to the Industries Development Commission for further considera-
tion. The terms of reference of any such referral will depend on the nature of the appeal. The
Government does not, however, consider it desirable that when appeals are referred to the


## p. 4210 (#316) ###########################################

4210
4 November
Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Industries Development Commission they should be restricted to appeals on an industry
basis rather than from segments of an industry. As members opposite will probably know,
one of the problems related to earlier references to the former Tariff and Development
Board was that they too often related to segments of an industry. As a result, changes by the
board caused anomalies with other parts of the tariff. I appreciate that elucidation of this
portion of the Bill has taken somewhat longer than is usual in a first reading speech, but I
considered it necessary at this stage to give the House some background to the legislation.
Clause 10 contains the transitional provision enabling the proposed tariff to be amended
with effect from 1 July 1978 at any date after the passing of this Bill if it becomes necessary.
When speaking about the Government's intention on appeal procedures, I indicated that
there may be some exceptional circumstances where this is necessary. In addition to a
revision of the restructured tariff, the Bill makes a number of amendments to the Customs
Act. The more interesting is clause 24, which provides for a situation where it may become
desirable to introduce a duty on exports. Although there is already provision in the Customs
Act to impose an absolute prohibition on exports by Order in Council-that is, in section
70-there are no means at present to take a less severe course and effect any desirable
controls by a duty mechanism. As at present, where import duties are levied by Order in
Council, it is intended that where export duties are applied validation by Act of Parliament
will subsequently be necessary, and section 131 of the principal Act is being amended
accordingly to provide for this.
Clause 25 is designed to supplement the various powers that already exist in the
Customs Act to impose or adjust customs duties in the public interest. It is, of course, a
contingency authority only. As is the case with other duties, an amendment to section 131 of
the principal Act will require that the imposition of any surtax by Order in Council will
necessitate confirmation by Act of Parliament. The clause also contains a subsection that
places a maximum on the rates that may be levied. At present, the import deposit scheme
derives its legal base from the Economic Stabilisation Act 1948. Although for practical
purposes the scheme is operated by the Customs Department, that Act is administered by
the Department of Trade and Industry. Because of this, and since the import deposit scheme
draws on the Customs Act for much of its interpretation, it is considered desirable to amend
that Act by tidying up the position, and this is dealt with in clause 27.
Finally, clause 36 makes it clear beyond doubt that the Customs Department has the
necessary authority to use the services of qualified medical practitioners when body searches
are necessary. Members will know that body searches are now being used in the war against
narcotics. As this is a potentially sensitive area in the civil rights field, I have taken care to
ensure that the basis on which these searches are used is strictly controlled. I have also asked
my department to make sure that our legal authority is absolutely watertight. Clause 36
simply spells out a power that is already quite legally exercised. Other minor amendments
included in the Bill involve changing the Royal Arms on the Customs Seal to the New
Zealand Arms, changing procedures in regard to warehouses licensed under the Customs
Act, and amending the provisions relating to accommodation provided for the use of the
department by the authorities in charge of wharves, airports, and container bases.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Rhodesia-Recruitment of Mercenaries
1. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui),
asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs: What steps is the Government taking to render illegal

Economy-International Factors
4. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Finance: What major factors in the
international economy persuaded him to consider the various measures contained in the
mini-Budget?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Finance. His answer is as follows: "As I said in my statement to the House on 28 October
1977 the present state of the world economy does not offer us much hope for a rapid growth
in the sales of our exports. The major economies are growing more slowly than last year.
Some economies, such as West Germany, have experienced no growth at all in the mid-1977
period. While some Governments have introduced or are going to introduce reflationary
measures, these do not appear to be substantial enough to offer us any hope of a significant
up-turn in international trade. It was in this context that the economic package was
determined."
Mr Courtney: What factor made the Minister decide to introduce tax cuts, which gave
little to low-income people, but $18 a week to the Prime Minister?

Hon. G. F. GAIR: There are two aspects to the point raised by the member for Nelson.
First, in the case of the lump-sum increase in the child benefit, there was a need to inject
money quickly into the economy so that it could have some effect upon the December
trading conditions. In the case of the taxation reduction of 5 percent consistently through all
levels, this was to ensure that the compression of incomes, which has been a feature in recent
years, was not allowed to reach the point where there was no encouragement at all for
people to work. The honourable member will appreciate that, every time there is a
compression in the income scales, margins for skill and responsibility become eroded. By
having a consistent percentage, this is avoided.

of a few days ago, as the brief answer to the question explained, increased the level of
activity in the local economy, because we cannot depend upon the stimulation we had earlier
hoped to get from a reflation of the economies abroad.

farmers and the spreading operators, and are discussed fairly fully with departmental
officials and farming interests before they are altered. I can see no differential subsidy being
provided for a certain area, as that would introduce all sorts of difficulties.
Mr Kirk: Could the Minister confirm that economically it is more feasible to distribute
fertiliser from the air than from the ground?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot confirm that. There is no doubt that once a subsidy is
introduced it creates some differences in costs that would not otherwise be there. However, I
am unaware of any occasion where it would be cheaper, under normal costing, to apply
fertiliser by air rather than from the ground.

Coromandel Peninsula-Foreshore Reserves and Farm Parks
12. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister of Lands: What area of land has
been set aside as foreshore reserves on the Coromandel Peninsula, and what is the total area
of farm land now purchased and established as farm parks?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The process of setting aside coastal reserves on
the Coromandel Peninsula has been going on from the earliest days of settlement in New
Zealand, but no cumulative record of reserve areas has been maintained. The coastal survey
of 1968 confirmed that much of the outstandingly scenic coastline and many of the beaches
were being considered for housing subdivisions, and that if some of these areas were to be
reserved for posterity early action was required. Since the special fund for the purchase of
reserves was established in 1972, 3840 hectares have been reserved on the Coromandel
coastline, including 3696 hectares in farm parks.
Mr Rogers: Is it the Government's intention to purchase more land in the Coromandel
area for this purpose?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The principle of having a trust fund for the purchase of coastal
reserves has been continued by successive Governments. In the Coromandel Peninsula and
other areas where there is a need for coastal land to be purchased the process will be
continued.

Deficit Before Borrowing
16. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram) asked the Minister of Finance: What will
be the deficit before borrowing for the current financial year after taking into account the
effect of Government measures announced to date?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Finance. His answer is as follows: "As I said in my statement last Friday, the effect of the
Government measures, together with the supplementary appropriations now tabled, are
expected to increase the deficit before borrowing for the current financial year by approxi-
mately $180 million. Adding this amount to the deficit in the July Budget of $382 million, the

RNZAF-Retention of Dakota
17. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Defence: What consideration
can be given to the retention of one RNZAF Dakota to be held at an RNZAF air base for
historical purposes?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence): When it was decided to withdraw the
six Dakotas from RNZAF service consideration was given to retaining one for historical
purposes, particularly as an RNZAF historical centre has recently been established.
However, while appreciating the Dakota's long and faithful service to the RNZAF and
therefore its part in military aviation in New Zealand, its most significant role in this country
was in the field of civil aviation. This has been appropriately recognised by the inclusion of a
Dakota in the aircraft display at the Museum of Transport and Technology, Auckland. With
this in mind, and in the knowledge that the ex RNZAF Dakotas have a not inconsiderable
commercial value, it was decided to dispose of them through the Government Stores Board.
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister confirm that many servicemen who served during World
War II and the Korean war had a long association with Dakota aircraft, and will see good
reason for its establishment as a museum piece?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY: Yes, the DC3 was used as a military machine, but,
basically, it played its major part with the commencement of NAC in New Zealand. We have
made one Dakota available for display in Auckland, together with other aeroplanes used
both in the civilian and military fields.

Both those clauses contain provisions that are completely unacceptable. Sir Guy


## p. 4222 (#328) ###########################################

4222
4 November
New Zealand SIS Amendment Bill
Powles's recommendations were set aside when the legislation was introduced and during
discussion in the Committee stage. He recommended that his proposals be taken as a
complete package, and said that any change would unbalance and destroy what he was
aiming for. Unfortunately, that is exactly what has happened. Sir Guy was seeking a greater
understanding of the Security Intelligence Service, and to some extent a greater and quite
understandable restraint on its operations. In this Bill we have neither.
In his report Sir Guy recommended that the Act should be amended by inserting a
proviso to section 4(1)(a) as follows: "Provided that intelligence shall not be obtained
regarding any person or body which is not actually engaged in espionage, sabotage, or
subversion, unless the advice of the Intelligence Council has been obtained. . . . Until the
Act is so amended the service should curtail its countersubversion activities in accordance
with the spirit of the proposed amendment." The Bill does not provide that the advice of the
council be sought; it simply states that the service will inform the council. Sir Guy clearly
meant that there should be consultation before the event, but the Bill has deliberately set out
a circumstance that applies after the event.
Clause 3 introduces a new power for the SIS to institute surveillance over "potential
subversion". No attempt is made anywhere in the Bill to define that term. During the
Committee stage the Opposition asked the Government to say exactly what was meant by
"potential subversion", but no answer was given. Where is the line to be drawn, and by
whom? How can there be surveillance of potential subversion that does not include
surveillance of lawful groups? The new subsection 2(b) of section 4, inserted by clause 3 and
passed in the Committee stage, provides that it will not be a function of the Security
Intelligence Service to institute surveillance of any person or persons by reason of his or their
involvement in lawful protest or dissent. Apparently if the SIS considers that something is a
lawful protest or dissent but is potentially subversive, or if the Prime Minister considers it to
be so, then surveillance may be instituted. But who determines when a lawful protest or
dissent should be categorised as potentially subversive?
Subclause 2(b) is meaningless. Sir Guy said in his report, and later on Radio New
Zealand, that in his view New Zealand did not, and does not, have a problem of subversion.
I ask the House who is better qualified to make that kind of comment than a very
distinguished New Zealander who has had the opportunity to examine the work of the SIS in
great detail? It would have been reasonable to expect that, in the light of Sir Guy's
comments, the Government would have tightened up the legislation, but its response has
been to introduce into this clause the vague and rather sinister term "potential subversion".
The Auckland District Law Society said that the term was limitless, and that it took the SIS
beyond the surveillance of unlawful acts and into the ill-defined and possibly limitless area of
potential acts. That is very disturbing, because the Bill goes well across the exhortation of Sir
Guy that the SIS should work within well-defined rules. The service must be seen to work
within well defined rules; and, to use Sir Guy's own words, they must be consonant with our
democratic way of life. That has been set aside in this clause.
I now turn to the discussion on clause 4, which is, as was admitted during the Committee
stage, the most critical clause in the Bill. The clause has been much amended by the
Government, but improved very little. The heart of public protest is to be found in this
clause, because it vests so much power in the Minister in Charge of the New Zealand
Security Intelligence Service. Everyone knows that the Minister is most noted for his lack of
judgment and intolerance of minority groups and anyone who is prepared to speak out
against the establishment because they think all is not well.
The Prime Minister has claimed that he is the only person fitted for this role because he
is the only person able to keep up with the play. However, he is going overseas once again,
which will mean he has been away 15 weeks out of 35. I question whether any Minister can
claim to be up with the play when, over a period of 35 weeks, he has been out of the country
for 4 days out of 10. At times the Deputy Prime Minister also has been away, and that raises
the question of how much anyone in authority would be up with the play. Perhaps
interception warrants will be announced in Korea or some other place, as was the composi-
tion of the Broadcasting Authority.
The power is in the Bill. Protection against abuse is not to be found. There is no redress
for a citizen against the wrongful issue of a warrant, no matter how much damage may occur
to his reputation; neither is there any time limit on the warrants, although one of Sir Guy's
specific recommendations was that there should be a time limit. It seems that the Govern-
ment rejected that recommendation out of hand. The new section 4A(2)(b) inserted by
clause 4 provides that a warrant may include the names of any number of people. If the two


## p. 4223 (#329) ###########################################

4 November
4223
New Zealand SIS Amendment Bill
provisions are run together, an indefinite number of people could be covered by a warrant
for an indefinite period. I cannot think of anything more contrary to the views expressed by
Sir Guy in his report. The new paragraph (aa) inserted in the new section 4A(2)(d) by clause
4 provides that the Minister may append to a warrant "Such other terms and conditions (if
any) as the Minister considers advisable in the public interest". That is a blank cheque.
Again, the Government has made no effort to define the boundaries within which the
Minister should properly operate in what is styled "the public interest". No wonder that
people from all walks of life are concerned about this measure.
The new subsection (3)(b) of section 4A inserted by clause 4 has the effect of involving
the community in the activities of the SIS. People can be requested to become involved.
Originally, as you know, Mr Speaker, State servants were to be required to be involved, and
would have had no redress. Fortunately, that provision was amended, but the whole effect of
the subsection will be to sow seeds of distress in the community, so that neighbour will be
lined against neighbour, teacher against pupil, and worker against worker. Perhaps that is
the Government's intention.
The new subsection (4) of the proposed section 4A relates to reports to Parliament. The
fear has been expressed publicly-and was certainly expressed in the Committee stage—that
there is an absolute lack of real accountability by the SIS. Most damaging of all, I think, is
the new subsection (5), which puts the SIS completely above and beyond the law. It can
commit the act of breaking and entering which, if committed by the ordinary citizen, would
cost him 10 or 12 years' jail. I believe that the SIS may even be involved in force, although
that is not clear. But it is clear that, according to the terms of the Bill, it can take “any
reasonable action necessarily involved in making or assisting to make the interception or
seizure". Who defines "reasonable action" and, given the secrecy surrounding the entire
operation, who will know whether an agent takes unreasonable action? Indeed, if an agent
were to take unreasonable action, what would happen to such an agent?
The provisions are just so much hocus pocus. No one could suggest that in peacetime, in
a community such as ours, people should be above the law. Sir Guy Powles said on page 24
of his report: "Certainly, complete secrecy from all forms of democratic control must be
avoided." I suggest that the very secrecy of these provisions runs counter to that comment.
The clause totally ignores that exhortation. Indeed, I believe that fears have been
compounded by comments made by the Prime Minister. As recently as 19 October-and this
matter was referred to in the Committee stage-the National Business Review reported a
comment made over Radio New Zealand by the Prime Minister: "There is nothing to stop a
Government from doing a mortal thing in this country, because we have no written
constitution-except the sanction of the public." That is very worrying.
The National Business Review went on to say: "He obviously meant that there is
nothing to prevent him or, indeed, any other Prime Minister from exceeding the bounds of
the Act. This amounts to a denial of the rule of law and clears the way for the despotic rule of
one man. If the Government is not bound by the statutes, all law and order becomes a
monstrous hypocrisy." And that, I suggest, underlines too much of the Bill.

quality of the debate during the Committee stage.
It was interesting to hear the change in direction that the debate took during the
Committee stage, and has taken in the speech given by the Leader of the Opposition. When
the Bill was introduced the Opposition categorised it as a "telephone tapping and mail
opening" Bill. The Opposition found those features of the Bill repugnant. It thought the Bill
legalised and authorised telephone tapping and mail opening. During the Committee stage it
was found that those operations were already legal, open ended, and uncontrolled; at
present there is no requirement for reporting.
The Bill does not extend the powers of the Prime Minister and the Security Intelligence
Service; it restricts the powers. The ground was taken out from under the feet of the
Opposition, which had been stomping the country and crying that the Bill would legalise
telephone tapping and mail opening. That argument has totally disappeared, so during the
Committee stage the Opposition had no alternative but to fall back on various drafting
points and try to make an argument out of whether a comma should be placed here and
another word there. The substance of the Opposition's initial resistance to the Bill had
disappeared from under its feet.
Section 34 of the Post Office Act provides that it has been legal for more than 100 years
to intercept mail by warrant for any purpose whatsoever-and that applies also to telegrams.
Any person may be directed to intercept mail for the purposes of security. We have it on the
authority of the member for Henderson, the former Minister of Justice, that that section was
used for that purpose. The Postmaster-General has also said that that section was used in
1974, quite legally, for security reasons by the then Labour Prime Minister. The Bill restricts
existing powers for mail opening. Section 158 of the Post Office Act, relating to telephone
tapping, has, as stated by the Prime Minister, been the law of the land for at least 20 years.
The provision is in the Post Office Act 1928. It seems that it probably came from an
immemorial provision, possibly prerogative, possibly common law, possibly of long usage.
Mr Lange: Read the Birkett committee findings.
Mr BRILL: The member for Mangere should read the Birkett Committee of Privy
Councillors report to find that they believe in all three provisions. He might also find that the
Birkett committee found in the case of Crown prerogative that when there are new
technologies and changes the prerogative changes take into account the alterations in
technology. The prerogative extends, and always has extended, to telephones. Be that as it
may, whether we rely upon the fact that the law has been here from time immemorial or
upon statute, the Solicitor-General and the former Attorney-General, the member for
Henderson, have advised us on that matter. I do not believe the Opposition has raised any
argument to the contrary. It is quite clear that the power exists, and that it has existed for
many years. The Postmaster-General has been able to intercept telephone calls for at least
50 years, and the convention is that he does it only for security purposes and at the request of
the Prime Minister. The Opposition's argument disappeared from under its feet because
wide powers have always existed for telephone tapping with no restrictions or reporting
requirements.
Sir Guy Powles was concerned about this matter. I believe one argument was that Sir
Guy Powles found it was not legal. In his report Sir Guy leaves the matter open. On page 58,
in paragraph 16, he gives his legal counsel's conclusions, and goes on at some length to say
that a contrary view has also been expressed. At the beginning of paragraph 17 he states:
"However this may be, it is clear there is a situation here which needs urgent attention." Sir
Guy did not find that at present it is unlawful to tap telephones and intercept mail for
security purposes. There is no reason to disregard the advice expressed by the member for
Henderson when he told the House the effect of the law in 1975. Sir Guy felt that the powers
were too wide and suggested that they be narrowed. The Bill has been introduced to narrow
and restrict the wide powers the service and the Prime Minister have at the present time.
I believe that if the Opposition had realised the legal position when the Bill was
introduced it would have applauded the Bill, and supported it throughout its passage. By the
time the Opposition was aware of the facts it was committed to its course, and had had
meetings around the country with the Socialist Unity Party and other leading opponents of
the Bill. It could no longer back down and say that the Bill had its support in the cause of
civil liberties. When asked what it would do about the Bill the Opposition said it would
repeal it. If the Opposition repeals the Bill we will revert to the existing law under which the
Prime Minister has total power to intercept mail and tap telephones without restriction. The
Opposition has said that it will bring back the Listening Devices Bill, which has nothing to do
with mail or telephones. That Bill expressly stated that it did not apply to telephones. The

Listening Devices Bill did not cover the problems faced up to by this Bill-that the powers to
tap telephones and intercept mail are too wide.
Similar debate has already taken place in countries similar to New Zealand. These
debates have been resolved on the basis that the Minister in charge of the Bill should issue
warrants and report. That is the position in the United Kingdom; and it has been debated
and the same conclusion arrived at in Canada and in Australia. It is now being debated in
New Zealand. New Zealanders will support the Bill, with the exception of a few who have
committed themselves to protest, and with the exception of the Opposition, which now has
no alternative, despite the fact that it has learned what the law is, but to continue to
undertake an insensate, blind blockage of the Bill because it is committed to do so, and
therefore would repeal it. The Opposition will gain no support from thinking New Zealan-
ders who are concerned about a democratic way of life and that the security service should be
accountable to its Minister for its activities. That is an essential civil liberty, and an essential
constitutional protection that the Minister must be accountable for the actions of the service.
This Bill will see that that happens.

being moved to the first amendment on the Supplementary Order Paper. When I say “first”
that does not necessarily mean what it says, because the Chairman, driven by some
inscrutable procedurual compulsion, put the amendments, not in the order in which they
appeared on the Supplementary Order Paper, but in some other mystifying and completely
confusing manner that had the House at sixes and sevens throughout.
Hon. David Thomson: What nonsense!
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: It is not nonsense. The House was at sixes and sevens
throughout the whole of that debate until the Chairman explained that he was not putting
the amendments in the order in which they appeared in the Supplementary Order Paper. All
this could have been avoided had the Bill been referred to a select committee. There, any
amendments contemplated by the Government could have been read into the Bill, and
members presented with the clean, completed copy we have before us today. There was
nothing to prevent that emerging from a committee with the amendments incorporated and
being voted on, without the closure depriving us of the right to debate most of the
amendments made to the operative clause of the Bill.
The fact is that the Government is sailing under false colours, flying the flag of Sir Guy
Powles, a flag it is not entitled to have at its masthead. Without being too outlandish, I say
with confidence that we speak for those who see that that flag is pirated and flying upside-
down.
The Prime Minister based most of his contribution to the debate on the aspect of
terrorism. I say emphatically, here and now, that we yield to no one in our detestation and
condemnation of skyjacking and urban guerrilla atrocities, and in our readiness to go to any
lengths to prevent and punish such activities in New Zealand. The Prime Minister's remarks
were illustrated by continual references to what may be called the Kirk incident, the details
of which are unknown to me. I was not privy to what was done at the time, and it was proper
that I should not be as I had no need to know. Two or three of my colleagues were involved.
The fact is that the incident involved a proved terrorist and a known victim. Like the Prime
Minister, I endorse what the then Prime Minister did to ensure that there was no danger to
that individual in New Zealand, or, as a very likely consequence, to other New Zealanders.
The act was taken with due regard to the proprieties, and with the proper chain of
consultation being followed. That would not be necessary under this Bill.
Incidentally, I take the opportunity to say that the Act aims in the wrong direction, by
aligning terrorist activities with something that must necessarily challenge the Government
or the community of New Zealand. I invite the Government to contrast that with the
definition of "terrorism" contained in the recommendations of the Hope Commission in
Australia, which suggested these words: "Terrorism: the organisation in Australia or
assistance for violent political activity in foreign countries." Unless the Government
redefines "terrorism" to make sure that objectives for which constraints can be imposed are
those that take place or are designed to secure an effect in some other country, and not
necessarily in New Zealand, then the definition in our Bill is defective.
The aspect that concerns me, and I believe the community, and which is at the root of
our campaign against the Bill, is the extension of SIS activities into the area of subversion.
Sir Guy Powles recommended that these activities be scaled down. He noted the propensity
of the service to confuse subversion with political criticism or dissent, and found that this
occupied too much of its attention at the expense of its true role of counter-espionage. This
Bill, far from scaling down such activities, encourages meddling in industrial and other
internal matters by the use of the misbegotten phrase and concept of "potential subversion".
One fact that alarms us is that the finger on the trigger is that of the Prime Minister,
notoriously and demonstrably impulsive-and, indeed, trigger-happy. He places much
reliance on intuition and he has revealed a relevant example of this disposition in the second
instalment of the new book of partial revelations and political mythology, which he deems
worthy of the entitlement, "The Good Book". In that, he discloses that he had an intuitive
feeling that the successful action for the breach of the New Zealand Superannuation Act was
launched at the instance of a solicitor. He immediately zeroed in on the plaintiff's counsel,
who was forthwith abused and defamed. This is relevant, Mr Speaker, because I am coming
back to it in a moment. The Prime Minister states in his book that he later found he was
mistaken, and said that he admitted this and apologised-a circumstance of which I have not
seen any evidence. Perhaps he did it privately. Who can doubt that if this Bill had been in
force at the time, the counsel for the plaintiff would have been treated as a subversive under
this legislation and subjected to the surveillance provided for in it?

What can be done about the Bill? It is here, the Government's majority will ensure that

I must concede that even if it were improved there would necessarily be some
constraints on full disclosures, in the interests of security. One has to admit that.
Other countries have tried to grapple with the same situation to ensure some supervi-
sion of the activities of their intelligence departments consonant with the needs of security.
The United States Senate has set up a committee of senators, which meets members of the
service and holds frequent conferences. A similar provision obtains in the House of
Commons, and I believe also in Australia. I must admit they have not proved phenomenally
successful as watchdogs; they have shown themselves to be less watchdogs than tame
poodles.
However, that should not deter us from making some attempt to impose a liaison
between the service and Parliament, and to have something more than the ineffective
reporting system provided in the Bill. I, for one, would subscribe to the consideration at least
of a bipartisan committee, preferably chaired by a stipendiary magistrate, to keep an eye on
and maintain a link with the activities of the SIS. The present director already has that status,
but I believe there would be some gain if an independent committee of that kind was set up.
One is not overoptimistic of its being an effective watchdog, but I think it is totally
inadequate simply to leave this organisation to operate with no more than the sanction of the
Prime Minister, and a kind of ineffectual reporting back to Parliament once a year, with the
paucity of detail that that report can contain.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Cigarette Prices
1. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central), on behalf of Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert),
asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: How can his department justify a price increase of
2c being approved to cigarette manufacturers on 3 October to be followed 10 days later by
reductions in prices of the same brands of cigarettes?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): The prices
approved by my department are maxima and do not prevent lower prices being charged for
competitive or other reasons. The reduction in price referred to by the honourable member
followed the introduction of a new low-priced brand by one of the manufacturers, and is
indicative of the competition within the industry.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is not one driven to the conclusion that the increase of 2c,
followed by a reduction of much more than that a few days later, shows that the original
increase was quite unjustified?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am not prepared to indulge in that criticism of the
secretary of the department, who is the initial pricing authority and acts with statutory
authority. He sets the barème for a return on shareholders' funds, assets, and so on. The
industry as a whole made an application for a price increase and was able to show that it was
achieving lower than that level, and the increase of 2c which he approved, in his
judgment would have brought it up to the level it was entitled to achieve. Then one firm
introduced a new brand at the reduced price. The largest firm in New Zealand came in
behind that and reduced its price, and then the first firm reduced its price still further. That is
private enterprise competition, despite the fact that price control still operates.
Mr Prebble: In view of the Minister's statement that he is not prepared to accept
criticism of his department, is he prepared to say that what happened means that cigarette
manufacturers are asking for approval of price increases which are completely unjustified?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am not prepared to concede that. Neither am I
critical of my department. I simply said I was not prepared to criticise the secretary in his
capacity as the initial pricing authority. The Labour Government put him in that position
under the Commerce Act. We supported it, and endorsed it in an amendment last year. At
the time he acted with statutory authority as the pricing authority, and made a decision on


## p. 4238 (#344) ###########################################

4238
8 November
Oral Answers to Questions
the basis of shareholders' funds. The industry had applied for an increase; it was entitled to
one and received it. But individual units in the industry still carry on competition, and in this
instance with a new brand one firm saw fit to make the price much lower than for other
brands which it was promoting. The other firms then followed suit
Mr Kirk: Can the Minister confirm that he consulted both firms about the proposed
price increase at the time the one firm applied for it?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I can confirm that I did not. I have no intention of
talking to the secretary or consulting with him on a matter in which he acts with statutory
authority. Neither would I talk to a Supreme Court judge or a magistrate on such matters. I
am prepared to talk about the regulations, and whether they should be amended or changed.
That is within the Minister's province, but in regard to pricing, an application is made by a
firm or a group of firms to the secretary as the initial pricing authority, and the Minister
would interfere at his peril.

Education-Spelling Ability
2. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Education: Has he read the
article in City News (Auckland) of 4 October, entitled "Growing concern over the 'new
English"" in which "a well-known proponent of sound basic education" states that it is
impossible for children taught English as a pictographic language to learn to spell with any
understanding, and, if so, does he have evidence to show that the average level of spelling
ability in schools is lower than it was 10 years ago, and, if he has, does his department have
any plans to improve the situation?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I am aware of the article referred to. It
is not possible from the article to know what is meant by the reference to "pictographic" in
this context. There is, however, recent evidence from studies conducted by the New Zealand
Council for Educational Research in 1961, and again in 1975, which shows that spelling
standards have not declined. The report of this national survey was published by the
NZCER in 1976, and is entitled "The Teaching of Spelling in New Zealand Schools". My
department, through its field inspectorate, through curriculum officers, and through advisers
is continuously engaged in activities that have as their aim improvements in teaching spelling
in the wider context of English language activities generally. One outcome of these activities
is the handbook "Suggestions for Teaching Spelling" published by the department in
1975. There are other materials, but I must add that I am concerned about the number of
misleading statements made in this article published in the City News.
Mr Prebble: I understood the Minister to say that spelling levels are not less than they
were 10 years ago. Have they improved, and, if not, is his department happy with the
average level of spelling ability in our schools?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: In 1961 Dr Arbutson produced the alphabetical spelling list,
which was derived from information received from 98 schools. I have here the results of the
average performance of the children in each standard class in 1961. The same test was
carried out by Mr Croft in 1975, and it could be said that in standards 1 to 4 and in form I
there was an improvement. It was only in form II that there appeared to be a slight lack of
improvement. I would not go so far as to say that it was an improvement, but it shows that
there has been no decline in the standard over the past 14 years.
Mr Prebble: Would the Minister answer the second half of my question, and say
whether the department is happy with the average level of spelling ability in our schools?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Naturally the department is always trying to improve it. I should
point out that the present primary school syllabus was first published in 1961, and the
secondary school syllabus in 1944. Those people who say there has been a decline over those
years cannot point to the curriculum that has been used. If the objective evidence we have is
accepted I doubt whether it can be said that there has been a decline in standards.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

short of appalling""?

Maori language. Since last September six marae-based courses have been held for principals
and senior teachers of primary and secondary schools. These aim to give these teachers a
greater understanding of Maori life and culture. Because of the recognition given to

teachers' colleges. Many more schools are now undertaking teaching in Maori, and many

INDUSTRIAL LAW REFORM BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the Industrial Law Reform Bill
be introduced. The Bill contains amendments to four existing Acts: the Industrial Relations
Act, the Aircrew Industrial Tribunal Act, the Waterfront Industry Act and the Agricultural
Workers Act. The purpose of the amendments is to create a new structure for the system of
voluntary arbitration that is part of existing wage settlement procedures. The new structure
does not mean any lessening of the emphasis on negotiation and conciliation beforehand.
Negotiation and counciliation are, and must remain, the major means of settling disputes
between employers and workers. As a last resort the parties have the option of arbitration.
The Government's aim is to provide arbitration machinery in which the parties will have the
fullest confidence. That is absolutely essential.


## p. 4247 (#353) ###########################################

8 November
4247
Industrial Law Reform Bill
Under the Industrial Relations Act 1973 an Industrial Commission was constituted to
provide arbitral services in disputes of interest. However, events have in effect prevented
that commission from undertaking the tasks it was established to perform. Instead of being
an arbitral body, it was required by regulations passed within months of its establishment in
1974 to become a wage control authority. The two duties are quite different, and indeed are
incompatible one with the other. The commission, under its President Mr George Whatnall,
shouldered the heavy burden thrust upon it. There will be other occasions when it will be
more appropriate to pay tribute to the work of Mr Whatnall and his fellow commissioners. In
the meantime, I make it clear that the abolition of the Industrial Commission proposed in
this Bill has been brought about by events beyond the commission's control and is no
reflection upon the members of the commission personally or on the commission as a body.
The Bill contains amendments to the Industrial Relations Act providing for the
establishment of a new Arbitration Court to take over the functions of both the Industrial
Court and the Industrial Commission. The total membership of the court will consist of no
fewer than three judges, plus two or more sets of members nominated by the New Zealand
Employers Federation and the Federation of Labour respectively. All appointments will be
on a career basis, whereas those of nominated members are at present on renewable terms.
A normal sitting of the court will comprise a judge and two nominated members. The court
will have considerable flexibility and it will be possible for two courts to sit simultaneously to
provide prompt service. Staffing of services for the courts will also be improved.
The opportunity has been taken to improve provisions to deal with disputed points of
law and to clarify provisions introduced last year covering the enforcement of disputes
procedures. After discussions with the parties involved a clause to clarify the vesting of
certain property in the New Zealand Waterside Workers Federation Industrial Association
of Workers has been included. The Bill also provides for a degree of common membership of
the various wage settlement tribunals. Amendments to the Aircrew Industrial Tribunal Act
replace the present one-man tribunal by a judge of the new Arbitration Court. Similarly, by
amendments to the Waterfront Industry Act the chairman is to be a judge of the new
Arbitration Court instead of a Government-appointed barrister and solicitor. The amend-
ments to the Agricultural Workers Act replace the president of the Industrial Commission as
the present chairman of the Agricultural Workers Tribunal with a judge of the Arbitration
Court. Similar provisions in respect of State servants and others were contained in the State
Services Conditions of Employment Bill introduced into the House last week.
The basic structures set out in the Industrial Law Reform Bill were approved by the
Industrial Relations Council at its meeting last week. Instead, certain amendments have
already been made to the original proposals as a result of the council's considerations. A
further meeting of the council next week will consider the Bill now before the House. Any
further amendments requested by the council and acceptable to the Government will then be
brought forward in the Committee stage. The Bill, read in association with the General
Wage Orders Bill-also to be introduced today-represents a significant move towards the
Government's objective of a wage settlement procedure containing a basis for consistency
between the decisions of the various tribunals, one that is flexible, and one that will enjoy
the confidence of the parties—which should assist the process of free wage bargaining.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): The Minister did not indicate-and he may do so
across the floor of the House-whether it is intended to send the Bill to the Labour
Committee.
Hon. J. B. Gordon: No, it was not the intention.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER: I believe he should. There are, of course, aspects of the Bill
with which we agree. The waterfront federation has been in touch with me about the

Hon. J. B. Gordon: No.

Hon. A. J. FAULKNER: Well, I understood there had been an agreement with the

concept had been set aside.

The explanatory note states that the court is to consist of not fewer than three judges

I understand the position, that would consist of a judge presiding over a court consisting of
two associate members; so, in practice, there are likely to be three judges and three sets of
nominated members sitting as a court of three presided over by a judge. However, the
judges can sit together, and I apprehend that to mean that they will take on the role of what
is familiar to lawyers as a full court, but one that is distinguished from a court of appeal
because there is provision in this Bill for matters of law to be referred to the Court of Appeal
in the ordinary way for a ruling on a disputed point of law. However, where there is not
necessarily a disputed point of law but a difficult point of law involved, the three judges who
would normally preside each one in his own individual court can sit together in a single court
as a full court to dispose of a difficult point of law.

Industrial Law Reform Bill
Basically, the Bill now before the House has been generally endorsed by the Industrial
Relations Council. We did our best to interpret the suggestions and implications-the
positive motion taken at last week's meeting was a clear indication of concensus there—and I
think my officers have succeeded in writing them into this quick draft, although not much
had to be changed. Basically, it was a change from the three-judge concept back to that of
the old Arbitration Court, but with one distinct difference which the member for Henderson
tended to overlook. It probably is not easily picked up on first glance at the Bill, but the
nominated members will be in two or more sets-and the member for Henderson was
correct there; there must be two sets if you have two arbitration courts sitting, and that
would seem to be practicable and highly desirable at a fairly early date. The third judge
would be sitting as chairman of the Public Sector Tribunal, as it is called in the new State
Services Conditions of Employment Bill, and he would have there other nominated people
from the State sector.
In point of fact, you do get three sets of nominated members with three judges. There is
nothing to preclude the judge that must maintain continuity with the Public Sector Tribunal
coming over to one of the other tribunals, but if members look carefully at this provision
they will see he cannot act on a matter pertaining to the Industrial Relations Act. The other
two judges do that with the two sets of nominated people from outside. The significant
change from the old Arbitration Court is that members are appointed permanently. We
hope to get the type of individual who would make this a career, as was done by two noted
members-one lately deceased-who virtually built a career late in life in the old Arbitration
Court. We want that built into some of the others. The nominated members will be straight
nominations from the Federation of Labour and the Employers Federation on the one hand,
and the Government and the State services on the other.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: That is in the State services tribunal.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Yes, the Public Sector Tribunal under the State Services nul.
Those nominees will have a career ahead of them. They will not have a 3-year appointment,
but will be there until they turn 72, the same as for a judge. The member for Henderson
raised the question of aircrew. I shall be quite frank about this. That proposition was mooted
informally to the Airline Pilots Association. I warned it of a potential change. It is having
talks with me tomorrow, having been unable to arrange such a meeting earlier. I shall be
listening very carefully to its comments, and, as this is not germane to the Industrial
Relations Council, if the parties prefer a three-man tribunal we could well look at that.
One of the advantages of establishing three judges is the better build-up of expertise in
industrial law-in which, I regret to say, New Zealand is sadly lacking by comparison with
Canada and, to some extent, the United States. As the legislation is drafted at present, the
only occasion on which the three judges are called to sit together officially in the form of a
court is triennially when they arbitrate on the formula for measuring the drift between the
public sector and the private sector for discounting State services pay. The Bill alludes to the
question of adequate back-up staff. Members probably will be aware of the move last year to
get both the Industrial Court and the Industrial Commission adquate servicing
staff-registrars, and so on-and there is bound to be cross-reference and mixing by the
judges. At this stage the Bill does not allow for the court to sit formally with three judges.

compare notes. The member for Henderson mentioned the right of appeal to three judges.

GENERAL WAGE ORDERS BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the General Wage Orders Bill
be introduced. This is the third in the package of industrial and wages legislation that the
Government proposes to bring down. Members will be aware that, for some years past, the
operation of the General Wage Orders Act 1969 has been suspended by regulations made
under the authority of the Economic Stabilisation Act 1948. The purpose of the present Bill
is twofold: first, to revoke parts of the Wage Adjustment Regulations and thereby abolish
the Wage Hearing Tribunal established under those regulations; and, secondly, to restore
the General Wage Orders Act in an amended form. These two purposes are part of the
Government's wider plan to accomplish a restructuring of wage settlement tribunals and a
relaxation of Government controls over wage bargaining.
The Industrial Relations Council supports the basic proposals and concepts contained in
this Bill. In particular, the Government has accepted the recommendations of the council on
the composition of the tribunal that will hear applications and make orders. In introducing
the Bill I shall refer only to those aspects in which the Bill differs from the 1969 Act,
presently suspended, and from the regulations at present in force. The tribunal hearing of a
general wage order application will be the Arbitration Court-established under the
Industrial Law Reform Bill that has just been introduced-presided over by the chief judge
of that court. This means that the tribunal will consist of three persons, the chief judge, plus
one employers' nominated member and one workers' nominated member. Under the
present regulations, the Wage Hearing Tribunal comprises the judge of the Industrial Court
plus two independent persons specially appointed by the Government after consultations.
Under the 1969 Act and its amendments the tribunal was the Industrial Commission. There
is provision for the court to appoint special counsel to assist the court.
The application of general orders has been widened from that under the 1969 Act to
include agricultural workers coming within the Agricultural Workers Act passed earlier this
session. The provisions of the 1969 Act are unchanged in that the application of general
orders to persons governed by awards of orders of other specialised tribunals is determined
by the provisions of the particular legislation governing those specialised areas. Therefore,
with some exceptions, general wage orders apply directly only to those persons governed by
agreements or awards under the Industrial Relations Act or the Agricultural Workers Act.
Under the present regulations, the direct application of orders of the Wage Hearing
Tribunal is wider. The matters to be considered by the court before making a general order
represent an amalgam of provisions applicable under the regulations or under the 1969 Act.
The court is required to give paramount importance to the economic stability of New
Zealand. The right to apply for a general order is restricted to the two central organisations
recognised under the Industrial Relations Act, the Federation of Labour and the Employers
Federation. The opportunity to be heard is to be given to representatives of those two
central organisations and also to representatives of the Combined State Service Organisa-
tions and the Government. Consistent with the right to free bargaining, there is provision for


## p. 4254 (#360) ###########################################

4254
8 November
General Wage Orders Bill
the court's general order to be incorporated within any later bargain between the parties. In
the area of wage bargaining, as in other areas, it is difficult to impose controls. However, to
remove those controls without undue disruption is even more difficult and I commend this
Bill to the House as one further deliberate step towards that most desirable goal.

NEW ZEALAND PLANNING BILL
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of National Development): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The purpose of this Bill is to give two organisations, the New Zealand
Planning Council and the Commission for the Future, a statutory foundation. The creation
of these two organisations reflects the Government's determination that it and the commun-
ity should be provided with a carefully thought out assessment of likely future developments
and the available options to respond to them. The National Party pioneered national
planning on a co-operative and consultative basis. It remains convinced that such planning is
essential-first, to solve our current problems, and, secondly, to enable this nation to play its
full part in an age of scientific and technological opportunity.
The 1975 National Party manifesto promised that a National Government would make
the National Development Council a more effective consultative system. The New Zealand
Planning Council, which is given a statutory foundation in this Bill, represents this promised
revitalisation of the national planning mechanism, which had fallen into disuse. The
manifesto also promised that a National Government would establish a Commission for the
Future, which would be incorporated by an Act of Parliament. This is being done in the
present Bill. Shortly after the National Government took office, it set up the now celebrated
task force to present a report to the Government on all aspects of economic and social
planning for the future of New Zealand. Under the able leadership of Sir Frank Holmes, the
task force reported within the 6-month deadline set. That report contains a very valuable
analysis of the main issues confronting New Zealand today, and also sets out a new planning
structure. The structure of the New Zealand Planning Council to be set up under this Bill is
based largely on those recommendations. Furthermore, the Government has appointed Sir
Frank as the first chairman of the new body.
Among the recommendations to improve the planning mechanism that the Government
has accepted in drafting the Bill are the appointment of an independent chairman, provision
of an independent secretariat able to devote its full time to planning, and provision for the
council to employ experts to assist in analysing major planning issues. The Minister of
National Development is to be a member to ensure there is a link at the highest level
between the Planning Council's work and the Government's decision making. The task force
did not envisage a ministerial member of the council, but I believe that this provision will
greatly strengthen the council's effectiveness. The granting of a statutory basis to the
Planning Council will, in itself, of course, stress to the community the significance placed by
the Government on the council's work.
The New Zealand Planning Bill also gives a statutory foundation to the Commission for
the Future. The organisation has been set up to provide the Government and the public with
an early warning of the major issues likely to arise in the future as a result of long-term
changes in the social, technological, and economic environment in which New Zealand's
development will take place. The commission is to give special attention to the implications
12-Vol. 415


## p. 4256 (#362) ###########################################

4256
8 November
New Zealand Planning Bill
of new and prospective developments in science and technology. Such changes have had a
major effect in shaping our society. They may be even more important in future. The
commission will be concerned with identifying issues rather than resolving them, and the
time span it is concerned with is very much longer than that of the Planning Council. It is
intended that the commission will initiate public discussion on the possibilities for the long-
term economic and social development of New Zealand. Special emphasis is to be placed on
ensuring that members of Parliament have opportunities to inform themselves on the future
issues discussed in the commission's reports.
A significant feature of the commission is that it is to be a bipartisan body, including in
its membership a member of Parliament appointed on the nomination of the Leader of the
Opposition. The commission is already in operation, with a member of the Opposition
participating fully in its deliberations. A Minister of the Crown and the Director-General of
the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research are also to be members of the
commission, and provision is made for an independent chairman. The first chairman is
Professor James Duncan of Victoria University, under whose leadership the commission is
rapidly developing its work programme.
The Bill consists of four parts. The first deals with the New Zealand Planning Council,
the second with the Commission for the Future, the third with relationships between the two
bodies, and the fourth with general provisions, including the secretariats of the two bodies. I
intend to discuss briefly each of these parts to elucidate the significant provisions. Part I
establishes the New Zealand Planning Council, the paramount function of which is to advise
the Government on planning for social, economic, and cultural development in New
Zealand. It is to assist in co-ordinating such plans, and to submit to the Government advice
on programmes for development in New Zealand, and on links between planning at the
national and regional levels. The council is to act as a focal point for a process of consultative
planning about New Zealand's medium-term development. To assist it to carry out these
functions, the Bill gives the council the power to prepare reports on any matter affecting the
economic, social, and cultural development of New Zealand, and to publish documents on
planning topics that, in its view, merit wide consideration and public debate. The Govern-
ment is, therefore, setting up the council as an independent organisation and giving it the
right to express its views.
The council will comprise not more than 12 members appointed by the Governor-
General on the recommendation of the Minister, together with the Minister himself and the
Secretary to the Treasury. The Minister provides a link with Cabinet, and the Secretary to
the Treasury a link with the Government machine. In recommending persons for appoint-
ment, regard is to be had, inter alia, to the need for a diversity of knowledge among
members, and to the capacity of the council to promote a sense of common purpose among
different sections of the community in planning New Zealand's future. It is intended that the
appointed persons will serve as individuals and not as representatives of any interest group.
The Government expects that the council will be a source of advice, and the means of
increasing public understanding on the issues of New Zealand's development. The council.
will, I hope, be effective in illuminating such issues, and in particular the constraints on
resources within which decisions must be made, and the strategies for removing those
constraints.
The work of the council should encourage Government departments, local bodies, and
private enterprise to consider in their decision making the long-term national interest as well
as their short-term aims. The council will increase the opportunities for constructive
consultation in the community about how the goals of different groups can best be
harmonised. I want to make it clear, however, that when the advice of the Planning Council
and of the Government's other advisers has been received it is the responsibility and
prerogative of the Government to make decisions.
Part II of the Bill establishes the Commission for the Future, the paramount function of
which is to study the possibilities of the long-term economic and social development of New
Zealand. The commission is charged with making information on those possibilities available
to all members of Parliament, and publishing it for wider dissemination. I mentioned earlier
the bipartisan nature of the commission, membership of which is to be not more than seven
persons appointed by the Governor-General on the recommendation of the Minister,
together with a Minister of the Crown, a member of the Opposition, a member of the
Planning Council, and the Director-General of the Department of Scientific and Industrial
Research. The commission is, therefore, being set up in a manner that ensures it is
bipartisan, can draw on the experience of the DSIR, has a link with the Planning Council,


## p. 4257 (#363) ###########################################

8 November
4257
New Zealand Planning Bill
and has contact with the Government at Cabinet level. It is an independent organisation,
and has been given the right to publish its views.
Part III is concerned with co-ordination between the council and the commission. It
simply spells out a framework for consultation and co-operation between the two organisa-
tions. One aspect of this is that they are required to submit their work programmes to the
Minister before the end of February each year, and he may convene a meeting to discuss the
relationship between the respective work programmes. During the Committee stage I shall
be moving an amendment to make it clear that this is the purpose of such meetings.
Part IV makes general provisions about the council and the commission. The most
significant aspect is that they are empowered to appoint officers and employees in agreement
with the State Services Commission. Similarly, they are empowered to commission experts
to report on relevant issues or questions. These provisions will greatly strengthen the
planning mechanism by giving it its own independent staff able to devote their full attention
to the work of planning, and of the commission.
I now want to refer to three amendments I shall be moving by way of a Supplementary
Order Paper during the Committee stage. The first of these amendments is to provide in
clause 10 for the appointment of an alternative to the ministerial member of the Commission
for the Future. The second proposed amendment is intended to clarify the purpose of the
meetings between the Minister of National Development and representatives of the council
and of the commission, for which provision is made in clause 13(3). The proposed
amendment is to remove the requirement that such a meeting agree on the work program-
mes of the two organisations. It is proposed that the purpose of such a meeting be simply to
consider the relationship between the respective work programmes. The third proposed
amendment is to correct an error in the description of the Government Superannuation
Fund Act in clause 21(3).
In conclusion, the Government has three objectives in the New Zealand Planning Bill:
first, to ensure that a sound basis for long-term policy is arrived at by a process of wide
consultation; secondly, to increase general awareness and understanding of the key issues
relating to New Zealand's development; thirdly, to ensure that long-term considerations are
brought to bear on policy decisions throughout the Government and the community.

In this country we need people of energy and imagination to take great leaps in

many more of his type around here. We want to see planning and forecasting that stretches
the imagination, that cultivates creativity, and that leads us every now and again to boggle at
the sort of changes that might occur. Forecasts are continually being confounded; sometimes
because they are fulfilled unexpectedly early, sometimes because social and political change
remains stubbornly slow in comparison with material possibilities.
In his book Future Facts, Steven Rosen, who has been looking at developments and
technology in the United States, talks of things as future facts because they are the sort of
things that medical teams and technological teams have already developed, which in the next
10 to 20 years will probably be influencing the lives of all of us. For example, as long ago as
1966 a medical team at Cincinnati University substituted certain fluorocarbon emulsions for
blood in experimental animals for a limited time. The animals survived in apparently good
health, leading to the possibility that some day synthetic liquids may well replace blood in
emergency transfusions. Many of us will have read of nuclear-powered artificial hearts
becoming a possibility. In the power and energy field we have the likelihood of solar power
from satellites, of cooking by sunlight, of bulk energy batteries, and the possibility of a
hydrogen-based energy economy. In food crops, the process of artificial selection is giving
higher yield crops; here we see big challenges for New Zealand.

The member for Raglan quoted an interview that Sir Frank Holmes gave to Better

saying that he was in favour of it, nor that he was against it. He continued: "We have a

what are the Government's objectives, and the carrying out of the Government's views." In

National Party has no scheme.

elements, of which the first was a clear statement of the Government's overall economic and
social objectives. That is something that we have not been given. All we have had has been a
series of platitudes from the member for Raglan and even more platitudinous statements by

taxpayers' money.
Parliament and the people are entitled to a clear statement of the Government's social
and economic objectives before the council starts work, not afterwards. This should not be
done in some secret session, with the Minister telling the council what to do. The Minister
should be saying here and now that he will be instructing it to look into certain areas. The
functions and powers of the council are set out in clause 5, which states in paragraph (a) of
subclause (1) that the general functions of the council shall be to advise the Government on
planning for social, economic, and cultural development in New Zealand. It is significant to
note the three areas the Government has set out as being prime areas for planning. Surely
the prime area for planning should have been the protection and conservation of the
environment. In the United States, where this subject has been debated in Congress,
President Carter has produced as his first planning priority the conservation of the environ-
ment. That is something that has been completely ignored by this Government. The
environment is mentioned in a mild way in paragraph (e). The council should be instructed
to produce viable economic policies that take account of the need to preserve the environ-
ment. It is highly significant that in drafting this Bill the Government has completely ignored
the environment.

The first thing to do is to determine your aim. The aim was given very clearly by Sir

The next thing to do is assess the factors, and that is what takes the time. That is where the

Planning Council can help assess all the factors, bring them together, look at the limitations,

ongoing study, and an ongoing body. I like the provisions in the Bill for the appointment of a
chairman and secretary, and for having the best brains that can be got. Planning is no
different, no matter at what level you do it. Having got a plan you must then maintain
momentum, and that was where the National Development Council of the 1960s failed. Its
momentum failed. This is a new exercise, and a very much better structure. Each year the
Planning Council will have to recheck the factors it considered before it produced its plan. It
must retain flexibility as new factors come up, and here again the commission can do a
valuable job by batting ideas about. The Bill states that the information from the commission
is to be available to members of Parliament, and so it should be. It is a grand concept. We
must keep working, and looking ahead.

and to assist the Government to co-ordinate such planning. Is there a need for a long-term
