clearly by Sir Frank Holmes and his committee in the report New Zealand at the Turning
Point, from which I quote: "All the evidence it has studied leads the task force to one simple
conclusion-New Zealand does not at present have appropriate techniques and institutions
to carry out the long-term appraisal of the trends, issues, and options which is necessary to
ensure that policy is geared to strike a wise balance in the development of our society." I
believe that concept is fundamental to the Bill we are discussing tonight.
If we look at only two of the problems facing New Zealand society-the problem of
urban development and the problem of industrial relations, for instance-perhaps we can
see more clearly what we are heading for. There is a need to avoid some of the past mistakes
in urban development, particularly in the newer parts of our cities. We tend as a community
to encourage people to shout out for their rights and not to say, "What can I do to help?" If
we do not tackle those problems, which are basic to our society, we will have more and more
misfits in our community, more dropouts in society, and more broken marriages-and
goodness knows, there are enough of those today, without projecting the numbers forward
into the future. We have to prevent those things happening, and snowballing.
Let us look at the problems of industrial relations, and question some of the principles
in that sphere that many people regard as inviolate. Take, for example, the right to strike. Is
there, in fact, such an inviolate principle today in our changing society? There is a
responsibility to contribute to society, and when someone strikes he withdraws his labour
from society and society loses production. Often that person who is on strike receives a tax
refund, and if he is on strike over a central issue he may eventually receive higher wages. Of
course, the community is the loser in all of this, yet that same person still cries out for free
education, free hospitalisation, and a family benefit. He enjoys what the community
provides for him, despite the fact that he has withdrawn his contribution. So, I say that we
should be questioning some of the things which we often do not question, because society
has changed and we need new methods of approaching the problems. The Government
considers that it is a question of who determines the priorities, what will be produced, how it
will be produced, and who will get the benefit from that production.
Is the member for St. Kilda, who is trying to interject, about to get excited again, as we
saw him get excited 2 or 3 nights ago? I wonder what particular problem excited him then
and caused him to wave his finger as he is waving it now. Perhaps he was disappointed at the
result of the local body elections in Dunedin, or perhaps he is apprehensive about the
prospects of his party in the 1978 election. Fortunately, that is not one of the problems that
either the council or the commission has to deal with. With regard to planning, we can either
leave it to individuals and to the market force to decide or the State can play its role, as it has
done for a number of years. It can modify the market force, it can institute a concept of
fairness, and it can see that the community develops for the benefit of the country as a
whole.

which, after less than 2 years in power, has had to introduce an emergency Budget in which it

realises, as all the people realise, that many of the policies put to the people in 1975 by the

Nothwithstanding the Bill, and notwithstanding the statements from the Government

nation and the people? The fact is that New Zealand has already had woeful experience of
planning under former National Governments—and I refer to the Agriculture Production
Council, which was an exercise in agricultural economic planning, and also to the National
Development Council. Those were two woeful experiments in planning under the National
Government in the 1960s. They were to be the panacea for all the evils created by
incompetent National Government economic policy and management. But they failed,
because the Government failed to back them with complementary policies. The Government

the people and the nation. The result was that the period from the mid-1960s on, which
coincided with the existence of the Agricultural Production Council and the National

and slowest economic growth since World War II.
If the proposals outlined in the Bill are to achieve the best results, the Government will
need the voluntary co-operation of all sections of the community in setting goals and
objectives, and in carrying them into effect. There will be those who question whether the
structure and approach reflected in this measure will enable that to be done. Government
speakers have yet to indicate how the participation of all sections of the community can be
satisfactorily achieved under the proposed structure. If the project is to be successful, it is
essential that that objective be achieved. So far we have had no real indication of how the
activities of the council and its objectives are to be co-ordinated and linked with the
industrial, productive, and social sectors of our economy.
What assurance is the Government prepared to give that this organisation will function
in the common good-not merely in the economic sense, but in a social sense as well? What
assurance is there, for example-and this is essential if the best results are to be
achieved that the benefits on the economic side will be fairly shared between the investor,
the producer, the labour force, and those in need? What assurance is there that the
requirements of those whose need is greatest in our community will be accorded a worth-
while priority? What assurance is there that social objectives essential to the well-being of
the people will be pursued? I think especially of the family and family life, of the young, the
aged, the handicapped, and the infirm. What assurance is there that policies will be pursued
to help eliminate the social deficiencies that are of so much concern in our society today, and
lead to crime and other major problems?
In view of the industrial unrest provoked by the policies of successive National
Governments, will the Government give an assurance that satisfactory complementary
industrial relations policies will be pursued to enable the country to achieve desirable levels
of industrial harmony in order to promote a co-operative approach to production and to
achieve the highest levels of productivity and full employment and the free flow of
production and productive resources? After all, one can have the best possible economic
policies and objectives in the world, but, if the Government pursues detrimental industrial
relations policies, there is never any hope of achieving the objective.
As for the planning organisation outlined in the Bill, the question is whether the
organisation has been structured correctly-first, as to representation, and, secondly, as to
the machinery and techniques to be adopted. As to representation, of course, the organisa-
tion can be either totally non-political, representative of both political parties and standing
apart from the Government-just as the Monetary and Economic Council is independent
and stands apart from the Government-or representative solely of the Government.
Although both the Government and the Opposition are represented on the Commission for

the Future, only the Government is to be represented on the Planning Council. Why the
inconsistency, particularly when Government speakers have alleged that the Government is
seeking a bipartisan approach to this project?
As to the machinery and techniques to be adopted, I suggest that if planning is to be
attempted in the short term, the medium term, and the longer term, as the Bill proposes, it is
logical that it should be the responsibility of one organisation and not two, as is proposed.
For example, the New Zealand Planning Council is to be concerned with short-term and
medium-term planning. The Commission for the Future is to be concerned with longer-term
planning. If one organisation undertakes full responsibility, a consistent approach is
achieved, with the application of consistent principles and the fullest co-ordination and
liaison of activities and interests involved, and the optimum linkage and flow-on of policies,
of know-how, of statistics, and of other resources. If one organisation is responsible it has
the benefit of a similar policy and management approach, the same staff and administration,
and the same statistics and research facilities. One avoids the wasteful, inefficient, and
ineffective duplication that can arise if what ought to be a sole responsibility is handed over
to two separate bodies.
Some would say there is need for parliamentary participation if we are to achieve the
best results in the long term. I understand that the New Zealand Planning Council is to be
linked with both Cabinet and the Executive. The planning secretariat of the New Zealand
Planning Council-that is to say, the workers of the council-are now to form part of an
expanded committee on public expenditure, a committee that formerly comprised a couple
of Government departments and that has since been expanded further. Some would suggest
that the secretariat should also liaise with select committees. I believe that this suggestion
has merit. The secretariat should key in at the departmental level and at the parliamentary
level, as it would through the Public Expenditure Committee and other select committees.
That would ensure continuity in aims and objectives at the parliamentary level which, after
all, is the decision-making, spending, and resources allocation level.
Much more could be said about this Bill, but it cannot be covered in a 20-minute speech.
Many questions must be answered by the Government before the House and the people can
be satisfied with the Bill. I repeat that even if the New Zealand Planning Council and
associated bodies achieve the highest level of perfection in their approach, in formulating
policies, in presenting a range of alternatives and options, in setting priorities, targets, and
goals, and in assessing resources and resource needs and ensuring that our resources are used
to the best advantage, it will be of no avail unless backed by realistic complementary
Government policies to ensure that the goals and objectives are achieved.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): The honourable member used many words, but he showed an
abysmal lack of knowledge of the processes the Government will achieve by the introduction
of this Bill. To understand the functions of the two proposed bodies one needs to go back to
the National Party manifesto which, in plank 32, sets out the basis for the establishment of
the Commission for the Future: "The main function of the commission will be to consider,
study, and recommend policy options for the future as might seem appropriate to determine
the impact on and consequences for the long-term development of New Zealand." One or
two of the earlier Opposition speakers had a better understanding of that function than did
the honourable member for Wigram. The Bill provides for the establishment of the
Commission for the Future and reiterates the functions primarily established in the National
Party's 1975 election manifesto. It complements the New Zealand Planning Council, which is
also provided for in the Bill. As the honourable members said, the Planning Council is the
result of recommendations in the report of the Holmes task force, New Zealand at the
Turning Point.
Some say that New Zealand is overplanned already. In fact, one Opposition member
has said that New Zealand is overanalysed, and I think there is a place for both those
comments. That sort of criticism indicates a misunderstanding of the need in a modern
society to set objectives and national goals. The functions of the New Zealand Planning
Council and the Commission for the Future, although related, are quite separate. The
Commission for the Future, a bipartisan body, has been established to look at the long-term
options open to New Zealand. Its functions are clearly set out in the Bill and emphasis is
given to studying all the possibilities for the long-term economic and social development of
New Zealand. The role and function of the New Zealand Planning Council is much more
short term and more specific. It emphasises that the council should advise the Government
on planning for social, economic, and cultural development in New Zealand; it should assist
the Government to co-ordinate such planning; and it should comment on the Government's

New Zealand Planning Bill
programme on social, economic, and cultural development in New Zealand. There is a

I can do no more than suggest that he read much more diligently the book prepared by Sir

I want to draw attention to the countries, both eastern and western, that have done so
well in assessing national objectives over the past 30 years. If one looks at Japan and
compares its economic and social progress with that of other countries one must appreciate
that it stands apart from other countries for certain reasons. The reason that strikes the
visitor to Japan is that the country has consciously set its objectives on a national basis. My
mind goes back to the decision, made by Japan a long time ago, to set the world on wheels.
That conscious economic planning decision was made in the best interests of Japan at that
time. The results can be seen throughout the world today-Japanese cars have set the world
on wheels. That is a good example of long-term, conscious, economic planning decisions that
should be made in the country's economic interests.
By contrast, New Zealand has tended to leave long-term economic decisions to the
different sectors. The Dairy Board has decided its goals and objectives in terms of the
promotion and growth of dairy produce; the Wool Board has decided its long-term
objectives; and the manufacturing sector has in some instances been leaderless without a
cohesive policy set by the Government or a quasi-Government body. The National Govern-
ment recognised that this was happening, and in the mid-1960s set up the National
Development Council, which set goals for growth, industrial decisions, and primary-
producing decisions. The decisions of the National Development Council made a very
considerable contribution to the country's growth in the late 1960s. The Labour Government
decapitated the National Development Council by taking away its ability to make conscious
decisions in the best interests of the country, and by taking away its leadership. The Bill
before us restores the decision-making machinery so that long-term decisions can again be
made. I do not think that many people would argue about that need.
Some Opposition members have argued that the two bodies to be established by the Bill
will be political bodies. The Commission for the Future is a bipartisan group, containing one
Opposition member and one Government member. It will make long-term recommenda-
tions, and there is no political advantage in that type of study. The Planning Council is
different, because its day-to-day function is to comment on the work of the Government and
its decisions. I can agree with Opposition members when they say that the Planning
Council's role is in part political. If the Planning Council's short-term advice is to assist the
Government in making the right decisions, then the council can be accused of being political.
There is no doubt that the Planning Council's task is to advise the Government so that it can
make the right economic and social decisions. It is nonsense to throw in the old skeleton that
the Planning Council may be a political body; it is being established to make studies and to
advise the Government about decision making.
I have little else to say. I subscribe to the view that we must avoid overplanning and
overanalysing. The task ahead is one of proper decision making based on sound studies, the
collection of data, and ensuring that the decisions made are in the best interests of New
Zealand, both in the short and the long term. I am confident that the steps being taken in the
Bill will help that process. The Commission for the Future and the New Zealand Planning
Council will make worth-while contributions in decision making.
The members of both bodies have been discussed, and I shall not say anything more

They have chosen people of their own philosophical outlook for the commission and the

Also, it is extraordinary that a Government that espouses the cause of totally free

I have a few examples to give the House. Town planners are well trained and can call on
long experience, yet fashions and objectives in town planning have changed in accordance
with the prevailing philosophy at the time. We used to have streets of maximum width, with
good vehicular access to all parts of the city. Twenty years ago the whole objective of town
planning was to have a uniform standard. Dilapidated buildings were torn down and
replaced by modern structures of uniform design with certain verandah levels. We have seen
the disastrous results, and the barren tasteless areas produced by that sort of planning, and
now the objective must be to reproduce the variety of the past, rather than worrying about
technical excellence. We have seen a total change in planning, because of a totally different
philosophical objective.
In the cultural field, where at last our consciences are being scraped, we see that,
because of a different cultural outlook, we have destroyed much that was of value to the
Maori people, both in their social life and in the prospects of a continuing attachment to their
own cultural background. Now, belatedly and with reluctance, we are starting to look at
planning considerations that will take into account the importance of the marae-something
we set out to destroy in our previous planning.
The determination goes back again to Goethe's statement that, having made the
decision on where we are going, we must then decide what is good and what is bad. The
philosophy of the legislation is to decide that we will go somewhere, get all the information,

wonder whether it was Chapman, Leay, and company who planned it as a long-term political

Future.
This legislation is long overdue, and should be welcomed by all concerned, including the
Opposition. It is disappointing that it has been treated as it has. I should have thought the
Opposition would have a common interest with the Government in seeing to it that we
injected some long-term and true assessment of national interest. Mention has been made of
the National Development Council and various other planning efforts. A great deal of
criticism can be directed at past efforts over a number of years and through the terms of
successive Governments. We should not become tied up in party political terms about this.
Largely because we have not narrowed our objectives sufficiently, we have attempted to
plan on too large a front over too long a timespan.
I caution very much against projecting the future on the basis of the crystal-ball gazing
done today. World circumstances are changing very rapidly. I should like to think that the
Commission for the Future will advise us well in advance about circumstances likely to make
an impact on this country, rather than projecting answers to problems we do not even know
about at this stage. Changes in world trade, changes in the world's political scene, changes in
the balance of power in the trading financial international scene, and the emergence of
multinational corporations-all these developments are altering the old terms of definition
and ways of doing things. I hope that the Commission for the Future will in a real sense bring
us, in our thinking at least, into the twentieth century. There is no suggestion that either of
the bodies will prepare some sort of blueprint that will act as a strait-jacket on our future
development; that is not the objective at all. The objective is to promote the kind of
intelligent forethought that will enable this country to cope the better in the future with the
kind of circumstance of economic difficulty that challenges all the old assumptions of the past
and invites us to meet the challenge by answering, first, this sort of question: what are we
already doing with the resources we have? Are we using them wisely? I repeat that I do not
think we are, because in the past we have allocated capital, particularly in the public sector,
on the basis I have already mentioned.
The other thing is the investment of private capital. How on earth can intelligent,
major, private-capital decisions be made except on the basis of some integrated land-use
appreciation? Yet that has been done. In one part of the North Island it seems that a great
deal of traditional farm land is about to be put into forestry, yet we hear talk of the
investment of millions of dollars in a meatworks, and industry based upon it. The time for
that is past, if we project the future, which is afforestation and not grassland farming in a
very large part of the North Island. Forward thinking must be encouraged, not only in the
public sector but also in the private sector.
I welcome this Bill, but not for what it will do in the short term. I have stated my view as
clearly as I can. The most necessary thing in the short term is to get to grips with resource
utilisation based on land-use appreciation. That is the compelling short-term need. I
welcome the prospect that in the longer term, beyond 5 years, we will begin to get the full
advantages of the two organisations established by the Bill. I congratulate the Minister on his
foresight in introducing this legislation, which inspires in me a greater confidence in the
future, even while I urge on the Government a greater concern for the needs of the present
and for action in the directions I have outlined.

CUSTOMS ORDERS CONFIRMATION BILL
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): Much as I should like to maintain the
tempo of excitement that has been generated by my colleague the Minister of National
Development, I do not think I will be able to. I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. When I introduced the Bill I explained to the House that its purpose is limited to
making provision for confirmation, in terms of section 131 of the Customs Act 1966, of all
Orders in Council made under section 124 of the Act on or after 1 July of the previous
session but before 1 July during the present session, and laid before Parliament in
accordance with the Regulations Act 1936. The Bill confirms a number of Customs Tariff
Amendment Orders made as a result of recommendations from the Industries Development
Commission. All parties having an interest in the changes have had an opportunity to make
submissions to the commission during its investigations. The Bill also confirms the Customs
Tariff (Clocks and Watches) Amendment Order 1977. This order was made to impose the
same rates of duty on clock and watch movements assembled but incomplete as applied to

BEER DUTY BILL
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. On the introduction of this Bill I said that its purpose was to modernise and
consolidate the existing legislation, which was no longer appropriate because of the many
advances in brewing techniques which have taken place in more recent times. The Bill does
not make any alteration to the amount of revenue received by the Government from this
source of taxation, although there are minor variations, both upwards and downwards, in the
rates applicable to particular kinds of beer. The Bill also removes the need for the
department's officers to carry out the cumbersome procedure of measuring quantities and
specific gravities of wort at the stage when it is pitched for fermentation, and substitutes an
audit check procedure of the brewery companies' records in a manner similar to that
undertaken by the department's sales tax inspectors in regard to the collection of sales tax.
Clause 1 provides that the Bill will come into force on 1 April 1978. Clause 2 deals with
various definitions necessary for the effective administration of the Act. Clauses 3 and 4 are
machinery clauses. Clause 5 makes beer brewed for sale subject to the control of the
Customs Department, and thereby ensures that the department may exercise effective
control in the collection of beer duty. This applies even where beer may be brewed illegally,
but it does not, of course, place any restrictions on home brewers, who are not covered by
the provisions of the Act when they brew beer just for their own consumption. That is the
current position. Clause 6 provides that it is an offence to brew beer for sale unless that is
done pursuant to a licence issued under the Act. Clause 7 deals with the necessary
procedures for obtaining a brewer's licence.
Clause 8 and 9 concern the grant of, refusal of, or suspension of licences. Clause 8
provides for renewal of licences not later than 31 January each year on the payment of the
necessary licence fee. Clause 10 allows any person who is refused a licence or is refused
approval to establish a depot to appeal to the Administrative Division of the Supreme Court.
Clause 11 empowers the Collector of Customs to require payment of the annual licence fee,
and it also contains the necessary transitional provision in respect of fees paid in 1978. The
fees will be prescribed on the same basis as at present—that is, on a graduated scale based
upon the quantity of beer produced.
The anti-evasion provision, clause 12, makes it an offence to alter the strength or
quantity of beer after the declaration of these for duty purposes has been made. Clause 13
translates existing provisions into the new legislation. Clause 14 provides in more precise
form the existing power of the Licensing Control Commission to approve or refuse
applications for the establishment of brewery depots or bottling stores. The Bill contains an
appeal provision in clause 10 against any adverse decision of the commission. Clause 15
imposes the rates of duty set out in the schedule to the Bill. The clause also ensures that beer
exported from New Zealand by a brewery does not pay duty, thus avoiding the necessity for
drawbacks of duty in these circumstances. Transfers of beer from one brewery to another are
also dealt with in a manner similar to that which applies under the Motor Spirits Duty Act in
respect of motor spirit transferred from one licensee to another. Clause 16 ensures that the
department has effective control over beer brewed for export.
Clause 17 ensures that beer consumed on the premises of a brewery shall pay duty.
Clause 18 allows the brewer to take beer for quality control. Clauses 19 to 23 are essentially
machinery clauses. Clause 24 embodies a provision in the present law permitting the
Collector of Customs to prohibit the brewer from brewing beer where duty due and payable
has not been paid. Clause 25 makes clear the liability of the brewery in cases where the rates
of duty payable are changed at any time. Clause 26 provides the power to require securities
to be given. Clauses 27 to 32 deal with refunds, remissions, and drawback of beer duty.
Clauses 33 to 36 provide certain powers to the department's officers. They include authority
for officers to question persons about the particulars shown in any document required to be
provided, and authority to require documents to be produced. These powers are necessary
to enable the department's officers to carry out the audit check of company records, which I


## p. 4284 (#390) ###########################################

4284
8 November
Beer Duty Bill
have already explained will replace the present system of measuring and testing the strength
and quantity of wort used in the production of beer. Clause 37 empowers the department to
take samples for the purpose of checking the alcoholic strength of beers to ensure duty is
being paid at the correct rate.
Part VIII of the Bill deals with offences and penalties. Offences include attempts to
defraud the revenue, knowingly making false or erroneous declarations, the production of
false documents, and making unauthorised structural alterations to the brewery or plant.
Clause 48 requires the brewer to keep sufficient business records to enable his liability for
the payment of beer duty to be readily ascertained. Clauses 49 to 53 are machinery
provisions. Clause 54 is the necessary transitional provision to cover duty payable on beer
brewed prior to the commencement of the new Act and delivered from the brewery prior to
its coming into force. This Bill modernises and consolidates the legislation relating to the
collection of beer duty and the control of brewing operations. The many changes which have
taken place in recent times in brewing techniques have made a complete review of the
legislation essential.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I do not think either the Bill or
the Minister's comments on it will disturb the froth on a single glass of beer. The Bill has not
stirred any reaction from either the brewers or the consumers, and I think that is all that
needs to be said about it.

POST OFFICE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This Bill is again an important and necessary but unexciting measure. Clause 1
relates to the short title and commencement. The Bill, which provides for the implementa-
tion of measures announced in the Budget, is deemed to have come into force on 1
September 1977. No action has yet been taken under the new provisions; recent changes to
interest rates were made under the existing legislation. Clause 2 relates to term deposits.
This clause amends the main Act to provide for the Post Office Savings Bank to receive
deposits to term deposit accounts, and is in line with similar provisions recently enacted in
respect of trustee savings banks and private savings banks.
Clause 3 relates to rates of interest on deposits. This clause amends the principal Act to
provide for the rate of interest payable on money deposited in securities under provisions
made in other sections of the principal Act to be fixed by the Post Office Savings Bank in
concurrence with the Secretary to the Treasury. In practice, all rates of interest will continue
to be fixed by the Minister of Finance except those in respect of deposits in investment
accounts, term deposit accounts, national development bonds, housing bonds, savings
certificates, and any other securities which may be issued under section 129E of the principal
Act.
Clause 4 relates to the calculation of interest. This clause repeals section 122 of the main
Act, and a new section is substituted. In addition to existing provisions, the new section
authorises the Postmaster-General, with the concurrence of the Minister of Finance, in
respect of deposits made to any class of account or depositors or group of depositors that the
Minister of Finance may specify, to direct that interest shall be payable on deposits entered
on the ledger record on or before the seventh day of the month. The change is of a
machinery nature, and is designed to simplify the processing of accounts. It will confer no
significant advantage or disadvantage on any depositor.
Clause 5 relates to investment accounts and term deposits. It repeals section 127 of the
main Act, which empowers the Minister of Finance to determine the rate of interest payable
on investment accounts and provides for the Postmaster-General to set the structure. In
substitution, clause 5 (2) authorises the Post Office Savings Bank to receive deposits into
investment accounts and term deposit accounts, and provides for the rates of interest in
respect of these to be determined by the Director-General of the Post Office with the
concurrence of the Secretary to the Treasury. Clause 6 amends the principal Act to provide
for every development bond to be issued for such a term as the Postmaster-General directs.
The present subsection provides for the bonds to mature at the expiration of 8 years from the
date of purchase. Section 129B is further amended to provide for the Director-General of the
Post Office, with the concurrence of the Secretary to the Treasury, to determine the rates of
interest payable in respect of money paid in development bonds.
Finally, clause 7 amends section 129E of the principal Act to provide that every security

NURSES BILL
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time.
An earlier form of this Bill was introduced in 1975 and, since its provisions affected all
categories of nurses, it was referred to the Social Services Committee to allow representa-
tions to be made by interested parties. As a result of representations from the Nursing
Council of New Zealand and the New Zealand Nurses Association, the select committee in
1976 accepted that there was a need to establish a roll for those at present called community
nurses. As this change involved extensive redrafting, the Bill was deferred on an undertaking
being given that a new Bill would be introduced in 1977 making provision for a roll.
This Bill repeats most of the contents of the earlier Bill, makes further minor
amendments, and re-enacts the Nurses Act 1971. The Bill amends the provisions of the
principal Act dealing with the registration of nurses, and includes new provisions for a
separate class of nurses to be known as enrolled nurses. It also opens all branches of nursing
to members of either sex, and excludes private charitable institutions from those institutions
that may be approved as schools of nursing. The class of "registered comprehensive nurse"
was created by the Nurses Amendment Act passed in 1975 to cover those qualifying from the
new programmes at technical institutes.
Under this Bill provision is made for entry on this part of the register of those who have
obtained registration in certain other branches of nursing. A new class, "General and
Obstetric", is created, and the class of registration to be called "Obstetric"-previously
"Maternity"-will be available only for registration of persons trained overseas in that
capacity. There is an historical background to this. Prior to 1957, the training course leading
to registration as a maternity nurse stood on its own, either as a 6-month course for the
already registered nurse or as a separate 18-month basic course. In 1958 a new scheme was
introduced whereby a nurse who had qualified in the basic 3-year general nursing course
could also obtain registration as a maternity nurse because obstetric nursing was included in
the programme. In 1970 the 18-month course was discontinued so that all new registrations
on the maternity register have in recent years been in respect of persons already registered as
general nurses. Under the terms of this Bill a further step is taken. The general and obstetric
qualifications are combined and a person obtains registration after the 3-year hospital


## p. 4286 (#392) ###########################################

4286
8 November
Nurses Bill
programme as a registered general and obstetric nurse.
During the hearing before the select committee strong submissions were made by the
New Zealand Nurses Association and the Nursing Council of New Zealand to the effect that
the class of nurses now known as community nurses should be entered on a roll of nurses and
be known as enrolled nurses. Before being accepted a great deal of consideration was given
to this change. People on this part of the register have qualified from an 18-month
programme and are not as highly qualified as nurses in the other parts of the register who
have undergone a 3-year programme. The title "community nurse" is not descriptive of the
duties of these nurses and is used overseas to describe a different type of nursing function
altogether. The title in the Bill provides the status of "enrolled nurse" for this type of nurse.
The category "male nurse" is abolished and in the terms of the Bill men qualify for any class
of registration or enrolment in exactly the same way as women. The nursing profession has
pressed for this for years. The Bill provides a system whereby nurses who qualify for
registration in all the branches of nursing included in the comprehensive programme will
obtain registration as comprehensive nurses. This has the merit of simplicity and easy
reference.
The Bill abolishes the minimum age for registration except in the case of enrolled
nurses, for whom the minimum age is reduced by 6 months to 17 years. The other classes of
nurse are registered after a 3-year training course following a school certificate qualification.
This means that it is not possible to obtain registration in those classes under the age of 18,
and a specific age registration therefore is unnecessary. At present there is provision for
private charitable institutions to be approved as schools of nursing. For some years there has
been no need for this provision. These institutions acknowledge that they do not wish to use
resources in this way, and this Bill excludes them from such a function in the future.
Other changes introduced by the Bill are of a minor administrative nature. The field
from which nurses may be appointed to the Nursing Council has been somewhat extended.
The 1971 Act provides, as two of the qualifications for nomination, employment as principal
tutor in a hospital school of nursing and employment in the Department of Health as the
chief nursing officer of a health district. Under the Bill, and in response to representations
made to the select committee, the field is now widened to any tutor in a hospital school of
nursing and any departmental nursing officer in a health district.
A number of submissions were made to the select committee in 1976 and all were
considered, though not all were adopted. For example, the Plunket Society advocated an
additional class of registration for Karitane nurses, but the committee was of the opinion that
Karitane nurses, while doing valuable work and filling a need in the community, do not
perform nursing functions comparable to those covered by the register. The Christian
Scientists submitted a case for registration for non-medical nurses who treat patients by
spiritual means, but the committee felt that registration should be confined to the medical
field.
Recently, this Bill was referred to the Social Services Committee to allow representa-
tions on clauses 16 and 17 only, which relate to registration and enrolment, to be made by
interested parties. Submissions were made that only those nurses who have undertaken the
comprehensive nurse programme offered by technical institutes should be entitled to
comprehensive nurse registration. The committee felt that it is fair that all those who in the
aggregate have substantially equivalent qualifications should be entered on the comprehen-
sive register. The changes contained in the Bill will not please everybody, but they have a
logical sequence. As far as possible they reflect the functions of the different classes of nurse
and remove discrimination against men in nursing.
I commend also the new system whereby the registration of one individual on several
registers will be progressively reduced since the comprehensive class includes those nurses
qualified in general and obstetric nursing, and either psychiatric or psychopaedic nursing. In
addition, the Bill ensures that due recognition is given to those whose combined qualifica-
tions are substantially equivalent to those gained from technical institute programmes thus
avoiding the establishment of an elite group within the profession. I thank all people who
made submissions to the committee in 1976 and 1977. Even where the submissions were not
adopted they assisted the committee in its deliberations. During the Committee stage I
propose to introduce for consideration a Supplementary Order Paper making some minor
amendments to clauses 47, 52, 60, and 62. These involve some redrafting for reasons of
clarity.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): As many members are aware,
the Bill has been being processed for a long time. Most of the contentious issues have been

CONTRACTUAL MISTAKES BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee, as part of its general
review of our law of contracts begun in 1971, reported to me in May of last year on the effect
of mistakes on contracts. This Bill implements that report. The law reform committee found
the existing law on this subject to be fragmented, relying on inherently meaningless tests for
mistake, and attracting remedies that are both drastic and inflexible. It has been suggested
that there is no demand for such technical legal legislation.
The law reform committee discussed in paragraph 6 of its report a trilogy of English
cases illustrating the different results that could be obtained at present even though the
factual situations were nearly identical. The committee concluded: "That such illusory
distinctions should exist and that such important consequences should depend upon them,
seem to us a reproach to the law." Other similar sentiments are expressed in the law reform
committee's report, and it is clear to me that the law in this area of contract is in need of an
overhaul. As introduced nearly 6 months ago the Bill contained a wide definition of mistake
as the law reform committee felt this was desirable to ensure that meritorious cases could be
brought before the courts. The law reform committee believed that there were adequate
checks in clauses 5 and 6 of the Bill to ensure that relief will be granted in appropriate cases
only. The select committee, however, after hearing the evidence concluded that it would be
undesirable at this stage to include such a wide definition. Clause 2 was accordingly altered
to define mistake simply as a mistake whether of fact or law.
A number of submissions to the select committee expressed concern at what was
thought to be the effect of the Bill on the certainty that normally attaches to a written
contract. While some of these submissions failed to take account of the existing law relating
to mistake, the select committee nevertheless felt it desirable to spell out that the general
security of contractual relationships should not be prejudiced by the Bill. This is to be found
in clause 3(a). Clause 4 provides for the Bill to be a code in respect of the relief that may be
granted where a contract was entered into by mistake. Clause 5 sets out the circumstances
that must prevail before relief may be granted. A number of submissions did not appear to
appreciate the mutuality concept of the clause—that is, that relief would be available only
where the mistake was made by both parties, or made by one party and known to the other.
The clause has been redrafted to make this point clearer. In addition to the mutuality
concept I have just outlined, the mistake must result in a substantially unequal exchange of
values or in the conferment of a benefit substantially disproportionate to the consideration
provided.
Some of the building interests making submissions were concerned that clause 5 could
upset existing practice where a tenderer makes a mistake in his tender. The normal practice
when a mistake is discovered is to draw it to the tenderer's attention and ask him whether he
wishes to withdraw or affirm his tender. Fears were expressed that clause 5 could permit an
affirmation followed by an application for relief for mistake. Clause 5(2)(b) makes it quite
13 Vol. 415


## p. 4288 (#394) ###########################################

4288
8 November
Contractual Mistakes Bill
clear that this cannot occur. The type of relief that may be granted is set out in clause 6. As
opposed to the existing rigid and inflexible rules relating to relief for mistake, the courts are
given a wide discretion to do as they think just in any particular case. This type of approach is
contained in the Illegal Contracts Act, and has been recommended by the law reform
committee in its report on misrepresentation and breach of contract.
The rights of third parties are protected under clause 7. This will ensure that a court
order under clause 6 made in respect of two parties to a contract will not affect the rights of a
person not a party to the contract who purchases the property in good faith and with no
knowledge of the original mistaken contract. Clause 8(a) was inserted by the select
committee to confer jurisdiction on small claims tribunals, while clause 8(b) confers
jurisdiction under the Bill on arbitrators. The power conferred on arbitrators may be
expressly excluded by the parties to a contract.
When the Bill was reported back from the select committee the member for Henderson
expressed some doubt about whether it was precise enough for parties to determine their
legal rights without recourse to the courts. In my view the Bill provides a vastly improved
framework for the determination of the effect of a mistake upon a contract than is to be
found in the existing law. It seems to me that it would be necessary to compile an exhaustive
list of all the situations in which a contractual mistake could occur, and the remedies
applicable in each case if the member's concern is to be met. Such a task would be virtually
impossible. It could also result in replacing an existing inflexible set of rules with one that
could be just as inflexible. At the moment a lawyer cannot advise his client with any degree
of certainty on the law relating to mistake. I believe that the enactment of this Bill will
enable any competent commercial lawyer adequately to advise his client whether he may
apply for relief, his chances of obtaining it, and its nature.

system and they would prefer that Parliament leave it alone.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I do not share the member for Auckland
Central's low opinion of the legal profession or of arbitrators, or his apparently high opinion
of a socialist academic whose case about the volume and the quality of Parliament's law was
blown to bits by a retired senior parliamentary counsel just a few months ago. As I said in
moving the second reading and in introducing the Bill more than 6 months ago, it is an
improvement on the existing law. As the law reform committee stated in its report, the most
important point against the present law is that the remedies available for mistakes in contract
are drastic and inflexible. If the member for Auckland Central, having discovered some
defect in the law that produces inequities, is content to leave the law unchanged, I am not.
The Government was elected to produce law that is fair and just to all parties.
Bill read a second time.
WILLS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. On 30 March 1973 my predecessor, the member for Henderson, referred to the
Property Law and Equity Reform Committee two alternative proposals-first, that a will
should be revoked automatically by the subsequent divorce of a testator, and, secondly, that
if a testator is subsequently divorced and is survived by his former wife, his will should be
read as if his former wife had predeceased him. The Bill in the main gives effect to the
recommendations of the law reform committee contained in a report dated November 1973
that a divorced spouse should not benefit under a pre-divorce will. The Bill contains
exceptions to this general principle in the case of wills expressed to be made in anticipation
of divorce, and also if the provision in the estate relates to a debt or liability owing to the
divorced spouse, but otherwise the divorced spouse is excluded from taking. For the
purposes of administering the will, the will is read as if the divorced spouse died immediately
before the person making the will.
Although this reform may be considered a novel reform in any English jurisdiction,
other countries in the Commonwealth have either passed legislation giving effect to the
reform proposal, or have indicated that they are about to do so. It is also worth noting that
the Ontario Law Reform Commission in its report on the impact of divorce on existing wills
has followed very closely the reform proposals contained in the New Zealand report. The
Bill was drafted in close consultation with the Public Trustee, and apart from a submission
received from a member of the legal profession in his individual capacity-which, I might
add, contained very useful submissions, some of which have been incorporated in the
present draft-no other submissions were received, although the New Zealand Law Society
and Trustee Companies Association perused the Bill.
Clause 2 has been redrafted to clarify the application of the Bill. This redrafting has in
turn removed the need for clause 2(2)(c) relating to wills made after divorce. It also resolves
the problem relating to the wills of people who have been divorced twice or more. Clause
2(1) of the Bill has been so drafted to ensure that while the divorced spouse is unable to take
a beneficial interest under a pre-divorce will, or assume a position as executor or trustee
under that will, the remaining provisions of the Bill take effect. This is achieved by providing
that the will shall be read as if the other partner had died immediately before the person
making the will. Clause 2(2) contains the exception, and, as mentioned above, the Bill does
not apply to wills expressed to be made in anticipation of divorce, or if the provision relates
to a debt or liability. This includes a liability under the Law Reform (Testamentary
Promises) Act 1949. A further exception should be added in the case of a codicil made after
the relevant decree or order or legislative enactment, but expressed to take effect notwith-
standing the provisions of the Bill, and I intend to introduce a Supplementary Order Paper
to provide for this exception.
Clause 2(3) has been redrafted to avoid the possibility of a testator inadvertently
confirming a gift by codicil to a divorced spouse without going so far as to require execution
of a new will when the codicil is simply re-executing or revising an existing will. This clause
requires redrafting to distinguish between a re-executed will and one revived by a codicil,
and I intend to reintroduce a further Supplementary Order Paper. Clause 4 provides that the
Bill shall apply to every will whether made before or after the commencement of the Act if
the testator dies after the commencement of the Act. In order to give testators and their


## p. 4291 (#397) ###########################################

8 November
4291
Wills Amendment Bill
testamentary advisers sufficient time to make alterations to existing testamentary arrange-
ments if considered necessary in the light of the new provisions in the Bill, clause 1 provides
that it should come into force on 1 July 1978. In addition, the Bill contains an amendment to
section 15 of the Wills Act 1837, which relates to the avoidance of gifts by attesting
witnesses. It remedies the situation that was disclosed in the case of In the Estate of Bravda.
Finally, the Bill contains a consequential amendment to the Wills Amendment Act 1955.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): In this legislation, which appears on the Order Paper in

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I did not, as perhaps I should have,

later, and he died some 20 years after the divorce, survived by his former wife. He had not

passed to the woman who had not been his wife for more than 20 years."
It is very evident from that quotation from the letter written by the then Minister of
Justice, the member for Henderson, that he was sufficiently concerned with what appeared
to be an inequity in the law to refer it to the law reform committee for study and report. The

3. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Works and Development: Is he
satisfied with the basis of the compensation settlement for the Ferentosh Homestead at Lake

made to replace the Ferentosh Homestead were entered into before I came into office. The

it was entered into. This case, as many members will know, has been a very difficult one
associated with most unusual circumstances. There are some aspects of the case about which

Industrial Relations—Waipa Sawmill
11. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) asked the Minister of Labour: In the light of the
supplementary question in the House on 3 November by the member for Grey Lynn, asking
what action the Minister of Labour had taken during the recent costly union dispute at the
Waipa sawmill, can he indicate whether this was an inter-union dispute; did the FOL
intercede and settle the dispute; and does this indicate that the policy of the Minister and the
Government is to refrain from interfering in domestic union disputes?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Yes, I can confirm that the disruption in the
timber industry arose as a result of domestic issues within the timber workers' union—and I
should add primarily one branch, South Auckland. At the invitation of the national office of
the timber workers' union the Federation of Labour interceded and put forward certain
proposals for the settlement of the dispute. As the issue was a domestic union matter, I
considered it was appropriate in the first instance that the union itself or the Federation of
Labour should have had the opportunity of resolving the matter. Any premature action by
the Government would not have led to a resumption of work, and indeed the position could
have deteriorated quite significantly. However, the Government is still watching develop-
ments closely and will act should the situation warrant it.
Mr Isbey: In how many disputes, apart from this one involving the timber workers, has
the Minister called in the Federation of Labour to assist?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It is not a question of calling in the Federation of Labour. I could
not say, and I do not think my officers could say, the number of cases on which there have
been consultations with the Federation of Labour. This case was clearly a domestic union
matter-a deplorable one from the point of view of union democracy-and I left it to the
Federation of Labour to clean up its own mess. It did so.
Mr Isbey: Will the Minister of Labour confirm that in this dispute the Federation of
Labour was of great assistance, and that it has been of great assistance to the Minister in
many disputes?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: No, quite the reverse. In this case the Government was not
involved. The Government deliberately kept itself out of union democracy and left the
Federation of Labour to clean up bad practices within unions.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Would the Minister therefore concede that comments here and in
other places downgrading the Federation of Labour are unhelpful to general industrial
harmony?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I do not know of any downgrading of the Federation of Labour,
but the Government believes in good trade unionism, properly practised under democratic
rules. We have seen that at work with the Federation of Labour dealing with the timber
workers' union. I hope it may long continue.

that the half-yearly survey increase granted to State servants with effect from 1 November
1976 and paid out earlier this year has not yet been paid to nurses employed at Waikato
Hospital, and, further, that there have been suggestions that the increase will not be paid out
before next year, whereas most other State servants received the back pay for this increase in
July or August, and, if so, could he advise, (1) why there has been such a long delay, and (2)
when payment will be made to Waikato nurses?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I had been informed that the half-yearly survey
increase that took effect from 1 November 1976 had not been paid to nurses at Waikato
Hospital. I am informed further that, as the Waikato Hospital Board is the prototype site for
the health computer system, it has been necessary to spread its staffing resources over the
implementation of its payroll on the new computer systems and the calculation of the arrears
of salary. Both have been major undertakings, and, as a result, the payment of back pay has
been affected. The Waikato Hospital Board has tentatively arranged to pay all nurses, other
than those employed at Waikato Hospital, during the week 14 to 18 November, and all
nurses employed at Waikato Hospital during the week 21 to 25 November.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Manawatu Gorge
17. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua). asked
the Minister of Works and Development: In view of his comments as reported in the
Dominion of 3 November on the new methods proposed for the improvement of the
Manawatu Gorge, could he advise the House of the steps he will take to implement what he
learned from Japan?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The National Roads Board
has asked for an appraisal to be made of the manner in which the Manawatu Gorge can be
upgraded to improve its safety and efficiency to the users. A possible solution to some of the
more difficult sections could well be the use of half bridging, as was witnessed by myself and
the Director of Roading in Japan. This suggestion will be followed up by those carrying out
the appraisal.

18. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) asked the Minister of Housing: How many people

Trade Training for Urban Maoris
20. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Maori Affairs: How many
young urban Maoris receive assistance from his department for trade training?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Maori Affairs): I am informed that in 1977, 82
young Maoris from urban areas, as classified by the Department of Statistics, were engaged
in pre-apprenticeship courses operated by the Department of Maori Affairs.
Hon. M. Rata: Can I take it from the Minister's answer that not one of the 82 young
urban Maoris engaged in pre-apprenticeship courses was receiving assistance for trade
training?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: I have given the honourable member the information I was
supplied with. From the information I have I am not sure whether they received additional
trade training. However, I will endeavour to find out for the member.
Hon. M. Rata: Assuming that none of the 82 young urban Maoris engaged in pre-
apprenticeship courses is receiving trade training, will the Minister take immediate steps to
ensure that in future a number of young Maoris can receive trade training assistance from the
department?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: There is work in this area. As the member will be aware,
provision was made in the mini-Budget for pre-apprenticeship training courses for young
people across the board, to be instituted in Auckland. He will also be aware, as a former
Minister of Maori Affairs, that there was some difficulty with the trade union movement
about special assistance being granted to young urban Maoris but not being available to
others.
Hon. M. Rata: What evidence does the Minister have for claiming that the trade training
scheme was hindered by the attitude of the trade union movement?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: My understanding is that the scheme was restricted to rural
Maoris because of the limited opportunities in such areas, but that if the scheme was to be
expanded to those living in urban areas it was considered it should not be racially selective.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

TAB-Annual Net Income
1. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: When was the
last time, if at all, that the Totalisator Agency Board showed a decrease in its annual net
income from the amount received in the previous year?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: The last time the Totalisator
Agency Board showed a decrease in its annual net income was for the racing year ended 31
July 1971. The figure for that year was $3,500,494, compared with $3,520,871 for the
previous year—a decrease of $20,377, or 0.57 percent.
(20/10/77)
Trotting Permits
2. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: Could he
indicate how many new racing and trotting permits have been issued for the period 1 August
to 1 October 1977, and, of these, how many are for weekday meetings?
Hon D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: Two new permits were issued
for the period 1 August to 1 October 1977. Both were for mid-week night trotting meetings
held in August, one by the Waikato Trotting Club and the other by the Cambridge Trotting
Club.
(20/10/77)
Off-course Betting Figures
3. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) asked the Minister of Internal Affairs: How much of
an increase/decrease has there been in off-course betting on weekday racing and trotting
meetings in the period 1 August to 1 October 1977 (not including meetings held as a result of
new permits having been allocated) in comparison with the 1 August to 1 October periods in
1976 and 1972?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs) replied: Off-course betting on mid-
week racing and trotting meetings in the period 1 August to 1 October 1977 (excluding the
two extra trotting meetings authorised during this time) amounted to $21,351,778. This was
an increase of $3,244,044 over the corresponding period in 1976, the figure for which was
$18,107,734. The 1972 figure was $5,698,343—that is, $12,409,391 less than in 1976 and
$15,653,435 less than in 1977. The great increase since 1972, and especially in the last 2
years, is undoubtedly due in great part to new forms of betting such as trebles and quinellas.
(20/10/77)
Forest Development—Thinning Programmes
4. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Forests: Is he aware that the
downturn in the building industry is having serious consequences for the Woodhill State
Forest because thinnings normally taken by contractors for particle board manufacture and
posts are now required only in small quantities, so that thinning is not being undertaken at
the level essential for maximum forest development, and, if so, does he intend to increase
Forest Service staff levels to maintain this work?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: I am aware that the reduced level of
activity in the building industry has had some effect on the sale of thinnings from the
Woodhill State Forest. Thinning programmes are, however, being maintained, the only
difference being that instead of being able to sell the thinnings for particle board manufac-
ture or fencing materials they are being left to waste. It is necessary to thin forest plantations
at prescribed times to maintain vigorous, healthy, and windfirm trees, and when there is a
downturn in the market there is no alternative but to waste thin. Of the 47 men laid off by
New Zealand Particle Board Ltd and the 10 men laid off by the thinning contractors, 7 have
been given jobs by the Forest Service.
(20/10/77)

Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied: Three public telephones have

Fisheries-Market Research and Development
7. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Fisheries: Can he specify what research
and market development is being carrried out by the Fishing Industry Board specifically for
small fishing operators?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied: The Fishing Industry Board has a
programme of market research and development which is intended to be of benefit to all fish
processors selling on domestic and/or export markets. No distinction is drawn between
relative size. However, as most fish processors would be in the small to medium category and
as the few large processors have market research and information services of their own, the
smaller processors would probably obtain proportionately greater benefit from the board's
activities in this field. The board has the following services: (a) a market intelligence service
providing data, statistics, and contacts for major and potential fish export markets; (b) a
producers' seafood buyers' guide, promotional literature, etc., to assist export and domestic
selling; (c) the board has printed a wide range of individual fish recipe leaflets for the
domestic market; (d) it employs two full-time economists who are engaged in a very
extensive promotional programme, including a lot of work with home-science teachers and
classes in schools; (e) the board's food technologist is available to assist companies with
handling, storage, processing, freezing, packing, quality, etc., matters; and (f) it has a food
technology research contract with Massey University for investigating specific problems and
developments.
(20/10/77)

Railway Houses, Milson, Palmerston North
10. Hon M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Railways: How many residen-
tial houses in the Milson area of Palmerston North does the Railways Department own; what
is the average age of these houses, and when were the oldest built; are any of these dwellings
considered substandard by the department, and, if so, how many; how many of the dwellings
have outside toilets, and how many dwellings have been altered or extended to bring the
toilets inside during the last 2 years; and what was the average expenditure per house in
maintenance or improvement to make them more habitable in each of the last 2 financial
years?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways) replied: The department owns 79
houses at Milson. Of these, 66 are of the older type averaging 50 years of age while the other
13, averaging 19 years of age, are of more modern design. The oldest houses were
constructed in 1926. None of these houses is considered substandard. Of the 79 houses, 39
still have outside toilet facilities. The toilets of 26 houses were moved inside during the last 2
years. Maintenance expenditure is not necessarily incurred every year on every house. In
year ended 31 March 1976, $6,000 was spent on 12 houses, an average of $500 per house. In
year ended 31 March 1977, $48,400 was spent on 35 houses, an average of $1,383 per house,
and $22,000 on the remaining 44. During the present financial year, $26,000 will be spent on
maintaining 35 houses, an average of $743 per house. Spread over the 3 years and the 79
houses, this amounts to an average expenditure per house per year of $432 on maintenance
and improvement.
(21/10/77)

National Advisory Council on Pre-school Education
16. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education: Can he supply the
following details about the National Advisory Council on Pre-school Education: (a) how
often does the council meet; (b) at what cost; (c) what changes have been effected in pre-
school education as a result of its consultations; and (d) what recommendations has it made
which have not yet been brought into effect?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: (a) The National Advisory Council
meets twice a year; (b) the cost is about $4,000 a year for the travel cost of the members; (c)
as the council has an advisory role and because it is the only national forum for discussion
and the sharing of views across the whole field of pre-school education, it has contributed
significantly since 1973 towards the development of early childhood education. It has done
so through its influence on the thinking of its members, who represent voluntary organisa-
tions, teacher organisations, Government departments, the universities, teachers' colleges,
and education boards with a direct responsibility in the pre-school field. Changes consequent
on the deliberations of the council have been made in the following areas: the work of the
district pre-school committees; policies for the education of handicapped pre-school chil-
dren; the growing responsibilities of education boards in servicing pre-school organisations;
the development of materials for the information of parents of pre-school children; the
rationalisation of the administration of early childhood care and education services; policies
relating to child care services; (d) recommendations are made to Government departments
and other agencies. All these agencies have, of course, the right to decide for themselves
whether they wish to act on any recommendation made by the National Advisory Council, to
adopt it in a different way, or to decline to adopt it. Among the recommendations made to
the Department of Education over the last year that are at present being studied and which
could influence further development in the pre-school field are: a review of the aims,
functions, and membership of the National Advisory Council itself; services for pre-school
children in hospital; intervention programmes for handicapped children; the training of
kindergarten teachers and child care centre personnel. The first of these recommendations
foreshadows a comprehensive study of the council by its own members which could lead to
discussions with the Government on the responsibilities it might assume in the future
development of policies within the whole field of services for young children.
(26/10/77)

## p. 4307 (#413) ###########################################

9 November
4307
Questions and Replies
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: Widows' benefits and other
income-tested social security benefits are based on need and designed to meet a specific set
of circumstances. It is appropriate, therefore, that the establishment of need be by way of an
income test. Additional benefit of up to $16 per week is also available, as well as telephone
and television licence fee concessions, rates rebates, and so on. On the other hand, National
superannuation is a retirement income, and for this group telephone and television licence
fee concessions are being phased out.

South Auckland Timber Workers Union
22. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa) asked the Minister of Labour: Did the Government
consider deregistering the South Auckland Timber Workers Union, and, if so, why did it not
do so at an early stage?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Disruption to the timber industry
arose as a result of domestic issues within the Timber Workers Union. It was therefore
appropriate in the first instance that the union itself or the Federation of Labour should have
had the opportunity of resolving the matter. Any premature action by the Government
would not have led to an early resumption of work, and, indeed, the position could have
deteriorated. As my colleague will now be aware, the proposals put forward by Sir Thomas
Skinner for a resumption of work have been accepted by the timber workers. However, if a
resumption of work had not taken place, the Government would have had to give very
serious consideration to any options available to it. Deregistration may have been one of the
options, either of the New Zealand or of the south Auckland Branch of the union.

Electoral Rolls
27. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Justice: Has he seen the report of the
comments of the Lower Hutt City returning officer in the Evening Post on 15 October that
"The option voters had of enlisting on either the local body or parliamentary roll for local
authority elections made ‘a bit of a farce' of the enrolment provisions relating to local body
rolls", and, if so, what is he doing to create the joint parliamentary and local body roll
promised?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: The present provisions whereby
enrolment on the appropriate parliamentary electoral roll enables a voter in a local authority
election to cast an effective vote is the first step towards a common roll. Facilities will be
available when the next local authority elections are held in 1980 for rolls to be provided for
local authorities from parliamentary electoral roll sources. However, a number of adminis-
trative questions have yet to be resolved. The main problem is that parliamentary electoral
rolls are based on residence alone, and any rolls compiled from them alone can contain
names of only those having a residential qualification. Persons with a ratepayer's qualifica-
tion are also entitled to vote in local authority elections, and ratepayers' rolls cannot be
produced from parliamentary roll sources.

the farmers concerned?

indicates there is no evidence to suggest that lambs will be more susceptible to either of these
conditions this year than in a normal year. I am informed that quite often the reverse is the
case, and that these conditions are more likely to occur in a dry year. At this stage I am not
prepared to make any commitment to institute a subsidy.

New Zealand investment in the port facilities, will he advise what stage has been reached in
the construction of the causeway?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade) replied: The
Saudi Arabian Ministry of Communications has appointed a Saudi-Danish team of consul-

of international contractors to tender in April 1978. Construction time is expected to be
about 4 years. The Saudi Abrabians have agreed to finance the causeway.

53. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) asked the Minister
of Social Welfare: As the annual report of the Department of Social Welfare shows that for
the first time there has been a reduction in the number of widow's benefit beneficiaries in
force in the year ended March 1977, can he explain how the decrease of 515 occurred?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: The department's annual
report shows that the number of widow's benefits have reduced in each of the last 4 years.
The reduction could result from remarriages, and we wish all widows who remarry well;
fewer dependent children, enabling those who wish to return to the work force to do so;
widows with the necessary qualifications transferring to national superannuation, which
places them in a better financial position; and possibly as a result of improving economic
conditions fewer husbands have died because of business stress and strain.

body, and interested persons in the community. It gives employment and experience to a
group of young Maori people who are endeavouring to improve their own skills. Many other
local bodies and community organisations are responding with similar initiatives.

Chatham Islands-Forestry Development
56. Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Forests: Are there any plans for the
planting and development of forests on the Chatham Islands, and, if so, what areas are being
considered and for what specific end use?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: The potential for any large-scale
development of forests on the Chatham Islands is extremely limited because of the severe
climatic conditions that prevail there, particularly the salt-laden winds that sweep over the
islands. For the same reason there is an obvious need to encourage the establishment of
shelter belts of resistant trees to benefit farming and the community generally. It has
therefore been the policy of the New Zealand Forest Service to encourage the establishment
of shelter belts and assist with designs and species composition. The total area of woodlots
that would be required to make the islands largely self-sufficient in sawn timber and fencing
materials has been estimated to be about 150 hectares. At present the area of woodlots is
only about 40 or 50 hectares.

for this?
14 Vol. 415


## p. 4320 (#426) ###########################################

4320
9 November
Questions and Replies
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department)
replied: I cannot confirm that former age beneficiaries are being taxed at the rate of 40c in
the dollar. What I can confirm is that it is possible that one or two superannuitants have
applied for a special tax code of, say, 40c. It would happen in this manner: a single person on
national superannuation without other income would face a tax deduction equalling 14.22c
in the dollar, or, if the superannuation was treated as secondary employment, a rate of 19c in
the dollar. Should he have other income subject to tax it is possible for him to apply to the
Inland Revenue Department for a special tax code. If that other income were of sufficient
magnitude and he wished to have all his total annual tax met by deductions from his national
superannuation then it would be possible for a tax deduction rate of 40c in the dollar to be in
force. That would be the justification.

## p. 4324 (#430) ###########################################

4324
9 November
Questions and Replies
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the Earthquake and War Damage Commis-
sion) replied: Following the Wellington and Hutt Valley floods of 20 December 1976 the
commission submitted a scheme for consideration whereby relief could be made available to
home owners for flood, landslip, erosion, or other disaster-induced problems affecting
residential sections. The proposal is that local authorities be empowered to set up local relief
schemes funded and administered at local community level, and tailored to meet the special
needs of the community. The commission's recommendation was referred to the Territorial
Local Government Council for consideration. A committee representing the council, the
Department of Internal Affairs, and the commission has met on two occasions to consider
the proposal. At the request of this committee the proposal is to be referred to the local
government consultative committee at its next meeting with the Minister of Internal Affairs,
which will be held about the end of next month. I feel the scheme proposed by the
commission is the only practicable and equitable way home owners can be provided with a
measure of relief for uninsurable property losses, and I have strongly urged that the proposal
be fully investigated with a view to early implementation.

Shipping Corporation
111. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) asked the Minister of Transport: In the light of his answer
in the House that the New Zealand Shipping Corporation was subsidised to an amount of $4
million, can he indicate (1) where this is shown in the annual report of the corporation; and
(2) whether this sum should be offset by the profit in the accounts?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied on behalf of the the Minister of Transport:
"The total cost to the Government for providing the Shipping Corporation service to the
Cook Islands and Niue and a coastal shipping service was, as I indicated on 19 October, $4.2
million for the year ended 31 March 1977. Page 11 of the Shipping Corporation's annual
report shows that $2.99 million was received from the Government by way of charter and
management fee. The remaining $1.2 million was paid directly to the Shipping Corporation
by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as reimbursement for expenses incurred in operating the
Cook Islands and Niue service. It was for this reason that this figure was excluded from the
corporation's annual report. In reply to the second part of the question, offsetting the profit
in the corporation's accounts against the subsidy paid would have the effect of cross-
subsidising loss-making services by profit-making services. This is not desirable. In directing
the Shipping Corporation to provide shipping services to the Cook Islands, Niue, and the
New Zealand coast, which operate at a loss, successive Governments have undertaken to
ensure that the corporation would not be financially disadvantaged."
