Kauri Sawn Timber-Price
117. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of Forests: Has he seen the statement in an
article in the New Zealand Herald of 3 October 1977 which claimed that an increase in the
price of State-owned kauri would lead to greater pressure for the purchase of kauri still in
private ownership, and, if so, does this statement clearly reflect the situation?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: Yes, I have seen the statement, but I
consider that it does not clearly reflect the situation regarding the sale of kauri in private


## p. 4331 (#437) ###########################################

9 November
4331
Questions and Replies
ownership. Kauri sawn timber has been exempt from price control since 1952, and selling
prices are determined by negotiation between the sawmiller and an intending buyer.
Because of the scarcity of this timber, and its intrinsic value for special purposes, such as
boatbuilding, prices obtained are high. The price obtained for State-owned kauri is calcu-
lated by deducting from the already determined selling price for sawn timber, reasonable
costs of logging and sawing the wood. It therefore follows that the real pressure on the
resource originates from the high prices users of kauri sawn timber are prepared to pay for a
scarce resource, and not from Forest Service log prices.

122. Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram), on behalf of Mr HUNT (New Lynn), asked
the Minister of Health: Has the Government excluded the elderly from the increases in the
GMS benefits when the elderly were included in the 1972 and 1974 increases?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: In discussions with the New Zealand
Medical Association when reviewing the GMS benefit it was agreed that the main area of
patient need was to increase the benefit for children, since it was apparent that some parents
were having difficulty in meeting fees charged by doctors additional to the benefit. The
Medical Association gave practical recognition of this by agreeing to recommend that any
charge made for children should be "nominal or minimal". The elderly will continue to
receive higher benefits, which are $3 for a consultation at the surgery during normal hours,
$4 for a visit to the patient during normal hours, $6 for a consultation at the surgery outside
normal hours, and $7 for a visit to the patient outside normal hours.

Kauri-Regrowth
135. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister of Forests: To what extent is the
regrowth of kauri being encouraged, and what areas are to be set aside for regeneration and
restocking?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests) replied: As far as possible, kauri forest areas are
being managed according to the kauri management policy, the prime objective of which is to
perpetuate kauri as a species in the interests of science, and for public enjoyment, both as
natural stands and managed forests. The policy is implemented to manage and regenerate
kauri by tending areas of natural regeneration by periodic releasing and thinning of pole and
immature stands, and by the artificial re-establishment of seedlings on selected sites. To
date, 400 hectares of kauri forest have been formed by direct planting or supplementing of
natural regeneration.

Dance Bands and Decibels
143. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North) asked the Minister of Labour: Under what union
are members of a dance band registered, and will the new regulations limiting the noise level
at work places to 85 decibels apply, and, if not, why not?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Persons employed in dance bands
would be eligible for membership of the New Zealand Musicians Industrial Union of
Workers. The only Acts at present administered by the Department of Labour that contain
noise control provisions are the Factories Act 1946, the Construction Act 1959, and the
Agricultural Workers Act passed this year. Consideration is currently being given to the
need to incorporate similar noise control provisions in other statutes administered by the
department so as to afford protection to persons in a wider range of occupations in which
excessive noise may be encountered. The reference to regulations limiting noise levels to 85
decibels is not correct, as no legislative change has occurred. The position is that a recent
review of the evidence relating to noise-induced hearing loss has indicated that a reduction of
the level originally adopted by medical officers of health as a basis for determining the
degree of hazard was necessary to protect a greater percentage of the work force.

that a married pensioner couple with a private income of $10 a week paid in 1975, after

increase over the 2-year period, in cash and as a percentage?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: The standard telephone rental

$5.10, or 59c a week. The standard telephone rental is now $20 each 2 months, which means
that a national superannuitant no longer eligible for the telephone concession is now
required to pay an extra $1.72 a week for his telephone compared with his position in 1975.
During the same period, the person's income has increased by approximately $21 a week as a
result of cost-of-living adjustments to the age benefit and the introduction of national
superannuation.

Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare) replied: The number of unemployment

duration of these benefits to date is not known, but, based on the situation over the 12

less, 2000, or 44 percent; between 1 and 3 months, 1635, or 36 percent; between 3 and 6
months, 728, or 16 percent; between 6 months and 1 year, 135, or 3 percent; and 1 year or

Fishing Vessels Regulations
157. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) asked the Minister of Transport: Has he any intention of
changing the present regulations covering the survey of fishing vessels to include craft of less
than 35 ft?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries) replied on behalf of the Minister of Transport:
"I have no immediate intention of changing the present regulations covering the survey of
fishing vessels of less than 35 ft in registered length. This matter is regularly kept under
review, but as there are over 1000 such vessels between 20ft and 35 ft in length to survey all
or even a proportion of these vessels would require a substantial increase in marine division
survey staff. Suitably qualified surveyors are extremely difficult to recruit at present, due to
an industry wide shortage. Discussions are being held between the marine division of the
Ministry of Transport and the Fishing Industry Board to find alternative means of ensuring
that fishing vessels under 35 ft in length are brought up to and kept in an acceptable standard
of seaworthiness."

Mobile X-ray Units
165. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) asked the Minister of Health: Is it correct that the number
of mobile X-ray units has been reduced over the past few years and that cuts have been made
in spending in this direction, and, if so, what is the justification for this?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: The number of mobile X-ray units was
reduced on 1 October 1976 from nine to six. The three units disestablished were in Gisborne,
Palmerston North, and Dunedin. There has been a steady decline in the number of cases of
tuberculosis diagnosed to 1.5 per 10 000 X-rays taken by the mobile X-ray service. The only
reduction in expenditure has been in the actual maintenance of the disestablished units, plus
the salaries of the technicians involved. The units in Hamilton, Wellington, and Christchurch
will continue to operate, if required, in the areas previously covered by the disestablished
units, and the medical officer of health need only request this service. I can assure the
honourable member that the Department of Health is keeping the matter under constant
surveillance, and should additional mobile X-ray services be needed they will be supplied.

Ahuriri River Diversion into Upper Waitaki
168. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Electricity: Is the department
considering proposals to divert the Ahuriri River into the Upper Waitaki hydro-electric
scheme?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Electricity) replied: The New Zealand Electricity Depart-
ment has no proposals to divert the Ahuriri River into the Upper Waitaki hydro-electric
scheme. However, the member might be interested to know that on 29 July 1977 the Waitaki
Electric Power Board advised the New Zealand Electricity Department of investigations of a
very preliminary nature into the possiblity of hydro-electric generation using the Ahuriri
River. The scheme envisaged at that stage was to divert water from the Ahuriri River, via a
channel, to a point about 2 miles down stream, and to discharge this water back into the
same river through a power station of about 2 to 2.5 MW capacity.

173. Mr LA VARIS (Taupo) asked the Minister of Labour, as an urgent question: Has he
had any reports of violence and victimisation against any timber or pulp and paper or other
workers who kept working during the recent troubles in the centre of the North Island, and
will he reassure the work force today that their personal rights will be protected, and,
further, that the Government will take positive steps to ensure that this untenable position is
rectified immediately?

(21/10/77)
Tourism-Coach Drivers' Dispute
174. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Labour, as an urgent question: Is he
aware that as of midnight tonight, 27 October, overseas tourists will be stranded throughout
New Zealand, and will he inform the House: (1) the present average coach-driver's wage,
the amount of increase sought, and the amount of increase agreed to; (2) the approaches he
has made to the employment group concerned to avoid this stoppage; and (3) what last-
minute moves he intends to make this afternoon to avert this situation which will cause
irreparable damage to our tourist industry?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: I am now aware that as a result of
proposed strike action by some drivers tomorrow overseas tourists and others who rely on
these services may be stranded temporarily-some for 24 hours. I am unable to give the
honourable member the present average coach-driver's wage as the remuneration of these
drivers varies considerably depending on the utilisation of vehicles, hours worked, tips, and
so on. When negotiations broke down the employers had offered a 7 percent increase in
wage rates, and were discussing an industry allowance of $6 a week and a rearrangement of
drivers' holiday entitlements. I am advised that the union sought a 30 percent wage increase
plus substantial improvements in other allowances and conditions in the award that would
have increased drivers' take-home pay considerably. I am also advised that the union has
now made a fresh application for conciliation proceedings, and that all parties have agreed
upon a conciliation council being set up on this application on 1 November. In view of this, I
am completely at a loss to understand why some drivers should take futile strike action
tomorrow when constitutional means for settling the dispute and the issue are under way.

TENANCY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This short Bill of four clauses is a companion Bill to the Rent Appeal
Amendment Bill, which is next on the Order Paper. As I explained before the Bill was
introduced, the only significant aspect is to transfer the administration of the Tenancy Act
from the Department of Labour to the Housing Corporation. The Tenancy Act protects the
rights of tenants in a limited number of cases in which tenancies existed before 1955, and
most of those tenancies involve State rental houses.
It was suggested during the introductory debate that the Bill was taking away something
from tenants by giving the supervision of their protection to what Labour speakers called the
biggest landlord in the country-the Housing Corporation. The Housing Corporation is
proud of its role as a landlord. I am sure this would be agreed to by, say, the member for St.
Kilda and the member for Manukau, both of whom have been Ministers of Housing. I am
confident, and indeed sure, that the transfer of the tenancy legislation to the Housing
Corporation will be applauded by anyone who has had any connection with tenancies. Far
from adversely affecting the rights of those tenants who will still have the protection of the
Act, the transfer will give them added confidence. Their tenancy problems will be dealt with
by people whose business is housing and related matters-people who understand what
tenancy issues are all about.
There is no question of the corporation acting as judge and jury with its tenants. As far
as the calculation of rentals and the circumstances relating to the tenant's occupancy rights
are concerned, the Act is explicit. I am informed by officers of the Department of Labour
that the amount of work involved in the administration of the Tenancy Act is very, very

receipts unless asked to do so.

RENT APPEAL AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As I explained during the introduction of this small Bill, the principal function is
simply to transfer the administration of the Rent Appeal Act from the Department of
Labour to the Housing Corporation. This is done in fulfilment of an undertaking given in the
National Party's 1975 election manifesto. It is the Government's belief that matters relating
to tenancies, rentals, and housing generally are better handled, where this is appropriate, by
a Government agency skilled in dealing with matters of this nature.
During the introduction debate there was some criticism of the proposals in the Bill.
The member for Grey Lynn called it "a gift from the National Party to the landlords of New
Zealand". To my knowledge he made no attempt to explain his claim or to justify it,
preferring, as most Opposition members seem to do today, to make a headline-grabbing
statement and then let the public imagination get to work on it. So, for the benefit of the
member, let me remind him of the true situation. The Rent Appeal Act was passed in 1973,
and under its provisions four rent appeal boards were established in Auckland, Wellington,
Christchurch, and Dunedin.
The boards were and are still composed of citizens with interests designed to ensure that
those who apply to them—whether as landlord or as tenant-get a fair deal in the
establishment of equitable rents. That will continue. The boards will retain their independ-
ence. They will continue to operate in the same way as they have in the past, and no changes
are proposed in the Bill to the matters they are required to have regard to in coming to their
decisions. In no way does the Bill or the transfer of their operations to the administration of
the Housing Corporation threaten the existence or independent functioning of these boards.
I want to re-emphasise that no changes of principle are involved. A few minor
administrative changes are proposed, that have been found desirable in the light of the
experience gained since the establishment of the boards. They have been discussed by me
with the four chairmen, and any matters that were not clear to them or on which some
explanation was needed have been satisfactorily resolved. Perhaps two of them need a little
elaboration.
Clause 4 of the Bill provides for the assessment of equitable rents by consent. Under this
provision, the applicant may give his consent to a preliminary assessment being made by the
Housing Corporation. If this assessment is acceptable to both parties, it is then referred to
the board, which may also accept the assessment and, without the need for a formal hearing,
endorse it, and make an order accordingly. But the initiative remains completely with the
board. It has complete discretion, it may proceed with a hearing, and may make its own
different assessment of the equitable rent if it wishes. I believe that this method may well
speed up the work of the boards and do away with much of the present formality.
Clause 5 requires the board in its written assessment to disclose those factors on which
its decision is based-or perhaps I should say three of those factors, which are all included in
clause 8, none being in contravention of that clause-the value of the premises as a
dwellinghouse, the existing rent (if any), and the amount assessed by the board as a proper
return to the landlord. These factors already have to be taken into account by the board in
coming to its decision. All we are saying here is that, when it makes its written assessment of


## p. 4357 (#463) ###########################################

9 November
4357
Rent Appeal Amendment Bill
equitable rent, it should state the facts on which the finding is based. Under section 8 of the
principal Act these have to be considered in any case, and, to assist in a greater degree of
uniformity in the presentation of assessments, I feel that the parties are entitled to know the
basic factors on which a decision is made. As I have already indicated, I have discussed the
changeover and the minor changes proposed with the chairmen of the four boards and with
one or two senior officers of the corporation, and I am positive that there are no difficulties
unresolved which might prevent a smooth transfer of responsibility in February next year.

ESTATE AND GIFT DUTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. Its main purpose is to implement the principles of the Human Rights
Commission Bill by removing, where appropriate, discrimination between males and
females.
Hon. David Thomson: Hear, hear!
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Yes. Most of the amendments were originally contained in
the Human Rights Commission Bill, but have now been transferred to the relevant revenue
amendment Acts. At the same time as the Estate and Gift Duties Act 1968 is being
amended, we are taking the opportunity of making some other amendments of a compara-
tively minor nature. Members will recall that last year the Government made substantial
reductions in the rates of estate and gift duties.
I turn now to the clauses of the Bill. Clause 1 relates to the short title and commence-
ment. Except where otherwise specifically provided, the amendments will apply to the
estates of people dying on or after the day the Act receives the Governor-General's assent,
and to all gifts made on or after that date.
Clause 2 is a machinery amendment to the definition of "group superannuation
schemes" to recognise that they now need the approval of the Government Actuary.
Previously, the responsibility for approving group superannuation schemes rested with the
Commissioner of Inland Revenue.
Clause 3 amends section 35 of the principal Act, which at present provides that a group
superannuation scheme pension payable to a widow for life or until remarriage is exempt
from estate duty, except to the extent that it exceeds $2,000 a year. This clause gives the
same exemption to a pension payable to a widower.
Clause 4 increases the amount of duty, interest, and penalty the Commissioner of Inland
Revenue can remit without the prior approval of the Minister of Finance. At present, the
maximum amount he can remit is $500 in any one estate, or $500 of interest or penalty on gift
duty which relates to a gift transaction. This clause increases the maximum to $1,000. The
amendment is in line with the increases proposed in the Income Tax Amendment Bill (No.
2).
Clause 5 provides for the exemption from gift duty in respect of certain elections by
members of group superannuation schemes to be extended when a widower, as well as a
widow, is a beneficiary. Clause 6 exempts from gift duty certain payments by employers to
the widowers of deceased employees. At present, the exemption applies only to payments to
widows. Clause 7 increases, from 1 January 1978, the maximum monetary fines that can be
imposed by the courts for offences against the Act. These increases are in line with the other
increases proposed in the Income Tax Amendment Bill (No. 2).
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): The Opposition will not
contest the Bill, although members on this side might not applaud with quite the enthusiasm
shown by one of the Government members when he heard that certain human rights were
being extended to males.
My only comment is on the clause that deals with the extension of the right of the
Commissioner of Inland Revenue to have a discretionary power to remit duty that may be
levied. I remember that quite a few cases came before me when I was Minister, and I agree
that, with increased taxation, the raising of the maximum from $500 to $1,000 will not make
a very great difference to the number of cases that will come to the Minister. I remember
that questions were asked in quite a few cases, but I never found it necessary to disagree with
the recommendation of the commissioner on larger amounts. Therefore the clause seems to
be concerned only with flexible administration and, as I indicated, the Opposition has no
objection.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I thank the member for sharing
in the general support for human rights. I agree with him on the discretionary power; I am
astonished at the number of cases that come forward. I am also extraordinarily appreciative
of the care which the commissioner takes in putting them up. I think this is in line with
general practice.
I am fairly new to this job, and should like a little more time myself to see just what the

LAND TAX AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The Bill contains a number of miscellaneous amendments to the Land
Tax Act 1976. There are only six clauses, and they are all of a comparatively minor nature.
The amendment in clause 3 is a substitute for the one originally contained in the Human
Rights Commission Bill. The amendments in clauses 4, 5, and 6 are in line with similar
amendments in other revenue Bills currently before the House.
Clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 is a machinery amendment to insert a definition of
"superannuation fund" with effect from the commencement of the principal Act. This was
overlooked when the Land and Income Tax Act was divided into two separate Acts last year.
Clause 3 provides that the spouse of a person absent from New Zealand in the service of the
Government of New Zealand is deemed not to be an absentee. Previously the provision
referred only to the wife of such a person. Clauses 4 and 5 increase from $500 to $1,000 the
amount of tax or late payment penalty which can be remitted by the Commissioner of Inland
Revenue without the prior approval of the Minister. Clause 6 increases, as from 1 January
1978, the maximum monetary fines that can be imposed by the courts for offences against the
Act.

Fishing Vessel Ownership Savings Bill
FISHING VESSEL OWNERSHIP SAVINGS BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. This measure is another
expression of the Government's commitment to the expansion and development of the New
Zealand fishing industry. In the short time that this Government has been in office, it has
introduced several measures designed to assist the industry. This one is to assist potential
fishermen to save sufficient capital to enable them to purchase their first fishing vessels. As
the House will be aware, the price of fishing vessels has increased dramatically, like the price
of most other commodities. It is a truism that prices increased most rapidly in the period of
the former Government. This measure is really an adaptation for the fishing industry of a
scheme that was introduced to help young farmers to save for their first farm. The scheme is
recognised as a valuable contribution to young fishermen, and has been welcomed up and
down the country. I believe that even the Opposition will support the measure to assist
young farmers-
Mr Wetere: Young farmers?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: The honourable member will not? I am disappointed.
Mr Wetere: I thought it was fishermen.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: The two main criteria to be satisfied if a depositor is to receive the
benefits offered are that the fishing vessel ultimately purchased must be the depositor's first
such vessel, and must be at least 9 metres long. The latter criterion is in line with the
Government's expressed desire to encourage the build-up of what I loosely call larger vessels
for the New Zealand fishing industry. I use the expression loosely because, in some overseas
fishing industries, 9-metre vessels would not carry the adjective "large". We want to
encourage investment in vessels that we believe will most beneficially fit into the New
Zealand industry. It is also intended to ensure that they are bought by people purchasing
their first boats, who are, or intend to become, bona fide commercial fishermen, so that
there is no risk of anyone benefiting unnecessarily from the scheme.
Clause 5 states who may open accounts. They may be opened by persons over 15 years
of age who are employed or engaged in commercial fishing in New Zealand. However,
provision is also made for young people attending secondary school, university, or a similar
institution to participate in the scheme if they intend to take up commercial fishing as a
career. We want to give those who intend entering the industry the opportunity to
commence saving at the earliest possible opportunity, because we recognise the difficulty in
saving over a short period. Eligibility criteria for opening accounts will be liberally inter-
preted if a consistent saver has a genuine desire to obtain a fishing vessel.
The special benefits available under the scheme are similar to those available in the
farming scheme. With an ordinary account, a tax-free purchase grant of up to $15,125 can be
paid at the time the depositor acquires his first vessel. Alternatively, a special account will
provide tax-free rebates equal to 45 percent of eligible savings up to a maximum of $22,500.
So account holders can deposit up to $4,000 per annum, essentially tax free. Deposits in
ordinary savings accounts cannot exceed $3,000 per annum. The amount of purchase grant
under the ordinary savings scheme is calculated on a graduated scale. If a depositor has had
an account for 5 years he can have a 25 percent grant. The grant becomes progressively
larger, up to a maximum of 50 percent of the eligible savings in the account if the money is
deposited for the full period of 10 years. The benefits can continue to accrue to widows and
dependants in the event of the death of a depositor.
To receive tax rebates a special account depositor also must have an initial deposit of
$250 this is similar for both types of accounts. The balance in the account must not fall
below that figure. Of course, that is very logical, because one could not buy a very big vessel
for $250. The tax rebates are calculated at 45c in the dollar on eligible savings. As I said
earlier, the savings in this account are not $3,000 a year, but $4,000 a year-or less, of
course, if the depositor's tax liability is less than $1,800 per annum. These accounts also must
be operated for a minimum period of 5 years. There is no maximum time the depositor may
save, but the maximum amount of tax rebates that a depositor may receive is 45 percent of
$50,000, or $22,500.
That is the basis under which the scheme has been put together, and brought forward to
the House in the hope that it will be passed. As I said earlier, I believe that the scheme has
been welcomed as a valuable addition by those endeavouring to expand the New Zealand
fishing industry. It is one of a number of measures we have brought in, and unquestionably it
is one of the more important ones.

WATER AND SOIL CONSERVATION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I move, That this Bill be
now read a second time. This is a short Bill designed to assist regional water boards to raise
sufficient revenue to meet their administrative expenses. This measure is complementary to
the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Amendment Bill, which has the same purpose. At
present the Government is providing catchment authorities with financial assistance for their
administrative expenses. As I said on the introduction of the Bill, $625,000 has been set aside
this year for that purpose. There are 20 catchment authorities in the country, and the
changes proposed, while they will not enable all authorities to obtain sufficient revenue, will
go some way to making them less dependent on Government assistance. The Bill proposes
that regional water boards should be able to fix an annual charge to enable them to recoup
some of the costs involved in monitoring and supervising water rights.
A maximum annual charge of $10 is set in the Bill. This will ensure that there will not be
an excessive financial burden on the holders of water rights, and that a lesser fee can be
charged if appropriate. The amendment proposed will mean that the holders of water rights
will bear some of the costs involved in the monitoring of those rights. At the present time
there is no provision for a regional water board to make any charge for the supervision of
water rights, and the expenses incurred by boards in carrying out this function are borne by
the boards' administration accounts.
The revenue from the water rate application fee-which is $4 at present, but which will
be increased to $30 a year-has proved inadequate to cover the costs of processing
applications and supervising water rights. As this is an important part of the water
management functions of regional water boards, it is essential that the boards' activities in
this field are not curtailed. At the same time, the additional revenue will provide some
measure of assistance to catchment authorities in meeting their administrative expenses, and
further promote the objectives of good water management throughout the country.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): This interesting Bill is in line with the

SOIL CONSERVATION AND RIVERS CONTROL AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): I move, That this Bill be
now read a second time. As I have already said, the Bill is complementary to the Water and
Soil Conservation Amendment Bill. The purpose of the Bill is the same-to assist catchment
authorities to raise the revenue required to meet their administrative expenses. The Bill
increases from 0.03472c in the dollar to 0.05c in the dollar the maximum administrative rate
that can be levied each year on a rateable property in its district. Before 1959 the maximum
rate permissible was 0.05208c in the dollar, but this was reduced following an examination of
catchment authorities' administrative expenses and the revenue available based on 1957
valuations.
In recent years some authorities have not been able to raise sufficient revenue to cover
their administrative costs despite charging a proper proportion against works and subsidised
projects. Although it will not entirely eliminate the need for central government grants, the
proposed amendment will assist catchment authorities to cover the increasing costs of the
improved services the authorities have been developing in recent years. Not all catchment
authorities will need to levy the maximum rate. At present about half the authorities are
levying the maximum, but for those authorities having difficulty meeting the deficit in their
administration account the measure will provide much needed assistance.
The clause that increases the unauthorised expenditure from $600 a year to $1,700 a
year matches the rate of inflation since the last increase in the allowance for unauthorised
expenditure was made. Members on both sides of the House know that in recent years there
has been a definite trend toward increasing unauthorised expenditure to allow local bodies to
meet their commitments. Clause 3 carries out that function.

PUBLIC FINANCE BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. This is a major consolidation of the law relating to the public revenues
and loan-raising activities of the Crown, and to the appropriation and expenditure of public
money. The Bill also amends the present law in several respects. In the area that it embraces,
the Bill gives expression to the constitutional principles that evolved over a long period in the
development of our parliamentary democracy. It is, therefore, of constitutional importance
in confirming and enhancing parliamentary control of appropriation and expenditure.
As the Minister of Finance explained in his introductory speech, the need to revise the
present legislation arose from the findings of the Treasury committee set up in 1973. The
principal changes proposed by the Bill are based on the findings of that committee. I set
them out, in brief, in sections, before detailing the clauses. The Works and Trading Account
will be abolished. The principal trading departments served by that account will become
accounts outside the Public Account. These are the Ministry of Energy-formerly electricity
and State coal mines-and the Railways Department, both of which will in this regard join
and be brought into line with the Post Office. The remaining departments and programmes
now coming within the Works and Trading Account will thereafter be financed through the
Consolidated Account.
The present limit on the Minister's power to raise loans on behalf of the Crown has been
abolished. Conversely, parliamentary control over the expenditure of loan money has been
strengthened by providing that loan moneys shall be annually appropriated in future. In
addition, provision is being included for transfers from the Loans Account to the Consoli-
dated Account, within the limit to be set in the Appropriation Bills each year. As an
outcome of the elimination of the several permanent appropriations covering a substantial
area of expenditure and their replacement with annual appropriations, the remaining
permanent appropriations will be confined to the traditional areas.
A number of provisions in existing Acts enabling the Minister of Finance to give
guarantees on behalf of the Crown have been amended so as to provide that such guarantees
will be given pursuant to clause 86 of the Bill. Thus the disclosure provisions in clause 86 will
apply to all such guarantees given. The present procedure for calculating the annual
contribution from revenue toward repayment of the public debt has been simplified.
Statutory recognition has been given in the Bill to the independence of the important office
of the Controller and Auditor-General.


## p. 4368 (#474) ###########################################

4368
9 November
Public Finance Bill
I shall now deal with the clauses in the Bill in order. Clause 1 relates to the short title,
and provides for the Bill to come into force on 1 April 1978. Clause 2 is the interpretation
clause. Clause 3 binds the Crown to the provisions of the Bill. Then the Bill is set out in six
parts. Part I, containing clauses 4 to 13, establishes the Treasury as a department of State,
and includes the normal supporting clauses for the appointment of a secretary and deputy
and assistant secretaries. There are the usual clauses enabling both the Minister of Finance
and the secretary to delegate their powers. Clause 12 re-enacts the present provision for the
secretary to be a member of the board of an organisation controlling or administering public
money. Clause 13 is new, and empowers the Minister to appoint committees to advise or
assist the Minister or the secretary on financial, economic, or other matters.
Part II of the Bill sets out more clearly what is implied in the present statute, namely,
the independence of the Audit Office. It also restates the functions, duties, and powers of
the office, including essential provisions relating to the access to information and the right to
report. Clause 15 establishes the Audit Department as a department of State, and provides
for the Controller and Auditor-General to be the administrative head of the department.
Clause 16 provides for the appointment of the Controller and Auditor-General, and clauses
17 to 20 set out the conditions of his employment. Clauses 21 and 22 relate to the deputy
controller and auditor-general on a similar basis to the controller. Clauses 25 and 26 set out
in detail the general functions, duties, and powers of the Audit Office. Clauses 27 to 29 give
further specific powers to the Controller and Auditor-General. Clauses 30 to 32 enable the
Controller and Auditor-General to issue a surcharge in certain circumstances when there has
been a deficiency or loss of public money or stores, or of the money or stores of a local
authority. Clauses 33 to 36 are of a miscellaneous nature, and include, among other matters,
provision for the Controller and Auditor-General to report on the public accounts, and other
accounts subject to his audit.
Part III relates to the Public Account, and establishes the framework within which the
Crown accounts for the moneys it receives, and for the expenditure of supply granted by
Parliament. Clause 37 establishes the Public Account, and describes which accounts and
funds are comprised within the Public Account. Clause 38 creates the Consolidated Account
in place of the Consolidated Revenue Account. All revenue receipts are to be credited to the
Consolidated Account. Transfers may be made to the Loans Account, Loans Redemption
Account, and Reserve Account of moneys in excess of the amount reasonably required for
the purposes of the Consolidated Account. Clause 39 establishes the Loans Account in place
of the National Development Loans Account, and, unless otherwise determined, the
proceeds of all loans raised under Part V must be credited to the Loans Account. Transfers
may be made to the Consolidated Account and the Loans Redemption Account, but a limit
is to be set each year by the appropriation Acts on the amount that can be transferred to the
Consolidated Account.
Clause 40 establishes the Loans Redemption Account, and provides that all money
borrowed or set aside for repaying the public debt shall be credited to that account. In the
event of there being more than what is required in the account, a transfer may be made to
the Loans Account. Clause 41 creates the Reserve Account in place of the Reserve Fund and
the General Purposes Relief Account. Money in this account may be invested with the
approval of the Minister of Finance. Clause 42 establishes the Trust Account, and provides
that all money received in trust by any accounting officer shall be credited to that account
unless otherwise determined. Clause 43 permits any account within the Public Account to be
overdrawn during a financial year, but not at the end of such year. Clauses 44 and 45 permit
the Minister of Finance to make temporary borrowings, principally on overdraft, in
anticipation of revenue and for the purpose of providing sufficient money to meet current
expenditure.
Clauses 46 to 48 empower temporary transfers between accounts, and enable the
Minister to enter into agreements with the Reserve Bank about the general banking business
of the Crown. The Reserve Bank shall also supply statements of account to the Treasury and
the Audit Office. Clause 49 provides that a sum equal to at least 1 percent of the public debt
shall be transferred from the Consolidated Account to the loans redemption account in each
year for the purpose of redeeming outstanding loans. Provision is being maintained for a
reduction in the amount so transferred to the extent of other moneys in this account. Clauses
50 and 52 relate to the investment of money in the Public Account, to the acceptance of
money on deposit, and for dealing with certain money that is trust money.
Part IV relates to the appropriation and payment of public money, and is a most
important constitutional part of the Bill. The Government has endeavoured to preserve the


## p. 4369 (#475) ###########################################

9 November
4369
Public Finance Bill
constitutional procedures that have been laid down over the centuries when important
measures apply both to ordinary expenditure and to the expenditure of loan money.
Different requirements are laid down under existing statutes. Clause 53 enacts the constitu-
tional principle that there shall be no expenditure of public money except pursuant to an
appropriation by Act of Parliament. The estimates for any financial year set forth the
Crown's demands for supply for that year. Clauses 54 to 56 provide three special applications
of the rule set out in clause 53. First, until an Imprest Supply Bill is passed, expenditure may
be made in the first 3 months of a financial year in anticipation of appropriation, of up to
one-quarter of the total sum appropriated in the previous year; secondly, during the period
between the passing of the last appropriation Act and the end of that financial year,
unauthorised expenditure may be made of up to 1.5 percent of the total appropriated by the
appropriation Acts. This percentage may be increased to 2.5 percent when in certain
circumstances there is an increase in State Service salaries; and, thirdly, expenditure may be
made without normal appropriation when a state of national or civil defence emergency has
been declared, or in the event of an emergency that affects the public health, interest, or
safety.
Clauses 57 and 58 provide that expenditure items in the estimates may be overspent in
certain circumstances, and that when money is appropriated for a certain restricted purpose
and not expended in that year, it may be transferred to the Trust Account until required for
that purpose. Clauses 59 to 61 provide that the issue of public money must be pursuant to a
warrant signed by the Governor-General, and for the procedural steps to be followed when
such money is paid from disbursement and imprest accounts. Clauses 62 to 64 enable the
Treasury to establish overseas accounts and, in certain circumstances, to allow payments
without receipts. Clauses 65 to 67 require the Treasury to prepare a statement of the public
accounts each year, and quarterly summaries, and for the Audit Office to report on such
statement and summaries. Clause 68 deals with the accounts of Government agencies known
as accounts outside the Public Account. New trading accounts made subject to this clause
are, as I have already said, those of the Ministry of Energy and the Railways Department.
Normal estimates of expenditure will, of course, continue to be prepared in accordance with
the amending provisions of the respective Acts. The accounts subject to this clause are set
out in the first schedule. Clause 69 makes certain provisions in respect of the accounts of
some other Government agencies, which accounts are set out in the second schedule. The
object is to enable Parliament to control individual agencies for which public moneys are
appropriated for expenditure.
Part V is important, and deals with loans to and by the Crown, and also securities for
such loans. It represents a consolidation of existing legislation, and will also provide a
governing authority for the registration of Government stock, which is being enacted in the
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act. Clause 70 prohibits the Crown from borrowing money
except pursuant to an Act of Parliament. Clause 71 authorises the Minister of Finance to
raise a loan if he considers it necessary or expedient in the public interest to do so. Clause 72
makes certain provisions applicable to the raising of loans. Clauses 73 to 75 authorise the
raising of loans by way of registered Treasury bills, Government stock, or a mortgage of
securities. Clause 77 details the functions of the Reserve Bank in relation to loans raised
within New Zealand. Clauses 78 and 79 relate to overseas loans, and to the appointment of
managers and loan agents. Clauses 80 to 84 make certain provisions relating to securities for
loans, and the issue thereof. Clauses 85 and 86 empower the Minister of Finance to make
loans on behalf of the Crown, and to give guarantees. Clauses 87 to 91 are miscellaneous
matters relating to loans and securities. Clauses 92 to 94 relate to the Public Debt
Commission, and the procedures to be followed in connection with its activities.
Part VI deals with matters of a general nature, and I shall briefly mention the more
important clauses. Clause 95 is new, and puts an obligation on the head of a Government
department or agency to take all practicable steps to recover any deficiency or loss of public
money or stores under his control. Clause 99 relates to the capital liability of the accounts of
Government agencies to the public accounts and the payment of interest and repayments of
such liability. Clause 105 establishes the Government Stores Insurance Fund and sets out the
conditions on which the fund will operate. A new provision specifies that a copy of the
accounts of the fund shall be tabled in Parliament each year. Clause 107 provides that unless
incurred in normal or unavoidable circumstances, or otherwise authorised, no public money
or stores shall be written off without the authority of Parliament.
Clauses 109 to 113 relate to offences under the Bill and authorise the issue of Treasury
instructions and regulations. Part VII relates to consequential amendments, repeals, and

4370
9 November

savings. Clauses 114 to 119 are savings provisions relating to the principal accounts within
the Public Account and certain other accounts. Clauses 120 to 159 make a number of
amendments to other Acts. The principal amendments are consequent upon the abolition of
the Works and Trading Account and the conversion of permanent appropriations to annual
appropriations. Clause 160 makes minor consequential amendments to other Acts, the
details of which are set out in the third schedule. Clauses 161 to 163 relate to savings and
repeals.
In conclusion, despite its length, in terms of its importance this is a succinct rationalisa-
tion and modernisation of our financial procedures. The Bill is of considerable importance to
Parliament. It confirms and extends some of our most important and revered parliamentary
procedures in requiring all appropriations and all expenditure to be approved by Parliament.

have engaged in this massive consolidation, particularly to a retired Treasury officer, Mr
Leathwick, for the tremendous amount of work, which I am sure will prove of very great
value to the House.

Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I want to speak briefly as the chairman of the Public Expendi-
ture Committee, and to confirm some of the points made by the Deputy Leader of the
Opposition, which were emphasised by the Minister. It is not always understood by members
that the Public Expenditure Committee has a vital role to play in parliamentary procedures,
and its relationship between Parliament and the Executive is a critical one. Members
themselves do not always understand the system of parliamentary appropriation and the
strictures and limits it places on the Crown, but there is a very real limit, which is being
reinforced by the Bill before the House tonight.
Crown expenditure cannot take place unless the money has been appropriated in the
House. I think it is worth reiterating tonight, in the simplest form, that Parliament
appropriates a certain amount for a certain expenditure, and it is then the responsibility of
the Minister to ensure that the appropriation takes place in the way intended by the House.
The Public Expenditure Committee, as a select committee of Parliament, has a responsibility
as the watchdog for Parliament. It has to ensure that once the money has been voted and the
appropriation has been made the money is spent, down to quite small details, on the purpose
for which it was intended. Each year the committee examines the Government's public
accounts in the light of the estimates approved by the House, and draws any discrepancies to
the attention of the House.
I mention those facts because the Public Finance Bill consolidates and restates some
fundamental parliamentary procedures-constitutional procedures accepted in the model
under which parliamentarians practise. It is my view, and I think it is correct to say, that in
some ways the principles are strengthened by the Bill. I was glad that the Bill was referred to
the Public Expenditure Committee before it was introduced to the House. That gave the
committee the opportunity to consider it clause by clause, and to examine the principles and
the changes proposed in the light of the underlying constitutional principles that are so
important to the functioning of the House.
As the Deputy Leader of the Opposition has said, by and large there was agreement in
the committee on the individual clauses, with perhaps some differences in emphasis. I can
record that there were no divisions at any stage on the changes recommended. Tonight I
want to emphasise what I see as the three very important aspects of the Bill. Most of the

Public Finance Bill
principles of the existing legislation are changed slightly by the Bill. I draw attention first to
the appointment of the Controller and Auditor-General and his deputy. This provision is
fundamental to the supervision of the whole of public spending, because, hand in hand with
the Public Expenditure Committee, the Controller and Auditor-General has a responsibil-
ity, in an independent way, to overview the spending by departments, public corporations,
and local bodies, and to report to the House.
In a paper presented to the committee, the Controller and Auditor-General emphasised
that, to do his job properly, he must enjoy five freedoms as the State auditor. As
parliamentarians, it is as well for us to bear those freedoms in mind, and I draw them to the

must have freedom from instruction on how to conduct audits. Thirdly, he must have
freedom from supervision in an administrative sense. Fourthly, he must have freedom to
secure financial resources to support his operations. Finally, he must have freedom to

introduced in the Bill, were conscious of the necessity to reserve to the Auditor-General
those five freedoms. If one looks at the part of the Bill that provides for his appointment and
functions, and the way in which the Controller and Auditor-General is allowed to operate,
one finds that the five principles and freedoms have been preserved.
The second point I want to make is that a very fundamental section of the Bill is based
on the recommendation of a review committee set up some years ago to report on
consolidating the old Public Revenues Act and the Loans Act. That committee made
recommendations relating to the public accounts that have now been incorporated in the
Bill. I shall refer to them briefly. One was that the public accounts should reflect the
Government's revenue-raising transactions and the expenditures financed therefrom. That
led, in the new Bill, to the provision that will place trading departments outside the public
accounts. If members reflect a little they will understand the reason, which is that public
accounts should reflect the Government's revenue and expenditure, not the trading of the
trading departments.
The second principle set out in the review committee's report, and incorporated in this
measure, is that permanent appropriations should be limited to traditional items. In the Bill
provision is made for the capital financing of all corporations and other agencies to be
appropriated annually. Members who are interested in the public accounts will appreciate
that those are two very important aspects of the Bill.
Finally, I draw attention to clause 55, which has not been referred to in any depth by
previous speakers. The clause defines the amount of unauthorised expenditure that any
Government is permitted to spend or the limits to which a Government can go without
infringing the provisions of the statute. It is important for parliamentarians to realise that the
Government or the Executive must act within the limits and the restraints placed upon it by
the House. Those members who criticise the power of the Executive-and there are one or
two who do that from time to time-should consider the restraints placed on the Executive
by the Public Revenues Act, the principles of which are now restated in the Public Finance
Bill. The Government is not permitted to spend without restraint. The Executive has no
unlimited power of spending taxpayers' money. Clause 55 sets out in clear language the
limits to which the Executive can spend without coming back to the House. This is a very old
principle, known to parliamentarians for a long time-not always understood by all members
and certainly seldom understood by those outside the House-and very important for those
particularly concerned about the role of the Executive. The provisions enacted in clause 55
were recommended to the Executive by the Public Expenditure Committee in 1976, the year
the committee looked at the limits of unauthorised expenditure.
I am not being political in any way when I say that at that stage we were concerned that
in the years 1975 and 1976 the limits had been exceeded to a very substantial degree, and
required validating legislation. The Public Expenditure Committee looked at the question,
and asked whether the limits set in the statute were realistic in the light of inflation and so
on, and it came down with recommendations for change. I shall refer to the statutory
provisions that have been incorporated in the Bill, which provides that in any financial year
the amount that the Government or Crown can spend shall not exceed a sum-this is
unauthorised expenditure-equal to the following percentage of the total of all sums
appropriated by the Appropriation Act or Acts for that financial year. The Appropriation
Act or Acts for the financial year determine the amount, and it shall not be exceeded by
"2½ percent in any year in which an increase in remuneration is paid to employees in the
State services. . . being an increase which (i) is in the nature of a general wage order, a

OVERSEAS INVESTMENT AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. This is a short Bill. Its purpose is to make a small number of changes to
definitions in the interpretation section of the principal Act. These changes are contained in
clause 2. In addition, the regulations section of the principal Act is amended in one respect.
Clause 4 enables regulations to be made controlling the commencement of business in New
Zealand by any overseas person.
I turn now to the individual clauses. Clause 2 introduces a definition of "building
society" and amends the definitions of “nominee” and “overseas person”. It has been found
that the principal Act does not cover "building societies"; therefore a definition has been
included and the words "building society" inserted, where appropriate, after the word
"company" in the principal Act. The definition of "nominee" is amended in two respects:
(a) an anomaly in the principal Act is removed so that a New Zealand owned company
owning shares in another company which is itself an "overseas person" will not also be
defined as an "overseas person" unless, as provided in the Bill, the acquisition of those
shares was entered into for the benefit of an overseas person.
Secondly, the definition of nominee is widened to prevent a situation where two or more


## p. 4374 (#480) ###########################################

4374
9 November
Overseas Investment Amendment Bill
overseas persons act jointly or in concert in any transaction. The main area in which this
would apply is the acquisition of shares in a New Zealand company when two or more
persons each purchase less than 25 percent of shares in a company and thus avoid the
Overseas Investment Regulations. The only other amendment relates to the definition of
overseas person. The definition is changed to include a company in which 25 percent or more
of any class of shares is held by an overseas person. The present definition catches those
companies in which 25 percent or more of the overseas shares are held by an overseas
person. This loophole will be closed to prevent the avoidance of the Overseas Investment
Regulations by some companies.
Clause 3 rectifies a clerical error. Clause 4 amends the regulation-making powers
relating to the commencement of business in New Zealand contained in the principal Act.
This extends at the moment only to incorporated bodies, and the amendment will enable
new Overseas Investment Regulations to be issued to cover the commencement of business
in New Zealand by overseas individuals as well as overseas companies.

RESERVE BANK OF NEW ZEALAND AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The proposed amendment to the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act
1964 covers three different functions of the bank: the executive committee of the bank, the
exchange control provisions, and the registration of securities. I shall deal first with the
executive committee of the bank. Section 6 of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 1964 as
substituted by section 4 of the 1973 amendment Act provides for the executive committee of
the bank to confer with the Minister of Finance, at his request, on any matter coming within
the scope of section 8 of the Act, and for any director common to both the Reserve Bank and
the Bank of New Zealand to be a member of the executive committee. Such an appointment
is unnecessary and has inherent dangers because of the conflict of interest which might arise.
The present section 6 would have given to any director who was appointed to both the
Bank of New Zealand and Reserve Bank boards a special means of communication with the
Minister, through the executive committee, not available to other members of the board.
This would not be conducive to the harmonious working and effectiveness of the board.
Moreover, the appointment of a common director could adversely affect the reputation of
the Bank of New Zealand as an independent trading bank competing fairly and evenly with
other trading banks. The present section 6 of the Act, which implies that there should be a
common director, is therefore undesirable.
The reason for the existing provision is unclear. No appointment has ever been made,
and it would appear that no good would be achieved by so doing. The special provision for
communication between the Minister and the executive committee is also unnecessary. The
Minister and the Associate Minister of Finance both have frequent consultations with the
governor of the bank who is well able to pass on the view of the directors. The fact that no
such appointment has been made leads us to the view that we should repeal this section
substituted by the 1973 amendment and replace it with the section in the original Act. The
effect of this would be to return to the directors the power to determine the membership of
the executive committee and to delete any reference to a common director with the Bank of
New Zealand or the Secretary to the Treasury being automatically members of the
committee. The reference to the committee discussing matters with the Minister would also
be deleted as unnecessary.
I shall now deal with exchange control provisions. A review of the relevant clauses of
the Act has been necessitated by a decision to promulgate up-dated exchange control
regulations, which are made in terms of the Act. This course was largely dictated by changes
made to relevant legislation and procedures in the United Kingdom which were reflected
significantly in the administration of the exchange control regulations in New Zealand. In
addition, the opportunity has been taken to correct some weaknesses in the regulations with
consequential amendments to the Act. Clause 3 of the Bill amends that section of the Act
which relates to the control of overseas exchange and other transactions. It clarifies the
regulation-making powers in the section, adds some definitions, including that of the term
"borrowing money outside New Zealand", and makes provision for the Minister of Finance
to determine, in cases of doubt, whether a person is deemed, for purposes of the section, to


## p. 4375 (#481) ###########################################

9 November
4375
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Amendment Bill
be ordinarily resident in New Zealand. Also included in subsection (13) is a provision which
avoids the present situation whereby a person who promises to provide a consideration in
New Zealand in exchange for a consideration outside New Zealand is deemed to have
completed the transaction outside New Zealand, thus escaping the regulation which
precludes the giving of a consideration in New Zealand for a consideration outside New
Zealand.
Clause 6 amends section 50 of the principal Act so as to rectify weaknesses in section 50
in regard to the Reserve Bank's legal powers to make inquiries into irregularities in the
exchange control area. The main weakness arises because the limitations on the bank's
powers to require information from financial institutions generally can be used to obstruct
inquiries into breaches of the exchange control regulations. Clause 7 relates to penalties for
offences. The penalties at present prescribed were last considered some 12 years ago. The
changes proposed reflect mainly the influence of inflation. Clause 8 inserts a new section in
the Act. It provides that certificates as to certain matters signed by the governor of the bank
shall, unless shown to be otherwise, be conclusive evidence of the matters stated therein in
any proceedings.
Part III of the Bill deals with registration of securities. Following the decision to
introduce the Public Finance Bill, which consolidates and amends the Public Revenues Act
1953 and the New Zealand Loans Act 1953, it was considered desirable to incorporate in the
Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act rather than in the Public Finance Bill that section of the
New Zealand Loans Act 1953 which relates to the registration of Government stock. This
particular section, Part III of the New Zealand Loans Act 1953, includes provisions relating
to the keeping of the register of Government stock. It is considered appropriate that such
provisions be more properly put under the umbrella of the Reserve Bank's own Act. Hence
this amendment, which is to come into force at the same time as the provisions of the Public
Finance Bill. The Reserve Bank also acts as registrar for loans raised by local authorities,
and the Local Authorities Loans Act contains a number of provisions similar to those in the
New Zealand Loans Act, relating to the keeping of the register of local authorities stock.
Clause 4 of the amendment takes these duplicated provisions out of both these Acts and
places them into one piece of legislation, for which the Reserve Bank, as registrar for public
sector securities, can be responsible.
The Reserve Bank, under its own Act, also acts as registrar for stock issued by other
statutory organisations-for example, the Housing Corporation and the New Zealand Dairy
Board. Clause 4 brings certain provisions relating to these operations within the Reserve
Bank Act. It is considered preferable that the criteria which the Reserve Bank applies to
transactions relating to stock registered on account of these organisations be clearly stated in
its own Act. The Bank has, until now, by agreement with these organisations, applied the
provisions at present included in the Local Authorities Loans Act. Having accepted the
necessity to introduce an amendment to the Act, it has been considered appropriate to tidy
up the existing legislation by amending and consolidating the provisions, where the bank acts
as registrar, of the existing Acts.
Clause 4 of the amendment inserts in the principal Act a new part VIA relating to the
registration and transfer of stock and other securities. The new part consolidates and amends
sections 16 to 35 of the New Zealand Loans Act 1953 and sections 67 to 79 and 81 to 83 of the
Local Authorities Loans Act 1956. It is consequential to the enactment of the Public Finance
Bill 1977. The provisions in this part will automatically relate to all securities for which the
bank is empowered to act as registrar now or in the future. Any changes to existing
legislation are of a minor nature only. They include a reduction in the age of infants who may
be registered as the holders of stock from 10 years and upwards to 7 years and upwards. This
amendment will bring stockholders under this Act into line with holders of inflation-adjusted
bonds and various savings accounts. The new provision for certification of transfers
formalises an arrangement of many years' standing between the Reserve Bank and members
of the Stock Exchange and other organisations that deal extensively in public sector
securities. Provision is also made for fees for the bank's services as registrar to be prescribed
by regulation.
In conclusion, it is not considered that there is anything contentious in the proposed
amendment, which is purely a tidying-up operation brought about, in the main, by the
introduction of the Public Finance Bill. The opportunity has been taken at the same time to
reinstate the section of the Act relating to the executive committee of the bank in the form
that existed before the 1973 amendment. In addition, it is considered appropriate to effect
minor changes to the existing sections of the Act that relate to the control of overseas

fidelity fund. The conditions under which a levy may be imposed are widened to cover a
likely insufficiency as well as an actual insufficiency. Clause 7 removes the present prohibi-
tion against collecting the annual fee payable to the fidelity fund if the net amount of the

CITIZENS AND ALIENS BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This Bill revises and consolidates the law relating to New Zealand citizenship. It
also incorporates the law dealing with the registration of aliens, which is at present contained
in a separate statute. As I will explain later, it is proposed that those provisions be removed.
At the outset, I should like to thank the chairman and members of the Statutes Revision
Committee for the careful consideration they gave to the Bill. As members will have noted,
the committee has proposed a number of amendments, all of which I am satisfied improve
the Bill and should be adopted, except for a minor change of a machinery nature that will be
incorporated in a Supplementary Order Paper. I am grateful to the committee for those
improvements.
The Bill, though not a massive measure, is one of major importance. It deals with
something of which all New Zealanders are rightly proud-their citizenship-which goes to
the very roots of our nationhood. New Zealand citizenship has existed since 1949. It was
created by the British Nationality and New Zealand Citizenship Act 1948, which came into
force on 1 January 1949. Before that, the legislation—the British Nationality and Status of
Aliens (in New Zealand) Act 1928-referred only to British subjects and aliens. British
subjects were either "natural-born" British subjects-and these included New
Zealanders—or people who had become British by the process known as naturalisation. The
Bill now before the House continues the emphasis that New Zealand, in common with other
countries of the Commonwealth, has been placing on its individual citizenship.
There are three ways in which New Zealand citizenship is acquired: by birth in New
Zealand; by descent—that is, by birth overseas to a parent who is a New Zealand citizen;
and by applying for and being granted New Zealand citizenship. The Bill does not change
those methods, but it introduces some refinements. The major change in the transmission of
citizenship, and indeed in the Bill as a whole, is to provide for citizenship to be transmitted
through the female line instead of only the male line as at present. The present situation is
regarded—and I think rightly regarded as discriminating against the female.
In placing emphasis on New Zealand citizenship, the Bill standardises the process by
which it is granted. Hitherto there has been a distinction between British subjects and non-
British subjects or aliens, as such people have commonly been called. The British subject
has acquired his New Zealand citizenship by registration, and the alien has had his conferred
by the process known as naturalisation. The terms "registration” and “naturalisation" are
being dispensed with and will be replaced by the common term "grant of citizenship”.
British subjects and aliens are being placed on common terms in all other respects also.
Hitherto, British subjects have been required to live in New Zealand for a period of 3 years
before being eligible to apply for citizenship, whereas a minimum period of 5 years'
residence has been required of aliens. The Bill lays down a common period of 3 years'
minimum residence, and includes provision for the Minister to reduce this to 12 months if, in
a particular case, he is satisfied that because of an applicant's age, or for other reasons
personal to the applicant, he or she would suffer hardship if held to the 3 years' residence
requirement.
As I mentioned, it is not possible under the present state of the law for citizenship by
descent to be conveyed through the female line. A married New Zealand father of a child
born overseas passes on his New Zealand citizenship to the child, but this is not at present
the case with the mother. The Bill provides in clause 7 that, for children born outside New


## p. 4378 (#484) ###########################################

4378
9 November
Citizens and Aliens Bill
Zealand to either a New Zealand father or mother, citizenship will be passed on equally
through the female line as with the male line, provided that such citizenship shall lapse if the
birth is not registered in New Zealand before the expiry of 2 years after attaining the age of
majority. So much for the children of the future. They will be New Zealand citizens by
descent if born overseas to either a New Zealand mother or father.
The Statutes Revision Committee also turned its attention to the children born in the
past to New Zealand mothers overseas. Such children have not been New Zealand citizens
by descent; in other words, they have been discriminated against. The committee sought a
means of conferring citizenship as of right-that is, without need of application-on any
person born before 1 January 1978 if at the time of birth the mother was a New Zealand
citizen. It was realised, however, that this could confer citizenship on people who might not
want it, because under the laws of some other country it might deprive them of the
citizenship of that other country. The committee has therefore modified the Bill to provide
that any person in this category-that is, who was born overseas to a New Zealand mother
before 1 January 1978-may apply for a grant of citizenship, and thereupon the Minister
shall be required to make such grant.
I am sure that the wording of the amendment proposed by the Statutes Revision
Committee inadvertently goes further than the committee meant. Under the present
legislation, and in this Bill, citizenship by descent is, by and large, limited to the first
generation born outside New Zealand. Clearly, the retrospective provision for children
born overseas to New Zealand mothers should be limited in the same way; it is undesirable
to provide for New Zealand citizenship to be available as of right to people who have no
connection with this country. Therefore, I intend to move by way of a Supplementary Order
paper that clause 9 (a) of the Bill be amended by the addition of the words "otherwise than
by descent".
Another important respect in which the Statutes Revision Committee has modified the
Bill is the inclusion in clauses 8 and 9 of provision for a grant of citizenship to people who
may already be New Zealand citizens by descent. The committee took note of the fact that a
citizen by descent only, unlike one by birth or grant of citizenship, cannot pass on his
citizenship to children born overseas. The committee contemplated that a person-a New
Zealander by descent only-leaving the country for several years and being fairly sure of
having a family during that time should be able to convert his or her own citizenship by
descent into citizenship by grant, in order to be sure that any children born overseas would
be New Zealand citizens by descent.
A further matter on which the Statutes Revision Committee deliberated especially
carefully was the provision relating to the taking of an oath of allegiance by persons for
whom the grant of citizenship has been approved. Clause 10 of the Bill refers to this. The
committee left this clause substantially as it was when the Bill was introduced—that is, to the
effect that the Minister may require such case or class of cases as he thinks fit to take the oath
in the form set out in the first schedule. The committee recorded the view, however, that
now that we have our own Queen of New Zealand it regarded the taking of an oath of
allegiance as desirable in all cases, even by other Commonwealth subjects who already owe
allegiance to the Queen by reason of their birth.
I promised to look at the practicability of this. I have done so, and have concluded that,
desirable though the proposal may be from the point of view of its symbolic importance, the
administrative complications that it presents rule it out as a practical proposition. I think it is
essential in this matter that the Minister have the discretion to make some compromise in the
interests of administrative convenience, especially as a very great increase in citizenship
work in the Department of Internal Affairs can be foreseen as a result of the liberal nature of
the Bill.
I would add that, as a matter of policy, it can be expected that all persons who do not by
reason of birth owe allegiance to the Queen will continue to be required to take the oath,
generally at civic ceremonies, and all other people will be required to subscribe to some
appropriate declaration at the time of application. I specifically draw attention to the second
schedule to the Bill, which specifies the countries whose citizens shall have the status of
Commonwealth citizen or British subject.
The enactment of the Commonwealth Countries Act has done away with the need for
the second schedule and clause 22. During the Committee stage I intend to move amend-
ments dealing with these points. It is necessary for me to mention that Cabinet has very
recently approved the abolition of the alien registration system. This will enable repeal of the
provisions relating to the registration of aliens, which are contained in the Aliens Act 1948,

refused, and, if it is refused, it should be open to judicial review.

One aspect of the Bill I welcome very much is that part which abolishes the previous
distinction between citizenship acquired through a mother who is a New Zealand citizen and
citizenship acquired through a father who is a New Zealand citizen. This aspect was praised,
not only by the National Council of Women, but also by the Committee on Women, both of
which were represented at one and the same time before the select committee. It was clear
that these organisations regarded those provisions as evidence of further implementation, by
this Government, of the report of the 1975 parliamentary select committee on the rights of
women.
I am happy to say that the Statutes Revision Committee was able to make an
appropriate change to the one aspect of the Bill which attracted some criticism from both
organisations. As drafted, the Bill made it possible for a 16-year-old to change his or her
citizen status. Both the National Council of Women and the Committee on Women
suggested that a change of citizenship was something too important for a 16-year-old-a
person who by the law of this country is regarded as a minor-to undertake. Both
organisations recommended that the age be increased to 18 years. The select committee
looked at the proposal with considerable care, and, bearing in mind that the Guardianship
Act already provides some jurisdiction in respect of minors up to the age of 18 years, agreed
that it would be appropriate to bring the Bill more into line with the provisions of other New
Zealand laws.
Another aspect of the Bill which was of some importance and attracted some comment
from a number of organisations-and the member for Henderson has referred to a
submission received from some academics at the University of Waikato-was the provision
contained in the present clause 9. In the Bill as introduced, provision was made that
citizenship by descent could be available only to first-generation members of a family born
outside New Zealand. As the member for Henderson has correctly pointed out, there may
well be persons in the academic community who are of a second or third generation born
outside New Zealand, and thereby, by a simple quirk of fate, denied New Zealand
citizenship by descent. This does not apply just to members of the academic community. It
applies also to members of the diplomatic corp who might have served outside the country
for some years, and to their families. It also applies-and this may perhaps be where we find
the most common application of the principle-to the families of missionaries. It was
originally suggested that clause 9(1)(c) gave sufficient ministerial discretion to deal with the
problem, but it was the view of the select committee, now embodied in the Bill, that the
provision should be expressly dealt with. We therefore proposed a provision to permit
citizens by descent to "perfect" their citizenship, and a further provision to give the Minister
of Internal Affairs a discretion to deal with what one might call "second generation cases" on
criteria that are not as rigid as the other criteria contained in the Bill. These proposals are
now embodied in the Bill.
The Minister, in introducing the second reading debate, referred to the problems that
arose from the transitional provisions of the Bill, and particularly to an error apparently
made by the select committee in trying to provide for equality of citizenship by descent
