through a mother with the previously favoured position of that of a father. It would be
inappropriate to comment on those proposed changes in any detail at this stage, except to
say that it was the select committee's intention that we should, as far as humanly possible,
"even up" the claim of citizenship through a mother with the claim of citizenship through a
father. However, we recognise the fact—and I am sure that the member for Mangere was
one of those who recognised it—that it would not be possible to completely turn the clock
back to 1949 when the present law came into effect, and that we could not alter the status of
those who had already acquired citizenship of another country by some means, and who
might in fact be adversely affected if we were to effectively backdate New Zealand
citizenship in some way. Therefore, what the select committee did to even up the situation
was the best that it could in the circumstances, without at the same time recommending
retrospective legislation.
I turn now to the proposal to delete Part III of the Bill. Personally, I have always found
the provisions requiring the registration of aliens to be anathema. They are the legacy of a
day and age when a person who came to this country from another country was regarded as
somewhat unusual. That should not be the case, because New Zealand is essentially a nation
of immigrants. All our ancestors at one time came from another part of the world—and I
readily concede to the member for Western Maori, who is trying to interject, that some have
been here just a little longer than others. However, the fact remains that the law at present
requires that those people must in some way register their status and set themselves apart,
despite the fact that the State, by Executive action, has said, usually by granting the right to
permanent residence, that they are permitted to remain here and that nothing is known or
believed about them that would prohibit them from remaining. I welcome the Minister's
intimation while introducing the second reading debate that it is intended to delete Part III
and thereby effectively do away with the status of alien, and, more importantly, do away
with some of the undesirable consequences of those provisions.
Finally I refer to the submissions that were made about clause 18, and particularly to the
comments that were made by the member for Henderson on that clause. Those who would
advocate a right of appeal in respect of a refusal to grant citizenship are confusing two quite
different situations. There is a very substantial difference between deprivation of an existing
citizenship on the one hand, and on the other a refusal to grant a person who is not a New
Zealand citizen the right to be a New Zealand citizen. It has long been accepted, and it is not
a matter of argument, that no one should be able to lose his New Zealand citizenship by
some form of ministerial fiat or action. But that does not apply, and has never applied, to a
decision to grant citizenship to someone who is not at the time a New Zealand citizen. That
is, and always has been, an Executive act that is not subject to review.
I know that the Labour Party has a great desire to do away completely with the Govern-
ment in New Zealand and to substitute judges. I can hear the member for Auckland Central
trying to interject. If he is interested in my electorate, perhaps he would like to stand against
me, otherwise he might like to await his opportunity and make his contribution, whatever it
might be, at a later stage of the debate. The Labour Opposition has clearly confused an
Executive function on the one hand with the function exercised by the courts on the other. It
is entirely inappropriate to confuse decisions to grant citizenship with decisions to take away
an existing citizenship right. When the Bill was before the select committee we received only
a relatively few submissions, but all those who made submissions, subject to the particular
comments they wanted to make on the clauses, enthusiastically supported the Bill—and that
applied particularly to those provisions that equalised the situation between men and
women. I personally welcome the second reading of this very important constitutional
measure.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): The member for Birkenhead was correct in two of
the statements he made during his speech. He pointed out that this is a very important Bill. It
is a very important measure, because in New Zealand we do not have a great deal of
constitutional law as such. As he correctly stated, the Bill is a constitutional measure because
it sets out who is and who is not a New Zealand citizen. It also sets out the way in which
people can become New Zealand citizens. We on this side of the House welcome the Bill in
the sense that it is a sign of the further maturity of New Zealand as a nation. It is important
that members should be aware of the fact that New Zealand citizenship was first created as
something separate from British citizenship. That came about as a result of the adoption of
the Statute of Westminster by the first Labour Government in 1948, and the passing of the
British Nationality and New Zealand Citizenship Act and the Aliens Act in 1948. Those two
Acts are being repealed by the Bill before us.

Citizens and Aliens Bill
Minister has said he is prepared to go some little way towards having an oath of allegiance to
the Queen made by people who are granted New Zealand citizenship. This question arises
because the Queen is no longer Queen of New Zealand through being Queen of England;
she is Queen of New Zealand as a result of an Act of Parliament, which makes that position a
separate legal entity from that of Queen of England or of any other Commonwealth country.
That being the case, people who become New Zealand citizens, no matter whether they are
citizens of a Commonwealth country or any other country, should be able to make an oath of
allegiance.
I am unimpressed by the answer that it would be too administratively complex. If it is
possible to demand, as the Department of Social Welfare does, that solo mothers should
regularly sign oaths in order to receive benefits, surely it is not too much to ask that a person
who is to get the right of New Zealand citizenship, which is a very important thing, and one
of the most treasured privileges this country can bestow, should make an oath of allegiance
to the Queen. Once it has been explained to them that the Queen of New Zealand is, in a
legal sense, a different person from the Queen of England, and therefore the allegiance they
owe to her as the Queen of England, if they are English, is different from the allegiance they
owe to her as Queen of New Zealand, they will be pleased and proud and willing to make
such an oath. It is not enough for a person to receive a letter from the Minister saying, "You
are now a New Zealand citizen." That downgrades the whole status of New Zealand
citizenship and, in a sense, downgrades New Zealand's importance as an individual
sovereign State.
In order to build up a sense of nationalism—in the best sense of the word—and a sense
that being a New Zealander is something special and precious, we should ask people who
have applied for and been granted the right to become New Zealanders to make a simple but
solemn declaration of loyalty to Her Majesty the Queen. That would not be too difficult to
organise. If it is too difficult to organise through the Department of Internal Affairs as
administered by the Government, some administrative changes are called for.
I think that the Minister has in mind a sort of mail order oath-that he should post out
some sort of declaration, which will be signed and sent back. I think there should be some
civic ceremony, such as other nations have. The United States, for example, makes a special
occasion of granting citizenship; in fact, it goes a great deal further than I would think
necessary, and a great deal further than what the Minister has in mind. A simple, solemn
oath and declaration of loyalty to the Queen would be appreciated by new citizens, and it
would also encourage some New Zealanders who tend to be a little hostile to new New
Zealanders to treat them in a more fraternal way.
As the Minister has indicated, he is introducing a Supplementary Order Paper for that
reason. He has indicated he has accepted some of the arguments put forward by members on
this side of the House. I believe he should go a little further. If the Department of Social
Welfare can demand an oath for solo mothers surely the Minister's department can demand
an oath for new New Zealanders.
In conclusion, members on this side of the House welcome the overall thrust of the Bill,
but are sorry that the Minister has not taken this opportunity to make it completely
bipartisan. The Bill should be bipartisan and all members should agree about citizenship. I
am sure the Minister can find some way to accommodate the three proposals put forward by
the Opposition.

MINING AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines): I move, That the Mining Amendment Bill be
introduced. The main purpose of the Bill is to amend certain of the provisions in the Mining
Act 1971 that relate to mining in national parks so that exploration may again take place in
these large and potentially important areas and be done in a manner that will ensure, and in
certain respects strengthen, environmental safeguards.
When the Mining Act came into force in April 1973, a new provision was introduced to
the mining law allowing the holder of a prospecting licence the automatic right to convert
that prospecting licence to a mining licence. The intention of the provision was to provide
the holder of a prospecting licence with security for his high-risk expenditure during the
prospecting stage. However, the effect of the provision has been to bring to a halt
exploration for minerals in certain areas of national parks.
The consent of the Minister of Lands is required before a licence can be granted over
national park land. He, in turn, is required to consult the National Parks Authority before
making his decision. With the threat of the automatic right of exchange, the authority felt
that approval of a prospecting licence was tantamount to approval of a mining licence.
Consequently, no mineral exploration has taken place in parks since 1973.
National parks cover a large percentage of New Zealand's land mass, much of it in the
most favourable geological environment for the possible location of economic deposits of
minerals. These areas should be explored, and the Minister of Lands agrees with me that the
hiatus that has followed the introduction of the 1971 Mining Act must end, and that the
resumption of exploration must be allowed.
The Bill provides what we believe to be the solution to the problem. For national park
land, and national park land only, it removes the automatic right of exchange, and replaces it
with a right in priority. Thus, when a prospecting licence is granted, a decision on a mining
licence is not committed. Mining proposals can be examined quite independently and at a
more appropriate time when an economic evaluation of a mineral deposit is available.
The mining industry has naturally been reluctant to see eroded what it considers as an
important right, but I believe I have been able to persuade the industry of the need for this
move in recognition of the special nature of national parks.
The Bill also requires that in future the Minister of Lands and the Minister of Mines will
have to act jointly in considering whether to consent to applications for prospecting licences
and mining licences in national parks. Formerly, the consent of the Minister of Lands only
was required. This way, park and mining interests will need to get together at the earliest
stage to discuss prospecting and mining proposals before any decision is made. This will
ensure that any conflicts are resolved before proposals are recommended. This is seen as an
essential step to ensure that both points of view-the mining and the environmental-are
sufficiently represented, as perhaps has not been possible in the past. It is particularly
important to the mining industry, which will no longer enjoy the security of a right of
exchange of a prospecting licence to a mining licence.
The Bill amends the present provision that requires the Minister of Lands to give his
consent before the Minister of Mines can grant an exploration licence over national park and
reserve land. It is replaced with a requirement that the Minister of Lands be given 28 days'
notice of the intent to grant an exploration licence. A new requirement is then introduced,
by which the holder of an exploration licence has to give reasonable notice to the controlling
authority of the park or reserve of his intention to enter the land. The holder of the
exploration licence also has to comply with any reasonable conditions imposed by that


## p. 4393 (#499) ###########################################

10 November
4393
Mining Amendment Bill
authority while he is in the area. Previously, once an exploration licence was granted, the
holder was not obliged to accept that his entry could be governed by conditions.
The exploration licence concept, again, is one that was introduced to New Zealand
mining law when the 1971 Mining Act came into force. The exploration licence is quite
different from the prospecting licence. It can cover an area of up to 200 square miles, and is
designed to allow the holder to undertake a regional investigation of the area applied for to
identify localised areas of potential mineralisation. Such areas can then be applied for and
examined in detail under a prospecting licence. Only large-scale exploration methods can be
used, the most common being aerial surveys. No work on the ground is permitted that might
harm the environment.
These licences are ideal for large areas such as national parks. They have only a short
term, the work undertaken cannot be detrimental to park values, and, most importantly,
they carry no automatic rights of exchange-only a right in priority to a prospecting licence.
Their grant is supported by park interests. Unfortunately, the present formal procedure for
obtaining the consent of the Minister of Lands is cumbersome and time-consuming,
considering the nature of the licence. Further, the requirement to obtain consent has not
proved to be the best approach to supervising activity in the park. This supervision needs to
be done on the spot, at the time of entry, and by the controlling authority. The new
provisions will meet these requirements. The Minister of Lands is still notified, but, more
importantly, the licensee has to give notice of his intention to enter, and the controlling
authority of the park or reserve.may require that entry to be subject to conditions.
The Bill is a significant one. It provides the means for the resumption of mineral
exploration in our national parks. This is important for New Zealand. We must know what
and where our mineral resources are, and what the costs of developing them may be. The
Bill ensures that we can make a proper evaluation of those costs. It establishes clear divisions
between exploration, prospecting, and mining in national parks. First, the exploration stage
can be approved and carried out quickly and efficiently with no environmental damage, and
has the purpose of identifying localised areas of mineral interest. Effective controls will be
placed on land entry during this stage. Secondly, without commitment from the exploration
licence, the Minister of Lands and the Minister of Mines must jointly consent before a
prospecting licence can be granted. The identification of economic mineral deposits can take
place in the knowledge that the costs of development can be fully evaluated, and without the
threat of automatic mining rights. Thirdly, any mining proposal must be considered jointly
by two Ministers, and a decision can be made having regard to the circumstances at the
time-not influenced by any previous commitment entered into at the prospecting stage.
As the Bill affects Crown land, it will be referred automatically to the Lands and
Agriculture Committee. I trust that the committee will complete its consideration of the Bill
without delay, because there is no reason why this amendment to the mining law should not
be passed this session.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Lamb Prices
1. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of Agriculture: Is he able to give the
estimated increase in lamb prices to farmers as a result of sterling revaluation?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Acting Minister
of Agriculture. On 8 November 1977-2 days ago—the value of the pound sterling against
the New Zealand dollar was about 1 percent greater than on 28 October 1977 when its recent
movements against the United States dollar commenced. If this 1 percent appreciation were
maintained it could result in about a 1.3c a kilogram increase in the PM lamb schedule at
present Smithfield prices. For a 13.6 kg lamb this amounts to 17.7c a head. However, it
cannot be assumed that the schedule will immediately increase by 1.3c a kilogram as it is only
partly determined by current realisations for lamb in the United Kingdom and other
markets.

Industrial Stoppages-Cost to Dairy Industry
9. Mr BIRCH (Franklin) asked the Minister of Agriculture: How much in export
earnings have industrial stoppages cost the dairy industry in the past 12 months?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Acting Minister
of Agriculture. The dairy industry has an admirable record in the field of industrial relations,
as evidenced by the fact that in the first 8 months of this year there was only one stoppage in
the industry involving three dairy companies. It is, therefore, fair to say that there has been
little or no disruption to export production on account of industrial stoppages. However, in
common with other industries, both agricultural and manufacturing, the dairy industry does
face disruptions on occasions that are the result of actions involving groups outside the dairy
industry, and occasionally export shipments of dairy products are subject to delays because
of industrial stoppages. However, no precise details are available on the loss in export
earnings, if any, to the dairy industry because of such stoppages.

Social Welfare Cheques-Theft
10. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Police: How many social
welfare beneficiary cheques have been reported as stolen during the last financial year, and
how many convictions resulted from investigations into these thefts?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Police. It is not possible to determine from police reports exactly how many beneficiary
cheques have been stolen, as the statistical data are categorised under the general heading of
theft. This encompasses all types of theft. It is possible, however, to determine how many
offences have been dealt with under the Social Security Act. These offences include theft,
false declarations, and general fraudulent activity surrounding benefits. For the 1976 year
182 such offences were reported and 169 of these were cleared. For the 9 months to 30
September 1977, 249 cases were reported and 178 were cleared. It should be borne in mind
that offences of fraud and theft relating to benefit cheques may also be dealt with under the
appropriate provision of the Crimes Act 1961, and may not necessarily be dealt with under
the provisions of the Social Security Act.

Social Welfare Cheques-Theft
12. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Social Welfare: Will he

toward fluctuations in the incidence of misappropriations by area and season, particularly in
summer resort areas such as Tauranga and the Bay of Islands?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I reply on behalf of
the Minister of Social Welfare. His answer is as follows: "Exact statistics on the number of
benefit payment orders that went missing during the last financial year are not available.
However, it has been ascertained that over a recent 4-weekly period some 2200 applications
were received for duplicate payment orders. In the same period 1658 orders were returned
unclaimed to the department. The 542 orders that were unaccounted for represented 0.05
percent of the total number of payment orders dispatched from my department's computer
centre at Upper Hutt each 4 weeks. There is no evidence to suggest that the incidence of
misappropriation of payment orders fluctuates on a seasonal basis in areas such as Tauranga
and the Bay of Islands."
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Based on past experience, how many of these 542 vouchers would
the Minister expect to be dishonestly cashed?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I suggest that a separate question should be asked of

question.
Mr Comber: Do beneficiaries have available to them the option of having their benefits
paid directly into their Post Office or savings accounts?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: That is not related to the original question, which asked how

Hon. R. O. Douglas: The original question asked what percentage was dishonestly
cashed. Does the Minister have an indication of the percentage for any past period?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: No, I have no other information. I have a note
which states that in the processing of paid documents for August 1976, 483 instances where
duplicate and original payments had been negotiated were detected. Of these, 376 were
cases where both the original and duplicate payments had been negotiated by the
beneficiary. Overpayments in these cases were recovered. The remaining 107 cases were
those where the original payment had been negotiated by a person other than the
beneficiary. A proportion of the overpayments in these cases is recovered if the offender can
be detected and prosecuted following police investigation. If the honourable member wants
information for a longer period he should ask a separate question.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Does the Minister have the value of the 107 cases?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: No, I do not. It would be better if the honourable
member asked a written answer, because a mass of detail would have to be given.

Industrial Unions-Unqualified Preference Ballots
16. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour: In view of the fact that the
Industrial Relations Act requires unqualified preference ballots to be conducted by awards
rather than unions and that few unions with more than one award have rolls by award, so
that in most cases it will be necessary for the Department of Labour to compile new rolls for
each award, how long does he estimate it will take to ballot the entire New Zealand labour
force?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Although it is true that a great number of
unions are covered by more than one award or industrial agreement the Industrial Relations
Act requires that the unions shall supply the registrar with a list containing the names and
postal addresses of those people entitled to vote. It is not, therefore, true to say that it will be
necessary for the department to compile new rolls. The department must be satisfied that the
list provided by the union is as complete as possible. If it is not satisfied other means, such as
newspaper advertisements, will be used. It is not possible to say precisely how long it will
take to conduct all the ballots, but, as has been previously stated in the Government's policy,
it will take a number of years.

BAY OF PLENTY CATCHMENT COMMISSION AND REGIONAL WATER BOARD
ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSES RECOVERY BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission and
Regional Water Board Administrative Expenses Recovery Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.


## p. 4406 (#512) ###########################################

4406
10 November
Bay of Plenty Recovery Bill
When the commission was gazetted in 1964, the agreed basis for apportionment of adminis-
tration costs was counties 62.90 percent, municipalities 37.10 percent, and there was an
agreement that the basis of this apportionment would be reviewed after each triennial
election, which was done more or less successfully until February 1972 after the 1971 local
body elections. When reviewing the basis for apportionment in February 1972, the counties
unanimously favoured a change from levies to the making and levying of a uniform rate on
all rateable property within catchment areas as provided for in section 23B of the Soil
Conservation and Rivers Control Act 1941. This would have altered the proportion payable
in reverse quantity-in other words, the counties then would have paid the 37.10 percent and
the municipalities the 62.90 percent.
A lengthy wrangle has ensued since that time, and I certainly do not propose getting
into that area. Suffice it to say that successive Ministers of Works and Development have
tried to bring the parties together to reach agreement, and to date all attempts at conciliation
or arbitration have been unsuccessful. The basis for apportionment was in dispute from 1
April 1973 to 31 March 1977, and during that period constituent authorities made contribu-
tions without prejudice as they saw fit. This put the future of the catchment commission
under some threat, and I am sure that no member would want to jeopardise its future
operations. To date the deficit on the administration account is about $133,000.
It might be helpful to say what the Bill does. It provides that voluntary contributions
paid to the commission, as set out in the first schedule, become a debt of the commission to
the constituent authorities concerned. The commission, by agreement with a constituent
authority, may offset this debt against payments due from that authority. Another point is
that in making the commission's administration deficit, as set out in the second schedule, a
debt of the constituent authorities due to the commission, which they are to pay over 3 years,
the debt is deemed to be a rate duly made and levied by the commission. The Bill sets out to
recover the deficit accrued for the period in question in the administration expenses of the
commission in a manner within the compass of section 23B referred to earlier.
On 13 December 1976 the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Council instructed the
commission to make and levy a rate on a uniform scale on all rateable property in the
catchment area, to take effect in the year commencing 1 April 1977; and here the situation is
clear. No difficulty is envisaged in the recovery of these administration expenses. The period
still in doubt, and the chief subject of this legislation, is from 1 April 1973 to 31 March 1977.
Clause 1(2) of the Bill as reported back provides that the Act shall come into force on a date
to be fixed by the Governor-General by Order in Council on the recommendation of the
Minister of Works and Development.
This is to give the parties to the agreement one last opportunity for conciliation binding
on all parties. I make an urgent plea to all members of the catchment commission to get
together once again, in the light of the long debate that has ensued over the last 5½ years, to
resolve their difficulties once and for all.
I made an observation at the beginning of the hearings of the Local Bills Committee,
which I think had the support of all members, that no select committee of the House was a
court of conciliation or a court of arbitration. As Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the
Minister of Local Government, I repeat what I have said about the need for local authorities
to resolve their problems themselves, without turning back to central government. This is at
the heart of the policy and the principles enunciated by this Government. I do not like
centralism. This is a happy compromise. It ensures that, if the parties do not get together
finally to resolve the question of the recovery of this administrative expense, the Minister
will be bound to act in the interest of the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission. I hope that
no such Order in Council is ever made. I hope that common sense will prevail, on all sides,
and that the parties will resolve the question of recovery of the administration expense.
This matter has gone on too long; all parties would have to agree that 5½ years is far too
long-indeed, it is getting on for 6 years now. It was only after the most careful consideration
in discussion with the various parties that the Local Bills Committee came back with the
recommendation that is now before the House.
Mr ALLEN (Tauranga): Speaking to the Bill that is being reported back, it is correct, as
the Under-Secretary says, that it is intended to recover the administration costs of the Bay of
Plenty Catchment Commission for the period 1973-77, yet the effect will be to double the
cost during that period to the municipalities and halve the cost to the counties-exactly the
reverse of the agreement made at the inception of the catchment commission, which stood
until 1 April 1977. Apart from that injustice-and I see it as an injustice-I have grave
doubts that this Bill should be reported back to the House.


## p. 4407 (#513) ###########################################

10 November
4407
Bay of Plenty Recovery Bill
I can respect the committee's wish to see arbitration, since that is what I have advocated
myself over the years, but, since arbitration is not provided for in either of the principal
Acts the 1941 Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Act, and the 1967 Water and Soil
Conservation Act-nor in this Bill, it may be a somewhat vain wish. But, the grounds for my
objection are more important-this should not be a local Bill, since the power to levy-and
this is what the Bill is all about—is provided in section 23B of the 1941 Act, and is a power of
the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Council, a Government body set up by legislation.
A catchment board or a catchment commission is delegated this power, and is simply an
agent of the council, and cannot be anything else. The argument that this Bill is of local
significance only does not stand up, since it purports to change an agreed apportionment of
costs made under section 23B of the 1941 Act, which is New Zealand-wide legislation, not
local legislation. More importantly, section 23B, which gives the power to make such an
agreement concerning catchment commission costs, gives no power to revoke the agree-
ment, although it gives power to amend the apportionment of those costs by agreement. It is
obvious then that, if section 23B is faulty-and, if this Bill is necessary, it must be faulty—it is
the 1941 Act that should be amended, and this Bill should not be reported back.
The next objection I have is that the administration costs included in the two schedules
to the Bill contain water board costs that, according to section 28(1) of the 1967 Water and
Soil Conservation Act, should be met by moneys appropriated by Parliament. That is what
the section states, plainly and bluntly. They have not been so met, and this matter is now
under appeal to the Supreme Court. So it seems that not only does the Bill propose to
override-in one instance only, the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission-existing legisla-
tion, but also to abrogate the power of the court. This is totally wrong on all counts.
I contend that the legislation will not be just to the people of the Bay of Plenty, who are
concerned with it, and that it contravenes existing legislation. It is retrospective legislation,
intended to legalise spending by the catchment commission for which it had no authority at
all. The power to levy is given under the 1941 Act to the Soil Conservation and Rivers
Control Council, and to nobody else. As the council did not exercise that power it is at fault,
and should be responsible until this matter is sorted out under the agreement which existed
at that time. It is not acceptable to cover up bad departmental advice—and that is what it
is-by bulldozing retrospective legislation through the House.
The claim has been made that the catchment commission is in serious financial
difficulties. I am not surprised. As a member of the commission in 1971, I voted against such
expenditure, and recorded my vote, and, as far as I know, I was the only one who did so. I
am not being wise after the event therefore; I saw it coming. But the fault is with the council,
which did not make the levies during the period 1973-77.
I therefore submit: first, that this is not a local Bill, since the catchment commission acts
only as an agent for that council; secondly, that there is no power to revoke under section
23B, except by this type of retrospective legislation-the worst type, since it commits people
to paying more to cover unknown and what has been until this time illegal expenditure;
thirdly, that the Bill breaks the original agreement that stood until 1 April 1977-right
through the period we are talking about-by doubling the charges to the municipalities and
halving the other costs to the counties, and is, therefore, an injustice; and fourthly, that the
Bill is against the wishes of most of the people of the Bay of Plenty.
The Bill should not be reported back, and I shall speak against its proposals if it gets a
second reading. Let us hope that common sense and good will in the Bay of Plenty lead to an
arbitration acceptable by all the parties and that the situation can be resolved.
Motion agreed to.

INDECENT PUBLICATIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Honourable members will recall that in introducing the Bill I said that it makes
important changes to the provisions of the principal Act governing interim restriction orders.
The purpose of those changes is to prevent copies of a book being sold-as happened in the
case of the book entitled Down Under the Plum Trees—between the time a decision has been
made by the Indecent Publications Tribunal, and an appeal against that decision has been
heard and determined. As the law currently stands, if the tribunal has imposed an interim
restriction order that order is automatically revoked when the tribunal has reached a
decision on the particular publication. This Bill repeals subsection (8) of section 14A of the
principal Act-the provision allowing that result-and replaces it with provisions under
which an interim restriction order may remain in force after the tribunal has reached a
decision.
Clause 1 relates to the short title. Clause 2 repeals subsections (4) and (8) of section 14A
of the principal Act and replaces them with a provision whereby an interim restriction order
imposed by the tribunal remains in force until the time allowed for appealing against the
decision of the tribunal has elapsed. The time in which such an appeal may be lodged is 28
days from the date of the tribunal's decision. If an appeal has been lodged, this clause further
provides that any interim restriction order shall remain in force until the appeal has been
heard and determined. The amendments in clause 2 do not affect the present position,
whereby the chairman of the tribunal, or the tribunal itself, may revoke any interim
restriction order. If this is done, however, a fresh interim restriction order may be imposed
by a judge after an appeal has been lodged.
As it is by no means in every case that an interim restriction is imposed, and as the


## p. 4409 (#515) ###########################################

10 November
4409
Indecent Publications Amendment Bill
chairman of the tribunal, or the tribunal, may revoke such an order, the new provision
should not greatly inconvenience those wishing to distribute and sell a publication that has
been cleared by the tribunal. On the latter point, it would not, in my view, defeat the
purpose of the amendment if the tribunal revoked an interim restriction order in any case in
which it was clear that there was only a remote possibility of an appeal being lodged. Such
would not be the case, of course, in respect of the book to which I have referred. If an appeal
is lodged, any such order may, of course, be quickly reimposed by a judge.
Clause 3 gives the Supreme Court the power to impose and revoke an interim restriction
order. Under this clause, if the tribunal has either not imposed an interim restriction order or
has revoked such an order, the person appealing to the Supreme Court may apply for an
interim restriction order. If the Supreme Court imposes any such order it comes into force on
the day on which the order is made and remains in force until the appeal is determined. The
clause also gives the Supreme Court or a judge the power to revoke an interim restriction
order made under the new section 14B inserted into the principal Act by this clause, either on
its own or his own motion, or on the application of any person interested in the proceedings.
These provisions will ensure that when any decision of the tribunal is rigorously
disputed in any future case a decision of the Supreme Court, if it is in the appellant's favour,
will have more than merely academic significance. In my view, the new procedure is fair. It is
a workable alternative to the present system, and I believe it provides a safeguard against the
sort of problems that a great many people have, with justification, been very concerned
about.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The Minister describes the Bill as important and
I suppose one could not dispute that, but in essence it is consequential upon proceedings that
occurred not very long ago and is, in the main, procedural in character. There is little that
needs to be said as to clause 2, because it simply follows the common pattern of matters that
are ancillary to legal proceedings awaiting appeal. For instance, if the master of a fishing
vessel is prosecuted for an offence under our fisheries protection legislation and, if, being
found guilty, his vessel and gear are condemned, and he appeals against that, the condemna-
tion of the gear continues until the outcome of the appeal. No one could dispute that a ruling
of the tribunal should continue to be enforced while an appeal against the proceedings and
the tribunal's findings is still in dispute.
Clause 3 gives a power that I believe will be rarely invoked. It enables the Supreme
Court to issue interim restrictions. Normally, of course, they would be applied for and
granted by the tribunal itself, but, as the Minister says, it is only the failure of a person to
make an application, or its rejection or revocation by the tribunal, that would bring this into
force. It is hard to imagine a person forgoing an opportunity of applying to the tribunal, and
then applying to the Supreme Court. Any case of that kind would, I think, be extremely
rare. The other one is perhaps a little more likely to occur, but I still believe that the power
will be invoked comparatively seldom.
There are one or two points of detail that occur to me in looking at the language of the
clause. The original application to the tribunal is one that may be made ex parte, and indeed
an application under the new subsection 14A(9) inserted by clause 2-where there is
extension, by which time certain people will have become interested-may even be ex parte.
But this one is to be made to a judge on notice-presumably notice to other people involved,
as for instance, in some other subsection under which notice has to be given to the registrar
and parties having become interested in the proceedings. As far as I am aware, this is a novel
use of the language-"on notice"-because normally the parties to whom notice is to be
given are specified, and one is left to read into this the implication that the parties to be
notified are those who are either respondents to the appeal or have in some other way
indicated some kind of interest.
It is a kind of telegraphic language that is not uncommon in American jurisdiction and is
something of a replication of the language found in the present Town and Country Planning
Bill, which speaks of "notified applications", and so on, meaning those which are for
specified departures, which must be given on notice. I just remark on the unfamilarity of the
language here and wonder whether it is a style that we will adopt in future when notice has to
be given to anybody, instead of our usual expanded clause saying to whom the notice should
be given-just a compendious two-word phrase, "on notice". Other than that we have no
comment to make on the Bill.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I thank the member for Henderson for
his thought on the measure. Certainly I will discuss with parliamentary counsel the style of
drafting, and perhaps we can deal with that when we come to the Committee stage.

What was being done under the Education vote for children who would remain at school
next year? The recently announced mini-Budget had set aside money for many thousands of
people who would be unemployed next year, especially school leavers. It had been estimated
that between 65 000 and 70 000 school leavers would be looking for jobs at the end of the
year-a record number-because of the very high birth rates in 1961 and thereabouts. If
there was no improvement in the economy, about 60 percent of people unemployed would
be under 20 years of age. A person could not register as unemployed until he was 16, and
many people in that category were school leavers. He had received a letter today from a
person in Rotorua who had read a series of articles in the New Zealand Herald on job
availability for school leavers. One article had stated that butchery apprenticeships were
available to people with university entrance, but little else. The writer had stated that it was
demoralising for fourth, fifth, and sixth formers to have to stay at school, go on the dole, or
take demeaning jobs below their capabilities. Was there any indication that the situation
would improve if the pupils stayed at school?
Several articles had appeared in the newspapers, but the one in Monday's New Zealand
Herald had hit home more for the people living in the Auckland province outside Auckland
city. The Opposition was aware that the figures published by the department did not fully
illustrate the extent of the problem, and, given the forecasts of employment, it was
concerned about what would happen in the early part of next year. The Opposition was
concerned about the effects on the lives and morale of young people. A quarter of the
registered unemployed were under the age of 18. When school leavers were added to that,
one had to be concerned. Schools had not closed for the year, and so no one had any real


## p. 4412 (#518) ###########################################

4412
10 November
Appropriation Bill (No. 2)-Supplementary Estimates
idea of how many people would be unemployed. University students would be looking for
work during the vacation, and many people had expressed concern about how they would
find employment. What provision for unemployment benefits would be made for university
and other tertiary students who were unable to find vacation work? The matter was of very
serious concern in the community, especially to parents of people in the affected age group.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) said that it had been suggested that between
60 000 and 70 000 people would be leaving school this year. He did not want to underplay the
problem, but it had not reached the crisis situation suggested by the Opposition. During the
year it had been forecast that 62 000 people would be leaving school. A Department of
Labour survey had found that, of the 62 000 people presumed to be leaving school in 1977,
19 000 had left school by September, 13 200 intended to go on to full-time tertiary education,
and by early October jobs had been arranged for 6500 people. So nearly 39 000 of the 60 000
had been catered for by early October. Those intending to leave school, but with no specific
job in mind by the end of October, numbered 12 400. Those awaiting examination results or
a job numbered 23 900. On past experience only a proportion of that group left tertiary
education and came within the responsibility of the Department of Labour. On that basis,
between 22 000 and 28 000 school leavers who did not have jobs arranged by early October
might be seeking jobs at the end of the year. With Christmas holidays, the normal turnover
in the labour force, and people retiring at 60 or 65, the Government did not expect anywhere

BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): Next week it is intended to take
legislation, which should follow the order set down in today's Order Paper. There might be,
and indeed there have been from time to time, requests for variations in the order, but as far
as possible the Order Paper will be adhered to. On Thursday we shall deal with local Bills, if
any. I also thought I should inform the House that following discussions with some of my
colleagues, I talked with the Leader of the Opposition this morning, and it has been decided
to refer the Children and Young Persons Amendment Bill to a select committee. There is a
clear understanding that legislation will be passed this year.
NOTICES OF MOTION-ADMISSIBILITY
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Before we come to notices of motion, perhaps I should draw
attention to the notices of motion I was asked to look at yesterday. I believe the one in the
name of the member for Onehunga is acceptable, as is the one in the name of the member
for Franklin. I think one word should be amended in the motion lodged by the member for
Manukau.
On the main point over which I have some sort of jurisdiction under the Standing
Orders Committee's recommendations, the question raised with me yesterday was whether
notices of motion could be authenticated—whether they gave the facts correctly. All I am
obliged to do is to decide whether the words used in the notice of motion reflect the words
used in the newspaper report on which the notice was based. I do not have to authenticate
the veracity or otherwise of the newspaper report itself. I have found that on all the
occasions referred to me the notice of motion has correctly used the words in the newspaper
report. On the notice of motion given by the member for Manukau, I think the latter part
contains an implication that is rather difficult to authenticate. Perhaps the member could
alter one word, and then the notice might be acceptable.

the member that the regulations, which were dated 1912, were superseded in 1921, since
when a variety of Governments, including three Labour Administrations, have had the
chance to review and remove them. Such an exercise would be a large one, and under the
present circumstances we do not have the necessary labour force. However, I will certainly
consider some sort of review.

Energy-Water-Powered Engine
20. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: Have any
plans been made for departmental officials to meet and discuss with Mr A. Blue, inventor of

his return to this country before Christmas?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): The answer is no.
Dr Shearer: Will the Minister indicate why no approach has yet been made?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The Ministry of Energy Resources does not believe it is possible to
use water as an energy source in the manner claimed by Mr Blue. His system divides water
into hydrogen and oxygen and then recombines in a vehicle engine. No more energy can be
released by the recombination than was used to divide the water.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Is the Minister aware that there has been substantial progress in the
development of dividing hydrogen from water for energy in the United States of America?
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I am not sure, but that question may be related in some way to
the original question. As it is Friday I suppose I can allow it.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I think the principles being used are vastly different from those
proposed by Mr Blue. As Minister of Energy Resources, I get several letters with bright
ideas every week, at least one of which includes an idea for perpetual motion.
Hon. L. W. Gandar: Can the Minister confirm that the same amount of energy was
required to separate hydrogen and oxygen in 1850 as in 1977 and will be required 100 years
from now; and that, no matter what developments may have occurred in the United States,
the position will not alter?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I am pleased to confirm that interesting observation from the
Minister of Science.

MUTUAL INSURANCE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Mutual Insurance
Amendment Bill be introduced. The main purpose of this Bill is to provide statutory authority
for the merger of mutual insurance associations. The Mutual Insurance Act 1955 regulates
the operation of mutual insurance associations which comprise members of the farming
community formed to grant to those members a wide range of insurance cover. There are
two mutual insurance associations in New Zealand, the Farmers Mutual Insurance Associa-
tion of Dunedin and the Taranaki Farmers Mutual Insurance Association of Eltham. These
two associations wish to merge their businesses to provide a more efficient service for the
insurance needs of the agricultural sector. The administrative rearrangements for the
proposed merger have been completed, and the ultimate merger is planned to take effect
from 1 April 1978.
The Bill provides the statutory authority for the merger to proceed. The merger will
result in an association with a total membership of about 40 000 throughout New Zealand.
Accordingly, the Bill increases to 14 the maximum number of directors a mutual insurance
association may appoint, and provides for such an association to adopt rules for the regional
election of directors. This will allow members from every part of New Zealand to be
represented on the board of directors. The opportunity also is taken in the Bill to remove the
administration of the Mutual Insurance Act 1955 to the Department of Justice so that all
insurance legislation is administered in the one department.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): Naturally, I was glancing at the Bill as the
Minister was explaining it. I did not hear him make any comment on the provision in clause 3
which enables membership of the company to be extended not only to the constituent

ALCOHOLIC LIQUOR ADVISORY COUNCIL AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Alcoholic Liquor
Advisory Council Amendment Bill be introduced. The main purpose of this short Bill is to
make adequate provision for the collection of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council's levy
from winemakers. A detailed examination of the levy provisions of the principal Act
disclosed a deficiency in the machinery provisions in this respect. As the Act stands at
present, winemakers are required to pay their council levy in a lump sum early in each
financial year. Their levy, however, is based on wine sold during that period and the
winemaker is therefore being asked to pay a levy based on sales figures that are unknown to
him when his levy is payable. The most sensible method is to make the levy payable on the
sales figures for the preceding statistical year, and this approach, found in clause 2, has the
approval of the Wine Institute of New Zealand.
Clauses 3 and 4 implement the request of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council for
authority to make superannuation contributions for its staff, to operate subsidiary bank
accounts, and to permit unauthorised expenditure of up to $500 in any financial year.
Clauses 5 and 6 relate to the calculation and collection of the council's levy. The council's
levy in respect of beer and spirits is payable at the same time as customs duty, and clause 6
exempts from the council's levy any liquor which does not attract customs duty. Navy rum,
ships' stores, and liquor purchased by diplomatic personnel are examples of the application
of this exemption.
The Government has decided that exported liquor should be exempt from both the
calculation and payment of the council's levy. As the levy is for problems within New
Zealand, it seems only reasonable to exclude exported liquor from the levy. The Bill has the
support of the Wine Institute and the council itself, and I believe it can be dealt with by the
House without referral to a select committee.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): There appears to be nothing which calls for
comment from the Opposition at this stage.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Status of Children Amendment Bill
STATUS OF CHILDREN AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Status of Children
Amendment Bill be introduced. After the introduction, I propose to ask the House to refer
the Bill to the Statutes Revision Committee for recess study, so that it may be enacted in
1978. The purpose of the Bill is to clarify and rationalise the Status of Children Act as it
applies to the administration of trusts and estates. Members will recall that the object of the
principal Act was to abolish illegitimacy as a legal status and to remove the legal disabilities
of persons born out of wedlock. It follows that a person born out of wedlock may succeed to
family property in the ordinary way, subject of course to the satisfactory establishment of the
parent-child relationship. However, some anomalies have emerged in the practical operation
of the Act which the Bill sets out to correct.
Clause 1 proposes a commencement date of 1 October 1978 because the Bill is a
technical one-and for that reason also I want it to be referred to the Statutes Revision
Committee for recess study. It is not a measure that can or should be rushed. Clause 2 inserts
a new section 5A and remodels section 6 of the Act. At present, the Act does not say whether
an applicant for a grant of letters of administration of an estate has to inquire about the
existence of ex-nuptial relatives who could claim an interest in that estate and therefore have
an equal or prior right to a grant of administration. On the basis of the general law, the
Supreme Court registrars, acting with the approval of the judges, have said, in effect, that
inquiries have to be made.
By way of contrast, section 6 says at present that an administrator or trustee is under no
obligation to make any inquiries about the existence of relatives who might be entitled to a
share in the property by reason of the Status of Children Act. Clause 2 resolves these
difficulties by requiring both an applicant for a grant and an administrator or trustee to make
reasonable inquiries about the existence of such persons. To avoid uncertainty, the meaning
of the term "reasonable inquiries" is spelled out. I believe that this approach accords with
the spirit of the original Status of Children Bill as conceived by the late Mr Hanan.
Clause 3 makes some changes to section 7 of the principal Act, which relates to the
recognition of paternity. It is made clear that paternity admitted by or established against the
father before the child is born may found a claim to property. The present wording suggests
that paternity must be established after the child has been born. There is also provision for a
Supreme Court declaration as to paternity, obtained after the death of the father, to found a
claim to property. Existing law says that paternity must in every case be established during
the father's lifetime if a claim to property is to be sustained. This rule seems unnecessarily
restrictive, having regard to the fact that the Supreme Court is specifically empowered to
make a paternity declaration regardless of whether the father, the child, or either of them is
living or dead.
Subsection (2) of section 7 is rewritten to confer a little more flexibility. It provides that
no distribution of property is to be upset by reason of a further claimant having established
that he has a right to share in the property pursuant to the Act. Under the present law such a
person cannot share in property to which other persons have become absolutely entitled,
even though no steps have been taken to distribute the property to those persons. This could
cause injustice in some cases. Clauses 4 and 5 are in the nature of tidying-up provisions only.
I remind honourable members that I shall be seeking their co-operation in sending the Bill to
the Statutes Revision Committee for recess study for its enactment next year.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The Bill deals with esoteric and technical
matters, and any comment at this stage would be premature.
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): Without looking at the principal Act, I am concerned to see
here that a child relates to offspring, and not necessarily to a child as we understand it—as a
very young person still at school or under guidance. Does the term offspring include adults?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): Yes, that is correct.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I move, That the Status of Children Amendment Bill be
referred to the Statutes Revision Committee for recess study, and that the proceedings of the
committee during the hearing of evidence be open to accredited representatives of the news
media.
Motion agreed to.

11 November
Education Amendment Bill
Bill be introduced. This Bill of 10 clauses makes miscellaneous changes to the Education Act
1964. They are necessary to bring various sections of the Education Act up to date, and to
improve present education policy.
Clause 2 deals with the provisions of the present Act relating to schools in the Chatham
Islands which at present are administered directly by the department as if they were Maori
schools, although there are no longer any Maori schools as such. The Bill includes the
Chatham Islands in the Canterbury Education Board district for administrative purposes,
and will come into effect on a date appointed by Order in Council after the necessary
arrangements have been agreed upon between the department and the board. Clause 3 deals
with secondary school councils. At present a member of a secondary school council vacates
that office if he is convicted of an offence punishable by imprisonment. The Bill brings the
provision into line with similar provisions by providing that a person is to vacate office only if
he is convicted of an offence punishable by a term of imprisonment of 2 years or more, or if
he is actually sentenced to imprisonment.
Clause 4 provides for secondary schools offering some form of technical education to
accept students who are not enrolled as students at that school in the same way as if the
school was a technical institute. Provision is also made for a school controlling authority to
set up a special committee to advise on the classes and courses, and for regulations at present
relating to technical institutes to apply also to those classes and courses. The Bill includes
provision for the status of principals and registrars to be established in the same way as the
same office holders in technical institutes.
Clause 5 relates to the rights of teachers to appeal against appointments. At present the
Act does not require applicants for division A teaching positions to be informed that they
have been unsuccessful. This amendment Bill requires them to be given notice by letter, and
also provides that appeals against non-appointment must be lodged within 10 days from the
one on which the notification that an application was unsuccessful was posted.
In the Education Act there are no provisions for the inspection of teachers' colleges, or
pre-school institutions funded by grants or public money, so this Bill provides for the
inspection of these institutions, and also, in the case of pre-school institutions, allows
adequate notice of intention to inspect.
In the last Budget a new programme for research was inserted in the Education vote.
The Bill makes clearer the director-general's power to spend money on educational
research, and to enter into contracts with persons undertaking research. Clause 9 deals with
the School Certificate examination, and this new section does three things. First, it expresses
in general terms that the director-general may have power to do whatever is necessary to
hold examinations; secondly, it empowers him to make regulations providing for internal
assessment, and to charge fees in connection with the examination; thirdly, to avoid doubt, it
declares that all existing regulations are valid as if the principal Act had been amended in the
manner indicated in the clauses at the time they were made.
Clause 10 deals with the authorisation to grant holidays on special occasions. Under the
provisions of the present Act, school committees are not empowered to grant school
holdiays, even though it is considered usual for them to do so. The Bill authorises the making
of regulations to empower school committees to grant holidays on special occasions. I have
discussed the provisions of the Bill with the Opposition spokesman on education, and I do
not think there is any need for the Bill to go to a select committee. The amendments are of a
machinery nature and can be dealt with adequately by the House.

GAMING AND LOTTERIES BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Gaming and Lotteries Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
This Bill consolidates and amends the law relating to gaming and lotteries and makes a
number of important changes to the law. However, despite the fact that the measure is one
of both important and topical law reform, an indication of its general acceptability is that it
attracted only nine submissions, together with comments from the Department of
Justice-which conveyed to the select committee the views of the Contracts and Commercial
Law Reform Committee-the Police Department, the Department of Trade and Industry,
and the Department of Internal Affairs, whose officials were advising the committee on the
Bill. The committee recommends a number of detailed changes to the Bill. I shall merely
refer to the major changes proposed, either as a result of the submissions or as a result of the
committee's further consideration of the Bill, and will deal with those changes essentially in
the order in which they appear.
The committee received a detailed submission from New Zealand News Ltd, presented
by the company's managing editor, Mr Ross Sayers, which covered a number of important
points. The company first suggested that the definition of "authorised purpose” in clause 2
should include specific reference to sports clubs, youth clubs, etc. The committee is,
however, satisfied that the definition already, in general terms, covers such organisations,
and recommends no change. New Zealand News Ltd also recommended a clarification of the
definition of a game of chance. The definition in the Bill provides that a game of chance is
one in which the outcome depends "entirely or substantially" on chance. The intention was
that the element of chance would be such that it would materially affect the outcome of the
game. The committee is satisfied that the present definition may not meet this intention, and
therefore recommends that the words "entirely or substantially" be deleted and replaced
with "wholly or partly".
The Police Department, in its discussions with the committee, recommended that the
definition of a prize competition be amended so that the performance of the activity depends
to some degree on skill or dexterity. The definition of prize competition was intended to
cover those competitions that may include a substantial element of chance, but which also
involve the participant in some activity involving skill or dexterity. It is recognised, however,
that even if a competition involves an element of chance it should continue to be a prize
competition, provided there is some facility for competitors to exercise knowledge, skill, or
dexterity. We recommend an amendment to clause 2 to give effect to this change.
Finally, the Police suggested that the definition of sales promotion schemes should be
clarified to make it clear that, if such a scheme is a prize competition and meets the
requirements of the Bill, it should not be subject to the legislation. We also recommend the
inclusion of one further definition related to "authorised persons", which I shall explain in a
moment. As at present drafted, clause 7 (2) makes it an offence to charge admission to
premises where games of chance are played. The committee has concluded that it will be
necessary to exempt chartered clubs from this provision, and accordingly we propose that if
an annual subscription charge is made it shall not be deemed to be a charge for admission to
premises.
Under clause 8 the Minister is empowered to grant licences to societies to conduct
games of chance provided that no money is paid to any person by way of remuneration or
commission for conducting such games. This provision was intended to prevent professional
games promoters from conducting their activities under the auspices of some non-
profitmaking society. The New Zealand Football Association suggested that this would
prevent the association's own paid staff-for example, secretarial staff-from undertaking


## p. 4442 (#548) ###########################################

4442
11 November
Gaming and Lotteries Bill
such work incidental to their main duties. The committee believes that, provided the staff
merely undertake the work incidental to their main duties and are not paid for it in addition
to their normal remuneration, no problem arises.
We do, however, recognise that some organisations-sports clubs, and even some
churches-employ people whose major responsibility is fund raising, and that could include
organising games of chance. We therefore propose in clause 2 a new definition of "author-
ised employee" as an employee or agent who is employed or engaged otherwise than
principally for the purpose of conducting games of chance, and further propose that such a
person, provided he is not paid by way of commission, should be able to be employed by
such a society without a special licence from the Minister.
This results in a number of further consequential changes to many clauses. Some
question has been raised regarding games of chance played on an "amusement device". As
worded, clause 10(1)(b)(ii) permits a jackpot of up to 20c to be given to a successful
participant, even if there is only a 1c investment. This was not intended, and we recommend
a change to the clause to make it clear that the prize from such a machine can be not more
than "the amount paid to play the game once".
Under clause 11, liability was imposed upon newspapers and other publications for
advertising illegal games of chance. New Zealand News Ltd suggested that it was unreason-
able to impose an onus on newspapers to ascertain whether an advertisement concerned a
legal activity. The committee agrees with this submission, although it also believes that there
must be some element of responsibility on those who publish such advertisements, and
therefore recommends an amendment to clause 18 to provide that it shall not be an offence if
the defendant proves that he neither knew nor had reasonable cause to suspect that an
offence had occurred. A similar provision is already included in the Bill in respect of prize
competitions and lotteries.
New Zealand News also drew attention to the provisions of clause 17 relating to illegal
prize competitions, and suggested that it would not be able to run its "Spot the Ball"
competition under these provisions, as it was not a society. The committee points out,
however, that this clause merely specifies the types of prize competitions that are illegal for
the purposes of the Bill. If a scheme falls within the clause, a society could still run the
competition so long as the terms of the legislation are fulfilled. When making his submis-
sions, Mr Sayers agreed, in answer to a question from the Minister of Justice, that it would
not be difficult for his company to establish a society for the purpose of running its "Spot the
Ball" competition, and in the result we recommend no change to the clause.
New Zealand News also submitted, in relation to clause 24, that licences authorising
prize competitions should permit them to be conducted at a stated regularity-say weekly, or
monthly. However, the committee considers that the Bill as drafted already makes it
possible for the Minister to issue licences on such terms, and therefore recommends no
change. Clause 33 allows lotteries to be conducted without a permit if the prizes do not
exceed $500 in aggregate. The Police have suggested that the provision should be redrawn to
prevent what are commonly known as "snowball" raffles, or progressive weekly draws in the
same raffle. The committee agrees with this suggestion, and recommends an amendment to
that clause.
The New Zealand Football Association, which generally enthusiastically supported the
provisions of the Bill, noted that under clause 25 it would be possible to seek ministerial
approval for the conduct of football pool competitions. However, it queried whether such
competitions could be conducted by the association, with ministerial approval, in conjuction
with an overseas promoter. The committee considers that it is difficult to comment without
knowing the details of a particular scheme, which necessarily would have to be judged by the
Minister on its merits. However, as a general principle, an overseas company-because it
would be a private company rather than a society-would not be permitted to operate a prize
competition on its own behalf under this legislation. It might be able to obtain a licence
under Part V, but this would depend upon the terms of its application to the magistrate's
court. The committee recommends no change to clause 25.
The organiser of the national lotteries has, through the Department of Internal Affairs,
indicated that he contemplates the possibility of paying "instant prizes", depending on the
marking or other identification of tickets, and as a result the committee recommends that
provision be made in clause 70 (2) for prizes to be made available otherwise than by way of
the customary "draw". I should report also that the select committee considered a report
from the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee in respect of Part VIII of the
Bill, which provides a code relating to the enforcability of gaming and wagering contracts.


## p. 4443 (#549) ###########################################

11 November
4443
Gaming and Lotteries Bill
Generally speaking, these contracts will continue to be unenforcable in courts of law; this is
in accordance with long-standing principles of public policy, and in accordance with the
traditional reluctance of the courts to give effect to gaming and wagering contracts. Despite
the law reform committee's view, the only change recommended by the select committee is
one that would permit a party to an illegal gaming contract-that is, one expressly prohibited
by the Bill-to recover, and, if necessary, sue to recover, from a stakeholder any money that
is held in respect of such an illegal bet, provided the stakeholder had not already paid out the
money under the wager.
Finally, I should note that after the date for receipt of submissions had passed the
committee received two submissions from Rothmans (NZ) Ltd and the National Association
of Retail Grocers, both concerned at the possible implications of those provisions of the Bill
relating to sales promotion schemes. Both submissions were carefully considered by the
committee. They centred, however, on a misunderstanding of the Bill's provisions-and
particularly on a mistaken belief that its provisions would permit the type of sales promotion
schemes in which some sort of prize is included, at random, with the item on sale. A recent
example, mentioned in both submissions was of a cigarette manufacturer who advertised
that some packets of a certain brand contained a dollar note. However, the committee is
quite satisfied that such competitions which are illegal under the present law, would not be
permitted under this Bill. Furthermore, both the Police Department and the Department of
Internal Affairs expressed opposition to any change to the Bill, which will slightly liberalise
the law in relation to sales promotion schemes.
On behalf of the select committee I should like to express particular thanks to the
officers of the Police Department and the Department of Justice, who attended most of the
committee's meetings on the Bill. Major assistance was, of course, rendered by officials from
the Department of Internal Affairs, who were responsible for the Bill, and also by

Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): Opposition members are mainly in agreement with

legalises the present situation: that the innocent office sweepstake, or the fund raising in
social and sporting clubs, that have been going on for at least the last 20 years, are not a
social evil, and should not be illegal. That is the prime purpose of the Bill.
The situation was correctly reported by the chairman when he said that the Police, the
Department of Internal Affairs, and those who made submissions, were in broad agreement
about the Bill, as are members on this side of the House. The department should consider
the Bill carefully, because Parliament intends to legalise the present position, and no doubt
one or two organisations will try to stretch the law. The department should be vigilant in
ensuring that the law exists for the benefit of voluntary organisations, such as sporting clubs
and religious groups, and not for professional gamblers. It is not intended that professional
organisations should be allowed to organise professional gaming.
Prize promotions schemes are those whereby companies advertise a product and state
that if you buy a can of beans, or whatever it is, you have a chance of a trip to Fiji, or some
other reward. I am opposed to that type of advertising-it is not good advertising.
Advertising is not bad if it does what it should do—give the consumer a better choice. What I
object to, as do many people in my electorate, is buying a product, and then being forced to
buy something else that is unnecessary, such as a one-in-a-million chance of a trip to
Fiji-which, of course, as a consumer, I pay for. The law has been liberalised to a limited
degree, although it has not been liberalised as much as many people who made submissions
would have wished.
The attention of the Minister of Trade and Industry should be drawn to the fact that the
Trading Coupons Act 1931 is still in existence, as was mentioned in a late submission to the
committee. At present, a number of trade promotion schemes are illegal under that
provision. The Bill provides that if such schemes are to be illegal they should not be illegal
because of the gambling aspect of the scheme, but because it is bad commercial practice
--something that should be dealt with under commercial rather than gambling law. The
Police made a good submission about that. The liberalisation of prize competitions does not
mean that members on this side of the House are in favour of that type of commercial
practice. The attention of manufacturers who may be anxious to take advantage of the Bill
should be drawn to the fact that laws such as the Trading Coupons Act prevent many
promotions that Parliament in the past has not found commercially desirable. It is pleasing

untouched by this Bill, it would still be illegal, and subject to the sanctions of the law. The
Bill does not in any way alter the Trading Coupons Act, which remains part of our law.

imprisonment. It is unthinkable that they should be accommodated in prisons designed to
accommodate adult prisoners, and which do at present accommodate child prisoners apart
