STATE SERVICES CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. When the Bill was introduced some time ago a lot of heat was generated on the
question of the penalty provisions, and they were dealt with at some length. Part VIII will
seldom if ever be used if the State unions continue their generally good industrial relations
record. I do not say that lightly. We mean it.
The more significant clauses in the Bill deal with the setting of conditions of employ-
ment in the State services on a routine day-to-day basis. First, the extent to which the Bill re-
enacts the provisions of the existing legislation is quite marked. Second, the extent to which
the new clauses have been drafted with the active participation of the State services unions,
is also marked. In hard terms that means over 20 hours of negotiations between the CSSO
and the Government committee of Ministers and Government members, and a further 27
hours with officials of the employing authorities and the SSCC, together with over 10 months
of intensive research and drafting activity by officials, culminating in my consultating the
CSSO. In most cases, contrary to the views expressed during the introduction, the clauses
that the employees objected to were redrafted until agreement was reached. In a number of
cases we had to agree to differ, and that basically applied to Part VIII. Nevertheless, our
differences were always amicable, and I believe each side generally maintained respect for
the other side's position.
I turn to some of the more detailed aspects of the Bill. The definition of "Education
service" in clause 2 was a point in dispute. The issue was whether student teachers should be
included and thereby come into the State services as employees. The Government was
bound to look at the similarities between student teachers, especially those at university, and
other students. The effect of bringing student teachers into the wage-fixing system would
have been to prejudice the current review of student bursaries being undertaken by my
colleague the Minister of Education. Our decision is, therefore, to retain the status quo for
the time being and to review this decision in due course in the context of the full-scale
bursary review. The CSSO asked that that point be stated categorically in the House, and I
do so on behalf of my colleague and myself.
Clause 3 provides that the Act is to bind the Crown. Clause 4 defines the State services.
It also enables certain classes of employees to be brought in or out of the State services by
Order in Council. However, when members of a State union are affected, the agreement of
the employee organisations must be obtained before that person or organisation can be
taken out of the State services. Clauses 6 to 12 set out the conditions of employment that fall
within the provisions of the Bill and list the criteria by which rates of pay, allowances, and
other conditions are actually determined. These clauses are almost wholly re-enactments of
the previous Act.
One notable change is that all determinations must be lodged with the new public sector
tribunal. This parallels a private sector provision, and will promote the co-ordination of
wage fixing between the sectors. All determinations must remain in force for 12 months, as
in the private sector, except if the tribunal consents to less, or when the procedures parallel
similar procedures in the private sector. Fair external relativity remains the principal
criterion in State wage fixing. Ease or difficulty in recruitment and retention of staff is now
explicitly included as a criterion in determining pay in cases in which the State is the major or
only employer in that occupation. In some instances, that provision would apply specifically
to the Railways. One change in clauses 10(d) and 12(h) is that the State is recognised as
having the right to decide, subject to health, safety of employees, and other safeguards, what
standard of service the State is required to provide, for which staff are needed.
Clauses 13 to 20 are mostly re-enactments setting up the various service committees that
represent the Government in negotiations with the service organisations. Clause 21 is new. It
requires the employing authorities, and the Public Sector Tribunal, to consult the Higher
Salaries Commission in cases in which co-ordination between those wage-fixing authorities is
needed. The Higher Salaries Commission has worked under regulations until now,
but a
Higher Salaries Commission Bill will be introduced, probably next week.
In Part II, clauses 22 to 26 re-enact, with minor alterations, the provisions governing the
18-Vol. 415


## p. 4448 (#554) ###########################################

4448
11 November
State Services Conditions of Employment Bill
issue of determinations. Clause 27 is important. This clause, which has the wholehearted
support of the State employee organisations, introduces voluntary mediation into State
wage-fixing procedures. During the introduction of the Bill I recorded that this request came
from one section of the Public Service Association, and I was delighted that the association
agreed to accept the present mediation service of the Department of Labour. It may be that
at some time in the future this provision will be changed, but the agreement indicates the
good will that was shown during those talks.
The main recommendations of the 1972 royal commission have been followed in clause
32. The object of the commission's recommendations on general reviews was to eliminate
the element of double counting that seemed to have produced a degree of leadership in some
State pay scales in 1972; it is suggested that some has continued. The essence of clause 32 is
that the average general movement in the private sector is paid to State employees as before,
but only after any general movement that has already occurred in the State sector has been
deducted. However, some of the average general movement in the State sector might
represent genuine improvements in staff productivity or the quality of personnel over and
above that in the private sector.
Subclauses (9) and (10) require employers to consult the unions on such matters as the
amount of general adjustment, as determined by the criteria of the Bill, and also the
effective date. Backdating up to 1 year is permitted. That particular section contains a new
and very complex mathematical formula enabling calculation of the amount, over 3 years,
that is to be discounted between the drift in the public and the private sectors. This was the
subject of quite extensive negotiation, and I think I can correctly report a consensus opinion.
I would not say that the Combined State Service Organisations were entirely happy;
they want to see this working, and they also raised the question of who would adjudicate on
the final formula. The CSSO at one stage wanted the Public Sector Tribunal to do this. The
Industrial Law Reform Bill will enable the three judges of the Arbitration Court to do this
every 3 years, but that was one point on which there was some slight difference of opinion
between the CSSO and the Government. Subclause (15) entitles the service organisation to
take these matters to arbitration if necessary.
Clause 33, in Part III, broadly re-enacts the provisions of the defunct pay research unit.
In Part V the old State Services Tribunal is renamed the Public Service Tribunal. The change
of name does not basically affect the Combined State Service Organisations, because the
tribunal will operate for their purposes in virtually the same way as did the State Services
Tribunal. We may be legislating next year in the local authority field, and it is possible that
there may have to be a correlation between local authorities and the Government in this type
of legislation. The change of name was not just semantics—there were other reasons for
changing the title.
The provision that the chairman should be a judge of the Arbitration Court constitutes a
major change. Consultations will be held with all parties on the appointment of judges in the
various sections of the Arbitration Court. I have sent a letter to the State services assuring
them that such consultation will take place before a judge-who will have to have a degree of
continuity as head of the Public Sector Tribunal-is appointed. There are no further
significant changes in this Part, except perhaps in clause 48, whereby the Minister can, by
notice in the Gazette, extend the jurisdiction of the tribunal to cover further Government or
quasi-Government organisations.
Part VI of the Bill establishes the single service tribunals on the same basis as before,
with a change to the same official member being appointed to each of them. Although that
point was in dispute, we have unanimously agreed to a continuation of the single service,
such as education, railways, and others.
Part VIII of the Bill has been lifted straight out of the Industrial Relations Act, with the
absolute minimum of modification for legal reasons. This would be the most controversial
issue, and is the one on which there has been no agreement. Obviously agreement could not
be reached in the limited time available for discussions between the ad hoc committee and
the CSSO. At the same time, the Government recognises that the tradition of good sense
and responsibility on the part of State employees is probably unequalled anywhere else. For
that reason Part VIII of the Bill will not apply to the vast majority of State employees.
Mr Reweti: Why is it there?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It is there in case the Government has to use it. If the member
had been listening carefully he would have heard me use the words, "the vast majority of
State employees". I hope, and concede to the member, that the Government does not have
to use the provision. I would be a very happy Minister of State Services if that applied.

demonstrated in the kindred legislation, the Industrial Relations Act.
İn Part IX the only clause of interest to the House is the prohibition on preference
provisions in line with Government policy and the law in the private sector. The remainder

No Government enjoys introducing penalties into industrial relations but, in the last
resort, what is the alternative? When one of the vital meat exporters is needlessly disrupted,
or when essential services are withheld from the public without adequate notice, in
accordance with clause 1 of the Bill the penal provisions can be brought in by Order in

a stopwork, or illegal action. It will not be used and cannot apply detrimentally other than in
the name of British justice. It must be done through the court. The suggestion that the
Government or I, as Minister, can inflict a penalty is incorrect. The Bill provides for
penalties only as a matter of last resort.
We have gone a long way in the Bill towards meeting the CSSO's wishes, save in that
one area of disagreement, Part VIII. Our reasons are clear. The Bill heralds important
changes in the State services, and I commend the CSSO for the wholehearted co-operation

day-to-day running of the State services. We ended our consultation on a harmonious note,
and the CSSO in turn expressed gratitude to Government members for making themselves
available for cross-examination and consultation. It was a very enjoyable experience. Where
agreement was not possible, the rights and interests of the wider community had to be met.
The Bill does just that.

Party-he said publicly that it was not easy to fine the unions. "Mr Gordon on Monday

We now have before us a Bill from the same Minister, which provides for the same
measures against State servants that the Minister said were unworkable against the freezing
workers. The Government lacks understanding, experience, and expertise in industrial
relations. Clause 65 deals with lockouts. Let us look at it. Two parties are involved in
industrial negotiations-the Government, or employer, on the one side, and the public
servants, or their organisations, as employees on the other.
Clause 65 gives the Minister the right to prosecute the employer for a lockout. That is
one absurdity in the Bill. The Minister said that the lockout clause is straight out of the
Industrial Relations Act, but he has forgotten that the Government in this instance is as
directly involved as the employer, whereas under the Industrial Relations Act a private
employer is involved, and therefore the Government can intervene. Under the clause in the
Bill dealing with lockouts, the Minister of State Services has the right to fine himself and the
Government if there is a lockout against State servants. That is the ridiculous position the
Government finds itself in, and it has done nothing about the clause. In fact, the Govern-
ment can be fined up to $1,500 by the Minister of State Services if there is a lockout against
public servants.
The State Services Remuneration and Conditions of Employment Act 1969 adequately
sets out a legal framework for the determination of conditions of employment and relation-
ships within the State services between State servants and the Government. The 1969 Act
follows the recommendations of the royal commission of 1968; the provisions were
negotiated and agreed upon between the National Government of that day and the
Combined State Service Organisations. On the Minister's own admission, the Act has
worked reasonably well without the penalties included in Part VIII of the Bill, and
relationships have been good. Under Part VIII, relationships are bound to deteriorate. A big
stick hanging over the head of public servants will antagonise them, and that antagonism is

COMPANIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Companies Amend-.
ment Bill be introduced. The Bill makes three amendments to the Companies Act 1955. The
first relates to the purpose for which the Registrar of Companies may exercise his power of
inspection; the second relates to the continuation of an inspection after the lodging of an
appeal against that inspection; and the third relates to the application of the Act's prospectus
provisions to loans raised overseas by the issue of a prospectus.
In 1973, the Act was amended to empower the Registrar of Companies to inspect and
make records of the books and papers of a company, subject, of course, to strict provisions
about the confidentiality of the information derived. The Act expressly limits the purpose of
an inspection to seeing whether or not the provisions of the Act are being complied with. For
some time the Government has been concerned that the purpose of an inspection should be
clarified to make it clear that such purpose includes the detection of offences against the Act
and the consideration of whether the registrar should exercise any of his rights under the
Act. Clause 2 of the Bill clarifies the purpose of an inspection in this way, and so will place
beyond doubt the authority of the registrar to inspect a company's records to see whether,
for example, it is trading fraudulently, and to consider whether he should petition the
Supreme Court for an order that the company be, wound up.
The Registrar of Companies has exercised his power of inspection frequently, but only
recently has it been subjected to judicial scrutiny. In August of this year the Supreme Court
carefully considered the scope of operation of the registrar's power of inspection. In doing
so, the learned judge was moved to note, and I quote his words, "that it is curious that there
is a right of appeal where speed could be of the essence". The learned judge did not go on to
explain his comment, but I think it is clear that he was alluding to the opportunity for
manufacturing, destroying, or concealing evidence—an opportunity provided by the defer-
ment of an inspection pending the outcome of an appeal. I think it is clear also that he was
alluding to the delay in remedial action, such as a winding-up petition, that may be caused by
the lodging of an appeal.
To ensure that inspection is not frustrated, clause 3 of the Bill makes it clear that an
appeal does not, in the first place, prevent the registrar continuing an inspection, and, in the
second place, does not excuse a company from producing its records for inspection in the
meantime irrespective of the outcome of the appeal. The Government is, however,
concerned to see that the effect of a successful appeal is not diminished, and accordingly
clause 3 provides for the destruction or expunging of records of information derived in the
course of an improper inspection, and provides that such information is not admissible in
evidence in any proceedings.
The third amendment contained in the Bill provides that in respect of a particular
overseas loan the Minister may, on the recommendation of the Registrar of Companies,
exempt a company from all or any of the prospectus provisions of the Act. The problem is
that New Zealand law relating to prospectuses may differ from the law and accepted practice
of the place where the loan is to be raised. The registrar has received representations about
the possibility of at least one New Zealand company raising a loan in this way next year when
the House may not be sitting. Consequently, the Government considers it desirable for such
an exemption to be made by the Minister of Justice, rather than have the House, if it is


## p. 4460 (#566) ###########################################

4460
15 November
Companies Amendment Bill
sitting, deal with what is an administrative matter. I wish to emphasise that any exemption
may relate only to a particular loan, must be notified in the Gazette, and may be subject to
such terms as the Minister may prescribe. I envisage that any exemption made will go only so
far as is necessary to allow a company to meet the practices and requirements of the place
where the loan is raised overseas. I have consulted the member for Henderson in the
preparation of the Bill, and I understand that the last provision about raising loans overseas
is acceptable.

SALE OF LIQUOR AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Sale of Liquor
Amendment Bill be introduced. This short Bill makes a number of minor amendments to the
Sale of Liquor Act, some of which are necessary to correct deficiencies arising out of last
year's amending Bill, which, as honourable members will recall, was a major one. I have also
taken the opportunity to include a number of minor amendments that have been sought by
interested parties. I believe those amendments are not contentious.
Clause 2 meets a request from the Wholesale Wine and Spirit Merchants Federation
that the requirement to sell beer in certain quantities in kegs be amended to take account of
modern packaging methods. In addition, the minimum amount of liquor a wholesaler may
sell at any one time is being reduced from 9 litres to 8 litres to give legal effect to what has
been a traditional practice. Apparently the sale of 2 dozen 340 ml-which I understand is the
old quart-bottles has always been regarded as satisfying the 9 litre requirement, although
the total amounts to only 8.1 litres.
At the request of the trotting clubs, clause 3 amends the hours available under 1 booth
licence, the effect of which is to extend the present closing hours from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m. on
Fridays and Saturdays. This provision mirrors the later hours available to hotels and taverns.
Clause 4, requested by the Wine Institute, removes the requirement that winemakers must
specify the quantity of wine they propose to produce each year. In addition, it is made a
condition of a renewal of a fruit winemaker's licence that he has paid his levy to the
Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council. A similar provision exists at present in respect of grape
winemakers. Clause 5 reinstates a provision inadvertently repealed by last year's amendment
relating to the removal of wine resellers' licences.
Clause 6 limits the application of a manager's certificate to particular types of liquor
outlets. At present, a manager's certificate entitles the holder to manage most licensed
premises. An amendment along those lines was sought in principle by the Hotel Association
of New Zealand, and is supported by the New Zealand Licensing Trusts Association. The
right of the Hotel Association to object to the grant or renewal of managers' certificates for
district or suburban licensing trust premises is removed. At the request of the Hotel
Association, clause 7 increases from 1 month to 6 weeks the aggregate period for which an


## p. 4461 (#567) ###########################################

15 November
4461
Sale of Liquor Amendment Bill
acting manager may be appointed.
Clause 8 was included as a result of a request from the New Zealand Liquor Industry
Council for a modification of the provisions relating to the suspension of licences. At present
a licensing committee is required to suspend a licence if it is satisfied that the health of those
using the premises is likely to be injured, or their safety endangered by the failure of the
licensee to comply with a health or fire requirement. The effect of the clause is to permit the
licensing committee to close the affected part of the premises rather than suspend the licence
completely in cases in which danger has arisen as a result of circumstances beyond the
control of the licensee.
Under clause 9, a new permit is created to allow general and ancillary licences to be
used for social gatherings such as weddings, where liquor may be supplied but not sold. At
present it is an offence to consume liquor on such premises outside the hours specified by the
commission, and this can lead to difficulties, especially when the premises are used by more
than one organisation. Clauses 10, 12, and 13 are purely drafting amendments arising out of
last year's amending Bill. Clause 11 meets the request of the Licensing Control Commission
that the holders of wholesale licences and club charters obtain the commission's consent
before making alterations to their premises. The Bill is a minor measure that does not make
any substantial changes to our liquor laws. Therefore, I do not intend to refer it to a select
committee.

LICENSING TRUSTS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Licensing Trusts
Amendment Bill be introduced. The principal purpose of the Bill is to permit district licensing
trusts to operate catering outlets. In addition, the Bill corrects two anomalies arising from
last year's Sale of Liquor Amendment Act and Licensing Trusts Amendment Act. Clause 3
permits district licensing trusts to operate catering outlets on exactly the same basis as the
holders of a caterer's licence may operate their premises under the Sale of Liquor Act. As
the law stands at the moment, a district trust may operate a catering outlet at which liquor
may be supplied but not sold.
At the request of the Invercargill Licensing Trust, I have agreed to sponsor this
amendment to put district licensing trusts on exactly the same footing as private caterers.
Like a private caterer, a district trust will be entitled to undertake the following: first, it will
be entitled to sell liquor for consumption on its catering premises to those attending a social
function at which food is consumed; secondly, it will be entitled to sell liquor from its
premises for consumption on someone else's premises, whether inside the trust district or
not, at which it is catering; and, thirdly, it will be entitled to obtain a permit to enable it to
sell liquor for consumption on someone else's premises at which it is catering, whether those
premises are inside the trust district or not. Caterers' licences for private operators may be
issued within a licensing trust district at present, and caterers outside the district may obtain
a permit to sell liquor at a function being held on premises inside the trust district. Under this
Bill, therefore, private caterers and district trusts will be competing on an even footing.
Clause 5 corrects an omission in last year's amendment. It puts both suburban and
district licensing trusts on exactly the same footing as the trade, by permitting extended
hours for hotels and taverns on Fridays, Saturdays, Christmas Eve, and New Year's Eve, to
be an addition to the permitted 11-hour maximum opening time in any one day. Clause 6 is
designed to clarify doubts that have arisen by making it clear that all licences and permits
that may be granted in a district trust area may be administered by the licensing committee of
the licensing district adjoining the trust area. Clauses 4 and 7 are machinery provisions, and
clauses 8 to 15 make the same amendments to the Masterton and Invercargill Licensing
Trusts Acts as are contained in Part I of the Bill, which deals with the other six district trusts.
The Bill is a minor measure, and I do not propose to refer it to a select committee.

trust's favour, and it could not appeal against the appeal decision. People in the Mt.

Licensing Control Commission or to any other authority. Clearly, the district wants these
rights. Why cannot clause 3 also include local trusts?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Deputy Leader of the Opposition
has misunderstood the effects of the Bill. It will not give greater protection to district
licensing trusts, but is intended to give them greater opportunity to compete on all fours with
the private trade. The problem in Invercargill is that although the trust can operate a
catering division or department to supply, it cannot sell; so the Bill enables it to sell. Nothing
in the Bill prevents the Mt. Wellington local trust from applying for a caterer's licence under
the Sale of Liquor Act, but it must do so on all fours with any other private caterer who may
be interested in setting up business in that part of Auckland. The Bill does not provide
security or safeguard against competition, but it improves the position of the district
licensing trust, and particularly the Invercargill Licensing Trust, which is at present
hamstrung when competing against the private trade. Because the ownership of these outlets
is not the issue, I believe that they should have the right to compete openly against private
enterprise. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition is not asking for that. He is asking for
protection.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: I am asking for the right to have a licence.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: At present they have a right to make application.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: To make an application is a very different thing.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: All right. They have the right to make an application in
exactly the same way as any individual citizen can, but under the present law they all have to
go through the procedure of notification, of objection being available to objectors, of a
hearing, and of a proper determination of an objective body.

GEOTHERMAL ENERGY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): On behalf of the Minister of Energy
Resources, I move, That the Geothermal Energy Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill
contains amendments to the Geothermal Energy Act, and makes three changes. The first
repeals section 5 of the Geothermal Energy Act, which empowers the owner of land that is
not in a geothermal energy area as defined by that Act to make surveys, investigations, and
bores in a search for geothermal energy. Such surveys, tests, and bores may still be made
under section 6 (2) of the Act, which gives the Minister the power to grant such authority to
any person, subject, of course, to the provisions of the principal Act. In this respect
geothermal energy is now in a comparable position with coal.
The second change relates to the setting of rentals for the use of geothermal energy,
while the third empowers the Ministry of Works and Development to develop geothermal
energy for sale to industry. Clause 3 deals with the payment of rentals to the Crown. In
October 1976 the Government announced its energy pricing policy. This stated, in part, that
when private development of geothermal and hydro energy resources is agreed to, a rental
should be negotiated on a case-by-case basis, which would reflect the worth of the resource,
having regard to the alternative energy cost. Suitable provision for escalation and review
would need to be made in each case. This policy was formulated because New Zealand
needed an orderly system of energy pricing as the foundation of its energy policy.
Large increases in oil prices since the crisis in 1973 have greatly increased the value of
New Zealand's own energy resources. The energy pricing policy set out to establish a


## p. 4467 (#573) ###########################################

15 November
4467
Goethermal Energy Amendment Bill
relationship between the energy resources in New Zealand, based on the true worth of the
resource, and also to encourage the wise use of energy. The Government has, in putting its
policy into effect, introduced the energy resources levy on coal and natural gas, altered the
structure of subsidies for manufactured gas, and increased the bulk electricity tariff. One
indigenous fuel remains priced far below its real value. This is geothermal energy, which the
present Act prices at 2.5c a gigajoule-equivalent to 60c for a tonne of coal, and less than
one-hundredth of a cent per kW hour. This virtual give-away of geothermal energy may have
been appropriate when energy prices were generally low, but it is certainly not appropriate
in the present circumstances.
Individual negotiations on a case-by-case basis would not be appropriate in the case of
small users, as the cost of undertaking such negotiations would be excessive in relation to the
benefits the user can obtain. A 40-terajoule lower limit for case-by-case negotiations, which
is that set out in the Act, is equivalent to 1700 tonnes of Waikato coal, or 11 000 000 kW
hours of electricity. This well exceeds the requirement of users such as the Rotorua Public
Hospital and virtually all other commercial and light industrial users of geothermal energy.
However, it is below the requirements of such large consumers as the Tasman Pulp and
Paper Co. and the proposed sulphur extraction plant at Lake Rotokawa, and their geother-
mal rental would be negotiated.
The Bill proposes also that as a general principle the ownership of deep geothermal
bores and field management should be retained by the Government so that this valuable
renewable energy resource can be developed safely and to the best advantage of the country
as a whole. Also, it simply recognises the present reality—that the Ministry of Works and
Development, because of its experience and knowledge, would be doing the work anyway,
as it has been at Kawerau at the request of the Tasman Pulp and Paper Co., and at
Rotokawa on behalf of Fletcher Holdings.
In addition, by using the capability of the Ministry of Works and Development in this
way, and by relieving potential users of the considerable financial risks involved in develop-
ing geothermal energy, it is hoped to encourage a wider use of this energy source and hence
relieve pressure on our fossil fuel resources. As a consequence, the Government will become
a vendor of geothermal energy. I am satisfied that this Bill will encourage the wider use of
geothermal energy in industry by making it easier to obtain a supply, while at the same time
encouraging the wise use of geothermal energy by allowing it to be priced at its true value in
relation to other forms of energy.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Before I put the question, I might make a brief comment. I
did comment the other day on the introduction of a Bill by the Minister of Energy
Resources, and I invited him to read again the report of the Standing Orders Committee
dealing with the introduction of Bills. This may be an exceptional case, but, excepting
exceptional cases, the introduction of a Bill should not be a lengthy process. In general all
that is necessary is an explanation from the Minister followed by a limited period of
questions. If the Minister has a long introduction, it makes it more difficult for me to follow
the instructions of the House that a brief period of questions should follow.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): No one would deny that geothermal energy is one of
New Zealand's most under-developed yet readily available sources of renewable energy, and
one hopes that a Bill of this nature will expand the use of such energy. However, the Bill
before us could be counterproductive to that objective, which itself appears to be secondary
to the Government's stated intention to develop geothermal energy. The Bill sets out to
expand the Government's pricing policies on our indigenous fuels. The Government has
already placed a levy on natural gas and coal, and that levy is now being extended to
geothermal energy. The levies on natural gas and coal net the Government about $40 million
a year, and users of electricity pay about $18.5 million a year in levies. What revenue does
the Government expect to receive in the first full year from the levy to be placed on
geothermal energy? The Minister said that the Tasman Pulp and Paper Co. and other larger
industrial users would be liable for the levy. I understand that the Caxton Mill could also be
liable. I take it from the Minister's remarks that the small users such as boarding houses,
motels, and swimming pool operators would not be liable for the charge.
Hon. L. W. Gandar: No.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN: The Minister says that is so. Does the Minister see the levy as a
disincentive to the further expansion of geothermal energy? I think it would be regrettable if
there was any such disincentive.
Clause 4 provides that the Minister may develop and manage any bore or group of dores
on any land for the purpose of selling geothermal energy to industrial or other users. I have

companies are not required to advise him.

Education-Vandalism in Schools
7. Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori), on behalf of Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori), asked
the Minister of Education: In view of the reports of widespread vandalism, especially in

Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The cost of repairing damage by vandals
and replacing equipment in schools for the period from 1 April to 30 September this year was
$260,781. In January 1974 the department issued a circular to all school controlling
authorities setting out recommended security precautions for school buildings. These
included outside security lighting, alarm systems, and, in extreme cases, security patrols.
Controlling authorities may apply for finance to install these measures, and for the period 1
April to 30 September this year $27,200 was spent on security alarms. The circular was
reissued in July 1976 to emphasise the need for security measures. The prime responsibility
for the protection of school property lies with the school controlling authority and the Police
Department.
Mr Reweti: Is there a definite pattern in the damage that has been done by vandals?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I cannot say if there are any patterns in the damage done, but
vandalism does seem to come in waves. I think to some extent the publicity given to these
acts of vandalism and possible arson tends to create a situation in which others may copy
what is happening.
Mr Lange: Have there been large-scale acts of vandalism in schools that have taken
advantage of the recommended security measures?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Obviously I cannot give a reply in relation to, say, burglar
alarms, but there are burglar alarms in a number of schools. I am not prepared to nominate
them. From time to time we also have portable alarms in schools, and they give an effective
increase in coverage. I cannot answer about vandalsim occurring in a school that had an
alarm, or may subsequently or previously have had an alarm.

Australia 97c, Great Britain $1, and Canada 73c.

CONTRACTUAL MISTAKES BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a third
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I feel I should report briefly what happened in the
Committee stage of this Bill. We on this side of the House indicated our opposition to the
Bill, but we did not move any amendments because we believed that the Bill was incapable
of being amended in a meaningful way, or a way that would make it comprehensible to the
layman or lead to constructive law reform. I was the Opposition spokesman on this measure,
and said that we do not believe the Bill represents real law reform; it only fiddles with the
law. It is an irresponsible measure; those who presented submissions to the Statutes Revision
Committee made it clear that it was unnecessary.
The idea behind the introduction of the Contractual Mistakes Bill was that the law on
contractual mistakes should be codified. The Supreme Court is to be given a new power to
make changes in contracts when a mistake has been made. The Bill will largely affect only
one area of the economy, the building industry, because that is the area in which contractual
mistakes occur. Those who presented submissions to the Statutes Revision Committee said
that, in the main, the building industry is happy with the existing law, and Opposition
members cannot see any point in changing the law when everyone it affects approves of the
present law.
We readily concede that the law on contractual mistakes is complex. We also concede


## p. 4478 (#584) ###########################################

4478
15 November
Contractual Mistakes Bill
that there are some British cases on mistake, the meaning of which is almost incomprehens-
ible. However, that does not mean that the laymen who have to administer the law have not
been able to find a way around it. In fact, they have. They have found a satisfactory method
whereby arbitration is used to resolve mistakes in New Zealand. In essence, if you make a
mistake in a contract, that is your bad luck. Frankly, I do not believe that businessmen would
like it to be any other way. When they go into business they contract as competent
businessmen. Why should Parliament provide some type of social welfare for those who are
incompetent?
I believe this measure represents a negation of a policy Government members say they
support. I believe also that the Bill should not be passed because of a different principle of
law, which I do not know that the Minister understands. It is desirable that the law be certain
and that the man in the street be able to understand it. The Minister said any problems
would be taken care of, because he believes that a reasonably competent commercial lawyer
will be able to give an adequate explanation of the meaning of the Bill. I ask the Minister to
say which of the very eminent lawyers who gave different opinions on the meaning of the Bill
to the Statutes Revision Committee were not adequate commercial lawyers. I submit that
each one was, but each gave a different explanation of the Bill's meaning. The Law Society
had a different idea about what it meant, and the Department of Justice had a slightly
different idea from that held by the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee.
In view of the uncertainty, the fact that the public does not want it, and the fact that
once again a person who wants to read the law, understand it, and look after his own affairs
will find that more rather than less difficult, it should not be passed into law. I emphasise that
in future it will be more difficult for a competent person to draw up a contract that will not be
the subject of court action. The Bill is a reckless measure, and I remind the House that the
evidence presented to the select committee was overwhelmingly against it.
Finally, I make one more point to the Minister once again. In 1960 the Labour
Government was able to govern the country by enacting only two volumes of legislation and
one volume of regulations. Last year, in 1976, four volumes of legislation were enacted and
three volumes of regulations were agreed to. I submit that this Bill is merely adding to the
legislative floodgate that is open at the moment, and which is causing grave concern not only
to academics and commentators but also to the public.
I am convinced that the Minister does not understand the Bill. Indeed, I do not think
anyone in Parliament is absolutely certain what it means. I am absolutely convinced that it
will lead to litigation that will go all the way to the Privy Council. Of course, it will be very
good legislation for the lawyers, but very bad for those who are caught up in its provisions. If
I can give any advice to the law students I shall advocate that they study this measure,
because a query about its meaning would be a very good examination question. I do not
believe we should be attempting to add to the problems of law students or to those of the
ordinary man in the street. We are adding to the profits of the lawyers who, despite their
protests, are doing very well without Parliament going to the ridiculous length proposed to
give them additional assistance.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): All the way through our consideration
of the Contractual Mistakes Bill the member for Auckland Central has spoilt his argument
by his determination to oppose the Bill for no better reason than that he is on the Opposition
side of the House. That has reduced his credibility almost to zero. He is developing a
doctrine of inaction on the reports of law reform committees, which are committees
comprised of eminent lawyers who are asked by successive Ministers of Justice to consider
certain aspects of the law.
The Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee, which recommended this Bill
because it found that the existing legislation on the subject was fragmented, relied on
inherent meaningless tests for mistake, and attracted remedies that were both drastic and
inflexible, was chaired by no less a person than Mr C. I. Patterson of Wellington, a very
eminent lawyer in this field of law. Other members of the committee were Mr Cameron, the
Deputy Secretary for Justice, Professor Coutts, Professor Dugdale, Professor Ellingham, Mr
Fox, Mr Henry, Mr Walter Iles, the Chief Parliamentary Counsel, Mr Wallace-who is now
a Queen's Counsel and Mr Wright of the Department of Justice, who was the secretary.
It may well be that the member for Auckland Central wants to confuse the issue by
making all sorts of assertions that have no or very little basis in fact. If that is so, I suppose
the extent to which the public does become confused will depend upon the credibility that it
vests in the member for Auckland Central. I am fairly satisfied that the people will not be
confused, and that they will see the Bill as a measure providing a wider variety of

the heading of law reform, and only when we are convinced that we are advancing the cause
of justice within the community should such legislation be passed. That can in no way be said
of the measure before us.
This Bill is the result of a report from the Property Law and Equity Reform Committee.
Briefly, the facts canvassed are these. A man who died had made a will many years earlier in
which he left all his money to his wife, whom he had divorced two decades before his death.
A lawyer wrote to the Minister saying he thought that was unjust. How can anyone say that a
man did not want to leave his money to his former wife? He may have wanted to do just that.
The basic premise of the first letter that led to this reform being advocated is not correct, and
the law reform committee itself was divided. The committee's report said that when a person
is divorced his or her will should become void and of no effect, even though the person who
made the will may be perfectly happy with it. Parliament is deciding that when a person gets
divorced the previous will is invalid.
A minority on the committee said that the new measure would cause as many injustices
as has the supposedly faulty provision this Bill seeks to rectify. Quite frankly, no one has
convinced me that the present law causes injustices. It is highly desirable that as many people
as possible, especially those who own land, should draw up a will. Unfortunately, every year
a large number of New Zealanders fail to do this, and it causes injustices. Some people
believe the will they drew up before they married is valid, but that is not the case. After
marriage a new will is required. A person buys some land and draws up a will. If he marries,
that will becomes invalid, and he must draw up another. If he gets divorced, the will is
invalid, and he must draw up another will. If he remarries, yet another will is required.
Mr Brill: He would have to do that anyway.
Mr PREBBLE: No, he would not. A number of people now divorced have wills leaving
their possessions to the same beneficiaries as before the divorce. They are quite happy with
such disposition. In the Committee I referred to the case of a man who was perfectly happy
to leave his possessions to his ex-wife. Maybe he was still very fond of her and did not even
want to divorce her. Surely he can leave his possessions to his ex-wife if he wishes; we should
not make his will invalid. A man with six children may be divorced and his will states that on
his death his widow will inherit his possessions and, in the event of her death, the six children
will benefit.
Mr Brill: It will go to the children. She is their guardian
Mr PREBBLE: No, the situation I am putting is quite different. Surely it is in the public
interest that a man, even though divorced, should continue to honour his obligations to his
ex-wife and to the children. We are saying exactly the opposite in this Bill. We are not
justified in tinkering with law reform. A reasonable man should be able to understand the
law and have some affinity with the law, knowing that it is designed for him. The law is being
changed every day, and not for the benefit of the man in the street. No mass application has
been made for this change. No one came forward to cite a single case of injustice other than
the one lawyer who took upon himself to say that the man involved in the case mentioned in
the report would have wanted to leave his money in a different way from that mentioned in
his will. Well, we cannot make such an assumption. This type of law reform is irresponsible,

and Parliament should not pass this Bill.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): This Bill came to the House because one person asked for it.
He presumed to know the mind of someone who had been divorced 20 years previously.
That person, who had died, let his will speak for him. It benefited his former wife. However,
the lawyer took exception to the will and presumed to know that that person would not have
had things that way if he had thought about them. Because of that one instance, every person
in New Zealand who has made a will leaving property to a former spouse will have to consult
a lawyer and have a new will drawn up before 1 July 1978. The committee was not of the
unanimous view that the law should be reformed. A majority thought such a reform might

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): What are the facts? In 1973, the Labour
Government's Minister of Justice, the present member for Henderson, identified an
injustice in the existing law of testate succession. He asked the Property Law and Equity
Reform Committee, under the chairmanship of Mr Charles Hutchinson-one of our eminent
Queen's counsel to study the law. As I told the Committee of the Whole, the reform
committee's report stated: "In your letter of 30 March 1973 to the chairman of this
Committee, you asked that the Committee consider the alternative proposals (a) that a will
should be revoked automatically by the subsequent divorce of the testator, or (b) that, where
a testator is subsequently divorced and is survived by his former wife, his will should be read
as if his former wife had predeceased him."
The committee set out the background, saying: "In your letter you stated that your
decision to refer this matter to the committee followed representations that you had received
from a practitioner arising out of a case in which he was involved. In that case the testator
has made his will during the last war leaving the whole estate to his wife. They were divorced
8 years later and he died some 20 years after the divorce, survived by his former wife. He had
not altered his will and, accordingly, his whole estate-which as it happened, was quite
substantial-passed to the woman who had not been his wife for more than 20 years.'
With one dissenting voice this eminent committee recommended the change to the law
set out in the Wills Amendment Bill. Two members opposite, the member for Mangere and
the member for Auckland Central, have continued with this development of their doctrine of
inaction to law reform reports. The member for Mangere told us there was no public demand
for or interest in this, as did the member for Auckland Central, yet we have this evidence of
a concern about an injustice from one of their own colleagues, the member for Henderson.
We know that other Commonwealth jurisdictions are introducing similar legislation, yet
those members say there is no demand for or public interest in it.
The suggestion has been made that instances of hardship or injustice are rare, but in the
Government's view that in itself does not justify legislative inaction. If there is an injustice,
then it must be done away with. That is the view of the National Government. It has been
said that the Bill has been designed to upset testamentary arrangements of divorced people
who are content to leave their wills as they are. The fact is that the majority of people make a
new will on divorce. If they are properly advised, they will. A minority do not, for two
reasons. One is inadvertence. In other words, they forget about it, or do not take the advice
of their lawyers. The other is that they are content to leave the will as it is.
This Bill guards against inadvertence or forgetfulness. In those few cases where a person
wants to leave his will as it is the Bill provides for him to confirm that by a codicil or by re-
execution. He does not have to go to the trouble of making a brand new will, no matter what
members opposite say. We have heard this nonsensical talk about promoting a lot of new
work for lawyers, but no lawyer will get rich on the provisions contained in this Bill. It is here
to correct an injustice. The National Party stands for correcting injustices, and rejects the
Labour Party's doctrine of inaction.
Bill read a third time.
HARBOURS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. The purpose of the Bill is to introduce a number of amendments to the
Harbours Act 1950. There has been no substantial amendment to the Harbours Act since
1968. The 77 clauses of the Bill cover various miscellaneous provisions as well as recommen-
dations of the commission of inquiry into harbour pilotage and other matters of concern to


## p. 4481 (#587) ###########################################

15 November
4481
Harbours Amendment Bill
local authorities, the Harbours Association, and other interested bodies. The amendment
also incorporates a review of a number of penalties imposed by the Act. They have been
revised and increased to more realistic levels. Many of these penalties have remained the
same since they were first imposed in the 1878, 1908, and 1923 Acts.
After its introduction the Bill was referred to the Local Bills Committee and to the
Lands and Agriculture Committee. Interested groups had every opportunity to make their
views known on the matters in the Bill, and a number of them did so. As a result, a number
of amendments to the Bill were recommended at the select committee stage and have been
incorporated in the Bill which you now have before the House. A number of clauses in the
Bill are of a machinery nature only. Because of this I intend to confine most of my time to
clauses of major significance.
Clause 2 amends or introduces certain definitions. The main effect is to clarify powers to
control moorings and rafts, to bring the definition of "local authority" into line with the
Local Government Act, and to line up the definition of "wharf" with the definition of
"wharf limits" in the Waterfront Industry Act. Clause 3 provides that the definition of
"limits of a harbour" can be revoked entirely. This cannot be done at present, and there is a
need, where temporary harbour limits are declared, to revoke them when they are no longer
required. Clause 3A clarifies the powers of the Governor-General in respect of harbours
where there is no harbour board and makes it quite clear that his power to make regulations
can be exercised in respect of individual harbours rather than harbours generally.
Clause 4 makes two important amendments to the provision under which various public
bodies can be given control of navigable waters. The first provides for the renewal of a grant
of control and that existing bylaws made by the control authorities will continue in effect.
The second extends the categories of bodies which may be given grants of control to include
commissioners of Crown lands for reserves administered by the Department of Lands and
Survey, and to any persons acting as trustees for the inhabitants of any locality. This will
allow groups such as tribal trustees to control water adjoining Maori lands.
Clause 9 makes provision for the backdating of an increase in a chairman's allowance to
the date on which the Order in Council providing for the increase comes into effect, and
allows a chairman's allowance to be increased once during his term of office. These
amendments bring harbour boards into line with territorial local authorities. Clause 10
makes a number of amendments to the powers of harbour boards to appoint honorary
wardens. This has been done because of a legal opinion that boards could not appoint
honorary wardens to enforce their bylaws relating to motor launches.
Clause 11 effects certain amendments to the appeal rights of harbour board employees.
It gives employees the right of appeal against suspension, and imposes limits on the time
within which an appeal may be made. The time limit is fixed for certain classes of appeal but
expressed as "a reasonable time" for promotion appeals. This has been done because of the
difficulty in some promotion cases of defining the time from which a fixed limit should run.
Clauses 12 to 16 deal with certain financial matters, including provisions which will
allow the use of databank direct credit facilities for the payment of moneys by harbour
boards, streamline the auditing and public inspection of harbour board accounts, and place
harbour board members on the same basis for remuneration as members of territorial local
authorities.
Part III contains a number of machinery amendments relating to harbour dues. Many of
the clauses in part III deal only with increases in penalties for certain offences. Other
provisions extend a board's rights to give credit for dues and amend the law concerning
payment of dues by certain categories of vessels-principally Commonwealth and foreign
ships of war, and Government ships.
Clause 23 is of some importance. It removes the upper limit on the amount of harbour
improvement rate that may be charged by a harbour board. Safeguards against an excessive
rate exist, as a harbour improvement rate may be set only by bylaw, and a bylaw may not
come into effect until the Minister has acknowledged it. There are also provisions in the Act
for the disallowance of bylaws and the refund of dues when an excessive rate has been
charged. The amendment is made necessary by the circumstances of boards-such as the
Northland Harbour Board-which rely on a harbour improvement rate for a major part of
their income and have been caught between rising costs and the presence of a maximum in
the Act. I considered the continuance of that maximum an anomaly because there is no other
maximum on the bylaw charges that may be imposed by a harbour board.
Clause 24 makes it clear that a board may enter into a contract to exercise any of its
functions or duties Clause 25 introduces a provision that will allow harbour boards to
19*


## p. 4482 (#588) ###########################################

4482
15 November
Harbours Amendment Bill
subdivide and sell land vested in them. The powers of sale will not apply to land which is
foreshore or a public reserve, or which is held by a board in trust for a particular purpose.
The need for such provisions has become clear in recent years. Many harbour boards own
land which has become surplus to their requirements because of changing trade patterns or
other circumstances. At present they have no power of sale, and their powers to subdivide
are, at best, unclear. In some cases boards own land that has been zoned for residential or
other purposes by the territorial local authority, but the zoning is frustrated because the
harbour board lacks the powers necessary to subdivide or sell the land.
The provisions of clause 25 make it clear that a board may exercise the powers only with
the consent of myself and my colleague the Minister of Finance, and only upon such
conditions as we may lay down. In all cases the appropriate provisions of the Town and
Country Planning Act, the Municipal Corporations Act, the Counties Act, and the Water
and Soil Conservation Act will apply. This is a much more restrictive power of sale than is
vested in territorial local authorities, which may subdivide and sell land without the need for
any outside approval. During the Committee stage of the Bill I propose to move an
amendment to clause 25 to clarify a doubt that has arisen about the scope of the power of
subdivision proposed for harbour boards.
Clause 26 amends the provisions of section 146A under which the taking of material
from the beds of harbours, lakes, and rivers is controlled. The amendments clarify certain
aspects of that section. Clause 27 repeals the provisions of the Harbours Act, which provide
for what are usually known as agricultural reclamations. This repeal follows representations
from a number of interested organisations and Government departments that the continued
existence of a provision under which large areas of land could be reclaimed without any
public involvement in the decision-making process is quite inconsistent with current thinking
on reclamations.
Members will know the concern expressed before the Local Bills Committee at the end
of last year when permission was sought to reclaim an area of the Manukau Harbour so that
the Auckland Regional Authority could extend a rubbish tip. Much of the concern expressed
at that time was against the principle of reclaiming tidal areas at all. I am sure members will
agree that if tidal lands are to be reclaimed, it should be only after careful public scrutiny.
Mr Rogers: I'll agree with that.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: When I hear a remark like that, I wonder if there might
be a mistake in the Bill. Clauses 28, 29, and 30 effect changes to the law concerning the basis
on which harbour boards and local authorities may licence the use of the foreshore. Clause
31 changes the basis on which the Minister may license the occupation of the foreshore and
seabed for various purposes. The main effects are to abolish the distinction between licence
and permit so there is just one procedure under which rights of occupation can be granted.
The other main effect is to provide that, when special circumstances make it desirable in the
public interest, the Minister is not limited to granting a 14-year term for a licence, but may
grant a term of up to 50 years. The need for this change has been made apparent by such
major developments as the proposal of the Golden Bay Cement Co. Ltd to redevelop its
facilities. That redevelopment would not be feasible if it had to be costed over a 14-year
term.
Clause 32 changes the law under which public bodies may be given control of the
foreshore and thus are able to license the erection of structures on the foreshore, and
control, through their bylaws, public activities on that foreshore. The main changes are to
provide that control can be given of the seabed also, to redefine the consents that are
required before control may be given to any particular public body, and to extend the classes
of public bodies that may be given control in the same way as the power to grant control over
waters is being extended.
Clause 33 adds "shall" to those items whose removal from within a harbour may be
controlled by a harbour board. Clause 33A redrafts section 168, which affects the law on
accretion against harbour works within a harbour. This rewording results from litigation
which disclosed that section 168 did not have the intended effect. The new section reflects
the principles that I believe should apply to the ownership of accretion within harbours.
Clause 34 amends section 173 to remove a doubt raised by the Marlborough Harbour
Board as to whether it could construct a new office building outside harbour limits. The
amendment makes it clear that a board's power to construct authorised works is not affected
by whether the works are situated inside or outside the harbour limits. Clause 35 to 44 make
substantial changes in the law on reclamations, other authorised works, and the consequ-
ences of carrying out unauthorised reclamations or works.

Harbours Amendment Bill
Clause 36 provides for the revocation of an Order in Council when the person
authorised to reclaim so requests. This change arises from a recommendation contained in
the Waitemata Harbour study. Clause 36 makes new provision for survey plans for
reclamation purposes, and is designed to meet the requirements of the Department of Lands
and Survey, which wants to ensure that reclaimed land is accurately surveyed. Clause 37
redrafts the provisions for vesting reclaimed land. They have not been separated from the
survey provisions with which they are at present placed.
Clause 38 introduces a new law concerning illegal works. At present, anybody who
carries out an illegal reclamation, or other work faces a maximum penalty of $200. Because
of the isolated nature of many such works, which are often carried out in remote parts of
mud-flat harbours or in other places where enforcement is difficult, a conviction for such an
illegal reclamation or other work is very difficult to obtain under the present law. The new
proposed sections increase the maximum penalty for illegal reclamation from $200 to
$20,000, and for other illegal works from $200 to $5,000.
It is noteworthy that, despite the wide circulation of the Bill, no one has criticised the
substantial increase in penalties; and many people and organisations have welcomed them.
The clauses also lay down a series of rules which should make the proving of an offence less
difficult than at present, without running the risk of innocent people being wrongly
convicted. Again, these provisions have been widely welcomed and have attracted no
criticism whatsoever.
The remaining provisions to the end of clause 38 set forth a code for the removal or
abatement of illegal works, and will allow the Minister, subject to the supervision of the
courts, to require that illegal works are removed or properly completed or disposed of in the
public interest. Clause 39 effects certain changes to the provisions under which the Minister
approves plans of work. Of particular interest is the change which will mean that in the
future the Minister must have regard to the public interest as a whole. This is in contrast to
the present situation which requires the primary regard to be for the interests of navigation.
There is also provision for the Minister to revoke old plan approvals under conditions which
protect the rights of applicants. Clauses 40, 41, 42, 43, and 44 effect certain consequential
and machinery changes. The most important is the introduction of a time limit for objections
under section 185.
Clause 45 changes the basis for the definition of wharf limits. At present a harbour
board may declare wharf limits subject to obtaining the Minister's consent. The effect of the
change is to provide that a harbour board may declare or amend wharf limits only with the
prior consent of the Governor-General in Council. This change reflects the new importance
given wharf limits by the Waterfront Industry Act. Clauses 46, 47, 48, and 49 are machinery
changes.
Part V encompasses clauses 50 to 61 and concerns a number of the recommendations of
the commission of inquiry into harbour pilotage. The principal amendments cover the
licensing of pilots, the expiry of pilotage exemption certificates if they are not used, the
circumstances in which pilotage exemption certificates may be granted, and penalties for
offences. The provisions relating to exemption certificates were the subject of submissions
before the Local Bills Committee from the ship owners and the Merchant Service Guild. The
committee accepted the submission from the ship owners that the provisions proposed in
clause 53 governing the expiry of exemption certificates should be changed, but did not
accept the submissions of the Merchant Service Guild that geographical limits in the present
Harbours Act should continue. The major factor influencing the committee was the new
power given to harbourmasters to require that a pilot be taken on board regardless of the
fact that a master might have a pilotage exemption certificate. The Local Bills Committee
considered that this was a sufficient guarantee of safety.
Part VI of the Bill contains a number of provisions about bylaws and regulations. Clause
62 redefines a number of bylaw-making powers, including the provision for the composite
charges now levied by many boards. It extends the powers to make bylaws for certain
categories of craft and contains additional powers necessary as a result of the change in the
law relating to pilotage.
During the Committee stage I intend to introduce an amendment to clarify the powers
of boards to enable their officers to check cargo and goods leaving the wharf. As well, I shall
introduce an amendment to provide machinery to allow the Commissioner of Crown Lands
to introduce bylaws where he becomes the controlling authority under clauses 4 and 32.
Clause 63 makes an important change to the law in respect of bylaws. The Minister has a
residual control over harbour boards' bylaw powers, because bylaws do not have to come

15 November
Harbours Amendment Bill
into effect until he acknowledges them.
Mr Lange: It will take a while.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I hope the honourable gentleman can understand this,
because it is pretty legal. The principal result of this is that the Government will be able to
keep an eye on bylaw changes and ensure that harbour boards with a monopoly on a
particular trade or trades do not levy excessive charges. The present Act does not require
acknowledgment when there are existing bylaws and a new installation is constructed. The
effect of the new section will be that when a new cargo-handling facility is provided within a
harbour by someone other than the harbour board, the bylaws of the board, in so far as they
apply to that facility, must be remade. This will mean that the bylaw can be scrutinised, that
users have the opportunity of objecting, and that the acknowledgement procedures will
apply.
Clause 63 was amended by the Local Bills Committee to ensure that it was restricted to
wholly new cargo handling facilities, and would not affect other operations of a board, or the
maintenance or extension of a facility. Clause 64 provides that when a bylaw is disallowed
the Governor-General may order a refund of part or all of the dues paid under the bylaw.
The purpose of this provision is to provide that any excess charge can be refunded. Clause 66
amends a penalty and deals with the issue of a harbourmaster's discretion to grant an
exemption from a particular provision of general harbour regulations. The approach
adopted in the general harbour regulations has been to set a very high safety standard, but
with power for the harbourmaster to grant exemptions when he is satisfied that it is proper to
do so. While the Bill was before the Local Bills Committee, my ministry received a legal
opinion which suggested that the Act itself did not empower the making of regulations that
would give such a discretion to harbourmasters. The new provisions in clause 66 do so, and
validate the existing regulations.
Clause 67 extends the empowering provisions under which motor launch regulations are
made to clarify matters such as the control of moorings and rafts, and removes any doubt as
to the manner in which water ski and other access lanes have been set apart under the
existing regulations-I think this is a very important part of the Bill. Clause 68 contains
empowering provisions for new regulations. The first of these is intended to empower
regulations governing traffic on foreshores. These regulations will be drawn so that they can
be used by local bodies throughout New Zealand as a standard code. This will have two
effects. First, with the same code applying throughout New Zealand there is a better chance
of the public knowing and understanding it; secondly, it will remove the need for each local
body that wishes to control traffic on beaches within its area to obtain a grant of control and
bring down its own bylaws.
Clause 68 also empowers the making of regulations to control inland harbours. They are
necessary in order to provide for stricter control over waters of particular recreational or
aesthetic quality, or where there are unusual risks to navigation. For example, it is proposed
that the waters of the Shotover River and the Kawarau River would be included within an
inland harbour so that there would be power to prohibit navigation except under strict
conditions. Honourable members familiar with those rivers will know the grave risk to life
and limb that unrestricted navigation by jet boats up and down the rivers would create.
Clauses 62, 67, and 68 introduce provisions for the control of rafts. They require the
insertion of further references to rafts so that the powers conferred will parallel those in
respect of vessels. I intend moving suitable amendments during the Committee stage of the
Bill. Clause 69 amends the law governing the dumping of ballast or rubbish on the foreshore
of tidal lands, and is part of the pattern already established by the changes proposed for
reclamation and illegal works. The remaining clauses are machinery clauses, and include a
number of changes in penalty.
I wish to comment only on clause 77, which amends the Auckland Regional Authority
Act 1963 to make that authority a local authority for the purposes of the Harbours Act. The
effect of that amendment is that the Auckland Regional Authority may be given grants of
water and foreshore control over waters and foreshores adjoining its regional reserves. At
present the authority is in an unusual position in that it cannot obtain such control adjacent
to its reserves, which are among the largest and best run in the country, while all normal
territorial authorities have the ability to obtain such control. I thank the members who
served on the committee that went through the Bill thoroughly.
Mr Lange: Has the Minister the power to stop?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: If some members, particularly some from the Auckland
area, are not interested in what I am saying, that is their funeral.

authority wanted a hold over any harbour board wishing to co-operate under the terms of the
Bill. The authority said it was opposed to the fixed maximum rate because many harbour
boards would then be in a position to amass large amounts of revenue and reserves, which
could be used to circumvent the authority's powers. I thought that if a harbour board was
able to amass a large amount of revenue it would be able to improve its port installations if it
wished, but that seemed to be contrary to the submission made by the New Zealand Ports
Authority, and on the department's recommendation the maximum was removed. It was
also pointed out that the only port operating the harbour improvement rate was that
controlled by the Northland Harbour Board.
The committee is to be commended for the Bill's provisions for policing South Island
rivers, especially the Shotover River. Users of such rivers, including tourists and boat
operators, need to be safeguarded.
I conclude by saying again that I hope the Minister will consider my suggestion about
the trust boards being included in the list detailed in clause 4, as the representatives of the
owners of lakes, rivers, and the land adjoining them would then have an opportunity for
discussion with the local authorities. It is often thought that communications between the
Maori people and their representatives fall down because of the lack of representation on
bodies that discuss matters of importance to the Maori people. It is important that
consideration should be given to this matter. As I said earlier, I hope the Minister will
consider the amendment I intend to move during the Committee stage.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I thank the member for Eastern
Maori for his contribution to the debate. I remind the honourable member that grants of
control are for the management of foreshores outside harbour limits, whereas the control of
waters and foreshores within harbour limits is the responsibility of harbour boards. Harbour
board representatives are elected, not appointed. Trust boards-and this point was emphas-
ised by the honourable member-can be granted control of a foreshore. I remind him that I
pointed out earlier that the Bill made specific provision for areas of foreshore and adjacent
waters to be managed under a grant of control by persons acting as trustees for the

I have given an undertaking that the Ports Authority Act will be amended, and I hope to
introduce the legislation at the end of the session so that it can be considered during the
recess. Everyone will then have an opportunity to consider the Bill, and the powers that are,
or are not, granted to the Ports Authority. It has been said that the authority should have
more teeth. There is a definite need for some control over marine activities in certair
waterways such as the Shotover River. I have nothing against people who enjoy water skiing
but other people have to be protected against its dangers.

I want to confine my remarks to Part VIII, which is headed "Unjustified Industrial
Action", and I am bound to say that I intend to draw heavily on external sources to the
extent that I might leave myself open to a charge of plagiarism. Before I do that, I should
like to direct attention to clauses 70 to 72. Clause 70 is headed "Penalty for failure to observe
procedures", and its effect is that when any determination is prescribed for a settlement of a
dispute of rights, no State employee is to become a party to, incite, instigate, aid, or abet a
strike concerning a matter within that procedure, and no service organisation shall, in similar
terms, incite, instigate, aid, and so on. When a dispute has been settled, no employee shall
become a party to a strike concerning the decision, and the clause goes on to the penalties
that are consequent upon activity of that kind being engaged in; if the charge against the
employee or person is established, he is open to a fine not exceeding $100, and a further fine
of a similar amount for every day the strike or lockout has continued. In the case of a service
organisation, a fine not exceeding $500 will be imposed, again to be repeated with a similar
amount for every daily continuation.
I should note, by way of introduction, the provisions of clause 1(3), which enable the
Government to suspend the operation of the clause and bring it into effect partially or
wholly, and relate it to different groups or classes of employees of the State services, or both.
I give the Government credit for good intentions in including this clause in the Bill, but I
believe it is misguided. The power to hang what are clearly disciplinary penalties over the
heads of State service organisations and their members and to dangle penalties up and down
in a tantalising and provocative way, with the threat that parts of them can be applied, lifted,
and reapplied, is an open invitation to play cat and mouse by Executive order and without
parliamentary scrutiny.

One of the relevant parts of the short and untimely-concluded address of the Minister of
Defence was the denial of a charge made by my colleague the menber for Roskill that the
powers contained in Part VIII are, as a result of this subclause, to be invoked in secret. I
