House. The regulations are passed in the secrecy of the Cabinet room and endorsed by the
Executive Council without publication. They are applied in secret, and the first intimation of
their being invoked is their publication in the Gazette, and their application immediately to
the organisation of the State services concerned.
As I have said, I want to draw from external sources to comment on this part of the Bill,
and I do so partly because of the authority of the person writing the article and the vehicle in
which it appears. I shall read from the Canterbury Chambers of Commerce Economic
Bulletin, which appears occasionally but is not regularly published. This bulletin came out 3
or 4 weeks ago, and the article is by Mr Don J. Turkington, lecturer in the industrial
relations centre at the Victoria University of Wellington. I see the Minister in charge of the
Bill has a slight curl on his lip.
Hon. J. B. Gordon: I have a pleasant grin.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: I am glad to accept that emendation. I think we would both
recognise the application that Mr Turkington has brought to this activity, and the authority
with which he speaks on the subject. I want now to quote at some little length from his
statements in the bulletin: "For those who see industrial conflict as deviant behaviour, its
attempted suppression by way of penalties is justified and worth while. New Zealand
Governments, with the limited exception of the 1973-75 Labour Administration, appear to
have followed this view. The I. C. and A. Act began with, and gathered more legal sanctions
against, strike and lockout action. The Industrial Relations Act of 1973 moved away from
the emphasis on penalties but did not eliminate them." I agree with that. "1976 marked a
return with a vengeance to the tradition of the penalty-laden I. C. and A. Act. That
year”—the first year of the National Government—“saw legislative changes by way of the
Industrial Relations Amendment Act, the Industrial Relations Amendment Act (No. 2) and
the Commerce Amendment Act." The Commerce Amendment Act was badly named in this
regard. "These amendments introduced or increased penalties for strike or lockouts in
disputes of rights, in essential industries, in meat export works and in respect of non-
industrial matters and of failure to resume work where the public interest is affected."
The writer then goes on to comment on the applicability of penalties generally.
"Penalties are intended to reduce direct action but tend to have the opposite effect." That, I
think, is a point the Government might very well ponder. "They discriminate against one
party in a situation, the existence of which requires the involvement of another. Each party
considers its interests and tactics to be legitimate, yet one of them is restricted by law in the
tactics it can use to pursue its interests. And that party is usually the union." For "union" in
this context we can read "State Service organisation". "Most of the penalty provisions relate
to both strikes and lockouts, but those on lockouts are redundant. Employers do not need to
lockout. If they wish to close a plant they can usually promote a strike and so avoid being
seen as the aggressor. Workers are therefore opposed in principle to penalties in industrial
relations."
So far, of course, what has been said relates to a situation in private industry; there the
parties are at arm's length, each approaches the appropriate tribunal as a stranger and comes
to it on a more or less equal footing. With this Bill the position is different. It has been said,
not quite accurately I think, that the Government can be judge and jury in its own cause.
The position does not go quite as far as that, but it is a very different one from that which
prevails when a private employer is seeking to impose the penalties contained in the
industrial relations legislation-if there is a breach it is left to the Crown to institute
proceedings, just as the Crown does in all criminal activities. Here, it is the Government
itself that is the prosecution. That is the party invoking the provisions, and it is in a situation
of familiarity, prejudice, and closeness to the tribunal that is not open to a private employer.
I quote Turkington again: "The application of penalties raises further issues. It is not
usually practical to charge all workers involved in a strike. This leaves the union
official"-the officer of the State services in this context-¨although a paucity of evidence
for the prosecution may make it impractical to charge even him. But assuming the official is
found guilty, the fine for a first offender may be laughably small." That has been the history
of industrial prosecutions in this country over many years.
I well recall the prosecution during the war years of the Huntly miners, and the penalties
imposed on them. Undoubtedly the position was serious at the time, but the amount the

Mr MALCOLM (Eden): The member for Henderson has given us, with the help of Mr

Hon. F. M. Colman: The wicked part.
Mr MALCOLM: It is the only part the Opposition seems to want to discuss. To put the
matter back into balance, I shall point out what the Bill is all about. It is the result of one of
the most extensive series of consultations ever held between the Government, as the
employer, and the Combined State Service Organisations, representing Government
employees. The consultations took place over 9 months and totalled 54 hours.
A large portion of the Bill deals not with penalties but with other aspects of the
relationship between the Government, as employer, and its employees. The Opposition is
glossing over parts of the Bill, because it suits members opposite not to make public servants
aware of its good parts. Much of the Bill is a re-enactment of existing clauses, and it contains
the recommendations of the 1972 royal commission, which the Labour Government of the
time was not prepared to touch.
One of the important things to remind ourselves of-and it is important to the
Government's relationship with State servants-is that the main criterion in State wage
fixing still remains fair external relativity. Recruitment and the retention of staff are now
included as criteria in determining pay when the State is the major or only employer in an
occupation. That is a forward step.
One other change I want to comment on, because I think it has a lot of relevance to the
direction in which the Government service might be heading, is that under this legislation,
subject to the health and safety of employees, and other similar safeguards, the State has the
right to decide what standard of service it is required to provide, and the number of staff
needed to provide that service. This is an important point, with implications that should be
explored. We are reaching the stage at which much Government service paid for by the
taxpayers should be logically rationed so that it is within the taxpayers' ability to meet the
demand for that service. As was recently said in America, "If you want to get the
Government off your back, try taking your hands out of the Government's pocket." That
could be recommended to a number of New Zealanders.
An Hon. Member: Confucius.
Mr MALCOLM: No, not Confucius. It is important to recognise that we are moving
into an era in which some difficult political decisions will have to be made by the
Government on behalf of the taxpayer-whether it can continue endlessly supplying services
to meet the public need in all areas-for example, health and social welfare. At what point
does one draw the line, and at what point does one continue to attempt to provide services? I
am not saying that the Government is thinking of cutting back existing services drastically,
but clearly its technological ability to supply services to the community is at risk-the risk of
outstripping taxpayers' ability to pay for those services. The provisions in clause 10(d) and
clause 12(h) recognise that in future the Government might have to make hard political
decisions not to provide the services it would like to provide, or thinks could be provided.
Another important part of the Bill upon which the Opposition has failed to comment is
clause 27, which provides for voluntary mediation similar to that existing in the private sector
to be introduced into the State wage-fixing procedure. Another important part seeks to

change some of the provisions about keeping State sector pay abreast of private sector

underpaid for some 6 months and then receiving backdated pay increases.
We have tried to introduce better ways of ensuring that the concept of fair relativity is

Again and again members opposite have laid stress on Part VIII, and in doing so they
have to some extent misrepresented its role. Part VIII does not come into effect automati-
cally with the passing of the Bill, but the Opposition has failed to make that clear, and failed
to mention that clause 1 (3) clearly states that Part VIII of the Act shall come into force on a
date to be appointed by the Governor-General by Order in Council, and that different dates
may be so appointed for the purposes of different provisions of that part, or for the purposes
of different groups or classes of employees of the State services or of both. That legalistic
wording means in lay terms that Part VIII does not come into effect automatically; and if it is
to come into effect it can do so in a manner that will influence only a small section of State
servants who are, by their actions, inviting the Government to impose the legislation upon
them. Even then, it would not affect other State servants. That is very important, because
the Government recognises that most State servants have a very good industrial relations
record.
There is no question of the Government's attempting to be provocative or to exacerbate
problems in the State services, as suggested by the member for Grey Lynn. He also asked
why the Government was bulldozing the Bill through the House, and why it did not go to a
select committee. He suggested that the Government did not want any scrutiny of the Bill.
That is not so. It is ridiculous to suggest that the Bill is being bulldozed through the House. It
is passing through the House at a very leisurely pace.
Members of the CSSO called on me at my home on Saturday to make representations.
Such people cannot call on members of Parliament if a Bill is being bulldozed through the
House. The member for Grey Lynn was not prepared to accept or concede-and I think he is
still doubtful about it, even though the member for Marlborough produced the proof-that
the reason the Bill did not go to a select committee was that the CSSO and the Government,
having had full discussions, agreed that there was no need for it to go to a committee.
Legislation of this nature has a particular function, because it is not only legislation, but
also, in a sense, is rather like the award under which the State servants act in relation to the
Government as their employer. The member for Henderson made some play about the role
the Government plays as an employer of State servants. He disagreed with the member for
Roskill and I am very glad he did because the member for Roskill said that the State
becomes judge and jury. The member for Henderson corrected him, and quite rightly said
that some people would say the State becomes judge and jury, but that he would not agree
entirely-he felt that was an overstatement. I commend the member for Henderson for
agreeing with me that the member for Roskill is subject to considerable overstatement at
times.
The fact is that there is no way of avoiding the somewhat difficult position in which the
Government finds itself as both employer and Government. That is a fact of life, which no
one can run away from; the Government is a representative of the taxpayer and is an
employer. If anyone can see a way of resolving that conundrum totally, finally, and
absolutely I shall be very pleased, because to me it appears insoluble. One has to rely upon
the Government of the day to tread the narrow path and not to act as judge and jury.
Opposition members have made a great deal of Part VIII, which provides for penalties.
They have not pointed out that the penalties will not apply to all industrial action nor to all
strikes. The Bill outlines the procedures to be followed in the event of an industrial dispute.
It provides that the parties shall take part in conciliation proceedings and mediation, and
eventually appear before a separate authority, which will make a decision. A penalty is
incurred only if the parties choose not to follow the procedures laid down. The claim that a
public servant who goes on strike will somehow be clobbered by the iron fist of the State is
simply not true. Public servants will be able to strike as much as they like, providing they act
within the framework outlined in the Bill.
The member for Henderson referred to the article written by Mr Turkington, and
implied that some people see industrial action as deviant behaviour and consider that it
should be clobbered by force. He also implied that the Government sees it that way. I can


## p. 4494 (#600) ###########################################

4494
State Services Conditions of Employment Bill
15 November
assure the member for Henderson that the Government does not regard industrial action in
that light. We see it as perfectly normal behaviour; it is part of our way of life.
However, we must consider who should rule the nation. Should it be the trade union
movement in the guise of the Federation of Labour, the Combined State Service Organisa-
tions, or any other organisation one might care to mention, or should it be the Government
on behalf of the people? Surely the answer must be that it should be the Government on
behalf of the people. Therefore, while the Government accepts industrial action as healthy
and normal in our society, it is also entitled to lay down certain guidelines and to say to those
involved in industrial action; "You can do certain things providing you follow certain
procedures, which are designed to lead you, if at all possible, towards a solution in
conciliation to the problem." That does not mean that everyone who takes part in industrial
action is being clobbered; it simply means that if people wilfully choose to ignore conciliation
provisions and go outside the law, they will risk a penalty.
It has been said that the proposed penalties will be very difficult to enforce. I believe the
Government concedes that such penalties are difficult to enforce, but that does not mean
that it should run away from the task.
It has also been suggested that the Government itself could be fined if it imposed a
lockout, and that that would be a hollow victory because the Government would hardly
notice the odd fine of about $1,500. The people who make that suggestion fail to realise that
the Government department responsible for the lockout and for paying the fine would have
to appear before the Public Expenditure Committee when the estimates were being
considered for presentation to the House. They fail to realise, also, that the Minister would
be responsible for explaining to the House, the Opposition, and the public how he became
involved in a situation in which his department was obliged to pay a fine of $1,500 for
instituting a lockout. With all due respect to any Government, the damage done in such a
situation would far exceed the $1,500 fine.
In fact, that provision in the Bill is a very real deterrent to Government involvement in
any lockouts. I suggest that what is likely to happen under this measure is that if either an
employer or an employee finds himself becoming involved in a conflict and considers taking
action that might possibly smack of an illegal strike or lockout, the first thing he or she will
do is run straight to the nearest industrial lawyer for some good advice on whether the
proper procedures are being followed.
It has been said that penalties do not lead to a reduction in industrial disputes. The
member for Henderson quoted-or, rather, misquoted-the 1976 figures. We concede that
there were many stoppages in 1976, but the member's implication that they were due to the
Government's introducing penalties is not correct. Fifty-five percent of those disputes were
directly related to the Government's attempt to control the wage-price spiral, and had
nothing whatsoever to do with the introduction of penalties.
At present, a different set of reasons apply to the industrial problem. We are trying to
move back to free wage bargaining, and employers and employees are establishing their
negotiating position.
I make a point that has not been made by Opposition speakers. It relates to the
important question of the status of teacher trainees under this Bill, and is a fine legal point
rather than a strong political one. Before the 1969 legislation was enacted there was no doubt
that teacher trainees were public servants. Through some oversight, the 1969 Act failed
specifically to place teacher trainees under the provisions of the State Services Act. That
shortcoming did not become clear until after the 1974-75 debacle when the Labour
Government introduced its standard tertiary bursary, which upset teacher trainees. Only
then did the limitations of the 1969 Act become evident. The Government of the day was
prepared to continue with the provisions that applied before 1969.
Now that we have a chance to tidy up the law, what is the correct thing to do? Are we to
continue with the status quo, or should we do what the Act was meant to do in 1969? The
Opposition, whose job it is to scrutinise these matters in order to help those who in some way
may be disadvantaged by a particular Bill, has completely failed to argue the case for teacher
trainees. I am not saying that they would be disadvantaged, but the matter needs to be
looked at carefully. We should resolve the correct way to put the intentions of the Bill into
practice.
In summary, the Bill is the result of much consultation with the CSSO. It makes a
number of improvements in the positions of both employer and employee. Part VIII, to
which the Opposition is directing most of its attention, is only a small part of the Bill.

MR SPEAKER-COURT SUMMONS
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I should inform the House that Mr
J. R. Harrison, Acting Speaker, has received a summons to attend as a witness at the
Magistrate's Court, Wellington, on Thursday, 17 November 1977, at 10 a.m. to give
evidence in respect of a charge of assaulting the police laid by Constable Fluit against one
David Grant MacPherson. Pursuant to section 260 of the Legislature Act 1908 the Acting
Speaker is required to submit the matter to the House of Representatives, and such order
may be made thereon as the House thinks fit. I propose to seek a resolution from the House
under section 260 exempting the Acting Speaker from attendance at the court. I do this
because I believe the Speaker should be summoned only when it is absolutely essential,
which is seldom likely in cases of summary prosecution. In this case the summons relates to
certain documents held by a commissioned officer who has already been summoned as a
prosecution witness. There can be no question of the Acting Speaker being called as a
witness because he did not see the incident.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Is it a summons simply to produce documents?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Yes. The summons reads: "You are required to bring with
you and produce any documents written by yourself, or copies thereof, relating to instruc-
tions you gave the police in your capacity as Speaker . . .”.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: That is different from a summons to appear and give evidence.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Yes, but the summons is to give evidence in respect of a
charge of assaulting the police.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: There are, of course, two forms of summonses.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I will read the summons, if that will help the honourable
member.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: You are unaccustomed to them, of course.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: Yes, as a matter of fact I am.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: So am I.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: The summons reads: "You are summoned at the request of
the defendant to appear as a witness at the Magistrate's Court at Wellington on Thursday the
17th day of November 1977 at 10 a.m. and on such other days as may be directed by the court
to give evidence in respect of a charge of assaulting the police laid by Constable Fluit against
David Grant MacPherson. You are required to bring with you and produce. . .". The
documents are held by a police officer who has already been summoned as a prosecution
witness, and I think the Speaker should attend only when it is absolutely necessary. I recall
for the information of the House that there have been occasions in the United Kingdom
when those who have sought to require the Speaker to attend have been taken into custody
by the House to signify its disapproval.
I move, That, pursuant to section 260 of the Legislature Act 1908, John Richard Harrison,
Acting Speaker of the House of Representatives, be exempted from attendance at the Magis-
trate's Court, Wellington, on Thursday, 17 November 1977, to give evidence in the case of Fluit
v. MacPherson.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): The Acting Prime Minister was
kind enough to advise me of this matter during the lunch hour, and I had an opportunity to
consult with some-though regrettably not all of my colleagues. However, those I did talk
with certainly concurred with the view put forward by the Acting Prime Minister. In the
event of the Speaker being a physical witness to an incident and the circumstances being such
that he could throw helpful light on the situation, Parliament might have had to consider the
matter in a different way from that proposed by the Acting Prime Minister.
However, it is quite clear that the whole question relates to documents, or statements,
issued for Parliament by the Speaker, and those documents are available to the court for
consideration of their contents; and an officer would be present who could obviously provide
any ancillary information required. I think there are some more than slightly interesting
implications in the suggestion that Mr Speaker, whoever he might be, could be summoned to

HIGHER SALARIES COMMISSION BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That the Higher Salaries Commis-
sion Bill be introduced. The Bill makes statutory provision for the first time for the Higher
Salaries Commission, which has previously been covered by regulations at present set up
under Part II of the Wage Adjustment Regulations. It is the last part of the legislative
package giving effect to the Government's wages and industrial relations policy. Since its
establishment in 1974, the Higher Salaries Commission has determined the salaries and
allowances of members of Parliament, of top executives in public and quasi-public bodies
and corporations, and of top positions in local bodies and the universities. The commission
surveys the salaries and allowances of top executives in the private sector, and, in accordance
with the criteria set out in the present regulations, determines the salaries of those people
over whom it has jurisdiction. The commission can make general reviews between 1 and 3
yearly intervals, and has the power to make interim adjustments between general reviews.


## p. 4499 (#605) ###########################################

16 November
4499
Higher Salaries Commission Bill
By and large the Bill follows the principles and procedures embodied in the Wage
Adjustment Regulations, with some modifications to which I shall refer.
Clause 1 cites the short title, and as in the other three Bills relating to industrial relations
and wages policy, provides for the Higher Salaries Commission Act to come into force on a
date to be appointed by Order in Council. Clauses 5 and 6 establish a three-man commission,
and provide for staggered appointments to allow for some continuity in expertise. Clause 12
sets out the jurisdiction of the Higher Salaries Commission, and, by and large, repeats the
jurisdiction it has at present. The Government has some modifications to this jurisdiction
under active review, which may result in some changes to the schedules of the Bill. A new
provision allows for the commission to make recommendations to the Minister of Justice and
certain other Ministers on matters relating to salaries and allowances and superannuation of
the judiciary. The commission will make recommendations to the Prime Minister on
questions relating to parliamentary superannuation.
Clause 13 allows for additions to or deletions from the first three schedules of the Act by
Order in Council, and is the operative clause allowing for modification to the commission's
jurisdiction. Negotiations between the Government and the Local Authorities Industrial
Committee on new career service and wage-fixing machinery in the local body area are well
advanced. It is proposed that empowering legislation setting up a joint council for local
authorities services be introduced later this session—that is, fairly shortly—and, with the
successful conclusion of negotiations, the jurisdiction of the Higher Salaries Commission in
the local authority area will be reduced.
Clause 15 is new, and provides for the publication of the commission's determinations.
The result of the commission's general reviews will now be public except in certain
circumstances where, for competitive reasons-for example, Air New Zealand-it would
not be in the public interest to publish the commission's decision. Determinations made by
the commission will be provided to the Minister of Labour, with the exception of those
pertaining to local authorities and the public bodies specified in Part II of the first schedule.
The commission's decisions on parliamentary pay and allowances will be published in the
Gazette 14 days after the Prime Minister, the Speaker of the House, and the Leader of the
Opposition are notifed.
The criteria to be used by the commission when determining salaries are given in clause
17. The first requires the commission to "achieve and maintain fair relativity" with the
private sector, and is slightly different from the reference to "achieve and maintain stability"
contained in the Wage Adjustment Regulations. Clauses 18 and 19 set out the rules
governing general reviews and interim adjustments. A limit to the amount of backdating to a
general review has been introduced. The 12-month rule relating to the duration of a
determination is also brought into the Bill in a similar way to that set out in the Wage
Adjustment Regulations. The various bodies and organisations that may make submissions
to the commission are referred to in clause 20. Any person may make a written submission,
but certain advisory committees may make recommendations, which must be given due
regard by the Higher Salaries Commission. The remaining clauses embody provisions similar
to those in the Wage Adjustment Regulations.
Discussions on this Bill have been held with the present Higher Salaries Commission,
the Federation of Labour, the Employers Federation, the Combined State Service Organisa-
tions, the University Grants Committee, the Local Authorities Industrial Committee-a
relatively new organisation—and a number of other organisations. Discussions are continu-
ing in some places, and following further consideration some modifications may be made to
the Bill after it is introduced. We have tried to introduce the Bill at the earliest opportunity,
so that copies can be distributed this week-if possible, today. I had not intended to refer the
Bill to a select committee, but, in line with a request made by an Opposition representative
during a discussion this morning, I propose to refer the Bill to the Labour Committee for
consideration next Wednesday morning-in exactly the same circumstances as the Industrial
Law Reform Bill and the General Wage Orders Bill were referred to that committee-to
give Opposition members an opportunity to cross-examine officials on various points in the
Bill. In doing so, I accept exactly the terms set out by the member for Roskill last week: if
necessary, we will be able to proceed with the second reading of the Bill, but with an
assurance that it will not go through the Committee stage until the procedure I have
mentioned has been followed. I consider that a relatively satisfactory, if not totally
satisfactory, resolution of the discussion held this morning.

could correct the matter in the Committee stage. I shall certainly look into this question.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
SUBMARINE CABLES AND PIPELINES PROTECTION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Submarine
Cables and Pipelines Protection Amendment Bill be introduced. The Submarine Cables and
Pipelines Protection Act was introduced in 1966, and since then experience has shown the
need to make a number of amendments. These are basically for the purpose of strengthening
the provisions of an Act that protects seabed cables and pipelines, such as the Cook Strait
power cable, the Maui gas pipeline, and Post Office telecommunication cables. Protection is
obtained by declaring a special area around the pipeline in which fishing or anchoring is an
offence. The main provisions of the Bill relate to the removal of abandoned cables or
pipelines that constitute a hazard to fishing operations, the tightening up of the offence
provisions, the seizure of fishing equipment found near a protected cable or pipeline, and the
empowering of suitable persons to order ships from the vicinity of a protected cable or
pipeline.
The Bill also contains provision enabling the Minister to exempt specified ships or
classes of ships from the prohibition against anchoring or fishing in protected areas. From
time to time cables or pipelines need to be repaired, and if they are to be repaired a ship
must anchor near them. Members of the House will be well aware that the Photinia was
recently engaged in repairing the Cook Strait power cable. The ship has precision navigation
instruments on board, which enabled it to anchor without fear of damaging the cable.
Although the present Submarine Cables and Pipelines Protection Order 1977 exempted the
Photinia from the prohibition against anchoring, it is an unnecessarily cumbersome process
to issue an amending order each time a repair vessel wishes to anchor near a protected cable
or pipeline. For that reason, this Bill provides for the Minister to grant that exemption by
notice in the Gazette.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): At first glance this Bill does not appear to be
controversial, and for that reason I am not asking the Minister to send it to a select
committee. After closer examination, however, we could have a different view. I should like
the Minister to elaborate on the penal provisions in the proposed new section 7A(2) in clause
5, which states in providing that certain activities are prohibited in protected and restricted
areas: "Every person who fails to comply with or acts in contravention of any Order in
Council under section 7 of this Act commits an offence against this Act and is liable on
summary conviction to a fine not exceeding $5,000." Under the 1966 Act the penalty was
$500 and/or 3 months' imprisonment. Am I correct in assuming that the imprisonment
provisions have been dropped and we have instead a 1000 percent increase in the financial
penalty?
Under section 6 of the principal Act, which deals with indemnity against loss of gear, the
provisions are most rigid-and rightly so-in regard to ships that may venture into an area
covered by the Act. If my interpretation of the proposed new section 6A is correct, an


## p. 4503 (#609) ###########################################

16 November
4503
Submarine Cables and Pipelines Protection Amendment Bill
obligation is being imposed on the owners of abandoned submarine cables or pipelines to
inform the Minister that they no longer propose to use the pipelines; if they do not do that,
an order can be made for their removal. That seems to balance the position between the
owners of fishing and other vessels that might unwittingly trespass into such an area, and the
owners of submarine cables who no longer want to use them. If my interpretation is correct,
this would appear to be a desirable and uncontroversial amendment. I should like the
Minister to clarify the position regarding the penal provisions.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The member is quite correct
about the penal provisions. We thought that the provision relating to imprisonment was a
little too harsh and that the financial penalties should be increased instead. The aim is to
deter people who leave cables or other gear on the seabed from taking the matter lightly,
because they could cause problems for others and interfere with fishing. The second point
was on the use of pipelines and cables. As the member knows, it is possible for apparatus to
be dug into the seabed and left there, thus impeding fishing operations. We felt there should
be some obligation on owners to remove such material. I do not think I can add any more,
except to emphasise that, increasingly, articles left on the seabed are impeding both boating
and fishing operations. This is an attempt to penalise more heavily those who do that, and
also to put an obligation on them to remove the articles. Big changes are taking place in
fishing, as the honourable member will know, and we thought this Bill was necessary to deal
with matters that the principal Act did not adequately cover.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): It is not quite clear from the

provisions of the Bill.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): In my introductory remarks I

looked at again to ensure that its provisions do not go too far. It states that a vessel in
suspicious circumstances can be asked to move. We were trying to guard the rights of the

would have to move if their presence endangered pipelines such as those mentioned by the

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I do not have the Bill in front of me, but I am referring to

1. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Prime Minister: What is the total cost,
including an allowance for the estimated cost of any trips undertaken or being undertaken,
of the overseas trips made by him since taking office in 1975?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): As any members who have
experience of Cabinet procedure will know, substantial delays are incurred in bringing to
charge expenditure on ministerial overseas travel. Indeed, it is expected that the 1978-79
estimates will include expenses of Labour Ministers for their 1975 travel. As a result, and
because it is impossible to include an allowance for specific travel items not yet charged
because of the generalised form of travel cost estimates, it is not possible to calculate the
total cost of the Prime Minister's travel overseas since 1975.
However, as at 31 October 1977 the total amount expended on the Prime Minister's
overseas travel-being the expenses of all members of his party, including the Prime
Minister himself, Mrs Muldoon, private secretaries, and officials from the Treasury, the
Prime Minister's Department, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, or the Department of Trade
and Industry, as appropriate, and on one occasion the Hon. M. Rata and Mrs Rata-was
$196,045. Of this amount $76,988 has come to charge in 1977, while the total estimated cost
of overseas travel for 1977 is $213,107.
Mr Prebble: Can the Acting Prime Minister read the last part of the answer again? He
was reading it so quickly I found it difficult to follow.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: However, as at 31 October 1977 the total amount expended
on the Prime Minister's overseas travel-being the expenses of all members of his party,
including the Prime Minister himself, Mrs Muldoon, private secretaries, and officials from
the Treasury, the Prime Minister's Department, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, or the
Department of Trade and Industry, as appropriate, and on one occasion the Hon. M. Rata
and Mrs Rata-was $196,045.

3. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Education: Is it correct that the Syllabus

syllabus in schools and that there have been no amendments since their introductic in 1929?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I assume that the honourable member is
referring to the amended regulations to the Education Act 1914, which appeared in the New
Zealand Gazette dated 10 January 1929, and which came into force on 1 February 1929.
These regulations have not been amended, but from time to time new syllabuses in
individual subjects have been approved by Ministers of Education.
Mr Lange: Is it the Minister's intention to repeal the regulations and to regulate for
syllabuses in terms of ministerial instructions from time to time?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: This matter is being looked into. A practice has grown up over
the last 30 years of a syllabus being approved by the Minister of Education and gazetted in
the New Zealand Gazette. The Government intends to introduce a consolidated education
Bill later in the session for recess study. This matter will be brought up and considered,
because the number of syllabuses that have been introduced over the years without the
sanction of regulation have been large, and such a ponderous situation would no longer seem
viable.

Land-use Policy
8. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) asked the Minister of Lands: What progress is being
made towards the development of a comprehensive land-use policy for New Zealand?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The development of comprehensive land-use
policies for New Zealand depends on the availability of adequate information. Progress is
being made with the assembly of information through a series of regional or subregional
land-use studies, such as the King Country and South Westland studies, from which regional
and New Zealand policy can be developed. In addition, the Land Use Advisory Council has
made good progress with the investigation of a New Zealand land information system, which
would ensure the ready availability of information to policy makers and assist in the
examination in depth of the options open.
Marilyn Waring: In view of the time taken to assemble the King Country land-use
survey, is the Minister satisfied with the present speed of progress?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The King Country land-use study took far longer than I expected.
It was, however, the first of a number of such studies, and I am sure that the departments
concerned will have learnt from that experience. We must ensure that the information in
various departments is readily available to the working groups involved in the regional study.

planning scheme in the absence of the information that this study will provide?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: Yes, but the information that has been made available through a
land-use study such as that on the King Country is of tremendous assistance to local and
regional bodies in formulating their district and regional schemes.
Marilyn Waring: Is any attempt being made by the Department of Lands and Survey to
rationalise the criterion used for deciding what grade will be given to an area—a question
about which I understand there is departmental conflict?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: It is really a question of the several departments involved making
sure that the information at their disposal is easily obtainable and in fact fits in with the
information of other departments-for instance, the water and soil division with the
Valuation Department, and with the Department of Lands and Survey-and ensuring that
the information is stored in a way that makes it readily available, and avoids a duplication of
effort.
Mr Wetere: Will the Minister adopt the method outlined in the King Country and South
Westland land-use studies for a comprehensive policy for the whole of New Zealand?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: No. Both studies are being evaluated. The South Westland study
involved State forest land and Crown land, and was essentially a study by the Department of
Lands and Survey and the Forest Service. It did not go much wider than that in terms of the
personnel involved. The King Country study was very much an inter-departmental study.
Somewhere between those two extremes-two departments on the one hand and a multiplic-
ity of departments and information on the other-we will come to a method of land-use
study that is practical, will provide the information we need, and will provide it faster than
the King Country land-use study was able to do.

## p. 4515 (#621) ###########################################

16 November
4515
Supplementary Questions-Speaker's Ruling
House itself should be master of the situation to a large extent. It seems to me that if there is
a closer adherence to the original question in both questions asked and answers given in the
search for clarification of the original answer, your task will be made considerably easier. If
either Ministers in reply or members asking supplementary questions stray too wide of the
original question-and I say "too wide" advisedly, because obviously some range must be
permitted-it is proper for you to move on to the next question because members have
digressed from the original question. However, I suggest that if the questions and answers
remain pertinent to the main issue it is better for the House to have an exhaustive discussion.
It seems to me that two sets of circumstances have developed, one being that raised by
the member for Wigram of a Minister straying from the question in his initial reply. Once
that has happened—and it happens all too frequently-there are real problems for the
member who wants to ask a supplementary question; he finds it difficult to keep closely to
the main issue because it had been sidetracked by the Minister's reply. If you were to
intrude, very properly, at that point and insist on a proper reply, and then require that
supplementary questions relate to the original question and reply, there would be no need to
restrain the House when members deal with questions at some length but in a way that is
completely relevant.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I think the real problem that has
confronted the Speaker and the House is that the member for Wigram is disposed to make a
speech before asking his question. I have been here for 20 years and have listened to him
doing that time after time. I think that is the fundamental problem.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: I am not sure how I can make it clear to honourable members,
but I thank them for raising the point. Perhaps, for the benefit of Ministers who are required
to answer questions, I could refer again to Standing Order 81, and remind them and those
who help them draw up the answers that the replies must be concise, confined to the subject-
matter of the question asked, and must not contain any argument or controversial matter. If
Ministers would abide by Standing Order 81 then, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed
out, a great deal of the difficulty we are faced with would not arise. By the same token, if
members who ask questions-and normally they are very good and do not infringe Standing
Order 87 in the way many do when asking supplementary questions-were to comply with
Standing Order 87, we might not be faced with so many problems either. Standing Order 87
is clear, and I shall not read it because we do not have much time, but I think all honourable
members are familiar with it and know what it is about.
Speaker's ruling 115/3 states that supplementary questions must arise directly from the
Minister's reply; they must be related to it not indirectly but directly. My friend, "Mr
Oxford", says in his dictionary that a question is a "sentence adapted by order of words, use
of interrogative pronoun or stop, or other means, to elicit answer". In other words, it is
something to elicit an answer. The honourable member for Wigram informed me that he was
having difficulty because, as he said, "In a subsequent reply I had to make a case." Well, he
does not give the replies; he can only ask the questions. He also said, “In a supplementary
question I had to rebut the answer from the Minister before I could ask a further question.'
He seems to have forgotten that this is a question and answer period; it is not a debating
period. Therefore it is a matter of asking supplementary questions that must arise directly
from the Minister's reply. They must be put to elucidate an answer, that is, to make clear or
to find out what the answer means.
I am trying to make it clear to the honourable member that this is a question and answer
period. Supplementary questions, put to elucidate an answer, must be directly related to the
answer given. This is not a period of debate. That follows when the questions are transferred
to the Supplementary Order Paper and we have an opportunity to debate them every
fortnight. If Ministers and honourable members will adhere strictly to the Standing Orders,
we shall not have too much difficulty. I should very much like it if honourable members were
prepared to restrict the number of questions they put down on the Order Paper. A
reasonable proposition is 20 questions. That gives members the opportunity to have their
questions answered in the House, and also gives those members top priority to ask
supplementary questions to elucidate replies given by Ministers. If I am to do that, obviously
we must make somewhat better progress than we made today.
I remind members that today we had 17 questions and 33 supplementary questions, a
total of 50, so we have not done too badly. However, I would prefer to give members the
opportunity to ask 20 questions and 20 supplementary questions. I am quite happy to allow
half a dozen or a dozen supplementary questions if they all seek further elucidation of the
answers given.

STATE SERVICES CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT BILL
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): As one would expect, the Bill sets the conditions under
which Government employees work. One would have hoped that the Government would
use the Bill to set the stage for better working conditions for its own employees, but no one
could say that about this measure, least of all Government members.
The Government, through the Bill, should have tried to provide job satisfaction for
State servants. It should have improved their working conditions, and given them confi-
dence, which they are entitled to expect from such a major employer. However, the Bill has
aroused resentment, hostility, and general opposition from public servants throughout the
country. Before the Bill was introduced, widespread public meetings were held by those
opposing it. The meetings in some of the main centres were attended by thousands.
The Bill takes the big stick to public servants; it relies on penal provisions. I believe that
the Minister and other Government members know that penal provisions do not work with
trade unions. They have never worked overseas, and they are unlikely to be any more
successful in this country. They will never work in an enlightened democracy, and that is why
the measure is resented by public servants. Apparently the National Government will never
learn how to handle industrial relations.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: A point of order, Mr Speaker. Five Government members are
on their feet and speaking in the aisles. My colleague the member for Petone is making an
important contribution to the debate, and it is totally unreasonable for this kind of situation
to prevail.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: We have a Standing Order that states that members shall be
seated in the Chamber. It is not conducive to good order to have members talking in the
aisles while another member is speaking. If members wish to speak to each other, they
should occupy the spare bench seat beside the member with whom they want to talk, or
perhaps they could make use of the lobbies for discussion. Normally, an exception is made
for the leaders on each side and for the Whips.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN: Apparently the present Government will never learn how to
handle industrial relations. Surely members opposite realise that the starting point for good
industrial relations is harmony between the Government and its own employees. I do not
think the Minister believes in penalties as such. I am sure he has not much faith in their
application, but he is a prisoner of his own caucus-we can hear some of its members
interjecting tonight. The right-wing element in the Government caucus provides the real
pressure and motivation for the penal provisions. Its members want to be able to take
punitive action against State servants.
Last night the member for Eden said that the Government had consulted with the State
Service organisations for 54 hours. It would not matter how long the Government spent on
discussing the measure with public servants if it contained Part VIII, and its penal provisions.
Government members could talk until doomsday; the public servants still would not be

That is one reason for not referring the Bill to a select committee. The Government did
not want other members or the news media to obtain at first hand an insight into the
opposition to the Bill. The Government is singling out the workers as scapegoats, and that is
one reason for the Bill's being before us now. If punitive action, including fines, is taken
against individuals or unions, the end result is likely to be the extension of disputes. If a

sections of the State unions will become involved. Surely, in industrial matters, the name of
the game is to confine a dispute. The smaller a dispute can be kept the sooner it will be
settled, but this measure, particularly Part VIII, will extend any conflict between the
Government and its employees, and the courts and jails of the country will not be large
enough to deal with everyone involved. Unions consider this to be a matter of principle; if
one is picked on, the Government buys a fight with them all. This will unite the State sector
of the trade union movement, and lead to a general withdrawal of labour.
The Government is the largest employer in New Zealand, and because of this it should
also be the best employer, and give a lead in good industrial relations to the private sector.
This Bill does not do that. It takes a negative attitude. It contains nothing positive, and if the
Government and its employees cannot achieve harmonious relations, who can? Good

industrial relations should start between the Government and its own employees, but the

Various United Nations conventions have recognised a worker's fundamental right to
withdraw his labour, but the Bill restricts the possibilities of a lawful strike. Putting workers
outside the law does not solve anything, although it could have certain advantages. Telling
the public that a worker's action is unlawful is a good way to stir up false sympathy, as
evidenced by events in 1951. However, it does not get at the source of tension between
employer and worker. In a civilised country that can be done only by negotiation. The
Industrial Relations Act, introduced by the Labour Government, stressed conciliation rather
than coercion.
Last year the National Government turned this approach upside down, and the
alarming increase in the number of strikes has proved that its action was wrong. Last year the
number of worker days lost in all stoppages increased by 130 percent, from 228 000 to 526
000. This year the position is even worse. For the 6 months ended 30 June, 176 000 worker
days were lost compared with 149 000 for the same period last year. The number of days lost
is 18 percent higher than last year, which was the worst year since the major industrial
upheaval in 1951.

The effect of the regulations introduced by the then Minister of State Services, the member
for Roskill, is as follows. Regulation 64A authorised the State Services Commission to
suspend from duty without pay any employee who refused or failed to carry out his normal
duties. Regulation 64B enabled employees to be laid off work without pay if, by reason of
the failure of any group or class of employees to carry out normal duties, there was
insufficient work for them to perform. Regulation 64C provided that nothing in the
regulation should prevent disciplinary action being taken against the employee. Those
regulations will be done away with by the passing of this legislation.

necessary to implement Part VIII, but it is there if it is needed. The Opposition should have

concentrating on Part VIII. The Government hopes that the machinery and the mediation
service provided by the legislation will be effective, and that State employees will work
within its provisions. The legislation provides a mediation service similar to that provided by
the Industrial Relations Act.
The Bill provides for annual reviews of remuneration rather than half-yearly surveys.
The measure will cut the number of wage escalations. The continuous rise in incomes has
been a problem, and an annual review will be better than the past system. The half-yearly
survey which includes three-quarters of the labour force, is weighted in favour of the areas of
population that include more State servants, and these areas tend to lead.
In small rural towns one hears continual concern expressed about State pay fixing.
Rural towns are not included in the half-yearly survey that measures movement in the labour
force. The rate applying in the State sector has become the ruling rate, and the new award
target in the private sector. When employers again pay above the award rate, wages escalate.

1968 royal commission. Then in 1972 there was another royal commission, and this
legislation follows its report. The Labour Government had the report for 3 years, and did

Apple and Pear Marketing Amendment Bill
APPLE AND PEAR MARKETING AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The purpose of the Bill is to make various amendments to the Apple and
Pear Marketing Act 1971. Most of the provisions in the Bill have been requested by the
Apple and Pear Marketing Board and the New Zealand Fruitgrowers Federation, which, of
course, represents the growers and the industry. The amendments proposed by the industry
follow consideration at the last two industry conferences of the Massey University market
research centre report, which was commissioned by the board and the federation. The
principal amendments empower the board to deal with other horticultural products as the
Minister of Agriculture may from time to time approve, to provide for an industry levy on all
sales of apples and pears, and to allow for the seasonal movement in the average price to be
between plus 10 percent and minus 5 percent instead of the present plus or minus 5 percent.
The cost of production criterion is removed from the list of criteria to be taken into
account by the Apple and Pear Prices Authority when fixing the average price, and any
distribution of board profits is to be subject to ministerial approval.
I shall now go through the clauses in some detail. Clause 2 amends section 11 of the
principal Act and empowers the board to handle such horticultural products-other than
apples and pears-as the Minister may from time to time approve. The clause also provides
for the board, with the consent of the Minister of Finance, to acquire shares in companies
not specifically dealing with apples and pears, if participation by the board in such a
company could conveniently be undertaken by the Apple and Pear Marketing Board in
association with its general powers and functions, and if this may be of benefit to the board.
It should be made perfectly clear, however, that there is no intention—I repeat, no
intention that the controlled marketing provisions that relate to apples and pears should
apply to any other product or activity with which the board may be associated. These
provisions are included solely for the convenience of the board, so that it is able to offer its
facilities for use by other horticultural products at times when those facilities are not being
used for apples and pears. The provisions will also enable the board to become a shareholder
in operations such as cold-store facilities. For example, when the Nelson co-operative was
being set up about 3 years ago with the intention of building a cold store for use by various
primary industry groups such as berryfruit growers and the fishing industry, it was hoped that
the Apple and Pear Marketing Board would be able to participate in the shareholding also.
Unfortunately, because there was no guarantee that the cold store would be holding apples
all the year round, the board found itself unable to acquire any shares in the operation. The
intention in this clause is that the board should be empowered, when it considers it
advantageous to do so, to participate in operations such as the cold store co-operative I have
just mentioned. The safeguard on the exercise of this power is that the consent of the
Minister of Finance is required in each case. Thus, there is no risk—and some members
opposite questioned this during the introduction debate of the board acquiring a variety of
company shares unnecessarily.
Clause 2 is intended also to allow a more rational use of board facilities. Any such
additional use would require the approval of the Minister of Agriculture, and would have to
suit the convenience of the board and its main functions in serving the apple and pear
industry. Essentially, the arrangement would be a marketing one, with either the board
offering its facilities at a market price for use by other horticultural producers, or a grower or
group of growers of a particular product approaching the board and asking it to pack, store,
or market their products as a commercial transaction. This is designed to provide a facility
for some smaller horticultural enterprises that at present do not have the size, facilities, staff,
and marketing expertise necessary to break into world markets. Before exercising his power
to approve the board's handling any other horticultural products, the Minister-and that
would apply to any Minister in charge-would want to be assured that both the board and
the growers of the product concerned were satisfied about the arrangements proposed.
I reiterate what I said a moment or two ago. Any other products handled by the board
would not be subject to any of the control marketing provisions in the 1971 Act, as Part II of
the Act applies only to apples and pears. Clause 3, which amends section 18 of the principal
Act, is a technical amendment only, and relates to clause 7 of the Bill. The effect of clauses 3
and 7 is to make it clear that the board has the sole right over exports of apples and pears.
This was always thought to be the case. However, it was found that the law did not actually
prevent the export of apples that had been designated for the local market and sold on the


## p. 4528 (#634) ###########################################

4528
16 November
Apple and Pear Marketing Amendment Bill
local market, but subsequently exported. These amendments are intended to make perfectly
clear the rule that the board has the sole right over exports of apples and pears.
Section 18 will now provide that Part II of the Act relating to the acquisition of apples
and pears shall apply to all apples and pears grown in New Zealand or imported into New
Zealand, which may be sold, or exported for sale for human consumption. This is putting
into precise legal language what was always understood to be the position, at least by 99
percent of the growers. The reason is quite simple. The quality of apple and pear exports is
of paramount importance in our international marketing strategy, and it is essential that our
status as a producer of quality exports be preserved-the more so when we look at the large
increase in production from New Zealand industry which will be placed on the world
markets in the very near future. I reiterate that in such an approach quality is a most
important and significant factor, and the Apple and Pear Marketing Board is the appropriate
organisation to ensure this objective is achieved. The sole right to export does not, of course,
apply to any other products that the board may handle from time to time at the request of
others in the horticultural sector.
Clause 4 amends section 27 of the principal Act, which relates to the determination of
the average price. Subsection (3) of section 27 lists the criteria the Apple and Pear Prices
Authority is required to take into account when determining the average price, and
subclause (1) of this clause removes the cost of production criterion from that list. The result
of this amendment is that the authority will be required to place emphasis on market returns
and prospects when fixing the price.
At the same time as the cost of production criterion is being removed, however, the
restriction on the seasonal movement is being widened. As I have said, clause 4 (2) of the
Bill will allow for changes in the annual price of between plus 10 percent and minus 5
percent, instead of the present plus or minus 5 percent. This brings the price stabilisation
provisions for the apple and pear industry into line with those operating in most of the other
primary industries. With the price being more closely related to market realisations there is
scope for allowing increases of up to 10 percent in the price, if market returns justify this sort
of increase. The essential feature of the amendments made by clause 4 is that the average
price is to be more closely related to market returns. I might add that the Bill will need to be
passed by the end of this month if the Apple and Pear Prices Authority, which will be sitting
this month, is to be able to take note of the new criteria and the new flexibility in setting
prices.
Clause 5 provides for the imposition of an industry levy on all sales of apples and pears.
This caused some controversy within the industry. The levy is to be fixed by the Apple and
Pear Prices Authority, the same authority that sets the prices, after taking into account the
cost to the board of processing apples and pears, the state of the industry reserve account,
and the state of the apple and pear growing industry generally. The levy will be payable by 31
August in any year, based on the sales of fruit over the 12 months ended on the previous 30
June. Provision is made for remission of the levy by the board in cases in which genuine
hardship is proved. The purpose of the levy is to help finance the cost of processing apples
and pears to reduce any deficit in the industry reserve account, and to promote the interests
of the apple and pear growing industry. Although this provision is being included at the
request of the industry, there has been some opposition to it. I am satisfied that the majority
of the growers, as expressed at the last two dominion conferences of the Fruitgrowers
Federation, are in support of the proposed levy.
As recently as yesterday I met representatives of one group of growers who were
objecting to the levy. I indicated to them that I was prepared to promote a small amendment
in the Committee stage that would require the Apple and Pear Prices Authority to consult
the Minister as it does when setting the price to the grower before determining the levy in
any given year. That was the group from Huapai. This additional safeguard went a long way
towards alleviating the concern expressed by that group. I am sure that other groups will be
happier now that the Minister is involved.
The rate of the levy is a very small one of only 0.25 of a cent per kilogram, and obviously
will have very little or no effect on the price that the consumer will pay for apples. It is worth
reminding ourselves that at the time the levy was first proposed the industry was facing
severe problems. Market returns were down and the board was facing another substantial
deficit.
It is equally wise to remind ourselves that production has continued to increase and the
present estimates indicate that the crop is likely to increase by 50 percent by 1985. Although
the board made a substantial profit this year and may well do so again next year, these results


## p. 4529 (#635) ###########################################

16 November
4529
Apple and Pear Marketing Amendment Bill
cannot be taken as indicative of a changed marketing situation on the world scene, because
they were substantially influenced by adverse climatic conditions in the northern hemisphere
that dramatically affected crops in that part of the world. The year 1979 is expected to be one
of substantial oversupply of apples on the world market, and the industry cannot afford to be
complacent, to say, "We needed the levy when prices were bad; they are now better so let us
throw the idea away", because, like all other primary products, prices unfortunately vary
substantially from year to year. As New Zealand's consumption has remained relatively
static for some years, the extra production must be either exported or processed into juice or
pulp. The preparedness of the industry to impose a levy demonstrates a willingness by the
majority of growers to help overcome their own problems. I commend that attitude, which in
turn has led to a greater willingness by the Government to assist the industry wherever
possible.
The Massey report, which is the basis for most of the changes that have taken place in
recent months, and many of those changes proposed in the Bill, was not a report to the
Government, but was commissioned by the board and the federation. After the report was
received, the industry instituted a number of far-reaching proposals designed to restructure
the pipfruit industry, and this industry levy is a part of that restructuring programme.
While there are arguments in favour of freeing the local market and doing away with the
board and its controls, the industry as a whole has not accepted these arguments. It has voted
by a substantial majority for the retention of the present marketing system—and the
Government must take notice of the industry's views on this matter. The board's marketing
system provides for a continuous supply of good quality apples-subject, of course, to the
vagaries of the weather-at prices comparable with those of other fruits, and consumers are
able to purchase apples direct from growers, either by mail order or at the orchard gate,
provided the quantity does not exceed two cases at any one time. I have covered the levy and
the board's marketing system at some length, but I have felt it necessary to do so to correct
some of the misconceptions that have arisen in some quarters about these two matters in
particular.
Clause 6 rewrites subsection (5) of section 33 of the Act on the disposition of any profit
the board may make. The effect of the clause is to provide that any disposition of profits by
the board will be subject to the approval of the Minister after taking into account the board's
economic position and the desirability of repaying as quickly as practicable any deficit in the
reserve account. This amendment brings the apple and pear industry into line with other
primary industries. It is felt that, with the determining of the average price being more
flexible, any payout of board profits should be subject to the Minister's approval to avoid a
large payout from profits in years when there is a substantial deficit accumulated from
previous years' trading.
Clause 7 makes it an offence to export apples or pears that are not packed and graded in
accordance with the specifications gazetted by the Director-General of Agriculture and
Fisheries. This is to ensure that the quality of export apples is of the highest possible
standard. Clause 8 is an amendment consequential on clause 5, which provides for the
industry levy. The clause provides for the making of regulations to cover the details of the
incidence and manner of collection of the levy.
This is a small Bill relating to a relatively small but important primary industry. The Bill
has the support of the majority of the industry members, and full consultations have been
held with industry representatives in recent months.
As I mentioned during the first reading, the industry is anxious that the Bill should come
into force as soon as possible, and certainly before the present season ends on 30 November,
when the pricing authority will make a final determination on the average price to be paid.
Because of the consultations that were held, the Bill was not referred to a select committee. I
did invite submissions from people who had a point of view they wanted to have considered,
but I have received only one submission. A group from Huapai came to see me yesterday,
and, after our discussion, went away feeling much happier about the provisions of the Bill,
particularly the minor amendment I intend to move requiring consultation with the Minister
before the levy is imposed.
I remind the House that the Massey report was commissioned by the industry because of
the difficulties it was facing, and the industry has taken many steps to bring about the
restructuring suggested in the report. Legislative amendments to the Act are now required to
finalise the restructuring and replanning of the industry. I should like to think that the House
supports this move.

I want to make one or two specific comments on various clauses. Clause 2, dealt with at
some length by my colleague the member for Nelson, principally enables the board to
dispose of products other than apples and pears. It also enables the board to purchase or to
acquire an interest in companies or operations involved in exercises other than the simple
sale of apples and pears. I suppose one should welcome at least a socialistic tendency on the
part of the Government in recognising that a producer organisation should be able to
embark on an exercise of this kind.
I want to deal more specifically with this matter of the sale of products other than apples
and pears, which has arisen, I believe, out of the recognition by the growers of the need to
spread the risk. For a long time now, pipfruit growers have been dependent, in the main,
solely on the production and sale of apples and pears. As I have mentioned, they have been
vulnerable in overseas markets. In more recent years it has been appreciated that it is
possible, on the kind of country that most of them work, to spread the risk by becoming
involved in other types of fruit production, notably boysenberries, and, more recently, kiwi
fruit. That has been helpful to many growers.
Allied with that, of course, is the development of the packhouse or the co-operative
concept, whereby growers, in Nelson and Hawke's Bay in particular, have come together in
large numbers to pack on a co-operative basis. The packhouses themselves have realised
that, with this type of administration, they are able to reach out and assist growers to
diversify into other forms of fruit production. Already packhouses are handling boysenber-
ries and involving themselves in the production of kiwi fruit.
In the main, this clause will accord with general tendencies in the industry. There are
some dangers, as my colleague the member for Nelson very properly pointed out, but the
ideal operation that allows diversification for the growers while giving them strength in terms
of marketing operations is one that is generally favourable to producers.
Clause 4 is probably the most critical provision in the Bill, because it allows the pricing
authority to widen its range of price changes over that of the previous season. The downward
change is restricted to 5 percent, in accordance with the present Act, but the upward change
is lifted so that it will be possible-and indeed the pricing authority will give serious
consideration to this when it meets a little later in the month—to lift the price to the growers
by 10 percent. The general purpose, it appears, is to allow a closer relationship between the
prices that the pricing authority agrees to and the market situation—and, fortunately for the
industry, that has changed markedly in the past 12 months from a severe deficit in the 1976
season to a marked improvement in the 1977 season, when apples were realising anything up
to $20 a bushel case on the United Kingdom market, and often $17 or $18 a bushel case on
the United States market as opposed to $9 or $10 in the previous season.
However, I think that the decision to remove from the consideration of the pricing
authority the recognition of the cost of production is a detrimental move. I know the
Minister says that, in essence, the growers have given that away as the quid pro quo for the
wider range by which it will now be possible for the pricing authority to lift the price. I
believe the danger is a very real one, in the sense of removing a necessary element of stability
that exists under present pricing arrangements. Although I accept that industry spokesmen,
on behalf of growers generally, have agreed to the Government's proposal, I still hold the
view that something of a standover tactic was involved and that they gave something away
unnecessarily. That is a matter to which the pricing authority should give proper recognition.
I want to refer to only one other provision, clause 5. That clause has apparently upset
the gate-sale growers in New Zealand in that it provides for a levy of up to 25c a kilogram, or
a little less than 5c a bushel case, to be applicable on all sales. The argument put forward by
the gate-sales people is that they do not have an obligation to meet any cost commitment of
the Apple and Pear Marketing Board. I have already referred specifically to the problem the
board has in absorbing any excess production in processing, to the problem it has in ensuring
that good quality fruit reaches distant markets in the interests of New Zealand generally, and
also to the board's specific problem in ensuring that New Zealand consumers receive a
decent supply of apples throughout most of the year. Each one of those factors has an
influence on the domestic market to the benefit of the gate-sales operator. I do not believe it
is asking too much at all to request the gate-sales operator to make a contribution—not a
heavy one, but some contribution.
