POTATO GROWING INDUSTRY BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The purpose of the Bill is to reconstitute the New Zealand Potato Board
and redefine its functions and powers. The Bill has been to a select committee, at which a


## p. 4537 (#643) ###########################################

16 November
4537
Potato Growing Industry Bill
number of submissions from interested organisations and individuals were heard. The Bill is
to replace the Potato Growing Industry Act 1950, which established the New Zealand Potato
Board, defined its powers and functions, and provided for the regulation of the potato
growing industry. While the Potato Board has done a very worth-while job since 1950, the
Act under which it was established had one major limitation-it related only to potatoes
planted after 1 August and delivered for marketing between 1 March and 30 November the
following year. In the trade that is termed the "main crop". This limitation severely affected
the board's ability to supervise the whole supply of potatoes on the New Zealand market
throughout the year. Early potatoes and early potato growers have not come under the
auspices of the Potato Board.
For the last 10 years, under 3 Governments, early and main-crop growers have sought
ways of getting closer together through a reconstituted Potato Board with responsibility for
all potatoes grown in New Zealand. The Bill is the result of those discussions, in which I
became involved after my appointment as Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of
Agriculture and Fisheries in 1975. Constant discussions were held with all sectors of the
industry before the introduction of the Bill. Submissions were made to the select committee,
and the Bill reflects the views put forward in all those submissions.
The Bill provides for an expanded Potato Board of nine members-three growers
nominated by the Potato Growers Federation, three growers nominated by the Vegetable
and Produce Growers Federation, and one member from each of the Agricultural Merchants
Federation, the Fruit and Produce Merchants and Auctioneers Federation, and the Ministry
of Agriculture and Fisheries. The new board will be responsible for all potatoes grown in
New Zealand, for operating a registration scheme for potato plantings, and for establishing
and maintaining minimum quality standards for potatoes sold in this country for human
consumption. It will be required to ensure an adequate supply of potatoes to local consumers
throughout the year, and, to this end, will administer, subject to ministerial supervision,
schemes for potato imports and exports as required.
The most contentious matters have been the disposal of and compensation for surplus
potatoes, and greater representation on the reconstituted board. While agreement was
reached on these issues at a meeting held in November 1976, groups have since emerged that
do not support the agreement reached. I consider that the revised form contained in the
Bill-whereby the two grower federations put forward their own nominees in the three
wards, but all registered growers are eligible to vote in each election-should overcome
some of the objections expressed at the select committee that the industry should not
continue to be divided into early and main-crop growers. The provisions for the board set
out in the Bill were supported by both the Potato Growers Federation and the Vegetable and
Produce Growers Federation, and they are the two main bodies representing early growers
and main-crop growers.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: That's not exactly right.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: The member for Timaru knows what happened at the select
committee. I cannot say whether the federations had a unanimous vote before they appeared
before the committee, but the submissions supported the Bill's provisions, and that is the
important thing. It is worth recalling that Opposition members on the select committee
voted against this clause after it had been deliberated on, and I have no doubt they will
mention that fact in the debate. I remind the House that for 3 years the Labour Government
tried-conscientiously and seriously, I believe-to bring the potato industry together and to
draft legislation acceptable to all sectors. It was unable to do that during its term in office. I
was able to get agreement to bring this Bill in, and I believe it has the support of most sectors
of the potato industry.
The provisions on disposal of surplus potatoes have also been considerably amended so
that the fund to be set aside for this purpose may be used for disposal of potatoes, as well as
the interest. The original Bill provided only for the interest to be used, but the fund can be
used also under certain conditions. It will also be possible to replenish the fund by means of a
special levy. Both the use of the fund and its replenishment by special levy will have to have
the unanimous support of grower members of the board, and the approval of the Minister.
That was agreed to by both Government and Opposition members of the select committee,
and it tidies up the Bill. The short title of the Bill was amended in the select committee to
read "Potato Industry Bill", which more accurately reflects the wide functions the Bill is
designed to cover.
The Bill will come into force 2 months after its passage, with the exception of the
registration provisions, which come into force on 1 April 1978. Clause 3 provides for the


## p. 4538 (#644) ###########################################

4538
16 November
Potato Growing Industry Bill
establishment of the New Zealand Potato Board, which consists of nine members-six
growers, two merchants, and one nominee of the Director-General of Agriculture and
Fisheries. In other words, it is a clear producer board, with six grower members and three
non-grower members. I cannot believe that such a producer board will do other than work
for the benefit of the total industry, and I dispute any suggestion to the contrary.
Clauses 5 and 6 provide for the election of grower nominees, and for their terms of
office. The procedures for the election of the grower nominees were considerably amended
by the select committee, so that all registered growers will be able to vote in elections for
grower nominees within their ward. Nominations for elections will be made by either the
Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation or the Potato Growers Federation, depending
on which federation nominated the nominee whose position has fallen vacant. To allow the
new board to take office as soon as possible after the commencement of the Act, before the
registration procedures are implemented and a register of registered growers would be
available, the first grower members of the board are to be nominated by their respective
federations without the need for an election.
Clauses 7 to 12 are standard provisions relating to the deputy chairman and meetings of
the board-the normal procedures in all legislation. Clauses 13 to 16 set out the functions of
the board. I draw the attention of the House to the requirement that the board maintain a
supply of potatoes in New Zealand. The principal aims of the reconstituted board are to
promote and assist the development of the potato industry, and to ensure the adequate
supply of potatoes. To achieve these aims the board is to institute a system of registration of
all potato plantings to enable the board to determine accurately the total area of plantings
and the likely yield, to ensure that an adequate supply is maintained.
The board is empowered to arrange disposal of surplus potatoes unable to be sold, and
to provide money for this purpose, as set out in clause 23. The board is to operate a legal
minimum quality standard scheme under which potatoes below a specified size and quality
standard may not legally be sold for human consumption. That provision requires a certain
quality for all potatoes sold in New Zealand. The present board has control over only one
sector of the industry.
Provision for the control of the volume of import and export of potatoes, maintenance,
advertising, research, and the dissemination and maintenance of statistics is also provided
for. It is provided that persons growing more than 0.5 of a hectare of potatoes must register
their plantings. They will pay the necessary registration fee, which will be set from time to
time. Provision is made for an assessment of an area planted, when there is some difficulty in
getting the grower to provide the necessary information.
Clauses 22 to 29 are the financial provisions. The most important clause is clause 23 and
the newly inserted clause 23A. These clauses provide for the establishment of the potato
surplus disposal account and for a special levy to replenish the account. Clause 23 provides
for the board to set aside money in this account to pay for the disposal of surplus potatoes.
Subclause (2) provides for the interest on the disposal account to be used solely for the
disposal of potatoes, and the fund is also to be used for disposals after the unanimous vote of
six grower members on the board and the approval of the Minister. This is a major change in
the Bill that went before the select committee. The safeguards are obvious in requiring that
there be the unanimous vote of growers and the approval of the Minister.
Clause 23 logically provides for replenishment, if necessary, of the disposal account by a
special levy, which is to be recommended to the Minister on the unanimous vote of the six
grower members of the board, and no more than one such recommendation may be made to
the Minister in any one year. In other words, the Government has accepted that there may
be exceptional circumstances and the fund may need to be replenished. In that case the
industry should be given an opportunity to express its point of view.
It is well known that the so-called early growers have been reluctant to be associated
with the surplus disposal arrangement. The submissions heard by the committee on this
matter clearly demonstrated the growers' concern. The schedules set out the three wards and
the boundaries thereto. It will be debated that there should be six wards with individual
members. The Government considered that proposal and rejected it, staying with the
proposal of three wards with two members in each ward in line with the agreement that I
obtained from the industry at a meeting I convened in November 1976. It is not a provision
that we thought up in isolation from the industry. Agreement was reached with the industry
in accordance with the industry's views at that time, both sides agreeing that there must be
some compromise if progress was to be made in the implementation of legislation to unify
the industry and to provide it with the necessary legislation to promote the overall welfare of


## p. 4539 (#645) ###########################################

16 November
4539
Potato Growing Industry Bill
potato growers, whether they are early growers or late growers, or whether they are at the
top of the North Island or at the bottom of the South Island.
I believe that the potato industry will benefit significantly from the passage of the Bill. I
believe that the industry, although somewhat concerned at this stage with some sections, will
recognise that it has a common interest in providing the consumer with high quality potatoes
right through the year. It will also realise that if, from time to time, there is a surplus that is
to be sold overseas it is essential that the surplus to be exported should be in high quality
condition. Members will recall the difficulty experienced this year in exporting surplus
potatoes. Quality standards were not maintained, and a quite disastrous situation occurred
that has unfortunately damaged the name of New Zealand potatoes, and that damage will
not be overcome for some time.
I agree with the majority view of the industry that we must face the problem of unifying
the industry—a problem that has been with us for the past 10 years or so, and that three
successive Governments have tried, without success, to resolve. In 3 years the Labour
Government was unable to make any progress.
The House should support the Bill unanimously. It should not divide on the Bill, as I
suspect Opposition members might, because the industry needs legislation to unify it. The
Bill will unify it, and I should like to think it has the support of both sides of the House.
Debate adjourned.
The House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.

should be set up should receive urgent attention". That recommendation has been acted on.

required. This study will include the question of whether a commission should be set up. It is

sight the recommendation that commerce regulate itself looks very attractive, but there are
obvious difficulties. The member will appreciate that commerce cannot be expected to
discipline itself in the way his own profession can, and clearly the Government must remain
responsible, in the public interest, for the continuation of certain inspectorial and regulation
duties. Therefore, although I am attracted to the recommendation, I do not think I should
wholeheartedly throw myself on one side at present. It needs more study.

is self-disciplined and disciplined by competition. It is from that that it derives its great
advantage over socialism.

than a Government agency as such?

suggest that we want such an enormous bureaucratic machine as the agency in the United
States to which he referred.

Mt. Ruapehu-Early Warning System
7. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Lands: Has he read the article
entitled "Radio System and Warning Device an Urgent Need on Mt. Ruapehu" in the
Evening Post of 9 November, which states that the National Parks Authority was responsible
for the delay in not approving funding for an early warning system on the mountain, and, if
so, is the statement true, and, if it is, what was the reason for the delay?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): Yes, I have read the article referred to and I
can assure the member that any implication that the National Parks Authority was respons-
ible for the delay in approving the necessary funding is not correct. After the 1975 eruption
on Mt. Ruapehu renewed interest in a warning system led to the Tongariro National Park
Board calling for a detailed report and preliminary costings. These reports required
considerable investigation and were not available until June 1976, when the park board
submitted a case to the National Parks Authority. At its meeting on 28 July 1976 the
authority authorised an approach to the Government for a special grant of $116,300 for a
volcanic warning system and essential radio back-up for Mt. Ruapehu. The Government
endorsed the expenditure in May of this year as part of the 1977-78 new policies review. The
newspaper article refers to the biggest problem being the amount of technical work needed
to design the system and the warning equipment to enable tenders to be called, and I have, in
fact, already taken this matter up with the Minister of Works and Development. Progress on
the VHF radio back-up system is proceeding satisfactorily, and at present the park board is
discussing details with the favoured tenderer.
Mr Wetere: When will this project be completed?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I have given the House details of the position at present. I sincerely
hope that the radio communication and early warning system can be installed by the next
operative skiing season. I am concerned about the need for good communications when
large numbers of people are on the mountain.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

NORTH SHORE DRAINAGE AMENDMENT BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I move, That leave be given to introduce the North Shore
Drainage Amendment Bill. This is a local Bill sponsored by the North Shore Drainage
Board. It has two operative clauses, which seek to amend sections 15 and 21 of the North
Shore Drainage Act 1963. The North Shore Drainage Board serves the area commonly
known as the North Shore and Auckland, and specifically the Takapuna and East Coast
Bays Cities and the boroughs of Birkenhead, Northcote, and Devonport, as well as part of
the Rodney County. Under the present Act the North Shore Drainage Board comprises 12


## p. 4550 (#656) ###########################################

4550
17 November
North Shore Drainage Amendment Bill
·
members, 2 from each local authority. Each authority appoints one member, and the other
member is elected at the triennial local body elections.
Clause 2 seeks to amend the provisions of clause 15 relating to the voting powers of
those members. Board members exercise a single vote on most issues, with the chairman
having both a deliberative and casting vote. However, provision is made for any member of
the board to demand that a poll be taken on any question or proposal before the board, in
which case each representative of a local authority is entitled to exercise such number of
votes as are the equivalent of the proportion which the amount of the assessment paid by his
district bears to the total amount of the assessments of all of the authorities. On the basis of
last year's assessments the proportion of votes would be-and I give them as percentages
rounded off to the nearest whole number-Takapuna, 48 percent; Devonport, 8 percent;
East Coast Bays, 18 percent; Northcote, 7 percent; Birkenhead, 15 percent; and Rodney
County less than 1 percent.
Because of the increase in the area of Takapuna City due to its natural growth and the
recent incorporation into its boundaries of the Glenfield ward of the old Waitemata County
Council, the Takapuna City Council is very close to the point where it could have control,
and ultimately control the board's affairs. This situation is thought to be unreasonable by
both the drainage board and the five other local authorities whose areas are served by the
board. Their view is that the North Shore Drainage Board serves the whole of the North
Shore and that it would be fair and proper that matters be decided by the board on a
majority basis.
Furthermore, the board points out that the Takapuna City Council's area is almost fully
reticulated for sewerage, and that unfairness could arise because of its voting power and its
control over areas where substantial development is still required. In addition, the board
feels that, because half of its members are elected by the people, all matters should be
decided by a simple democratic majority vote. The present voting provisions are further
complicated by the fact that the two members from each authority are entitled to exercise
half of their council's vote, and that in theory, one member could vote one way and one
member vote the other. I understand that a poll has been demanded only twice in the board's
history. Clause 2 seeks to repeal the part of section 15 of the principal Act that provides for a
poll to be taken.
Five of the six local authorities-those other than Takapuna City Council-support the
Bill. I have received telegrams confirming that from the clerks of each of those authorities
and I am willing to table those telegrams and make them available to the Local Bills
Committee. Understandably, the Takapuna City Council is opposed to the Bill, and I am
certain it will make its views known to the select committee. I should also add that I know
that the Minister of Energy Resources, whose electorate of North Shore covers most of
Takapuna city, shares the opinion of his local authority and will doubtless make his view
known to the House at a later stage. The remaining clause is a machinery provision only,
which deletes the words "secretary manager" and substitutes the word "manager" as the
statutory description of the board's chief executive officer. The present wording is consi-
dered by the board to be too restrictive.
Motion agreed to.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
ELECTORAL AMENDMENT BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Electoral Amendment Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. As the
House knows, this Bill-with one or two exceptions-amends the Electoral Act by repealing
those aspects of the Electoral Amendment Act 1975 that were opposed by members of the
present Government when in Opposition. As will have been apparent from the debate on
the introduction of the Bill, there are strong differences of opinion between members on
each side of the House as to the necessity for these changes, and these divisions were
reflected in the discussions, debate, and voting during the select committee's deliberations.
The Bill attracted five submissions, and one more that I shall mention at the end of my
report. Two of them were supported by appearances in person. At my request, the secretary
of the committee contacted the two main political parties that are not represented in
Parliament-the Social Credit Political League and the Values Party-to see whether they
wanted to make submissions. Copies of the Bill were made available to them. The Values


## p. 4551 (#657) ###########################################

17 November
4551
Electoral Amendment Bill
Party made submissions, and its secretary, Mr McDavitt, appeared in support, but the Social
Credit Political League said that it did not wish to make submissions.
The House will recall that the provisions of the Electoral Act 1956 were the subject of a
major review by a special select committee, which sat during the term of the previous
Government. The changes made by the Electoral Amendment Act 1975 resulted from that
committee's recommendations. Because of the very wide nature of that review, I also
arranged for the secretary of the Statutes Revision Committee to contact those who had
made submissions to the previous select committee on matters covered by the present Bill to
see if they wished to be heard again on the present amendment. Four substantive submis-
sions were received, together with a written indication from the New Zealand Law Society
that it did not intend to make any submissions. I shall be referring to these various
submissions in my report on the individual clauses of the Bill.
Clause 2 removes from section 30(3) of the principal Act references to school teachers,
the effect being to require that school teachers must take leave without pay during the period
of the election campaign. The 1975 amendment had caused considerable difficulties for the
Department of Education and, although his party opposed the clause, Mr McDavitt of the
Values Party confirmed that such difficulties had arisen with Values candidates. The
committee understands that problems with the 1975 amendment were so manifest that on
various occasions they had to be referred both to the Ombudsman and to the Crown Law
Office. It should be emphasised that the purpose of the 1975 amendment-and this was
made quite clear at the time by the report of the select committee-was to benefit not school
or university teachers, but rather their pupils. As I have indicated, the 1975 amendment has
caused considerable confusion, and it is specifically at the request of the education
authorities that the amendment is made. In addition to the reservations expressed by the
Values Party, the Opposition members of the committee voted against the clause. No other
submissions relating to the clause were received.
Clause 3, which clarifies the meaning of the term "ordinarily resident in New Zealand",
was inserted at the request of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and is a consequence of
lowering the voting age. The clause was specifically supported by the Values Party, and was
agreed to unanimously by the committee. Clause 4 relates to the qualification of electors,
and reverts to the situation before the 1975 amendment, when a person had to reside in an
area for at least 3 months. There was some confusion about this clause; there were those who
assumed that it amounted to some form of voter disqualification, whereas it merely specifies
where a person may vote, not whether he may vote. Most of the opposition to the clause
seemed to result from this misunderstanding. The committee recommends, by a majority,
that the clause should proceed without amendment.
Clause 5 reinstates the pre-1975 disqualification as an elector imposed upon all persons
who are detained, pursuant to convictions, in a penal institution. This was in accordance with
a clear statement by the National Party when in opposition in 1975, and is a majority
recommendation of the committee. Clause 6 removes those provisions that were included in
the principal Act by the 1975 amendment requiring advertisement of candidates' nomina-
tions and polling places. This provision was supported by the Values Party, but was opposed
by Dr Alley and Mr Halligan of the School of Political Science and Public Administration at
Victoria University of Wellington. By a majority, the committee recommends that the clause
should proceed without amendment.
Clause 7 repeals that aspect of the 1975 amendment that permitted a person to register a
special vote if he were qualified to be registered but was not in fact registered on the roll,
provided he believed on reasonable grounds-to be set out in an application for a special
vote that he should have been registered as an elector. The committee unanimously agreed
that this aspect of the 1975 amendment had caused considerable difficulties. In fact, to quote
one Labour member, "No one was happy with the way the section had worked." One
submission on this clause was received from a Mrs E. V. Holmes of Hamilton, who related,
in strong and persuasive terms, an experience she had had in local body voting, and
expressed concern that this clause might perpetuate that problem in a general election.
However, the officials advising the committee have confirmed that the problem raised by
Mrs Holmes was in no way affected by clause 7 of the Bill, and the committee has agreed that
I, as chairman, should write to her explaining the correct position and indicating that her
concern is unfounded. The committee, by a majority, recommends that clause 7 should
proceed without amendment.
Clause 8, which increases the maximum allowable election expenses for an individual
candidate from $2,000 to $4,000, attracted some comments. The Values Party felt that the


## p. 4552 (#658) ###########################################

4552
17 November
Electoral Amendment Bill
figure was too high and suggested $3,000 instead, and this view was echoed by Dr Alley and
Mr Halligan. An interesting alternative view was put forward by the New Zealand Council
for Civil Liberties, which suggested that there was no credible justification for limiting an
individual candidate's expenditure. The view expressed by the council was that for New
Zealand at present no limitation is probably preferable. This view did not find favour with
the committee. By a majority it recommends that clause 8 proceed without amendment.
Clause 9 repeals the provision inserted by the 1975 amendment that permits a candidate
to use a loudspeaker in any public place during the period of 1 month before polling day.
This aspect of the 1975 amendment had been strongly opposed by the then National
Opposition. The New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties, while recognising that it would be
inappropriate to permit the use of loudspeakers in residential areas, suggested that Parlia-
ment should legislate to allow the use of such equipment without local body approval in non-
residential-for example, shopping-areas. However, the committee considers that
parliamentary intervention would be inappropriate and that these matters can best be left to
individual local authorities to decide in accordance with their bylaws and local practices. The
committee is not in any way convinced that the old law was abused by local authorities. By a
majority it recommends that clause 9 proceed without amendment.
Clause 10 inserts a new section 147A in the Electoral Act prohibiting the publication of
an advertisement intended to promote or procure the election of any candidate unless
authorised by the candidate. The clause also defines, with greater accuracy than in the past,
those costs that would form part of a candidate's election expenses. Dr Alley and Mr
Halligan of Victoria University strongly endorsed this provision, and, although the Opposi-
tion voted against it in the committee, there was no real dispute as to the substance of the
proposed amendment. Finally, I should note that today I personally received a submission
on the Bill from the Women's Electoral Lobby, Nelson branch. Although the submission
was received too late for specific consideration by the committee, copies will be made
available to all members of the committee. I have carefully read the WEL submission, and
confirm that all the matters set out in it have been included in the submissions received from
other organisations and individuals and which have, of course, been given the most careful
consideration.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I am outraged at the way the Bill is being handled in
the House, and at the manner in which the chairman reported on the committee's
deliberations. My recollection of the matter is completely different from his, and the report
is a complete distortion of what happened. The Electoral Amendment Bill is one of the most
important Bills introduced into Parliament in my time in the House, and, if passed, it will
determine how members of Parliament are to be elected. In other words, we are fixing the
rules for elections. The way in which the Bill is being handled is one of the worst abuses of
the parliamentary system I have seen. The Bill was introduced on 3 November, and, despite
its constitutional importance, no advance publicity or warning was given, and speeches by
Government members gave a completely misleading idea of what the Bill contains. Much
was made on its introduction about voting rights for prisoners and the use of loudspeakers.
Nothing was said about the fact that the Bill proposes a massive tightening in registration
which will disqualify up to 100 000 New Zealanders in the next election.
The clerk of the committee told me that on 4 November he telephoned the organisations
he thought would be interested, but no letters were sent out, no copies of the Bill have been
made available, and the contents of the Bill have not been advertised. Submissions opened
on 4 November and closed on 16 November, giving less than 2 weeks in which to make a
submission. Copies of the Bill are still not available in my home city of Auckland.
Even more outrageous is the fact that, although a well written submission was received
from two lecturers at the school of political science and public administration at Victoria
University, it arrived on 16 November, the day submissions closed and the same day on
which submissions were heard, and no member of the committee had an opportunity to read
that submission. The submission was put in my hand at 10 a.m., and at 1.30 p.m., even
though I mounted a one-man filibuster against the Bill, the committee rose, and I had no
opportunity to read the submission. I have since read it, and it is excellent. I make it clear to
those people who appeared as witnesses that it was obvious from the deliberation in the
committee that the National caucus had made a secret decision about the Bill and was not
interested in any submissions that were made, because members had no opportunity to
consider the amendments. Labour members found themselves in the ridiculous situation of
asking the officials to look at one or two amendments from a bipartisan point of view; and at
the normal finishing time of 12.45 p.m., after one committee member had left and no


## p. 4553 (#659) ###########################################

17 November
4553
Electoral Amendment Bill
member had indicated that he would speak, it was announced that the Government would

Mr PREBBLE: She also recorded the cases of other people not on the roll who were not

The New Zealand Council for Civil Liberties made a good submission, but regretted
that it had not been given time to make a proper submission. The council placed in front of
the committee the basic principle that "democracy means the voice of the people. Implicit in
the proposition that so far as possible it should be the voice of all the people, not merely
some of the people. Therefore, the emphasis should be on enfranchising as many citizens as
possible, not on disenfranchising them." The council maintained in its submission that the

covered in clause 10.

other, it is the electoral branch of the Department of Justice. I say that with sadness and with
the benefit of personal experience. Many of its functions have now been transferred to the
Post Office, and that addiction towards administrative convenience should certainly not be
encouraged.
The following extract is from the submissions put forward by the New Zealand Values
Party: "The Prime Minister justifies it"-the amendment-"in terms of the administrative
convenience of returning officers whereas we believe that a prior principle guiding the
Electoral Act should be the maximisation of democratic rights to vote. We are not suggesting
that the Prime Minister and his Government do not also believe this, but we point out that in
cases where there is a conflict between the two points, as in clauses 2, 4, and 5, the Bill
invariably sides with the administrative convenience of returning officers and restricts
democratic rights to vote. The mainstream of electoral reform in New Zealand has been to
extend democratic rights-some of the proudest moments of our country's history have been
in that tradition. This Bill, we believe, steps outside that mainstream.".
The submissions also had this to say: "Given the rather short time allotted for preparing
submissions on this Bill, we have had time only to consult with national-level standing
committees and office holders of the party review party files on the matters covered, and
read up on first reading speeches and press statements. We would have preferred, for a more
democratically based submission, to consult our general delegates meeting, but this is
impracticable. In general we are increasingly concerned about the shortness of time allotted
between reference to a select committee and deadlines for submissions. We do not believe
that this enables either the soundness of submissions or the best of legislation." That is
enhanced and emphasised by the member for Mangere's reference to the fact that only today
we received another submission dated within the time scale allowed for the giving of
submissions—not presented to the committee, but given to us in the House as the report
back is being debated. At least we should have an opportunity of considering that timely
submission within our committee.
On introducing the Bill the Minister of Justice said that it would limit the activity in next
year's election campaign of groups such as the Capital Club. Clause 10 of the Bill is nothing
but a Capital Club or Bob Jones clause. That causes me to quote some remarks attributed to
that gentleman, because in an Evening Post report he is credited with this somewhat
mysterious statement: "The National Party dissociated itself from the Capital Club advertis-
ing in 1975, but Mr Jones says he did not promote any particular candidate except in the case
of the Labour candidate, Mr F. D. O'Flynn, for the Kapiti electorate." I am sure Mr
O'Flynn relished the support he got from the Capital Club in that campaign. I am not so sure
whether the present member relished it quite so much. However, the ostensible purpose of
this clause is to limit unauthorised expenditure on behalf of a candidate.
We have been referred to some English cases in which it was said that an advertising
campaign in opposition to a candidate must be construed as support for the rival candidate or
candidates, but of course Mr Jones's objective is not to oppose a particular candidate in any
specific election but to deal with a very personal grievance against an individual. This clause,
therefore, would not have the slightest effect on his continuing vendetta, for which he
became so notorious a few years ago and which he apparently intends to continue during the
next election campaign. This would encourage him in that kind of personal campaign, and
for the Minister to say that this clause provides protection from such a possibility is simply to
misconstrue or misunderstand the purpose of the clause.

BAY OF PLENTY CATCHMENT COMMISSION AND REGIONAL WATER BOARD
ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSES RECOVERY BILL
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. This Bill of eight clauses and two schedules enables the recovery of levies for the
financial years ended 31 March 1974, 1975, 1976, and 1977 by the Bay of Plenty Catchment
Commission. The commission was established under the Soil Conservation and Rivers
Control Act 1941 as a regional water board in accordance with the provisions of the Water
and Soil Conservation Act 1967 and provided for its estimated annual expenditure in such
sums and on such terms as have from time to time been approved by the Soil Conservation
and Rivers Control Council.
The council has not levied or directed that an administrative rate be levied on all
rateable properties within the Bay of Plenty catchment area, nor have the local authorities
within the area agreed to apportion money themselves and pay sufficient money to meet the
administrative expenditure of the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission and Regional Water
Board in any of the years mentioned. The general administration levy suspense account of
the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission and Regional Water Board was in deficit as at 31
March 1977 to the extent of $468,153. Some local authorities within the catchment area have
from time to time made voluntary contributions towards the general administrative expenses
of the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission and Regional Water Board. It is desirable that
the general administrative expenses incurred by the commission be recovered on an orderly
basis over a period of years and that a refund be made to the local authorities which have
voluntarily contributed more money than would have been due had a rate been levied
pursuant to the Soil Conservation and Rivers Control Act 1941.
Clause 1, the short title, has a new subclause (2), which states that the Act shall come
into force on a date to be fixed by the Governor-General by Order in Council on the
recommendation of the Minister of Works and Development. Clause 2, interpretation, has
been slightly amended, as has clause 3, which deals with the administration deficit to be met
by local authorities. Under clause 4, voluntary contributions made by local authorities since
1973 are to be refunded or set off against the amount due to be paid. It is intended that the
expenses recovered from local authorities shall include the general administrative expenses
incurred by the commission in its capacity as a regional water board.


## p. 4569 (#675) ###########################################

17 November
4569
Bay of Plenty Recovery Bill
The payments set out in clause 5 are to be spread over a 3-year period, the first payment
falling due on 28 February 1978. Clause 6 states that the share to be paid by each constituent
authority shall be calculated as if a rate has been made and levied on a rateable property
within the catchment area. Contributions will be assessed as if rated on the basis of an
equalised rateable capital value. Clause 7 validates the deficit shown in the catchment
comraission's account during the period covered to maintain compliance with the Local
Authorities Loans Act 1956.
I trust that the Bill will overcome any anomalies and misunderstandings of the past. The
matter of payment of regional water board rates was decided in the Supreme Court in 1975,
but the cities of Rotorua and Tauranga and the borough of Mt. Maunganui have refused to
pay any contribution in view of an appeal that is set down tentatively for November of this
year. The appeal will be in no way affected by the passage of the Bill. The schedules show
the deficit the commission is trying to cover-namely, $133,012. That is the difference
between the money paid to the commission over the 4 years and the amount of debt that
I would have been incurred if a rate had been set in 1972.
Bill read a second time.
MANUKAU CITY RATING RELIEF BILL
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The Bill
comprises only two clauses. The Manukau City Council was formed in 1965 from the old
Manukau County and Manurewa Borough. Since 1967 the city council has promoted two
local Bills to help resolve rating problems which have beset the substantial rural lands within
the city boundaries. It is now proposed that those local Bills be repealed and that any future
alteration in the incidence of farm land rating in the city be accomplished by means of the
differential rating provisions of the Municipal Corporations Act 1954 as amended in 1976.
The first of the two previous local Bills-introduced in 1967-gave relief only to farmers
close to the urban fringe, where rates levied on that part of the rateable value attributed to
the urban potential were postponed to be written off after 5 years. That empowering Act did
not offer relief to farmers in the outer areas as such lands were not subject to urban
development in the near future. In 1969 a further local Act allowed the occupiers of any farm
land having more than a specified rateable value to apply for a postponement of the rates.
That legislation did not provide an equitable answer, and some bona fide farmers were
paying more in rates than their gross farming profit during the period of low farm prices in
1975. The council now intends to use the differential rating provisions of the Municipal
Corporations Act 1954 to provide relief to those farmer ratepayers.
Differential rating was designed to provide councils with the greatest possible flexibility
in apportioning the rates burden between owners of different types of property, and it is
hoped that it may eventually supersede the various complicated systems of adjusting the
rating incidence now in existence. I support such a move and accept the undertaking given by
the Manukau City Council in its submissions that it will provide absolute relief to the genuine
farmers on a better basis than that provided at present.
Bill read a second time.

Citizenship Bill
The member for Henderson then raised other matters. Let me repeat now, so that it is
on record, that the Supplementary Order Paper members opposite said they had not
received was distributed on 16 September. The Clerk's office is adamant that the
Supplementary Order Paper was given the normal, full distribution, and I hope that

The right of appeal against a refusal of citizenship was another matter raised in the
Committee. Let me put on record that there has never been any such right of appeal; it
would be an undesirable restriction of ministerial discretion. Any aggrieved person can
approach the Minister, and departmental recommendations are subject to scrutiny by the
ombudsman, who looks into the advice given to the Minister. I believe that is sufficient
protection for anyone refused citizenship.
Dealing with the rights of aliens to acquire property, the member for Henderson was
concerned that the restrictions on the rights of aliens in section 3 of the Aliens Act 1948
would lapse for a period through most of the provisions affecting aliens being deleted by the
Supplementary Order Paper. There will be no such gap. As I explained in the Committee,
clause 31 repeats the current restrictions and that clause has had only a minor change made
to it by the Supplementary Order Paper. In any case, section 3 of the Aliens Act and clause
31 of this Bill provide that aliens have the same right to property as have others. As a result
of the Supplementary Order Paper the Aliens Act will be repealed by this Bill as from 1
January 1978. Apart from the deportation processes, which will be incorporated in the
Immigration Act by an Immigration Amendment Bill that is to be introduced for recess
study, any other provisions which need to be continued following the abolition of aliens
registration are incorporated in this, the Citizenship Bill.

Mr WETERE (Western Maori): This Bill consolidates and amends the Potato Growing
Industry Act 1950 and incorporates certain provisions of the Potato Board Election
Regulations 1951 and the Potato Growing Industry Regulations 1951. As was pointed out by
the Minister, the Bill has been around the House and through various Ministers and Under-
Secretaries. The Opposition concurs with most of the provisions in the Bill. However, when
the Bill was reported back from the select committee I gave notice of the Opposition's
intention to move in the Committee of the Whole an amendment to clause 4, which refers to
the composition of the board and, more particularly, board areas. The Minister, in his
second reading speech, referred to the Opposition's intention to do that.
I intend now to elaborate on the submissions made to the select committee. The
Department of Agriculture in its report demonstrates quite clearly that the majority of
organisations support the concept of six wards; for example, Federated Farmers, the Potato

Potato Growers Association, and the Temuka Potato Growers Association. The ministry
also made this comment in its report: "The ministry realises the proposed membership is by
no means ideal, but considers it is a workable compromise which will bring all sectors of the
industry together." Even the ministry itself had some doubts.
Hon. J. B. Bolger: It was a workable compromise
Mr WETERE: Yes, a workable compromise, but I think the inference to be taken is that

Hon. J. B. Bolger: They said the same thing.

viewpoints arise from historical factors as well as an opposing view on the methods for the
disposal of surplus potato supplies. Federated Farmers must express its disappointment that
the two sectors of the industry have not been able to submerge their differences to an extent
which would permit the elimination of separate potato grower bodies. The federation is


## p. 4573 (#679) ###########################################

4573
Potato Growing Industry Bill
concerned that the embodying of these divisions in statute will perpetuate the existing

The federation said that New Zealand should be divided into six wards with the
following boundaries: ward 1, North Auckland and south Auckland; ward 2, Waikato and
Hawke's Bay; ward 3, Rangitikei, Wairarapa, Taranaki, and Ohakune; ward 4, Nelson,

fundamental question of industry representation would render unnecessary the definition of
early and main crop potatoes. The composition of the board as set out in clauses 4 and 5 was
accepted as promoting the best interests of the potato industry, and clause 4(2)(b)(i) and (ii)
would require restructuring to deal with the six representatives to be elected by the potato
growers. Similarly clause 5 would need to be amended by deleting references to sectional
interests and substituting the establishment of the potato grower election system.
The federation also said: "The federation has been placed in a difficult position in
commenting on the provisions of this Bill. While acknowledging that the Bill goes some
distance in bridging the differences between the two sections of the industry, we are
concerned that the compromises embodied in the legislation will, in themselves, serve to
perpetuate the divisions which we consider largely to be unjustified. We make a strong plea
that in the interest of industry unity all parties continue to actively work towards an early
amendment to delete or amend the offending clauses." The Potato Board said that in the
event of its proposal as to membership being unacceptable, the alternative should be the
establishment of six wards, and that provision should be made for representatives of those
wards to be elected by registered potato growers.
I understand that the Temuka Potato Growers Association, which comes from the
electorate of the member for South Canterbury, had some very strong feelings on this
section of the Bill, and its representations were confined generally to that aspect. It said: “A
three-ward system as proposed in the Bill would have geographical and administration
disadvantages in having board members with affiliations to either the Potato Growers
Federation or the Vegetable and Produce Growers Federation on it and that would not be
conducive to the smooth running of the board." It was felt that the grower representatives on
the proposed board should be elected by ballot from six wards within New Zealand, with
each registered grower having one vote. The association felt that for the industry to be
united any reference to early and late crop growers was detrimental, unnecessary, and would
cause undemocratic decisions to be made.
From those remarks in the submissions I believe that there is a case for six wards rather
than the proposed three wards under the provisions of clause 4. Wider representation will
bring about a more congenial atmosphere among board members and in the industry at
large. It is fair to say that all Ministers who have been working towards consolidating the
industry have come up against the same problem. In their concluding remarks the New

principles involved except as will provide for a more practical application of those principles.
We appreciate the opportunity of making submissions, and at the same time thank the
succession of Ministers and Under-Secretaries as well as departmental officers who have

INDUSTRIAL LAW REFORM BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. The Bill contains amendments to four existing Acts, namely, the Industrial Relations


## p. 4581 (#687) ###########################################

17 November
4581
Industrial Law Reform Bill
Act, the Aircrew Industrial Tribunal Act, the Waterfront Industry Act, and the Agricultural
Workers Act. The purpose of the amendments is to create a new arbitration structure. This
does not mean any lessening of emphasis on negotiation and conciliation. Indeed, the
contrary applies, because negotiation and conciliation must precede any arbitration.
The Bill provides for the establishment of a new Arbitration Court to take over the
functions of both the Industrial Court and the Industrial Commission. The total personnel of
the court is to consist of at least three judges and at least two sets of nominated members.
The present Industrial Commission consists of five members, and the present Industrial
Court consists of a judge and one set of nominated members. A normal sitting of the
Arbitration Court is to consist of one judge and one set of nominated members. It will be
possible to have two courts sitting simultaneously, which should reduce delay to a minimum
and enable better geographical coverage. The Bill aims to achieve a fair measure of
consistency between decisions of the various wage settlement tribunals by means of a degree
of common membership.
A clause has been included to clarify the vesting of certain property in the New Zealand
Waterside Workers Federation Industrial Association of Workers. It was at the association's
request, and this is a practical time to include it. The basic structures set out in the Industrial
Law Reform Bill have been approved by the Industrial Relations Council. Certain amend-
ments have already been made to the original proposals as a result of the council's
considerations. The Industrial Relations Council met again on Tuesday, after the Bill had
been introduced, and after it had had a look at it, and recommended a series of changes.
Such of those recommendations as are accepted by the Government will be introduced by
Supplementary Order Paper at the Committee stage. I will refer to the recommendations in
the next few minutes as I deal with the various clauses.
Clause 1 relates to the short title, and is quite straightforward. Clauses 2 to 9 make up
Part I of the Bill, dealing with amendments to the Industrial Relations Act 1973. Clause 3
abolishes the Industrial Commission and repeals Part III of the Industrial Relations Act
1973. Clause 4 replaces Part IV of the Industrial Relations Act 1973 and substitutes new
sections 32 to 62B. This new Part IV deals with the setting up of the Arbitration Court. The
new section 32 establishes the Arbitration Court.
The new section 33 provides that the personnel of the Arbitration Court is to consist of
not less than three judges, plus two or more sets of nominated members. One of the judges is
to be appointed chief judge of the court, and the Supplementary Order Paper will provide
that the chief judge will be the present judge of the Industrial Court. In the printed Bill his
retirement date is 12 months from the commencement of the Act by Order in Council. There
will be a small change in the Supplementary Order Paper spelling out the date as August
1979. I should be happy to discuss with any member opposite the reasons for that. It has
been unanimously accepted by parties who know the reason, and that will be one of the
items appearing in the Supplementary Order Paper. Half of the nominated members are to
be appointed on the nomination of the New Zealand Employers Federation, and the other
half on the nomination of the Federation of Labour.
The new section 34 re-enacts an existing provision. The new sections 35 and 36 provide
for purely machinery matters. The new section 37 provides for the appointment of judges of
the Arbitration Court, who shall be barristers or solicitors of at least 7 years' standing-the
same status as for the Supreme Court. The new sections 38 and 39 deal with administrative
matters. The new section 40 authorises the appointment of temporary judges in certain
circumstances. The new section 41 provides for the appointment and retirement of the
nominated members. The Bill at present provides for these to be career appointments with
retirement at age 72. On Tuesday, the Industrial Relations Council recommended that the
term of appointment should be 5 years, which will be renewable. The age of retirement is to
remain the same, at 72. I should say that the Industrial Relations Council requested that in
changing from the longer term to one of 5 years renewable by the nominating parties, or with
the nominating parties being consulted, a superannuation scheme should be looked at by the
Government with a view to adding to the attractiveness of a career appointment. I suppose it
could be likened to members of Parliament, who are covered in another Act, but the
Government has undertaken to look at a superannuation scheme for nominated members.
The new sections 42 and 43 enable the appointment of acting nominated members. The new
sections 44 to 47 substantially re-enact existing provisions. The new section 48 spells out the
jurisdiction of the Arbitration Court, which will be a combination of the jurisdiction of the
former Industrial Court and Industrial Commission. The court's jurisdiction will be
protected from challenge except on narrow jurisdictional grounds. The new sections 49 and


## p. 4582 (#688) ###########################################

4582
17 November
Industrial Law Reform Bill
50 re-enact existing provisions. The new section 51 is a modified version of an existing
provision. It gives the judge the right during the course of proceedings to refer the matter to
the Court of Appeal for its opinion. It will be noted—and I think the member for Henderson
will be interested-that any such reference will be to the Court of Appeal, not the Supreme
Court. We see the Arbitration Court as having slightly less jurisdiction than, but something
of the same status as, the Supreme Court. There was a suggestion that the right of appeal
should lie to the Supreme Court, but we have decided to make it the Court of Appeal.
The new section 52 relates to the sittings of the court. A sitting of the court will consist
of a judge, one member who has been appointed on the nomination of the New Zealand
Employers Federation, and one member who has been appointed on the nomination of the
Federation of Labour. There will be an addition to this part of the Bill as a result of the
deliberations on Tuesday. When a dispute of interest is to be heard by the court, any one of
the parties to the dispute of interest will be able to call for a full court hearing, which it is
recommended will consist of the judge, plus four nominated members-the judge, plus two
from each side. That was a request from the Industrial Relations Council on Tuesday; it was
accepted by the Government today, and will be on the Supplementary Order Paper that will
be brought into the House and circulated as soon as we can get it out.
The new section 53 re-enacts the existing law relating to the quorum and the decision of
the court. The Industrial Relations Council has recommended that the parties to disputes of
interest should have the right for matters in the dispute of interest to be heard by a full court.
The new section 54 re-enacts the substance of the existing law relating to the appearance and
representation of a party to any proceedings before the court. The new sections 55 to 62 are
really re-enactments of existing provisions. The new section 62A provides for appeals to the
Court of Appeal on questions of law only. The new section 62B enables the Court of Appeal,
instead of deciding the appeal itself, to give advice to the Arbitration Court to enable it to
reconsider the matters to which the appeal relates.
Clause 5 substitutes a new subsection (6) in section 124A of the Industrial Relations Act
1973. It clarifies the provisions relating to the enforcement of disputes procedures. Clauses 6
to 8 cover consequential amendments, repeals, and transitional provisions. Clause 9 clarifies
the vesting of the property of the Waterside Workers Federation Industrial Association of
Workers, alluded to earlier.
We come then to the Industrial Relations Council's recommendations and the extension
of section 118 of the old Act, relating to the interpretation of awards and collective
agreements. We propose to give the Arbitration Court the power to decide on the validity of
collective agreements. At one stage it was just to be on the interpretation, but now it can
decide on the validity. That has been accepted by the Government, and will be covered by
the amendments brought forward in the Supplementary Order Paper.
Clauses 10 to 12 make up Part II of the Bill, and provide for amendments to the Aircrew
Industrial Tribunal Act 1971. Clause 11 provides for the replacement of the existing one-man
Aircrew Industrial Tribunal, at a date to be arranged, by a judge of the Industrial Court. We
have had consultations with the parties concerned since the introduction of the Bill, and at
their request the Supplementary Order Paper to be considered in the Committee stage will
include a proposed amendment to replace the one-man tribunal with a judge of the
Arbitration Court plus a set of nominated members. It will therefore equate the Waterfront
Industry Tribunal, the Agricultural Tribunal, and other similar bodies. I am glad to report
that we had unanimous agreement from the parties on that proposal. We left the choice to
them; they asked for that alteration, and the Government has agreed to it.
Clauses 13 to 17 make up Part III of the Bill. They provide for minor amendments to the
Waterfront Industry Act 1976 and replace the present chairman of the Waterfront Industry
Tribunal with a judge of the Arbitration Court. Clauses 18 to 20 make up Part IV of the Bill.
They provide for amendments to the Agricultural Workers Act 1977 and require that a judge
of the Arbitration Court shall be the president of the Agricultural Workers Tribunal. The
four schedules set out consequential amendments to the Industrial Relations Act and other
enactments.
Having given a technical description of the Bill, there remains but one thing to be said. I
commenced my second reading speech by indicating that the Bill has come into the House
after negotiation and conciliation. No one would pretend that the Bill, if it is passed, will
provide the perfect answer to industrial relations in New Zealand. I do not think any
enactment passed by this House, whichever Government is in power, will achieve that end. I
believe the Bill will work only if it has the complete confidence of the various parties that
comprise the dissenting groups in industrial strife in New Zealand.

GENERAL WAGE ORDERS BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. Members will be aware that for some years past the operation of the General Wage
Orders Act 1969 has been suspended by regulations made under the authority of the
Economic Stabilisation Act 1948. Of course, it has been suspended under both Govern-
ments. The purpose of the present Bill is twofold. First, it revokes parts of the Wage
Adjustment Regulations, and thereby abolishes the wage hearing tribunal established under
those regulations, which had a general wage order hearing last year. Secondly, it restores the
General Wage Orders Act in an amended form. These two purposes are part of the
Government's wider plan to accomplish a restructuring of the wage settlement tribunals, and
a relaxation of Government controls over wage bargaining. That, I think, should be
welcomed.
The basis of the Bill is to provide a system for either of the central organisations under
the Industrial Relations Act, namely the Federation of Labour and the Employers Federa-
tion, to apply to a tribunal for a general wage order. The tribunal will be the Arbitration
Court established under the Industrial Law Reform Bill, with which we have just dealt. It
will consist of three persons: the chief judge of the Arbitration Court, plus one employers'
nominated member, and one workers' nominated member. It is proposed that when we call
for nominations we shall call initially for a senior nomination, and the other nominated team


## p. 4588 (#694) ###########################################

4588
17 November
General Wage Orders Bill
can act as deputies if need be, but in that way we achieve our first arbitration court for a
general wage order hearing when necessary.
The Industrial Relations Council supports the basic proposals contained in the Bill. In
particular, the Government has accepted the recommendation of the council as to the
composition of the tribunal that will hear applications and make orders. Further questions
relating to this Bill were raised at a meeting of the Industrial Relations Council this week,
but I must report faithfully to the House that the council could not reach agreement on the
issues discussed. The views of the parties are under consideration by the Government at
present, but only a small change may be made to the Bill in relation to those aspects.
Clause 1 is the short title and commencement. Clause 2 is the definition clause. It
provides that for the purposes of the Bill the word "award" shall include awards or
agreements under the Agricultural Workers Act 1977. They are brought in for the first time.
Clause 3 spells out the general purpose of the Act. It provides for the Arbitration Court to
make just and equitable reviews of the rates of remuneration in awards and collective
agreements. In making such reviews, the Arbitration Court will be required to give
paramount importance to the economic stability of New Zealand.
Clause 4 deals with the constitution, procedure, and jurisdiction of the Arbitration
Court in making general wage orders. The court may appoint a solicitor, counsel, or other
expert to assist it-and I emphasise the word "assist”-in dealing with applications for
general wage orders. In clause 5, provision is made to enable either the Employers
Federation or the Federation of Labour to apply to the court for a general order. In this
respect, the clause follows the equivalent provision in the Wage Adjustment Regulations,
rather than the 1969 Act, which allows applications by any union or association of employers
or workers. The clause retains the requirement for intervals of at least 6 months between
orders.
Clause 6 spells out the matters to be taken into account by the court in deciding on a
general wage order application. The paramount consideration is the economic stability of
New Zealand. The court is required also to consider whether an increase should be granted
to maintain living standards, and to consider the maintenance and promotion of industrial
harmony. We were requested to make some change in priority there. My feeling is that it
may amount to semantics, but I am looking at that before we go into the Committee stage. It
is to have regard to exports, and, above all, full employment. The court will also consider
movements in the consumer price index, and other matters it thinks relevant. These criteria
are an amalgam of the existing provisions under the 1969 Act and the Wage Adjustment
Regulations, which were tried out for a general wage order last year.
Clause 7 requires the court, before making a general wage order, to give an opportunity
to be heard to representatives of the Federation of Labour, the Employers Federation, the
Combined State Service Organisations, and the Minister of Finance. There was some
disagreement about whether it should be the Minister of Finance. In the regulations last year
it read as the Minister of Labour, and the Minister of Labour made an appointment that was
referred to as the "Minister's man". It is suggested that fundamentally the Minister of
Labour should deal with industrial relations and industrial harmony, and not offend people
by participating in a general wage order, in which there is sometimes a degree of conflict, or
at least opposition.
Clause 8 re-enacts an existing provision. Clause 9 spells out three cases to which general
orders will not apply. These are: first, rates of commission and similar payments; secondly,
rates of incentive or bonus payments; and thirdly, awards and collective agreements having
State linkage clauses. This clause derives partly from a provision in the Wage Adjustment
Regulations, and partly from the old 1969 Act. Clauses 10 to 12 are largely re-enactments of
existing provisions. Clause 13 relates to the duration of general wage orders.
A subsequent award or agreement can be drawn so as to have the effect of ending the
application of a general order to that award or agreement. Clauses 14 and 15 are re-
enactments of existing provisions from regulations and the Act. Clauses 16 to 18 make
consequential and transitional provisions. Basically, the Bill follows fundamentally on the
criteria set out last year in regulations, on which a general wage order hearing has been
based. The personnel who heard it last year are changed to the extent of two, unless the two
who heard it last year are nominated by the nominating parties. Otherwise, the same
chairman will adjudicate.

The 1953 regulations read: "In making a general order the Court shall take into account

"paramount", making it the primary consideration of the court, whereas in the other general

affecting finance, trade, and industry." The other criteria are then listed, having an equal
basis and asking the court to take them into account. The main change in the present
legislation is that the Court must give paramount importance to the protection of the
economic stability of New Zealand. That first section supersedes all the criteria below it,
because the court is asked to give it paramount importance. It does not say that the court

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I move, That the Social Security
Amendment Bill (No. 2) be introduced. This Bill makes a number of changes to the Social
Security Act. Most of the changes are of a machinery nature, but I should like to draw
members' attention to a number of the more important ones. Clause 2 will remove an
anomaly in the national superannuation scheme whereby a married person with an un-
qualified spouse receiving the married couple rate of national superannuation subject to an
income test receives less cash in hand than a married couple, both of whom are qualified for
national superannuation. The reason for the anomaly is the differing tax liability for two
categories of superannuitants.
Under clause 3, half the amount of national superannuation payable under section 16 of
the Social Security Act to a married person with a non-qualified spouse will be paid to the
unqualified spouse, and that half will be regarded as the unqualified spouse's income for tax
purposes. This will have the effect of reducing the couple's tax liability and placing them in


## p. 4603 (#709) ###########################################

18 November
4603
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
the same cash-in-hand position as a married couple who are both qualified for national
superannuation in their own right.
Clause 5 implements a recommendation of the recent Domestic Purposes Benefit
Review Committee. Under the present provisions of the Act, a domestic purposes
beneficiary can qualify automatically for continuation of her benefit after her youngest or
only child ceases to be dependent irrespective of how old she is at that time. The review
committee considered that this automatic entitlement should be abolished on the ground
that beneficiaries without dependants can be expected to join the work force unless their age
is such that it would be unreasonable to expect them to take up employment. The
Government agrees with the views of the review committee, and clause 5 withdraws, as from
1 April 1978, the right of a woman alone with no dependent children to a domestic purposes
benefit, unless she becomes a woman alone after reaching the age of 50. Such a woman will,
of course, be entitled to a sickness or unemployment benefit, subject to normal conditions.
The existing rights of a woman alone to the domestic purposes benefit are preserved, which
means that the new provisions will apply only to those beneficiaries whose youngest or only
child ceases to be dependent after 1 April next.
Clause 20 legislates for the Government's recently announced decision to pay an
additional $25 for each dependent child for whom the family benefit, the orphan's benefit, or
the child's war pension is payable. These additional payments, which are to be paid on 29
November, will be of material assistance to families faced with additional expenses over the
Christmas period, and are further evidence of the Government's concern to ease the
financial difficulties being experienced by people with dependent children. Clauses 17 and 18
validate the increases in the rate of social security benefit in January and July 1977 in
accordance with the Government's policy of reviewing benefit rates every 6 months in line
with movements in the consumer price index.
Part II of the Bill deals with increases in medical benefits and other related benefits. As
from 1 January 1978, the general medical services benefit payable for children in receipt of a
family benefit will increase as follows-consultation at surgery during normal hours: an
increase of $1.75 to $4.75; visit to a patient during normal hours: an increase of $2 to a new
total of $6; urgent consultation at surgery at night, weekends, and public holidays: an
increase of $1 to a new total of $7; and an urgent visit to a patient at night, weekends, or
public holidays: an increase of $1 to a new total of $8.
Clause 25 provides for travelling fees, previously known as "mileage fees", to be fixed
by Order in Council. This clause will come into force on 1 January next. Clause 26 amends
the principal Act relating to specialist medical services and will come into force on 1 January
1978. It increases specialist medical services benefits as follows-for the first occasion on
which specialist medical services are provided by a specialist, physician, psychiatrist, or
neurologist: an increase from the present $5 to a total of $20; for services provided for a child
in receipt of a family benefit: an increase from the present $3.50 to a total of $10; and for
services not specified above: an increase from $3.50 to $5. For each subsequent occasion
related to the first occasion on which specialist medical services are provided, the fee for a
child in receipt of a family benefit is increased from $3 to $4.75. There is no increase for
persons other than children. The benefit remains at $3 for patients who are beneficiaries or
pensioners, and $1.25 for other persons.

18 November
Social Security Amendment Bill (No. 2)
In the 1976 Budget, a substantial taxation concession worth $6 a week for those on
lower incomes was introduced for families with children under 5 years of age. In the 1977
Budget that concession was increased to $9 a week for children under 5 years, and there was
also a concession for families with children under 10 years of age if there was only one
income. That was worth $4 a week; so, all in all, the concessions given are equivalent to $13 a
week, and that excludes the 5 percent across-the-board income tax reduction in the mini-
Budget. We believe this is a more effective way of assisting the family unit than merely
increasing the family benefit.
The member for Southern Maori referred to clause 2, which amends the definition of
the principal Act to make it clear that war pensions granted under the War Pensions Act are
to be regarded as income for social security purposes. The definition of income in section 3
of the Act is amended to make it clear that war service pensions granted under the War
Pensions Act are treated in the same way as war veterans' allowances and war economic
pensions in assessing social security benefits. Section 72 of the Act provides that a social
security benefit cannot be paid in addition to a war veteran's allowance, a war service
pension, or a war economic pension. In fact, there is no change to the existing Act; the Bill
merely clarifies the position.
The member for Southern Maori also referred to clause 3, which relates to an alteration
in taxation if there is a non-qualified wife. At present the Act provides that when a man
applies for national superannuation on behalf of his non-qualified wife—that is, a wife who
does not qualify in her own right for national superannuation-the total benefit is paid to the
man and is treated as income, and he is taxed as a married man. Alternatively, when both
husband and wife qualify in their own right, the married couple rate of national superannua-
tion is divided equally between them, and they are taxed as single people. The difference in
the rate of taxation is $2.49 a week. This was not intended when the Act was introduced;
therefore this amendment corrects an acknowledged anomaly. It will come into effect as
from 1 April next.
The member also referred to the collection of maintenance, and wondered whether
anything was being done to rectify the matter. Something is being done, but this is a matter
for the Department of Justice. I assure the honourable member that the Government has
done a tremendous amount of study on this, and that some novel methods of collecting
maintenance have been worked out and will be introduced shortly.
The member for Wanganui commented that this was an opportunity to come to grips
with matters of social concern. He said he thought the Bill was a backward step. Anyone
who reads the Bill from cover to cover will see that practically every clause provides either
for an improvement in the method of payment to beneficiaries or an increase in benefits of
one kind or another. I wonder why the member for Wanganui believes it is a backward step
to give people better benefits and to provide them with improved conditions?
The member for Mangere asked whether the Bill had been introduced in response to
our election promise to increase the allowance for dependent children by $1.25 a week. No,
that is not in this measure, but I can assure the honourable member that it will be covered in
other legislation to be introduced shortly. The member for Mangere also raised a valid point
about the length of time it takes for a maintenance order claim to be heard. I acknowledge
that there is a large waiting list at present, but I assure him that the novel methods I have
referred to, which will be introduced shortly, will overcome the problem.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Are you going to do away with the hearings?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No. The seven lawyers on the caucus committee, and the
departmental officers who dealt with the matter, believe that the new measures will bring
about a big improvement, and will result in a substantial increase in the amount of
maintenance that is collected That is a matter for the Department of Justice, which, I can
assure honourable members, has it well under control.
The member for Mangere then referred to clause 5 and asked how a woman who has
brought up a family can return to the work force when her children cease to be dependent
upon her. The Bill provides that this clause applies only to women who are under 50 years of
age. Indeed, the main thinking behind the provision was that if a girl aged 15 or 16 had an ex-
nuptial child and decided to keep it-and she would be entitled to a domestic purposes
benefit if she had taken out a maintenance order against the father of the child-she would
be only 30 or 31 years of age when the child ceased to be dependent on her. The Horn
committee recommended that when a child ceased to be dependent the mother should be
helped to return to the work force. However, if a woman is over 50 years of age when her
youngest child ceases to be dependent, that provision will not apply.
