WAR PENSIONS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister in Charge of War Pensions): I move, That the War
Pensions Amendment Bill be introduced. The purpose of the Bill is to validate increases in the
rates of war pensions in 1977, and also to validate the special additional payments made to
income-tested war beneficiaries in December 1976. The rates of income-tested war pensions
have been increased twice this year. They are the war, economic, and wife's pensions, the
war veteran's allowances, and the war service pensions. The rates of those pensions were
increased from 12 January 1977 by $3.64 a week for married couples, and by $2.18 a week for
single pensioners. The second increase was from 27 July 1977, when the married couple's
rate was increased by $4.84 a week, and the rate for single pensioners was increased by $2.90
a week. The Bill validates both those increases.
War disablement and war widows' pensions that are not income tested are reviewed at 1
April each year in accordance with an agreement between the Government and the New
Zealand Returned Services Association on the basis of movements in the consumer price
index. The review at 1 April 1977 resulted in an increase in pensions for total disablement of
$3.55 a week to $29.45 a week. Pensions for other degrees of disablement were increased
proportionately. War widows' pensions were increased by $2.65 a week to $21.75. Clothing
allowances for pensioners who have lost a limb as a result of service in the forces were also
increased from 1 April 1977. The Bill validates those increases. Finally, the Bill validates the
special additional payments made to income-tested war pensioners in December 1976. The
additional payments were equivalent to 1 week's pension.

PRIMARY PRODUCTS MARKETING AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture): I move, That the Primary
Products Marketing Amendment Bill be introduced. This is a small four-clause Bill, with one
substantive clause. The Primary Products Marketing Act 1953 authorises the making of
regulations establishing a wide range of producer-controlled marketing authorities and
setting out their powers, functions, and responsibilities. One of the bodies established by
regulations under the Act is the Egg Marketing Authority, whose responsibility it is to
ensure an adequate supply of eggs on the New Zealand market. As a means of stabilising
production, the authority operates a licensing scheme that establishes the number of birds a
poultry farmer is entitled to farm.
Recent advances in disease control and bird strains have resulted in a substantial
increase in eggs produced from each flock, so reducing the total number of birds required to
meet national egg requirements. Because world prices are below New Zealand production
costs and losses result if surplus production is sold overseas, egg production is basically
restricted to local market needs. That is the basis of the problem faced by the New Zealand
industry. It is almost impossible to export eggs or egg pulp at a profit. The poultry industry
has recognised this factor of overproduction and has imposed reductions of up to 20 percent
on licensed bird numbers, but further reductions in the national flock are still necessary.
The Bill empowers the making of regulations allowing the egg marketing authority to
buy from poultry farmers and cancel surplus entitlement licences. This provision has been
requested by the industry, and the funds to purchase these entitlements and then cancel
them will be provided by the industry itself. The industry has asked the Government to take
a responsible approach in seeking provision for additional regulation-making powers. This
gives the Egg Marketing Authority the capacity to regulate the production of eggs at a level
in keeping with New Zealand demand. That is the substantive purpose of the Bill.
Section 3(6) of the Act provides that regulations made pursuant to that Act are to be
tabled within 28 days if Parliament is in session, or within 28 days of the start of the ensuing
session. Regulations tabled pursuant to section 3(6) and to section 4 are to be validated or
passed during the session in which they were tabled. This provision has caused some
problems with sessions such as the 1-day session in February 1977, when it was not practical
to table regulations or to validate or confirm them by an Act. Accordingly, clause 2(2)
amends section 3(6) so that regulations made purusant to the principal Act are to be tabled
within 16 sitting days after being promulgated. The regulations still need to be validated or
confirmed as before. This is a technical amendment that allows the same time, but the time
will not be interrupted by small or 1-day sessions. Sixteen working days are equivalent to 4
weeks of Parliament, or 28 days. There are further minor amendments to do with the
validating and confirming of regulations, and one inserted at the request of the Audit Office.
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson): I rise to ask the Minister a few questions about this Bill
because I am not convinced of the need for its introduction. The Minister has not justified
any real need for it. Clause 2(1) provides for regulations to be made authorising the
marketing authority to acquire, whether by compulsory purchase or otherwise, licences,
issued in the past by that marketing authority, entitling the person to whom they were issued
to keep certain hens and ducks for the production of eggs for sale. That in itself justifies the
need for this Bill to go to a select committee. The Minister has not told us that it will go to a
select committee, and I suspect that it will not go. That seems to be the case with so much
legislation this Government puts before us.
The Minister has played the Bill down as machinery legislation, but it threatens the
security of the people in the poultry industry. As my colleague the member for Onehunga
has said, it is eroding their security. Here we are giving the Egg Marketing Authority power
to take away licences by compulsory purchase, and also to cancel licences. People's freedoms
are being eroded continually by the National Administration, but that approach is typical of
the Government. It is governing by fear and insecurity, and egg production will be affected.
The Government is just injecting a little more fear and insecurity into that area. The purpose
of the Bill is to give greater powers to the Egg Marketing Authority, and, as I have said, it
will give the authority power to purchase licences compulsorily, or cancel them, resulting in
further control of the production of eggs.
Mr Lithgow: What would you do with the surplus?
Mr COURTNEY: Here we have the Government asking the alternative Government
what it should do with the surplus. I will tell the member in a moment what we will do with
the surplus.

Employment and Pay Between Christmas and New Year
2. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert) asked the Minister of Labour: Is there anything to
prevent employers laying off staff 2 weeks prior to Christmas to avoid having to pay them for
the 4 days between Christmas and New Year, and has an employer any obligations if he re-
employs the same workers during January?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I reply on behalf of the Minister of
Labour. There is nothing to prevent any employer terminating the services of an employee at
any time provided he is justified in doing so and complies with the provisions of the relevant
award or collective agreement on termination. If a worker is unjustifiably dismissed the
personal grievance provision of the Industrial Relations Act would have application. Most
awards and collective agreements and the Factories Act 1946 provide that workers become
entitled to payment for any statutory holiday if they have been employed at any time during
the fortnight ending on the day the holiday occurs. Any worker not employed during the
period does not become entitled to payment for any such holiday. If any dismissed worker is
re-engaged after the holidays the employer would have no obligation in respect of the
statutory holidays involved, but that is subject to the condition that the worker would qualify
for payment if he were employed at any time in the 14 days before the statutory holiday.
Hon. W. W. Freer: As I have been advised that some manufacturers, disturbed by their
present liquidity problems, are considering such action, would the Minister be prepared to
ask them to honour their normal employment commitments?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Obviously that question should be commented on by the
Minister of Labour, but if the member has any authentication of what he advances as a
rumour I am sure the Minister would want to know and would be very concerned about it.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Ironsand Processing
4. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Has the
technology developed by New Zealand Steel Ltd for the processing of ironsand been
adequately protected by patent rights, and is any benefit likely to accrue to New Zealand
from the application of this technology by overseas steel makers who are now seeking to
exploit the local process?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry): I
reply on behalf of the Minister. Licence fees and patent rights for the process used by New
Zealand Steel Ltd are covered adequately by reciprocal agreements by that company and the
proprietors of the process, whereby improvements made to the process and the benefits
arising therefrom are shared between the parties. In addition, New Zealand Steel Ltd
receives benefits accruing from operating know-how acquired by it during the development
of the process. These benefits include financial returns from fees charged for information,
access, advisory services, and manpower training supplied to such countries as Indonesia, El
Salvador, Columbia, and Japan.

development of this technology and its application overseas?

have the information with me. If the questioner wants to ask the Minister that question I am

15. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister for the Environment: Has he seen

discharge?

Evening Post of 10 November. The sulphide that caused the death of the herrings originated

facilities for all the industrial wastes to be passed into the trade and waste sewer rather than,

WOOL INDUSTRY BILL
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Commit-
tee to present the report of the committee on the Wool Industry Bill. The committee
recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table. The main purpose of the Bill is to provide for the amalgamation of the present
Wool Board and the Wool Marketing Corporation into a new board to be called the New
Zealand Wool Board. The merger was widely supported by those who made submissions to
the committee. Certainly, none of the 14 submissions received and studied opposed the
proposed amalgamation.
The Bill contains little that is new. Mainly, it incorporates the provisions of the Wool
Marketing Corporation Act 1972 and the key provisions governing wool income stabilisation
from the Wool Income Stabilisation Regulations 1976. Most of the provisions were therefore
given full consideration by the committee in 1972. For that reason there are few significant
amendments to the Bill proposed by the committee, although there are a number of minor
drafting changes proposed as the result of the examination by the committee in the light of
the submissions made. The amendments proposed in no way alter the intent of the Bill.
Many are simply refinements to clarify certain points.
The committee gave deep consideration, as it did in 1972 on the Wool Marketing
Corporation Bill, to the referendum provisions relating to the introduction of Part V on
annual pooling and marketing of wool. In their submissions, several grower organisations
expressed concern that a referendum could be sprung on growers without sufficient warning.
The committee, while considering such an event unlikely, concluded that it would not be
unreasonable to require the board to give some notice of a referendum, in order that the
question of the introduction of Part V could be fully debated within the industry, thereby
allowing sufficient time for each individual grower to reach a view on the matter. Accord-
ingly, the committee proposes an amendment requiring the board to give 3 months' notice of
the date on which it intends to hold a referendum.
Several submissions were received on the composition of the directorate of the
proposed board. The committee recognised that there are many people and many members
of different organisations who could make a worth-while contribution to the industry should
they be directors of the board. Against this, however, the committee considered that for the
business of the board to be conducted efficiently, the directorate must be of a manageable


## p. 4627 (#733) ###########################################

18 November
4627
Wool Industry Bill
size. Many submissions welcomed the concept of a producer board on which growers with
considerable interest in the future of the industry are represented by six grower directors.
The committee concluded that the composition of the directorate as provided in the Bill
should not be changed.
The method of appointment of directors to fill extraordinary vacancies among the
grower directors did not arise in 1972 with the Wool Marketing Corporation Bill. Grower
directors of the corporation are members of the present Wool Board. The proposed new
board, however, will have grower directors elected by the electoral committee. The Bill
provides for the remaining grower directors to nominate a person to be appointed as a
director to fill a vacancy left by a vacating grower director. As a result of submissions, the
committee proposed an amendment providing for extraordinary vacancies among grower
directors to be filled by election in the normal manner when the residue of the term is 1 year
or more. When the residue of the term is less than 1 year and hence an election is not
practical, the vacancy could be filled on the nomination of the remaining grower directors.
Several submissions were received by the committee concerning the power of the board
to control the sale, disposal and export of wool. The need for the board to have the power to
prohibit certain activities was questioned. The committee examined the matter carefully,
and was convinced that the board needs the power to achieve any degree of control when
other avenues, such as agreement with concerned parties, fail. The committee gave a good
deal of consideration to the inclusion or exclusion of dag wool from the three levies, and
eligibility for minimum price protection. It concluded that such wool should be excluded
from the levy and such protection in view of the relative unimportance of the wool, the
problems that could arise from its inclusion, and the improbability of dag wool receiving
minimum price supplementation because of the way it is sold. The committee therefore
proposes an amendment to the appropriate clause to exclude dag wool.
The committee proposes a further amendment to the provisions relating to the
minimum price scheme as it affects privately sold wool, the importance of which has
increased over the last decade. The committee proposes that privately sold greasy wool
should always be eligible for minimum price protection, provided that the wool is appraised
by the board at certain designated collection points. The amendment will provide added
security for growers who sell their wool privately-for instance, to grower co-operatives. At
present such protection is provided only when the Minister of Agriculture so approves.
The committee received several submissions on Part IV, which relates to the individual
grower income levy retention scheme. Some thought the provisions of the scheme should be
retained in regulations under the Economic Stabilisation Act 1948, and others thought they
should be included in a new and separate Act altogether. The committee considered that this
part should remain in the Bill because it was a portion of the wool income stabilisation
package agreed to with the industry last year, and that it should remain with the other
portion of that package, which constitutes Part III of the Bill. Much consideration was given
to whether or not money held in the retention account, over which a security is held, should
be paid at the end of the retention period to the grower who originally paid the grower
retention levy, or to the holder of that security. The committee proposed an amendment to
the Bill providing for refunds from the retention account to be paid only to the grower who
originally paid the levy, or to his estate or successor as the case may be. That will maintain
the present position, provided by the Wool Income Stabilisation Regulations 1976.
With the passing of the Bill the new board will achieve greater administrative efficiency
than has been possible under the structure of divided responsibility. It will facilitate greater
co-ordination among the research, marketing and promotional activities of the wool industry
generally. It will give the growers a single statutory producer-controlled board, responsible
for their industry-a board through which growers can become more directly involved in the
marketing of their product. The future direction of the industry will be a matter that growers
themselves ultimately decide.

Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I shall reply very briefly to the remarks made by the

growers. That is democratic; it is the way the industry wants it, and the way it will have it.

Queen Elizabeth the Second National Trust Board Bill
QUEEN ELIZABETH THE SECOND NATIONAL TRUST BOARD BILL
Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Commit-
tee to present the report of the committee on the Queen Elizabeth the Second National
Trust Board Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as
amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. The Queen Elizabeth the Second
National Trust Board Bill substantially enacts the National Government's 1975 election
promise to establish a national trust to ensure that sufficient open space is provided for the
needs of New Zealanders. The trust will formulate its own open space policies, and
encourage their acceptance. It will also encourage the co-ordination of existing agencies with
responsibilities for open space.
Before the introduction of the Bill, extensive discussions were held with Federated
Farmers about incorporating the principles of their similar Heritage Trust proposal into the
National Trust, and this was successfully achieved. In those discussions, and also in the
interdepartmental discussions, the need was stressed for the trust to be an independent
statutory body using government agencies for administration and servicing. The committee
received 18 submissions, only one of which was opposed to the legislation in its present form.
This confirms the considerable consensus of agreement on the principles set out in the Bill.
Notwithstanding this general agreement, very helpful suggestions were put forward and the
committee has recommended minor amendments to seven clauses. The enthusiasm of the
committee for the concept of the trust was matched by those making submissions.
Mr WETERE (Western Maori): The Bill is the result of the work of the committee, and
the great assistance given by the Opposition. A major amendment deals with land donated
to the trust. A new subclause (3) is to be added to clause 21: "Notwithstanding paragraph (b)
of subsection (2) of this section, where any land has been transferred to the trust by way of
gift, the board shall not dispose of that land by way of sale or exchange unless it has first
offered the land, on such terms and conditions as the board thinks fit, to the donor or (in the
case of a gift of Maori land) to the descendants of the donor.” That amendment is very
important, because the original donors or beneficiaries will now have the right to take back
land if the trust has no further use for it for the purpose for which it was donated. That has
considerably tidied up the Bill.
Motion agreed to.

Mutual Insurance Amendment Bill
MUTUAL INSURANCE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill amends the Mutual Insurance Act 1955 to provide statutory authority
for the merger of mutual insurance associations, and is prompted by the wish of the only two
mutual insurance associations to merge their businesses and provide a more efficient service
for the insurance needs of the agricultural sector. Clause 2 amends the definition of Minister,
and reflects the transfer of the administration of the Act to the Department of Justice so that
all insurance legislation will be administered by the one department. Clause 3 amends the
power of an association to hold shares in a company if, among other things, all members, or
all members excepting one, are associations or trustees of associations. The two associations
are the only members of a private company requiring at least two members. As a result of
the merger there will be only one mutual insurance association, so it is necessary to allow
some other person to become the second member of the company. The member for
Henderson raised that on the introduction. I wish to confirm that the intention is that this
second member will be an officer of the remaining larger association, and that he will hold
only one share.
Clause 4 increases the maximum number of directors that an association may have from
12 to 14 to allow for regional representation, and clause 5 authorises an association to make
rules providing for regional representation on its board of directors. Both these clauses will
meet the wish of the two associations that the members throughout the country of the
remaining larger association be assured of representation on the board of directors. Clause 6
provides for the merger of associations if each association passes a resolution authorising its
board of directors to effect the merger. This clause refers to resolutions passed before the
clause came into force because the necessary resolutions were passed at meetings of the two
associations last year, and no point is seen in requiring the associations to repeat that
exercise. Clause 7 makes several further amendments needed to complete the removal of the
administration of the Act to the Department of Justice.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The Opposition has carefully examined the Bill,
and has not found anything objectionable in it. Accordingly it does not propose to take up
the time of the House in a debate that would be to no purpose. Certain minor questions were
raised on the introduction. They have now been satisfactorily answered, and I propose to let
the matter rest.
Bill read a second time.
ALCOHOLIC LIQUOR ADVISORY COUNCIL AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As I said when introducing this short Bill, its main purpose is to make adequate
provision for the collection of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council's levy from winemak-
ers. Clause 2 provides that, for the purposes of the sections of the principal Act relating to
the payment and collection of the council's levy from winemakers, the amount of wine sold
shall be the same as the amount sold in the preceding statistical year. As the principal Act
stands at present, winemakers would be required to pay their council levy early in each
financial year on sales figures for that entire year. That is unworkable, and the proposed
amendment overcomes the problem and has the support of the Wine Institute of New
Zealand.
Clauses 3 and 4 relate to amendments sought by the council itself. These two clauses will
permit the council to subsidise staff superannuation schemes and operate subsidiary bank
accounts, as well as permitting unauthorised expenditure of up to $500 in any financial year.
Clause 5 excludes exported liquor from the figures used for calculating the council's levy.
This is in line with the Government's view that exported liquor should be exempt from both
the calculation and payment of the council's levy. This view is fully supported by the Wine
Institute.
Clause 6 deals with exemptions from the council's levy. The council's levy in respect of
beer and spirits will be payable at the same time as excise or beer duty is paid. The intention
of the clause is that if no such duty is payable the council levy need not be paid. This is
because no machinery provisions for the collection of the council's levy in such cases will
exist. In addition to exported liquor, liquor such as navy rum—and I might add that the


## p. 4631 (#737) ###########################################

18 November
4631
Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council Amendment Bill
Royal New Zealand Navy is the only navy with a rum issue-and liquor purchased by
diplomatic personnel will be exempt from the council's levy. I am advised that the definition
of customs duty in the Customs Act is not sufficiently wide to give effect to the intention of
clause 6. Therefore, I propose to introduce a Supplementary Order Paper during the
Committee stage to make it quite clear that customs duty includes excise duty, beer duty,
and sales tax as well as customs duty under the Customs Act.

EDUCATION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. The Bill contains 10 clauses and makes a number of miscellaneous changes to
the Education Act 1964. These are necessary to bring various sections of the Education Act
up to date, and to provide improvements to present education policy. Clause 2 deals with the
Chatham Islands. Under the provisions of the present Act, schools in the Chatham Islands
are administered directly by the department as if they were Maori schools, even though there
are no longer any Maori schools as such. The Bill will include the Chatham Islands in the
Canterbury Education Board district for administrative purposes, this provision to come into
effect on a date to be appointed by Order in Council after the necessary arrangements have
been agreed upon between the department and the board.
At present, a member of a secondary schools council vacates that office if he is
convicted of an offence punishable by imprisonment. Clause 3 brings this provision into line
with similar provisions in the Act relating to education boards and teachers college councils.
It provides that a person is to vacate office only if he is convicted of an offence punishable by
a term of imprisonment of 2 years or more, or if he is actually sentenced to imprisonment.
Clause 4 relates to the provision in secondary schools of some of the forms of technical
education at present provided by technical institutes. The governing body of any specified
secondary school may be authorised by the Minister to offer classes and courses in technical
subjects to persons who are not enrolled as students at that school. Provision is also made for
the setting up of a special committee to advise an authorised controlling authority on the
classes and courses to be offered. Each special committee will include such qualified persons
appointed as directed by the Minister. Under the provision contained in this clause, the
Technical Institute Regulations 1968-with the exception of those clauses relating to the
appointment of principals and assistant principals, and to the grading of institutes-will
apply to employees in those technical divisions. It is also proposed that the Secondary and
Technical Institute Teachers Disciplinary Regulations 1969 and the Tertiary Bursary Regula-


## p. 4632 (#738) ###########################################

4632
18 November
Education Amendment Bill
tions 1976 will apply. Senior technical divisions will be attached to a secondary school in
Gisborne, Wanganui, Tauranga, and Timaru.
Clause 5 deals with the rights of teachers to appeal against appointments to vacancies,
and requires that division A applicants be informed of non-appointment by a letter posted to
their last known address. The clause also requires that appeals against non-appointment
must be lodged within 10 days of the date of posting of the notification of an unsuccessful
application.
There are no provisions within the present Act for the inspection of teachers' colleges or
institutions offering pre-school education funded by Government grants. Clauses 6 and 7
provide for the inspection of these institutions on the same basis as the inspection of schools,
technical institutes, and community colleges. Provision is also made for adequate notice of
intention to inspect to be given in the case of institutions offering pre-school education.
In the last Budget, provision was made for a separate programme in education to
identify expenditure on research. Clause 8 makes clear the director-general's power to
expend money on education research. Provision is also made for the director-general to
enter into contracts with persons for the undertaking of research.
Clause 9 deals with the School Certificate examination. When the internal assessment
scheme was introduced, doubts were expressed about the validity of the examination. The
Bill therefore does three things: first, it expresses in general terms the director-general's
power to conduct the examination; secondly, it empowers the making of regulations
providing for internal assessment and for the charging of fees in connection with examina-
tions; and, thirdly, for the avoidance of doubt, it declares all existing regulations to be valid.
There has been some misunderstanding about the part of the Bill dealing with internal
assessment in schools. The purpose of this part of the Bill is to put internal assessment on a
firmer legal footing. It is not, as some people might have presumed, the final green light of
approval for the internal assessment of School Certificate. I must make this clear, because I
have seen one newspaper editorial that could have misled people. The investigation of
internal assessment initiated by me in 1976 has not been affected by the legislation. In March
1976, in a statement published in the Education Gazette, I referred to the fact that I had
asked the School Certificate Examination Board to continue the investigation of School
Certificate internal assessment, and that the present system-which is a combination of
internally and externally assessed components-would remain in operation until at least the
end of the 1978 school year.
Now, nearly 2 years later, my position is still essentially the same as it was at the
beginning of 1976, when I said that no new scheme that was not generally acceptable to
teachers and the general public would be introduced on a national basis. Any method of
internal assessment should, I believe, include adequate controls to ensure satisfactory
standards and maintain public confidence. In the meantime, the School Certificate Examina-
tion Board and the department have obtained useful information on the effect of internal
assessment on schools, pupils, and teachers, through surveillance of the limited trials that
were set up in mathematics, English, and science. However, it is still too early to evaluate
formally the effects of those trials. As I have requested, the School Certificate Examination
Board and the department will continue to work towards internal assessment for school
certificate. In view of the fact that there is a continuing need for further discussion and
investigation, the present system will remain at least until the end of the 1980 school year.
Finally, under the present Act, school committees are not empowered to grant holidays
even though it is the usual practice for them to do so. Clause 10 authorises the making of
regulations to empower school committees to grant school holidays on special occasions.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT AMENDMENT BILL (No. 3)
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Local
Government Amendment Bill (No. 3) be introduced. This Bill revises the law relating to the
constitution and procedures of the Local Government Commission. Last year the Govern-
ment promoted some changes to the Local Government Act to bring the powers of the Local
Government Commission more into line with the policy on which the Government was
elected, and to facilitate the implementation of its well publicised philosophy that it wanted
the views of the local community to prevail in the restructuring of local government.


## p. 4637 (#743) ###########################################

22 November
4637
Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 3)
The Government has now decided to go further and completely reconstitute the
commission and its procedures, so that the legislation will more clearly reflect the Govern-
ment's policy. This action is necessary because it is evident from a number of regional
schemes issued by the commission that, despite the changes made by this Government, the
law is still capable of being interpreted—and in fact is being interpreted-more in keeping
with the Labour Party's policy. That policy was one of imposing reform on people whether
they liked it or not. In contrast, the National Party's policy is one of consultation and
negotiation. Furthermore, in cases where strong objections are voiced by the people it wants
the question to be reviewed.
The Government has therefore completely reviewed the legislation governing the
constitution and procedures of the commission. This Bill is the result. It reduces the size of
the commission from a minimum of five members to a total of three-the chairman, one
member nominated by the New Zealand Counties Association, and one nominated by the
Municipal Association of New Zealand. There is no need, in the National Government's
opinion, for a commission of five or more members. The previous Labour Minister had a
commission of seven, which reflected his wish to push through reform without any real
regard for the wishes of the people. Provision is made for the appointment of a temporary
member when the commission is required to consider a proposal affecting a special purpose
authority. This temporary member will have a special knowledge of the type of ad hoc
authority involved.
Different procedures are laid down for the constitution of new regions on the one hand,
and for the consideration of reorganisation proposals on the other. The existing provisional
regional schemes will be either carried through to completion or abandoned-in which event
a fresh start will have to be made. I would not expect any existing provisional regional
scheme to be abandoned unless there is a substantial degree of opposition to it. Quite clearly
the existing Wellington scheme cannot be permitted to continue in the face of the hostility it
has aroused in the Horowhenua area. The Otago and Aorangi scheme are two others in the
same category.
The Bill places a great deal of emphasis on consultation and negotiation at a much
earlier stage than hitherto-especially before the issue of a formal provisional scheme, which
is the stage where legal processes begin to take over. For new regional schemes the
commission will be required to appoint one or more of its members to discuss its ideas with
every local authority likely to be affected. If, after these initial discussions, the commission
decides to proceed with its proposal-either as originally proposed or with amendments-it
must give public notification of its intention, stating the nature of its proposals. It will then
be required to gauge public reaction, even to the extent of holding public meetings if it thinks
fit. Only then, if the commission is satisfied it has the right scheme and has public support,
will the legal procedures be set in motion by the issue of a provisional scheme. From then on,
the procedures will be as they are now.
There will be a statutory right of objection and every objector must be given the
opportunity to be heard, but there is one important difference in the procedural require-
ments. The Bill gives the Minister the right to refer a final regional scheme back to the
commission for reconsideration of any aspects of it with which he is dissatisfied. This is a
most important innovation and one that recognises that there is a final political responsibility
to ensure that a scheme is not imposed on people against their wishes.
The procedures for dealing with boundary alterations and the union of territorial
authorities are altered to provide for more discussion with local authorities before the issue
of a provisional scheme. For this purpose the commission is empowered to appoint a
conciliator who need not necessarily be a member of the commission. If, after the initial
negotiations, the commission is satisfied that the reorganisation scheme should proceed and
that it has a reasonable measure of support, it is to issue a statement of its intention to
proceed. It is at that stage that a survey of the degree of public opposition to the proposal
will be undertaken if 15 percent of the electors of a district seek such a survey. Each elector
will be sent a form with a request that it be returned if the elector wishes to record his
objection. If more than half those on the roll record their objection, the proposal will not go
ahead. If less than half record an objection, the commission will be empowered to institute
the formal implementation of its proposals by the issue of a provisional scheme, which will,
of course, still be open to objection. Because public opinion has been surveyed at an earlier
stage, there will be no right to a poll on a final reorganisation scheme.
As I have said, the whole emphasis of this Bill is on consultation and on seeing that real
regard is paid to the wishes of the people in the area affected by a proposal. We want to


## p. 4638 (#744) ###########################################

22 November

ensure that the new commission really does take heed of public opinion and does more than

Association and the Municipal Association when an Auckland Regional Authority Bill was
introduced in 1963. I shall leave that passing reference there, but point out that antagonism
arises under this type of constitution.
Clause 17 relates to regional schemes, and states that every authority shall be linked to
some region by 31 December 1979. The existing commission has introduced some advanced
policies for regional authorities. Will its work be scrapped, and will the new commission start
again, or to what extent will the work of the present commission be acknowledged? It would

would be unjustified. More often than not we have found that the regional schemes have
become acceptable. Much of the legislation needs to be thoroughly culled. People with a
deep-seated interest in local bodies will not appreciate the legislation.
I was concerned to hear the Minister say he intended setting up the new commission by

through the House before the session finishes. I am bitterly opposed to that, because it is not
fair on local government or the communities. If the Minister thinks that is democratic he

constitutional measures like this. The Minister and the Government have already heard
objections from groups such as the National Council of Women, the Law Society, Federated
Farmers, and others who feel that important legislation is pushed through without thorough
consideration. We no longer have a second Chamber to review legislation. Committees have
been set up to study legislation, but the Government is determined to ride roughshod over
the people. That is not good enough, and I object to pushing through legislation. Many
people and organisations will want to make submissions about the Bill. I hope that it will be
referred to a committee, with adequate time given to hear submissions. Members know the

to see the number of Bills before that committee.

delayed until a consensus can be reached. For instance, in the Aorangi region there is strong
objection at the north end and the south end, but there are proposals that will be acceptable
to the territorial local authorities involved, and that will be workable. This legislation is not a
backward step; it is a step forward towards regional government. I support the introduction
of the Bill.

Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 3)
What members opposite do not appear to appreciate is that the good will that now exists
between the Counties Association and the Municipal Association did not exist 10 years ago.
There is a spirit of co-operation, and a desire by both associations to strengthen local
government. Two of the greatest advocates for a form of regional government and for the
strengthening of local government are the presidents of those two associations today. That is
why we are able to recommend with confidence that the two representatives be from the
Counties Association and the Municipal Association. The Government's known desire is
that both associations move as quickly as possible towards a strong form of regional
government and a strengthened reorganisation of all local government throughout the
country.
Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): The more the Minister tries to explain and justify the
Bill, the more reasons are found for opposing its introduction. The Bill will not achieve the
Minister's stated objectives, as is abundantly plain to anyone listening to the debate. The Bill
will not rationalise or reform local government as the Minister, most members of the House,
and local government members believe it should be reformed. The Evening Post a few days
ago put its finger right on the reason for the introduction of the Bill: it is touching sensitive
political aspirations of the Government. The Government caucus decided to introduce this
measure, not because it wanted to reform local government, but because some of the
Government's marginal seats are in jeopardy as a result of the commission's operations.
As the Deputy Leader of the Opposition said, the tail will be wagging the dog. The
Minister is abdicating his responsibility to Parliament and to local government. If he wants to
consult people, as he says is his intention, the Bill should go automaticaly to a select
committee. It should be considered in depth by Parliament and by all those people—and
there are tens of thousands-who have some interest in the matter. Does the Minister intend
to give the Municipal and Counties Associations a blank cheque with which they can make
their own rules, set their own pace, or maintain the status quo?
The Minister said the Bill will hurry up the rationalisation and the regional structure of
local government. However, the explanatory note states that it will be a requirement for one
or more of the commission's members to discuss regional schemes with all local authorities
likely to be affected. Does this mean that the commission, the membership of which has
been reduced from five to three, will be required to talk with every local body about the
proposal? If so, what is the time allotted for such discussion, and at what stage do
commission members consult together, or with the Minister? If the proposal is changed in
any way, will the commissioners be required to discuss it again with each local authority? If
so, the process will be very time consuming, and will have the opposite effect to that hoped
for by the Minister. It could take months, if not years, to get some regional structures under
way.
66
Paragraph (g) of the explanatory note states: " . . . If the Commission then decides to
proceed with the proposal, it must give public notice of its intention, and there will then be a
right of 15 percent of the electors on the roll to demand that a survey”—not a poll-"of the
electors on the roll be conducted. . .". Who will interpret the findings of such a survey,
which is different from a poll of electors? A survey can be interpreted many ways, whereas
the result of a poll is clear. Who will carry out the surveys? Will the commission staff do the
job; and, more importantly, will the local bodies involved with the proposal also help with
the surveys? If so, they could be their own judge and jury, which would not be democracy in
action by any stretch of the imagination.
It is regrettable that the Bill is not to go to a select committee, because, as I said before,
many local body representatives would want to make submissions so that various aspects of
the legislation could be considered. The Minister said he wishes to consult about this
measure, yet he also says he intends to pass the legislation during the present session, which
at the most will be another 3 or 4 weeks. As the Bill will lie on the table during that time and
will not be sent to a select committee, what opportunity will those interested people have of
putting forward their suggestions? The referral of such an important measure to the Local
Bills Committee for further consideration is a fundamental principle that the House should
not lightly forgo.

Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 3)
Generally speaking, most members opposite come from urban electorates, and have no
real understanding of local government in rural or provincial areas. The 32 members
opposite go along with the editorials of the major metropolitan newspapers, which have
stated for many years that bigger is better. They state that a local authority has to include all
others on its boundary, after which rates will be reduced, as will be the cost of sewerage and
water reticulation, and all will be well. However, we know that is not true. With this
legislation, members of Parliament will not endure the undesirable situation in which
members of the Local Government Commission-appointed by statute and based in
Wellington-although doing a job to the best of their ability, refuse to take into considera-
tion community of interest.
The people of Queenstown, Wanaka, and Otago Central, areas which were included in
the Otago region that extended from the Gates of Haast to the Otago Peninsula, and totalled
3 500 000 hectares, have no interest in what takes place in Dunedin. They are more
interested in their own bailiwick. I emphatically state that the Otago Central seat is not
marginal; nor has there been any caucus decision to suggest that any Government seat was in
jeopardy because of regional proposals made by the Local Government Commission. People
decide who their local representatives will be and where they will meet, and they put their
hopes and aspirations and trust in the people they elect.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: Order! I am reluctant to interrupt the honourable member,
but his speech is more relevant to a second reading. He should put forward an argument as to
why the motion, which is that the Local Government Amendment Bill (No. 3) be
introduced, should be agreed to or rejected.
Mr COOPER: The principal change in Part I gives the Minister the power to involve
himself, certainly not in the final say, but in the progress of the restructuring of local
government, so that the will of Parliament, or our requirement and desire for a regional form
of government-decentralisation-is clearly seen. The commission will study the final
situation after a decision has been made locally. A conciliator will be able to go into an area
and conduct a series of public meetings to seek local opinion, the local authorities will be
involved, and the Local Government Commission will be concerned in the poll provisions.
The Mayor of Wellington has called this a great step backwards, but in my association
with local government over the last 7 or 8 years I have often heard that comment from
metropolitan mayors. We are looking right across the board at the restructuring of local
government by consultation, not by bulldozer tactics. We put a date on it, and frankly I think
we can head off that date considerably. General public opinion is in favour of the legislation.
I do not take too lightly the fact that we have been able to reduce membership of the
commission from five to three, because many members of the Government caucus feel it is
time we looked at the membership of commissions and advisory boards, and at possible
savings. We have an economic problem, and every New Zealander must face it. If we reduce
the commission membership to three, with the ability to appoint a temporary conciliator, we
will be moving along according to the National Government's attitude towards local
government, which is that it should be a partnership and that there should be no bulldozer
tactics. We will be moving forward with a land strategy that will be in the best interests of
New Zealand.
The House divided on the question, That the Local Government Amendment Bill (No.
3) be introduced.

Housing Target
1. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) asked the Minister of Housing: Can he give an
assurance that the Government's housing completion target for the current year—namely
26 000-28 000 units-will be met, and, if not, will he advise the House of his amended
estimate?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I cannot give the assurance the
honourable member seeks. The targets set at the beginning of the financial year were based
on an assessment of the likely demand and reflected a level of activity that it was hoped could
be sustained by the building industry. No purpose would be served by making an amended
estimate of the targets, and I do not propose doing so.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: In view of the alarming statement made by the president of the
Master Builders Federation that the actual completion might reach only 21 000 or 22 000,
how can the Minister square off that probability with the statement he made only 5 days ago
that it was still desirable to maintain the industry at an activity level as near to the original
target as possible; and does the Minister consider that 22 000 housing completions are as
near as possible to 26 000 to 28 000 completions?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: The honourable member has used so many figures that I am
not sure what he means. I do not propose trying to square anything off. I do not accept the
figures used by the president of the Master Builders Federation; nor are they the best
estimates I have at the moment. What I regard as the level of building activity is not simply
that related to the construction of houses. Builders also build other things-for example,
kindergartens and schools—and they do a large number of repairs. If the real demand for

Oil Exploration Data-Hunt International
2. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) asked the Minister of Energy Resources: What
procedures are currently adopted to ensure that the New Zealand Government is constantly
and fully briefed on all scientific and geological data relating to oil exploration at present
being carried out by the Hunt International Petroleum Co. of New Zealand aboard Penrod
74 in the Great South Basin area?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): The Government is kept fully
informed of the progress of drilling under section 47E of the Petroleum Act, which is
administered by the Mines Department, which follows procedures to ensure that the Act is
complied with. All data is also received by the Ministry of Energy Resources as a
requirement arising from the participation agreement between the Government and Hunt
International Petroleum. Daily drilling reports are received by telex, and specialised reports
are received as soon as they are available. Examination of materials from wells is progres-
sively made at geological survey during operations to provide information on the strata
penetrated.
Mr W. R. Austin: Does this procedure involve the placement of any New Zealanders on
board to check it, and is the Minister fully satisfied that it is foolproof?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The New Zealand element of the exploration is kept well informed.
At any time a special feature of interest develops, New Zealand officials from the Ministry of
Energy Resources, the Mines Department, and sometimes the DSIR, are located at the
drilling site.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Does the data supplied justify the optimism expressed by the
Prime Minister during his present trip to America?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: There was evidence of hydrocarbons at Kauau 1A, and the testing
programme to establish the degree to which these hydrocarbons indicate sources of either
gas or oil and the approximate size of these resources will proceed as soon as the problem of
two broken anchor chains is resolved. Until fine weather is experienced, the problem cannot
be remedied.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

5. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Education: In view of the

returning to school as a result of the lack of suitable jobs, and has he discussed with the
Ministers of Labour, Social Welfare, and Maori Affairs the steps necessary to remedy the
situation?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): My department, with the assistance of
the Department of Labour, has conducted a survey of 1977 school leavers which will give an
indication of the number of young people who may return to school in 1978 because of the
lack of suitable jobs. I have not discussed this matter with my colleagues, but at my request
my department is having continuing discussions with the Department of Labour, the
Department of Social Welfare, and the Department of Maori Affairs.
Hon. M. Rata: In the light of that survey, what steps does the Minister now propose to
take?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It is too early to say exactly what the survey will reveal at the
beginning of the next school year. Information we have so far gleaned shows that there are
slightly fewer who might have to be absorbed. About 24 000 were absorbed into employment
last year. This year the figure will be 22 900. Last year we had 2400 notified vacancies, while
the figure for this year is 2200. The figures are much the same, but we are watching the
position very carefully and have made preparations at technical institutes and community
colleges. We are currently examining ways to see if we might absorb more children into
secondary schools.

Economy-Balance of Payments
7. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) asked the Minister of
Finance: What action does the Government intend to take immediately to correct the
deterioration of New Zealand's balance of payments situation, which has now been revealed
as extending over the two quarters of the current financial year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): The Government is acting
continually to improve the balance of payments both in the immediate future and in the
longer run. The Government's policy of domestic restraint has reduced the demand for
imports. The latest figures from the Government Statistician show that forward orders for
imports have dropped. This means we can expect a reduction in import volumes in the next
few months. The Government has also taken active measures to boost the export drive. The
livestock incentive scheme is providing a basis for sustained growth in primary exports.
Incentives have been extended for non-traditional exports, including services. Policies have
been set in train to stimulate the development of efficient import replacement industries and
to accelerate the development of indigenous energy resources.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: In the face of these continuing measures which the Minister has just
listed how did the revision of the provisional figure for June of $837 million take the actual
figure to $914 million for the June 1977 year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am sure the member is aware that provisional estimates by
the Government Statistician have to be corrected. There is a large increase in the element in
relation to imports of services, with higher payments there, and a reduction in income from
overseas, which unfortunately had to be taken into account in the final assessment.
Hon. P. I. Wilkinson: To what extent has the balance of payments fallen from the 14-
percent deficit which the Government inherited from the Labour Government?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am sure the House is aware that the balance of payments,
as one of the key indicators, has shown a continuing improvement since the change of
Government from the high level of a 14-percent deficit in 1975 to a 6- or 7-percent deficit this
year. In fact, the deficit has been halved, and that is true for the other major indicators, too.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: When these continuing measures were predicated on the basis of the
estimated figures for the June year, and it was discovered that the true deficit was almost $80
million worse, did the Government revise the measures it was taking to cure the situation?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am sure the member is thoroughly aware that the
Government's measures are based on a total approach to the economic situation. The
balance of payments position has improved overall. It will not improve continuously, but the
Government is moving and acting continually, as it did in the Budget and the mini-Budget,
to improve a balance of payments position that was in dire straits when the Labour
Government went out of office.
Mr Quigley: Can the Minister confirm that the current account receipts for the year
ended August 1975 were $2,253 million, whereas for the year ended August 1977 they were
$4,142 million, and that the current account deficit as a percentage of the gross national
product is substantially lower because of that increase in current account receipts?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: In terms of the debate on our overseas trading position I
think it is correct to use the current account figures, which show a marked improvement in
our trading position. The balance of payments problem results from the payment for
services, which has increased because of the rise in oil prices.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Is it not a fact that notwithstanding the Government's promise
to significantly reduce the balance of payments deficit it is still running at an abnormally high
level-equivalent to the level it criticised in 1975?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: That is incorrect. In reply to an earlier supplementary
question I said that the balance of payments deficit had been halved since the Government
took office. In 1975 the deficit was running at 14 percent of the gross national product; today
it is running at about 6.7 percent. The Government does not have a budget deficit of $1,000
million or an accelerating rate of inflation, and has the problem under control.
Mr ACTING SPEAKER: The Minister has taken his answer well outside the question
asked.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Coffee Price
16. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North), on behalf of Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt),
asked the Minister of Trade and Industry: Is his department keeping a close watch on the
retail price for coffee now that world coffee bean prices have fallen by about 40 percent?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry): I
reply on behalf of the Minister. "I am advised by the Secretary of Trade and Industry that


## p. 4654 (#760) ###########################################

4654
22 November
Oral Answers to Questions
the Stabilisation of Prices Regulations 1974 provide for an appropriate reduction in a
manufacturer's selling price and, as a consequence, the retail price to reflect a net reduction
in the manufacturer's total cost of production. The department has advised me that it is
monitoring the timing of lower priced raw coffee beans into each manufacturer's cost of
production. When the fall in world coffee bean prices is reflected in the total cost of the
product of the domestic coffee manufacturer an appropriate reduction in price will be
required."
Hon. W. W. Freer: Would the Under-Secretary give some indication-because of the
nature of the stocks held by manufacturers-when the first reduction at retail level will
occur?
Mr ALLEN: It is very difficult to estimate. As the questioner would realise, the world
price for raw coffee beans peaked in early March 1975. It was not until after mid-May 1977
that manufacturers were permitted to increase their selling prices. Even then the local
instant coffee prices did not reflect the peak world prices, partly because manufacturers'
stocks still contained some earlier lower costing purchases, and partly because the manufac-
turers, of their own volition, kept their prices below that justified by the regulations. Since
then a marked fall in domestic sales of instant coffee, following the increased prices, resulted
in a reduced draw-off of high priced stocks of coffee beans. This will further delay the time
when a price reduction could be required.
Mr MacDonell: If there is not a substantial drop in the price of coffee shortly-in view of
the 40 percent drop in the price of coffee beans-will the department take action?
Mr ALLEN: As I said in my original reply, the department is monitoring the system.
The New Zealand price of coffee depends on the stock of coffee beans being used in New
Zealand. At present manufacturers are working with old stock.

4656
Adjournment-Rail Passenger and Freight Charge Increases 22 November
freight charges of the New Zealand Railways, for which there has been no adequate
ministerial justification offered. On top of the announced fare increases I also refer to the
allegations made in the Dominion of Monday, 21 November, that the New Zealand Railways
has lost millions of dollars in freight contracts since road haulage restrictions were eased last
month, and to the further allegation that the department was running $20 million more into

national wastage of resources in the midst of an energy crisis, but which will inevitably
impose a greater burden for passengers and the taxpayer if urgent corrective measures are
not taken. The matter, finally, is in need of urgent Government action since, in the absence
of any Government moves to finalise a formula for the new road distance charge, together
with the latest freight charge increases announced over the weekend, there is every
indication that the Railways trading situation will deteriorate further."
Standing Order 90 states that the statement of the matter proposed to be discussed on a
motion for the adjournment of the House under the preceding Standing Order shall not be
framed in general terms but shall deal with a particular case of recent occurrence that
requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government, and involves the
administrative or ministerial responsibility of the Government. I have read the letter
carefully in the light of this Standing Order. The particular case to which it refers is stated to
be the weekend announcement of further increases in both passenger and freight charges of
the New Zealand Railways. This, it seems to me, conforms with the requirement of the
Standing Order.
However, the letter goes on to list a number of other matters, referred to as allegations,
regarding losses by the Railways, the situation relating to the 150 kilometre road haulage
limit, and a matter covering all three questions. These further issues appear to be added in
order to broaden the scope of the debate. They do not so closely conform with the Standing
Order as does the matter raised as the primary issue. Allegations contained in newspapers,
even though of this day's issue, do not constitute the "recent occurrences" envisaged by the
Standing Order. These are, of course, the events, not the reports of them; and it is the events
that must be recent. I would particularly point out that the issue of the extension of the road
haulage limit to 150 kilometres was effected some time ago, and has already been debated in
the House. I do not consider that that matter should be traversed in any debate on the matter
now under consideration. Indeed, in seeking to move the adjournment of the House under
Standing Order 89, a member should restrict his case to cover only those matters that are
covered in Standing Order 90. Subject to these comments, it appears to me that the matter
raised by the member's letter is one covered by the Standing Order. Will members who
approve of the proposed discussion rise in their places?

I draw the attention of the House to the adverse effect this will have on suburban

especially. As so often happens with this Government, those affected can least afford to pay,
have no alternative transport, and are compelled to use public services. They are captives,

would agree with him, but his action has reacted against the Railways. According to the

freight trains are being cancelled, and in some weeks the revenue has been as much as

I refer also to the Dominion of 21 November, which reported that the secretary of the

The National Government came into office criticising its predecessor's policy of holding
rail charges. It was sharply critical of the Labour Government's policy of containing the
charges. In the last 2 years, freight charges and many rail fares have been increased by more
than 100 percent, and this year the rail system will run at a loss of $70 million. In 1975-76, in
spite of the controlled charges under the Labour Government, the loss on rail operations
only was $57.5 million. Yet, after increasing charges by more than 100 percent, the estimated
loss in this financial year, assuming the Railways figure as quoted to its employees is correct,
will be $20 million more than the $50 million loss budgeted for. The extra deficit has to be
met from somewhere, so the Government has cut and slashed rail services at every turn.
According to the New Zealand Herald of 1 October 1977, the General Manager of the
Railways Department said that the Railways would fight to hold its share of freight traffic,
and would accept smaller margins in some areas in order to compete. He admitted that the
Railways would have to fight hard in the face of new competition, but thought it could be
done by adjusting margins and using the cross-subsidisation system.
The Minister's action in increasing rail charges at this time is contrary to the public
statements made by the general manager that the Railways are out to compete. The
Railways need more stock, more encouragement, and more Government backing. When
road transport has been given an extension of the haulage limit to 150 kilometres and is
setting out to undercut the Railways at every turn-and I shall not refer to the price war
between road transporters—the last thing the Railways needs is the Government stabbing it
in the back with a further increase of up to 12.5 percent on freight. If the general manager is
achieving some success in his declared objective the Government is ensuring that it is very
limited. The Minister has an obligation and a duty to give the reason for the increases in rail
charges. It is known that the Railways Department had set out to become more competitive,
to reduce its margins in some operations, and to make every effort to become as efficient as
possible with the resources at its disposal—as people expect it to do.
On 18 November, when addressing the Chartered Institute of Transport in Auckland,
the Minister said that the Railways would continue to be a major force in transport. He did
not release his announcement about the increases until the next day. He also said that
economic conditions were affecting many sections of the economy. He had reached this
conclusion because traffic carried both more than and fewer than 150 kilometres had been
affected to almost the same extent. Surely the Minister knows the Railways Department is
being undercut by road transport within the 150 kilometre limit, and that he is making it
more difficult for the department by imposing increased charges from 4 December. He
should also know that, through subsidiaries and mergers, road transporters can travel further
than the 150 kilometre limit.
In his address to the Chartered Institute of Transport, the Minister said the Railways
had a role to play in the country's transport system, and would continue to be a major force.
The key to an efficient transport system is an efficient rail link from the North Cape to the tip
of the South Island. However, as I said yesterday, the Government appears to be hell-bent
on destroying the efficiency and competitive element of the Railways.
The Minister's statements do not line up with the consequences of his actions, or those
of the Government. He should urgently justify the increases, which will apply from 4
December, and say why rail services are being cut. The department should be given a fair
chance, especially as it operates a publicly owned service. The people are entitled to an
explanation from the Minister.

FINANCE BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. This is the annual washing-up Bill relating to miscellaneous financial
matters. Part I contains provisions that are expected to continue in force for some time. Part
II, on the other hand, contains validations and other provisions of short duration. Clauses 2,
3, and 4 re-enact various provisions contained mainly in earlier Finance Acts, and consoli-
date and simplify those provisions that still have effect. Clause 2 empowers local authorities
controlling public passenger transport services to provide free travel for disabled servicemen
from the two world wars. Clause 3 repeals and replaces two sections in old Finance Acts
dealing with the Nauru and Ocean Island phosphate trade. These sections contain a number
of provisions relating to an amount of $600,000 authorised to be borrowed in 1920 for the
