CUSTOMS ACTS AMENDMENT BILL (NO.2)
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. Before coming to the individual clauses I intend making a few general remarks,
which should be taken in conjunction with the comments I made when I introduced the Bill a
fortnight ago. I said that between the introduction and the second reading my department
would be contacting various representatives of commercial bodies to explain the provisions
of the Bill, and at the same time give the organisations an opportunity to make any
comments they might wish to make at that stage. Discussions have been held with the New
Zealand Manufacturers Federation, the New Zealand Retailers Federation, the Associated
Chambers of Commerce, the British Trade Association, the Bureau of Importers and
Exporters, the Sports Industries Federation, the New Zealand Customs Agents Society, and


## p. 4666 (#772) ###########################################

4666
22 November
Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
the Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association.
Interest in the proposals has been considerable within the commercial community.
Approval for the new format of the tariff has been expressed, and questions have been asked
about the appeal provisions. My officers have stressed that there is no time limit for the
appeals to be lodged, that in exceptional circumstances appeals will be considered before the
implementation of the tariff on 1 July 1978, and that an opportunity should be given for the
new rates to be tested before an appeal is considered. It should also be emphasised that
appeals should be on an industry basis rather than on an individual company basis.
In recommending the various rates, the Tariff Review Committee followed procedures
similar to those used for the current tariff. In general, where protection of a domestic
industry is not a factor, the lowest possible rate, having regard to our international
commitments-usually 5 percent or free-applies to industrial raw materials. Recognition is
also given to various identifiable stages of processing goods in New Zealand, such as
packaging, fabricating, and so on. At the same time, developments in New Zealand industry
since the tariff was last reviewed have been taken into account, and protection accorded
where this was considered necessary. Traditional revenue items, such as spirits, have been
maintained as well as those items which contain an element of protection and revenue-for
example, jewellery.
I think it is fair to say that no local industry at present protected by tariffs has lost that
protection unless the current protection is meaningless, the goods are exempt from import
licensing, or the information available to the committee indicated quite clearly that duty
protection was no longer necessary. Some trade interests hoped for a level of protection that
virtually would have excluded competition from imports. A scrutiny of the new tariffs
reminded them that the review committee's brief was to allow an industry an adequate—not
a total-level of protection.
In the discussions with commercial organisations, interest was shown in whether or not
there had been any amendment to goods that now enter the country under the concessionary
provisions in Part II of the tariff. In general, if a tariff concession is granted the goods are
either free of duty or subject to a 5 percent duty in line with our international commitments.
No changes have been made to those goods, except in a few instances where a whole tariff
item is subject to concession-the concessionary rate now becomes the substantive rate, and
the need to apply for concessionary entry is eliminated.
Some interest has been expressed in the imports from developing countries. The
position is that 588 developing country rates have been reduced; 695 have been
increased generally to maintain the present margin between the developing country rate
and the normal tariff rate; 30 new rates are proposed; and 47 are eliminated. Looking at the
proposed tariff as a whole, the main reasons for tariff increases are: first, the protective
requirements of an industry for tariff purposes have not been considered since 1962, and
between that year and the present time there have been major industrial developments in
New Zealand-for example, the iron and steel industries; secondly, local production of basic
raw materials, which is given a protective rate and means increasing the tariff for further
local processing of those raw materials; thirdly, rationalisation of the tariff structure-in
many of these instances the concessions in Part II will be used to maintain the present
position if such action is compatible with the normal policies for granting concessionary
entry; and, fourthly, the Government has approved increases on related items following a
Tariff and Development Board hearing.
Some reasons for a decrease in rates are: first, the current rates are historical because of
trade classification, and are not now necessary; secondly, where current rates are meaning-
less either in terms of review or protection; thirdly, where current rates are too high in
relation to similar goods, particularly when such goods have been reviewed by the Tariff and
Development Board; and, fourthly, rationalisation of the tariff structure. Apart from
changes arising from amendments to the structure of the tariff, no significant changes have
been made to the rates for textiles and apparel as these goods are at present under
comprehensive study by the Tariff and Development Board.
I indicated in my introductory speech that about 10 industries are to be the subject of
further investigation, and in due course the Government will be making decisions on how
this might best be done. I would point out to members that some of those industries, such as
the plastics, footwear, and wine industries, have already been considered for some form of
industry study. The Government has also decided that consideration should be given to the
customs tariff being kept continually under review. This is particularly important in relation
to items having specific or threshold rates of duty as well as to those items that are subject to


## p. 4667 (#773) ###########################################

22 November
4667
Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
increasing development in local manufacture.
All in all, the Tariff Review Committee received about 1835 submissions-887 from
manufacturers, including trade groups, and 948 from importers and users. These latter
submissions related principally to the continuation of current tariff concessions. In many
cases the 1835 submissions covered a multitude of tariff items; the committee thus received
valuable co-operation from interested parties. In my comments I have tried not to go into
great detail about individual items in the tariff. I realise that honourable members might
have some questions to ask about some of the specific changes, but, as I said when
introducing the Bill, a customs tariff is a complex document, and I should hope technicalities
can be avoided.
The proposed tariff, if it is to come into force on 1 July 1978, must be approved by the
House this session. For statistical purposes, its implementation must coincide with the
commencement of the trade year, and the Government Printer requires some months to
have public copies of the tariff printed. It is intended to publish a key showing the
relationship between items in the present tariff and the new tariff, and also to conduct
training courses for all interested parties as well as for Customs Department staff throughout
the country.
In addition to the revised and restructured customs tariff, the Bill makes a number of
miscellaneous amendments to the Customs Acts. Clause 11 revises various existing defini-
tions in the Customs Act, and adds certain new definitions. Clauses 12, 14, 16, 20, 29, and 33
are consequential upon the provision relating to export duty in clause 24. The effect of the
amendments is to extend the existing provisions in so far as they relate to import and export
duties. The amendment in clause 28 is also consequential. It will enable the f.o.b. value to be
used as the basis for calculating export duty. Clause 13, a minor one, changes the Royal
Arms on the customs seal to the New Zealand Arms. The use of the latter is considered to be
more appropriate to this country's independent sovereign status.
Clause 15 deals with the accommodation required to be provided for customs officers by
the controlling authorities of wharves, container bases, and airports. Previously this accom-
modation had to be provided without charge, but by agreement the Crown now proposes to
pay for such accommodation. The amendment ensures that accommodation will be up to the
required standard. Clause 18 relates to section 52A of the principal Act, which makes it an
offence to remove goods from customs control except with the permission of the collector.
The amendment in clause 18 also makes it an offence for the person having custody of the
goods to deliver them, except pursuant to permission given by the department. Clause 19
relates to section 62 of the principal Act. Under section 62 goods that are removed under
customs control from one port to another must on arrival at the receiving port be directed to
an examining place. The amendment made by this clause allows them to go directly to any
warehouse licensed under the Act. This will save importers time and expense.
The amendment made by clause 21 will allow goods, other than dutiable goods on which
duty has not been paid, to be stored in a warehouse licensed under the Act. This, together
with the amendment made by clause 35, will allow earlier payment of drawbacks of duty to
manufacturers who export goods. Once the goods have been entered into the warehouse,
and are therefore under the department's control, the drawback may be paid back even
though the goods would not be exported until later. Clause 22 increases fees for licensed
warehouses to ensure that the return to the department is in line with the actual cost of
carrying out control and supervision of those warehouses. Clause 23 extends the controls on
the removal of goods from warehouses licensed under the Customs Act to warehouses
licensed under the Distillation Act. The original legislation was deficient in this regard.
Clause 24 provides for the introduction, where necessary, of a duty on exports. This, of
course, would be used only in exceptional circumstances, since the general thrust of the
Government's policies is to provide incentives for exports rather than disincentives. An
export duty is conceived as a possible alternative to the more drastic course of introducing an
export prohibition. Section 70 of the principal Act gives authority for prohibition, either
general or conditional, to be placed on exported goods by means of an Order in Council. At
present there are no means for similar prohibitions to be made by export duty. Other
countries have found such a duty to be an appropriate tool. For example, Australia has used
such a duty in the past as a ready means to recover subsidies or bounties paid for domestic
production. In New Zealand's case, circumstances arise from time to time where some curb
on exports becomes desirable-where, for example, a disparity between the price structure
of a commodity on the domestic market and that ruling overseas provides an artificial
structure for export that acts against the national interest.


## p. 4668 (#774) ###########################################

4668
22 November
Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
An export duty provides a simple administrative means of recovering a subsidy imposed
for domestic purposes. It can be used to bridge any difference between the domestic and
world price without going so far as to prohibit exports. It can encourage the retention of
commodities in short supply for local use. In this latter respect the amount of an export duty
has to be assessed carefully to reflect the extent to which the Government might be prepared
to move to protect local interests against international trends. Export restrictions in their
various forms are receiving increasing attention in international forums-again a realisation
that national resources are not infinite. Generally, an export duty applied selectively is a
more internationally acceptable constraint than an absolute prohibition. The clause would
therefore provide a useful additional tool should a particular need arise.
Subclause (3) indicates the type of situation in which its use might be appropriate.
Subclause (6) provides for the possibility whereby a business association or other arrange-
ment between exporters and importers might write into the value for export duty purposes
less than might be expected from an arm's-length transaction. In such a situation a collector
of customs is given authority to determine a normal value based on the cost and profit
margin normally applied by an independent seller. This is subject, however, to a right of
appeal to the Minister as provided for in subclause (7). As at present when import duties are
levied by Order in Council, provision for validation by Parliament is made by appropriate
amendment to the principal Act.
The intention of clause 25 is to complement the fairly considerable authority at present
contained in sections 124 and 125 of the Customs Act to improve or vary customs duties on
imported goods by means of Order in Council. It provides for the possibility of a
surtax-that is, duty additional to any other duties already in force-being used to good
effect. It is interesting to note that in Australia, for example, there is already provision for
the contingency of a possible surcharge on imported goods, but it is on customs tariff that
empowers an additional rate of duty of 20 percent applied on classes of goods produced or
manufactured in such countries as are specified in the Order. Subclause (5) of the New
Zealand Bill limits the discretion to impose a rate of surtax to a minimum of either 20
percent on the current domestic value, or 25 percent of the total duty otherwise payable.
Clause 26(1), which amends section 131 of the principal Act, will require that the imposition
of any surtax be validated in a confirmation Bill submitted pursuant to that section.
Clause 27 intends to convey any power that does not already exist, and is largely
directed at presenting a more appropriate base for the administration of an import deposit
scheme. The present scheme was introduced by the Economic Stabilisation Regulations
1976, which were made pursuant to the Economic Stabilisation Act of 1948. The Act,
however, is administered by the Department of Trade and Industry, whereas it was decided
that it would be more practicable to effect administration by the Customs Department. In
fact, the regulations are drawn upon the Customs Act for interpretive purposes. For
example, there is a relationship to entry-taking requirements pursuant to sections 22 and 53
of the Customs Act. The deposit itself is based on current domestic values as determined for
customs purposes.
Several terms used in the regulations draw on the Customs Act for definition. For those
reasons it is considered that the provision of a statutory basis for the scheme within the
Customs Act would be preferable. It would also remove the administrative anomaly
whereby the impression is given that overall responsibility for the actions of the Customs
Department in administering the scheme lies with the Minister of Trade and Industry, by
virtue of that Minister's responsibilities under the Economic Stabilisation Act.
Clause 38 makes clear the class of vessel that is forfeit in smuggling cases. This proposed
amendment will give the power to seize any vessel under 50 tonnes gross-which is
important in view of the growing use of high-speed launches as pick-up boats in connection
with the illicit importing of drugs. Clause 36 makes completely clear the authority of the
customs officers to use assistance in relation to the search of persons. This is important when
the services of qualified medical practitioners are used for body searches of persons
suspected of carrying narcotics and other controlled drugs.
Clauses 37 and 44 are designed to assist winemakers who require fortifying spirit to use
in the production of dessert wines such as sherry and port. Clause 39 brings in changes in the
classes of denatured alcohol used in the manufacture of perfumed spirit and toilet prepara-
tions that have been agreed to at the request of the industry. As a consequence of this, the
industry has agreed to the elimination of the concessionary rate of excise duty on the
undenatured alcohol used in the manufacture of these preparations. Clause 9 removes this
concessionary rate of excise duty.

Clause 42 aligns the definition of "motor cycle" in the Sales Tax Act with that used in

These are the main provisions in the Bill.

and how they contribute to the high cost of living. Over the past decade, National
Governments have talked of replacing import licensing with a comprehensive tariff system;
and the Minister of Trade and Industry will remember speaking for many years about the
replacement of the present licensing system with a tariff system. We now have the tariff
system, but no suggestion of abolishing import controls, because the Government realises
that it is not possible to do away with quantity controls that, although not popular with many
importers, are effective and fair.
Hon. L. R. Adams-Schneider: We've no proposals to do that.
Mr MacDONELL: It is all very well for the Minister to say we have no complaints about
it, but he was the Minister who said that the National Government would introduce a tariff
system.
Hon. L. R. Adams-Schneider: No, I've never said that. I said there would be a
combination of tariff and import licensing.
Mr MacDONELL: The Minister said that his Government would do away with the
import licensing system and bring in a tariff system over a 5-year period. I remember him
saying that, but he now denies it. If the Government intends to phase out import licensing,
has it carried out a full industry study to ensure a proper productive environment? I do not
think so.
The rates on pharmaceutical products have been reduced. That indicates a greater
influx of imported drugs and medical preparations from the world's larger pharmaceutical
suppliers, and a probable rise in the cost of medical aid. Surely, if it is at all possible, we
should be encouraging pharmaceutical manufacturers such as Kempthorne Prosser to
increase processing in New Zealand.
A matter of some concern is the introduction of the new tariff in the middle of major
trade negotiations under GATT. Why was the introduction not held back until the maximum
negotiating advantage under GATT was extracted? How can you negotiate on tariff changes
that have already been introduced? The Minister mentioned the import deposit scheme,
which has been slightly amended in the Bill; but that will not alter the fact that the scheme
has been a disaster. It has had an adverse effect on small business in the country, and, when
officials were questioned during discussions on the estimates of expenditure, it was found
that at least one company had gone into liquidation because of this scheme. That was
admitted by departmental officers.
The savings made have been minimal, a few million dollars at best-we are talking
about $4,000 million over the last year. Our import bill has been running at the highest level
ever since this Government came to power. I appreciate that the work has been done, and
done well, by the Tariff Review Committee. Although we do not accept all its recommenda-
tions, Opposition members recognise its diligence and hard work.
The Minister referred to miscellaneous clauses. One that attracted my attention deals
with body searching by the preventive service or the uniformed branch of the Customs
Department. The Minister said tonight, and also when introducing the Bill, that a great deal
of care would be taken by departmental officers to see that there was no abuse of human
rights. It is a matter that concerns the Opposition—and I am sure every member in the
House-when body searches are carried out at airports by departmental officers looking for
drugs. It is particularly important that the rights of individuals should be protected.
The preliminary estimates of the balance of payments for the September quarter have
just been released, and reveal an alarming situation. The September figures show a deficit of

$966 million. It was predicted that we would reach $965 million by March next year—and we
have reached this already. In spite of the Prime Minister's claims during the last election
campaign that imports would be controlled and that these figures would be brought down, it
appears that the balance of payments is getting out of hand, and the ineffective measures
taken by the Customs Department and other departments are unable to control this serious
situation. We have now reached the figure that was predicted for March next year, which
indicates that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Customs, and others have not been able to
control the situation. The Bill will not help in any way at all. I hope that the Minister, when

Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa): We have had a fairly gloomy and predictably
pessimistic response from the member for Dunedin Central; but this is another example of
the National Government completing work that the Labour Government was unable to do.
The customs tariff provides for domestic manufactures a flexible means of protection for
local industry. Although the tariff is not the sole means of protection, it is the principal
means of insulating domestic industry, a matter that has been of major concern to
Government members, and to the Minister in particular. We have also been concerned
about the protection of jobs within the manufacturing industry. The new tariff is a far better
document technically than the present tariff-and I should be surprised if any Opposition
member refuted that statement. The proposed duty rates are far more realistic than the
present rates. Most importantly, the Bill achieves one of the Government's principal
objectives: a reasonable level of protection for the domestic industry. Using that as a base, a
platform, and a springboard, it will play a major part in decisions on the future of the
industry.
The member for Dunedin Central said that there had been insufficient canvassing of
interested parties. I shall deal with that later. It should be pointed out that some 2000 items
were excluded, and a time factor had to be observed when reaching a final decision. It was
imperative that the Bill be brought into the House this session, for reasons that the Minister
has outlined. As for the canvassing of opinions of interest groups, it is noted that the
committee's terms of reference and the reasons for the review were published in the Customs
bulletin of May 1975. Interested parties were called upon to make submissions by completing
two forms, one designed for manufacturers or producers, and the other for importers. In
many instances those forms were supplemented by written material. Discussions were held
with the council and officers of the New Zealand Manufacturers Federation, with the various
trading groups within the federation, and with the Bureau of Importers and Exporters and
the Retailers Federation. Therefore, there has been a widespread canvassing of views from
interested parties, including supplementary information obtained from a variety of Govern-
ment departments, other trade organisations, and individual firms. I think the Government
has proceeded from the best base and with the best knowledge available in the time at its
disposal.
I shall briefly mention the potential effect on domestic industry. In general, no local
industry which at present has tariff protection will lose that protection, unless—and this is
important—the present protection is meaningless, the goods are exempt from import
licensing, or the information available to the committee really shows that protection is
unnecessary. No industry has been denied some level of protection. In this context it is
important to remember that the committee's terms of reference, established by the former
Labour Government, had been to decide whether or not the existence of an industry was
justified. To sum up, ample opportunity was given to the commercial community to make
submissions, and provision has been made for appeals. The terms of reference for the review
of the appeal procedures are similar to those agreed to by the former Labour Government,
and import licensing protection still remains for most domestic industries. I see little
justification for the sort of carping criticism that came from the member for Dunedin
Central, and is now coming from the member for Mangere, who is trying to interject. I have
pleasure in supporting the Bill.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): I did not intend to speak to this measure, but I want
to protect the member for Manurewa from himself. His first remark was that the present
Government is taking action that the Labour Government was unable to take. In his second
to last sentence he said that the terms of reference were as laid down by the Labour
Government. The Labour Government commenced the exercise that has resulted in the
document now before us. If the member for Manurewa knows anything about education I
advise him to stick to that, because it is obvious from what he has just said that he was
parrotting material given to him—either by the research unit, or someone else—and that he

When my colleague the member for Dunedin Central was speaking, the Minister of

disturbed. I wonder if some of the manufacturers in his and other electorates will take

Acting Prime Minister that, "It has particularly in mind”—he is talking about the Govern-
ment's tariff review-"the possible modification of New Zealand's generalised system of
preferences affecting certain products in which ASEAN countries have expressed interest."
We are all aware that a major change in Australia's tariff flooded that country with
products from South-east Asia and other low-cost areas. We now have on one hand the
member for Manurewa in his ignorance saying that everyone is secure, and on the other the
Acting Prime Minister, when addressing ASEAN heads of mission in Wellington 4 days ago,
saying that the Government was looking at the degree of preference. I should have thought
that the Government Whips would have had somebody a little more knowledgeable than the
member for Manurewa speaking on this issue.
As was stated by the Minister when moving the second reading, and supported by the
member for Dunedin Central, it is very difficult to overhaul the tariff. That is why the
Minister said there would be no statutory limit to the time in which a group, a company, or
an individual could appeal to the department because of an error, or the likelihood of an
adverse impact on their own economy, as a result of changes in the tariff. That is how it
should be; there is no political argument. The procedure is so complex that there must
always be the opportunity for change. People who read the frequent documents from the
Customs Department listing tariff changes are aware that the tariff is continually changing; it
cannot be rigid.
Earlier this evening I was at a function at which some prominent commercial people
were talking about the changing circumstances in the world. Once upon a time you knew tha
the pound was worth a certain amount of money, and that it was likely to be that value in any
foreign currency for a long time. That has now changed. Once upon a time you also had a
tariff that was nearly inflexible. With all due respect to some of our senior officials who lived
with this for a long time, I think some of them could accept that many years ago the
adjustments in the tariff were not as we see them today. This is the result of the continual
commercial change, not only in this country, but also in each country with which we trade.
In his excellent speech the member for Dunedin Central said that this matter must be
continually reviewed by Parliament; therefore during the Committee stage there will be an
opportunity to look at certain issues in this Bill. The Opposition concurs with the general
principle that from time to time there must be a general overhaul and review of the tariff.
The details in the Bill will be resolved in two ways: in the Committee stage, and even beyond
that, with the department and the Minister making the decisions that they must quite
properly make from time to time in consideration of appeals made in the normal and proper
way.
As I said earlier, I take some comfort from the fact that tonight, by way of interjection,
the Minister of Trade and Industry gave an assurance that the Government did not intend to
'essen protection for manufacturers. Lord only knows there could be no more dangerous
ime than now to weaken any protection. I take some comfort, as will many manufacturers,
rom the fact that the Minister has given that assurance, and I hope it is solemnly honoured
by his Cabinet colleagues. If it is not, the future of not only the manufacturers and the
thousands of people they employ, but also of New Zealand as a developing manufacturing
economic unit is gravely in doubt.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): Like the member
for Mt. Albert, I had not intended to speak in the debate, but I think I should because on this
matter of protection I did reply by way of interjection and this specifically affects my
portfolio and my relationship with manufacturers. The National Party's 1975 election
policy and I played a considerable part in drafting it-clearly stated that we would protect
New Zealand industry by import licensing and the tariff. At no time can I recollect saying
that we would dispose of import licensing and use the tariff only, although the member for
Dunedin Central seems to recollect my saying that at some time in my career. I should be
grateful if he could show the statement to me. I do not remember making it, it is not in our
policy, and it has not been in my thinking. We support both of those concepts, and I support
the Bill introduced by the Minister of Customs because it does likewise. Admittedly, it
makes adjustments to the tariff.

Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
The member for Dunedin Central was critical of some reduction for pharmaceuticals.
He will correct me if I did not get it right, but I think he suggested that this could mean a
greater importation of pharmaceuticals because of a lowering of the tariff barrier. All that is
being done is to effect in the tariff what has been the practice of both National and Labour
Governments in the past, in that they have given a special duty concession on pharmaceuti-
cals that are necessary to New Zealand but are not made here. What has happened is that Mr
Norman Laking and his committee have picked those things up and adjusted them in the
tariff, instead of by means of a duty concession.
The member for Mt. Albert quoted something said by the Minister of Overseas Trade
recently. I have not got the statement, but if it said that we were adjusting the tariff under
the generalised system of preferences, or the Pacific Islands development scheme in the
GSP, or something like that, that is something that it is quite competent for the Government
to do. But I assure the House that there is no intention, if we do adjust the tariff, to abolish
import licensing at the same time. That is the main means of protection.
To some of the developing countries, particularly in the Pacific Islands and those that
are in the GSP, we have made initiatives. I think both Governments have made initiatives
when in office. Certainly at the UNCTAD meeting attended by the Minister of Overseas
Trade many years ago we started on the pathway, and at last year's UNCTAD meeting in
Nairobi we made a major initiative in respect of our tariff. We placed most items-all except
300 to 400-under the generalised system of preferences. That was a move to assist the
developing countries. But we did not remove import licensing for those products, and we will
not. It is a matter of providing favourable access through the tariff under the import licensing
system. We have no intention of changing the policy on which we were elected, which was to
maintain import licensing and the tariff as a flexible means of protecting New Zealand
industry.
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): First, I thank my colleague the member
for Manurewa for taking part in the debate, and I also thank the Minister of Trade and
Industry, who gave his usual excellent contribution. My one fear was that, as he warmed to
the subject, he might use most of my reply speech material, but he left me some. I remind
the House that during the review hearings a number of trade interests sought a level of
protection that would have virtually excluded competition from imports with some products.
The end result will remind those interests that the review committee's assignment was to
produce a tariff that would give New Zealand industry an adequate, but not a total, measure
of protection.
There was very little that I disagreed with in what the member for Mt. Albert said. He
showed a good deal more constructive knowledge of the subject than his colleague the
member for Dunedin Central did. I agree that the tariff is, and should be, a dynamic
document, subject to and receptive to continuing change. The House has been told that the
new tariff was constructed with this flexibility in mind. We have had some very favourable
comments about the format of the new tariff. I am disappointed in the contribution of the
member for Dunedin Central. I had thought we would get something of a slightly higher
quality. It may have been the evil influence of the member for Mangere sitting next to him,
but the fact remains that this time he fell short of his usual constructive approach. He
suggested that this document was inflationary, and picked out a couple of products as
apparently conclusive evidence of that.
The member for Roskill, who is trying to interject, may be interested to know that
overall some $7 million less duty on imports is to be collected as a result of the new tariff.
That, according to the member for Dunedin Central, makes it an inflationary document. It is
that type of financial reasoning that got us into the kind of troubles we are in today. Framing
the new tariff was first and foremost an administrative exercise. It incorporates no
revolutionary changes in trade policy. It is not to be seen as a form of commitment on the
Government's part towards dismantling our import licensing system and moving towards the
tariff as a sole means of protection. Not only do I not recall the Minister of Trade and
Industry giving an undertaking about the tariff along the lines suggested by the Opposition,
but I also feel that it should be pointed out that in our 1975 manifesto—
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Which one?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The glossy one-there is no undertaking whatsoever that the
National Party would, when it became the Government, move towards tariff as the sole
means of protection. The member for Dunedin Central asked-and, frankly, I could not
understand this-how we could negotiate on tariffs that had already been introduced. If he
had read the terms of reference he would have realised that one of the main points in


## p. 4673 (#779) ###########################################

22 November
4673
Customs Acts Amendment Bill (No. 2)
undertaking a new tariff was to incorporate various changes that have been brought about as
the result of new commitments, new trade alignments, and the like, since the current tariff
was introduced. The terms of reference make it quite clear that this would be done. If that is
the case, he should be reminded that the terms of reference were originally drafted by the
Labour Government.
The member was on stronger and more responsible ground when he was talking about
the arrangements for and the law relating to body searches in the course of our work against
illegal narcotics importing. First-and he will just have to accept my assurance-personal
concealment of drugs on the persons of drug carriers is becoming a very much more frequent
offence. I have given strict instructions that no body search is to take place unless there is
reasonable cause for believing the person to be suspect. One day we will probably search
someone and find he has no drugs on him, but I want it to be clearly understood by the
House and everyone concerned that Customs officers must have reasonable cause for
believing that a person has drugs concealed before they bring in the medical officers for an
examination. I am also concerned about the civil rights aspect; that is precisely why I wanted
a review of the existing law, to ensure that the law is watertight. The whole purpose of clause
36 is to give that degree of certainty. The House may be interested to know that I have
looked at the departmental instructions on personal searches, and I have also asked the
ombudsman to consider them, and he is satisfied that the procedure laid down is a proper
one.
As I said at the outset, the preparation of this measure has been a massive exercise, and
those who have taken part in it over a protracted period deserve our gratitude for the work
they have done. Ample opportunity has been given the commercial community to make
submissions, provision has been made for appeals, and the tariff does not incorporate any
major or revolutionary new changes in our policy. I trust that the House will give the Bill its
full support.

APPLE AND PEAR MARKETING AMENDMENT BILL
In Committee
Clause 5. Industry levy on apples and pears.
(1) The principal Act is hereby further amended by inserting, after section 31, the following
section:
"31A (1) Every grower shall pay to the Board, before the 31st day of August in each year, a
levy, to be called the industry levy, on all apples and pears to which this Part of this Act applies,
sold, or exported for sale, by him during the year that ended with the previous 30th day of June.
"(2) All industry levy due and payable shall constitute a debt due to the Board which shall be
recoverable accordingly by the Board in any Court of competent jurisdiction.
"(3) The rate of industry levy payable on apples and pears in every year ending with the 30th day
of June shall be fixed by the Authority by notice in the Gazette before the preceding 1st day of
December; and the Authority may fix one rate for apples and another for pears, or fix a zero rate in
respect of apples or pears or both of them:
"Provided that the rate of the industry levy in respect of apples for the year ending with the 30th
day of June 1978 shall not exceed 0.25 cents per kilogram."
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture) moved to delete from subsection
(1) of the proposed new section 31A the words "to which this part of this Act applies,"
Amendment agreed to.
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Acting Minister of Agriculture) moved to insert in subsection (3)
of the proposed new section 31A, after the words "by the authority", the words ",after
consultation with the Minister,”.
Amendment agreed to, and clause as amended agreed to.
